title: fix(memory-ingest): refuse to advance state when gbrain imports fewer pages than staged
body:
## Summary

`gstack-memory-ingest` can report `N written` while writing nothing to the brain, and mark every one of those sessions as ingested in state — so no later run ever retries them. On the install where I found this, state claimed **1013 sessions ingested** while the brain held **391 pages**. Transcripts from ~2 days were gone with no error anywhere.

This PR makes that failure loud instead of silent. It does not change the happy path.

## The bug

`written` is counted from the **staged** set, never reconciled against gbrain's own totals:

```js
for (const p of prep.prepared) {
  if (failedSources.has(p.source_path)) continue;
  state.sessions[p.source_path] = {...};   // marked ingested
  written++;                                // counted as written
}
```

`failedSources` comes from `readNewFailures()`, which reads **per-file** failures out of `sync-failures.jsonl`. When `gbrain import` collects *zero* files, there are no per-file failures to report — gbrain never saw them — so that set is empty, every prepared file is state-recorded, and the pass reports success.

`importJson.imported` holds the truth. It's used in exactly one place: the `console.error` summary a few lines below. It is never compared to anything.

## Why it triggers in practice

`gbrain import` honours `.gitignore`. `bin/gstack-artifacts-init` writes `.gitignore = "*"` into `$GSTACK_HOME`:

```
bin/gstack-artifacts-init:21   #   2. Write .gitignore = "*"  (ignore everything; allowlist is explicit)
bin/gstack-artifacts-init:213  cat > "$GSTACK_HOME/.gitignore" <<'EOF'
```

`makeStagingDir()` stages into `$GSTACK_HOME/.staging-ingest-<pid>-<ts>/`. So on any machine that has run `artifacts-init`, **every** staged file is invisible to `collect_files`, forever.

Only affects the local-gbrain path. In remote-http MCP mode the code takes `makePersistentTranscriptDir()` and never calls `gbrain import`, so those users don't hit it.

## Clean-room reproduction

No reference to my setup — reproducible on a fresh checkout in about two minutes:

```bash
export H=$(mktemp -d)
bin/gstack-artifacts-init --remote "file://$(mktemp -d)/remote.git"   # GSTACK_HOME=$H
cat "$H/.gitignore"        # => *

D="$H/.staging-ingest-1-1"; mkdir -p "$D/transcripts/x"
printf -- '---\ntitle: probe\n---\nbody\n' > "$D/transcripts/x/probe.md"

gbrain import "$D" --no-embed        # Found 0 markdown files   <-- silent loss
cp -R "$D" /tmp/control
gbrain import /tmp/control --no-embed # Found 1 markdown files  <-- control
```

Same bytes, same filenames, same directory shape. The only variable is whether the path sits inside an `artifacts-init` home.

## The fix

Reconcile `imported + skipped` against `prepared - failed` (`skipped` is a content-hash no-op, which *is* a successful landing). On a shortfall: error, return `written: 0`, and **leave state untouched** so the next run re-prepares and gbrain's `content_hash` dedup short-circuits the re-import.

This mirrors the existing `"exited 0 but emitted no parseable --json payload. Refusing to advance state."` branch directly above — same intent, one failure mode further along.

The error names the likely cause and the staging path, so the next person sees it in one line rather than bisecting a 70KB file.

## Test

`test/gstack-memory-ingest.test.ts` gains a `collectNothing` option on the existing `installFakeGbrain` shim: gbrain exits 0, reports `imported=0`/`total_files=0`, and writes **no** `sync-failures.jsonl` entry — the exact silent-loss shape.

The test asserts the state file stays empty. **It fails without the source change** (verified by reverting the fix and re-running).

```
bun test test/gstack-memory-ingest.test.ts   # 24 pass, 0 fail
bun test                                      # full free suite, exit 0
```

## Notes for the maintainer

- **No VERSION bump or CHANGELOG entry included** — those collide with whatever lands first, and your CLAUDE.md scopes them to `/ship`. Happy to add both at whatever version you want this to land at, just say the word.
- **The deeper fix is arguably to stop staging inside `$GSTACK_HOME`** — ephemeral scratch in a directory that syncs to a GitHub artifacts repo is uncomfortable regardless, since transcripts can carry PII. I left that alone: `checkOwnedStagingDir()` hard-requires "direct child of `$GSTACK_HOME`", so moving it means changing that contract and its tests. Reconciling the counts makes the failure visible either way, and seemed like the right smallest first step. Glad to follow up if you'd prefer the relocation.
- No test asserted that staged pages actually land after import, which is how this shipped. The new one closes that gap narrowly.
- This comes from a fork, so the eval/E2E CI jobs won't receive base-repo secrets and will fail on empty-env auth. The free suite (`bun test`) is unaffected and passes. Push the branch to the base repo if you want a full green run.

title: Windows: bun link shim is unrunnable when bun came from npm — gbrain.exe can't find bun.exe on %PATH%
body:
## Summary

On Windows, `gstack-gbrain-install` runs `bun link` and reports success, but the resulting
`gbrain` is unusable if bun was installed via **npm** rather than the official bun.sh installer.
The generated `gbrain.exe` shim resolves `bun` through `%PATH%` and looks specifically for
`bun.exe`, which an npm install never puts there.

Related but distinct from #1271 (that one is bun's `[eval]` failing to parse shell redirects in
gbrain's postinstall). This is about the linked shim being unrunnable after a successful link.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11 Enterprise 10.0.26200, MINGW64 (Git Bash via Claude Code's Bash tool)
- gstack: v1.61.0.0
- gbrain: 0.42.74.0 (latest HEAD)
- bun: 1.3.14, installed via `npm i -g bun`
- Path picked: 3 (PGLite local)

## What happens

`gstack-gbrain-install` completes the clone, `bun install --ignore-scripts`, and `bun link`:

```
gstack-gbrain-install: running bun install --ignore-scripts in /c/Users/<you>/gbrain (Windows shell detected)
gstack-gbrain-install: running bun link in /c/Users/<you>/gbrain
```

`bun link` genuinely succeeds — `~/.bun/bin/gbrain.exe` and `~/.bun/bin/gbrain.bunx` both exist.
But running the shim fails:

```
$ ~/.bun/bin/gbrain.exe --version
error: bun is not installed in %PATH%

Please run the following command, or double check %PATH% is right.

    powershell -c "irm bun.sh/install.ps1|iex"
```

The remediation it suggests is wrong for this case: bun **is** installed, and re-running the
bun.sh installer is a second parallel bun rather than a fix.

## Root cause

An npm-installed bun lays out:

```
%APPDATA%\npm\bun            <- POSIX shell script (works in MSYS bash only)
%APPDATA%\npm\bun.cmd
%APPDATA%\npm\bun.ps1
%APPDATA%\npm\node_modules\bun\bin\bun.exe   <- the actual Windows executable
```

`%APPDATA%\npm` is on `%PATH%`, so `bun` resolves fine in bash and PowerShell. But
`node_modules\bun\bin` is **not** on `%PATH%`, so there is no `bun.exe` anywhere on it. The
`gbrain.exe` shim that `bun link` generates does a Windows-native lookup for `bun.exe`, finds
nothing, and bails.

Confirmed by putting only that directory on PATH and changing nothing else:

```
$ export PATH="/c/Users/<you>/AppData/Roaming/npm/node_modules/bun/bin:$PATH"
$ ~/.bun/bin/gbrain.exe --version
gbrain 0.42.74.0
```

Second, smaller half of the same problem: `~/.bun/bin` is itself not added to `%PATH%` in this
configuration (the bun.sh installer is what normally does that), so even a working shim is not
callable as `gbrain`. The installer's own D19 check reports this correctly —
`bun link completed but 'gbrain' is not on PATH` — but on this machine it never got that far,
because the `jq`-based version read at `bin/gstack-gbrain-install:174` aborts first (that part
is #1675 item 2, still open).

## Impact

`/setup-gbrain` cannot complete on Windows + npm-installed bun without manually discovering the
`node_modules\bun\bin` path. Nothing in the error output points at it, and the one hint that is
printed actively misleads. Every downstream step is blocked, since they all shell out to `gbrain`.

## Suggested fix

In `gstack-gbrain-install`, after `bun link` on Windows, validate that `bun.exe` is resolvable
Windows-natively (not just that `bun` resolves in the MSYS shell) and, on failure, print
remediation that names this case:

```
gbrain.exe resolves `bun` through %PATH% and needs bun.exe specifically.
Your bun came from npm, which only installs bun.cmd/bun.ps1 there.
Add this to PATH:  %APPDATA%\npm\node_modules\bun\bin
```

Deriving the directory from `dirname $(command -v bun)/node_modules/bun/bin` covers the npm
layout without hardcoding. A more robust alternative is to stop depending on the linked shim
on Windows and invoke `bun <install-dir>/<entry>` by absolute path, which also sidesteps
`~/.bun/bin` not being on PATH.

## Workaround for anyone hitting this now

Append both directories to the user PATH, then re-run `/setup-gbrain`:

```
%APPDATA%\npm\node_modules\bun\bin
%USERPROFILE%\.bun\bin
```

Setup then completes end to end. For the record, the rest of the run was clean once past this:
PGLite + a local `ollama:nomic-embed-text` provider indexed 1,559 pages / 16,186 chunks, and the
MCP registration reported `✔ Connected`.

title: gstack-question-preference --write accepts never-ask on one-way ids: preference stores, --stats reports it configured, --check refuses it forever
body:
## Summary

`bin/gstack-question-preference --write` accepts `never-ask` on a `door_type: 'one-way'` question_id, exits 0, and reports success. `--check` then refuses that same preference forever. The result is a preference that is **stored, counted by `--stats`, surfaced by `/plan-tune` as configured, and can never fire**.

The asymmetry is inside one file:

- `--check` (bin/gstack-question-preference:61) calls `isOneWayDoor()` **first** and returns `ASK_NORMALLY` before the `switch (pref)` is reached.
- `--write` (bin/gstack-question-preference:139) validates only that the string is in `ALLOWED_PREFS = ['always-ask', 'never-ask', 'ask-only-for-one-way']`. It never looks at `door_type`.

## Reproduction

Verified on `1.60.1.0`, macOS arm64, starting from an empty `question-preferences.json`:

```console
$ cat ~/.gstack/projects/<slug>/question-preferences.json
{}

$ gstack-question-preference --write '{"question_id":"plan-eng-review-arch-finding","preference":"never-ask","source":"plan-tune"}'
OK: plan-eng-review-arch-finding → never-ask (source: plan-tune)
$ echo $?
0

$ gstack-question-preference --stats
TOTAL: 1
ALWAYS_ASK: 0
NEVER_ASK: 1          # ← reads as configured and working
ASK_ONLY_ONE_WAY: 0

$ gstack-question-preference --check "plan-eng-review-arch-finding"
ASK_NORMALLY
NOTE: one-way door overrides your never-ask preference for safety.

$ cat ~/.gstack/projects/<slug>/question-preferences.json
{ "plan-eng-review-arch-finding": "never-ask" }
```

`plan-eng-review-arch-finding` is declared `door_type: 'one-way'` in `scripts/question-registry.ts`. 12 of the 53 registered ids are one-way, so this is reachable on ~23% of the registry.

## Why this is worse than the failure it protects against

The one-way gate exists so a `never-ask` cannot silently auto-approve something destructive. That is the right gate and it works. But the failure it produces on the write side is the more dangerous shape of the two:

- A preference that **wrongly auto-decides** is loud. The user sees a decision they did not make, within one session, and goes looking.
- A preference that is **silently inert** is self-congratulatory. `--stats` says `NEVER_ASK: 1`. `/plan-tune` renders it as set. Nobody audits a setting that reports it is working.

The `NOTE:` on `--check` is real, but it prints into the agent's check output at question time, not into the surface a human inspects. `--stats` is the human-facing surface and it carries no warning.

## Suggested fix

Any one of these closes it; (1) plus (3) is the honest combination:

1. **Reject at write.** `--write` resolves `door_type` via `getQuestion(id)` / `isOneWayDoor()` and exits non-zero for `never-ask` and `ask-only-for-one-way` on a one-way id, with a message naming the door type. Cheapest, and it fails at the moment the user can still do something about it.
2. **Accept but annotate.** Store it and have `--stats` / `/plan-tune` render it as `never-ask (INERT — one-way door)`. Preserves the write for a future registry reclassification, which matters if an id later flips to two-way.
3. **Make `--stats` truthful regardless.** Have `--stats` run each stored preference through the same one-way check `--check` uses and report the inert count separately. This is the piece that fixes the inspection surface, and it is needed even if (1) lands, for preferences written before the fix.

## Related observation on `ask-only-for-one-way`

Reading the same block: on a one-way id both `never-ask` and `ask-only-for-one-way` are refused above the `switch`; on a two-way id both fall through to `AUTO_DECIDE` (:81-92). So `ask-only-for-one-way` has no behavior distinct from `never-ask` at any door type — the one-way protection it names is already unconditional.

That is arguably fine as a no-op alias, but the name reads as the safer middle setting, which is exactly why a user reaches for it. If the redundancy is intentional, documenting it as an alias would help; if not, it is a separate bug. Happy to split it out if you would prefer it tracked on its own.

title: Question Tuning preamble points at a relative `scripts/question-registry.ts` that does not resolve from a project cwd, so agents silently fabricate question_ids (21/21 unregistered in one session)
body:
## Summary

The Question Tuning preamble tells the agent to look up `question_id` at a **relative path that does not resolve from a user's project directory**, and offers "make one up" as the alternative in the same sentence. The result is that agents silently fabricate `question_id`s instead of using the registry, and every fabricated id is a singleton that no per-question preference can ever attach to.

`scripts/resolvers/question-tuning.ts:26`:

```
Before each AskUserQuestion, choose `question_id` from `scripts/question-registry.ts` or
`{skill}-{slug}`, then run `${bin}/gstack-question-preference --check "<id>"`.
```

Note the asymmetry inside that one sentence: the **bin** path is interpolated absolute (`${bin}` → `~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin`), the **registry** path is hardcoded relative. Agents run with cwd set to the user's project, not the gstack install:

```console
$ pwd
/Users/<me>/Documents/<my-project>
$ ls scripts/question-registry.ts
ls: scripts/question-registry.ts: No such file or directory
```

The file exists only at `~/.claude/skills/gstack/scripts/question-registry.ts`. The lookup fails, the documented `or {skill}-{slug}` fallback succeeds, and the agent proceeds with an invented id and no error anywhere.

This line is emitted into every generated `SKILL.md` — I count it in ~40 of them (`plan-tune`, `autoplan`, `cso`, `plan-eng-review`, `design-*`, `ios-qa`, `learn`, `pair-agent`, …), so it is not skill-specific.

## Observed impact

One `/plan-eng-review` session on a real plan emitted **21 question_ids, 0 of them registered**:

```
plan-eng-review-arch-1-delta-lineage        plan-eng-review-quality-1-hook-durability
plan-eng-review-arch-2-parity-gate          plan-eng-review-perf-1-cumulative-rebuild
plan-eng-review-ov-3-subagent-transcripts   plan-eng-review-tests-2-client-tier
plan-eng-review-scope-challenge             plan-eng-review-todos-batch            …
```

Every one was generated from the agent's own section headings. The registry has five perfectly good `plan-eng-review-*` ids (`arch-finding`, `scope-reduce`, `test-gap`, `outside-voice`, `todo-add`) that these map onto cleanly — `arch-1-delta-lineage` and `arch-2-parity-gate` are both `plan-eng-review-arch-finding`, `tests-2-client-tier` is `plan-eng-review-test-gap`, and so on.

The one id that *was* logged in an earlier session, `plan-eng-review-step0-scope`, is also unregistered — the registry name is `plan-eng-review-scope-reduce`.

## Why this defeats the feature rather than degrading it

Per-question preferences are keyed on `question_id`. Tuning requires the same id to recur enough times to establish a pattern. With heading-derived ids:

- Each id fires **once, ever**. The next session produces 21 different ids from different headings.
- No count per id ever exceeds 1, so no threshold — the user's, mine, or any future automated one — is ever reachable.
- `door_type` is unknown for every fabricated id, so the safety classification falls back to keyword-matching prose (`scripts/one-way-doors.ts`), which that file's own header says is too weak to be the primary gate.
- `/plan-tune`'s history and stats views show 21 unrelated one-off rows instead of 5 ids with counts.

This is the same failure as the `hook-<hash>` ids that the skill's "Audit unmarked questions" section exists to surface, except louder: a heading-derived id *looks* legitimate and registered. `hook-<hash>` at least announces itself.

## Suggested fix

1. **Interpolate the registry path the same way the bin path already is.** One line, one file, propagates to every skill via `bun run gen:skill-docs`:

   ```diff
   -choose `question_id` from `scripts/question-registry.ts` or `{skill}-{slug}`
   +choose `question_id` from `${gstackRoot}/scripts/question-registry.ts` (read it — do not
   +guess); only if the question genuinely has no registry entry, fall back to `{skill}-{slug}`
   ```

2. **Demote the fallback.** As written, `A or B` reads as two equal options and B is the one that always works. Making the fallback explicitly conditional on a failed lookup is most of the fix on its own.

3. **Flag marked-but-unregistered in the audit path.** `/plan-tune`'s "Audit unmarked questions" currently greps for `hook-`-prefixed ids. It could equally check emitted ids against `getAllRegisteredIds()` (already exported from `scripts/question-registry.ts:623`) and surface the unregistered-but-marked ones. That catches this class at inspection time even when the instruction is misread, and it is the louder version of the problem the section already targets.

4. Optionally, have `bin/gstack-question-log` stamp a `registered: true|false` field per event so the fragmentation is queryable after the fact rather than needing a transcript audit.

Fix (1) is the one that stops new bad data. (3) is what would have caught this without a hand audit.

title: fix(codex): use flags that codex exec resume actually accepts
body:
## Problem

`/codex` consult mode saves a thread id and offers "Continue the conversation" on the next run. That resume path has never been able to work: `codex exec resume` accepts a much smaller flag set than `codex exec`, and the skill passes it two flags it rejects.

Verified against codex-cli 0.147.0:

```
$ codex exec --help | grep -E '^\s+-(s|C)'
  -s, --sandbox <SANDBOX_MODE>
  -C, --cd <DIR>

$ codex exec resume --help | grep -E '^\s+-(s|C)'
(no matches)
```

Result, using the exact command from the skill:

```
$ codex exec resume $TID "..." -C "$_REPO_ROOT" -s read-only -c 'model_reasoning_effort="medium"' --json
error: unexpected argument '-C' found
exit=2
```

## Safety angle

The `-s read-only` removal is not just a flag rename. Without an explicit sandbox override, a resumed session inherits the sandbox policy from the Codex CLI's own config file. So a conversation that starts read-only on round 1 could gain write access from round 2 onward. `-c 'sandbox_mode="read-only"'` pins it on every round, which matches the skill's stated "Never modify files. Codex runs in read-only sandbox mode" rule.

## Changes

- `-s read-only` becomes `-c 'sandbox_mode="read-only"'` on the resume call
- `-C "$_REPO_ROOT"` becomes a `cd "$_REPO_ROOT" &&` prefix on the resume call
- `< /dev/null` added to all Codex invocations in `/codex` and `/autoplan`. `codex exec` reads stdin and prints `Reading additional input from stdin...`, which can hang a non-interactive run
- Inline note documenting the flag asymmetry so the `-s` form does not get reintroduced

Templates edited, then `bun run gen:skill-docs --host all`. Split into two commits per the bisection convention in CLAUDE.md: template change, then regenerated output.

## Verification

End to end against a real Codex thread in a throwaway repo:

```
OLD (-s + -C):              exit=2, error: unexpected argument '-C' found
NEW (cd + -c sandbox_mode): exit=0, agent_message: OK2
thread continuity:          same thread_id returned
context retention:          asked what it replied in round 1, answered correctly
```

`bun test`: 5 failures before this change, the same 5 after, zero regressions. For transparency those 5 pre-existing failures on a clean `main` checkout are the 3 golden-file ship baselines, `gstack-uninstall > clean system outputs nothing to remove`, and `gen-skill-docs > package.json version matches VERSION file`. None are touched by this PR.

One test did legitimately catch a mistake in an earlier draft: my explanatory note originally spelled out the Codex home path, which tripped the `zero Codex paths` guard in `gen-skill-docs.test.ts`. Reworded to describe the file without the path.

## Not included

No VERSION bump or CHANGELOG entry, to avoid conflicting with your release flow. Happy to add both if you would like them in the PR.

title: fix(deploy-config): stop greedy sed from mangling scheme-bearing URLs
body:
## The bug

`generateDeployBootstrap` (`scripts/resolvers/utility.ts`) parses the persisted deploy config with `sed 's/.*: *//'`. `.*:` is greedy, so it cuts at the **last** colon on the line instead of the label separator. Against the format `/setup-deploy` itself writes:

```
- Production URL: https://example.com   ->   //example.com
```

Every URL with a scheme is affected, which is every real production URL.

## Why it matters

`//example.com` does not resolve, so on any project that persists a Production URL:

- `/land-and-deploy`'s post-deploy canary curls an unresolvable address and reports the deploy as unverified.
- The Step 1.5b dry-run table prints the mangled URL, so a correctly configured project looks misconfigured. That is the failure mode I hit: the table said the prod URL was unreachable while the site was serving 200 the whole time.

`PLATFORM` uses the same pattern. It happens to survive today because platform values rarely contain a colon, but it has the same latent bug, so I fixed both.

## The fix

```diff
-  PROD_URL=$(echo "$DEPLOY_CONFIG" | grep -i "production.*url" | head -1 | sed 's/.*: *//')
-  PLATFORM=$(echo "$DEPLOY_CONFIG" | grep -i "platform" | head -1 | sed 's/.*: *//')
+  PROD_URL=$(echo "$DEPLOY_CONFIG" | grep -i "production.*url" | head -1 | sed 's/^[^:]*: *//')
+  PLATFORM=$(echo "$DEPLOY_CONFIG" | grep -i "platform" | head -1 | sed 's/^[^:]*: *//')
```

Anchor at the start, stop at the first colon. A comment above the lines explains the trap so it does not get "simplified" back.

## Verification

Against the real config format:

| input | output |
|---|---|
| `- Production URL: https://example.com` | `https://example.com` |
| `- Production URL: http://localhost:3000/health` | `http://localhost:3000/health` |
| `- Platform: Vercel (auto-deploy on push)` | `Vercel (auto-deploy on push)` |
| `- Production URL: example.com` | `example.com` |
| `- Production URL:https://no-space.com` | `https://no-space.com` |
| `- a line with no colon` | unchanged |

The last two confirm no behavior change where the old pattern was already correct.

End to end on a real project, the parsed URL went from `//<host>` to `https://<host>` and the health check returned 200.

## Notes for review

- The fix is in the generator source, not the generated `SKILL.md`, per CONTRIBUTING.
- `land-and-deploy/SKILL.md` is the regenerated output from `bun run gen:skill-docs --host all`, included so the `skill-docs.yml` freshness check passes. `gen:skill-docs --dry-run` exits 0 with zero STALE.
- `bun test` passes (exit 0, no failures).
- `bun run skill:check` exits 1 on `claude/SKILL.md — generated file missing!`. That reproduces identically on a clean tree with my changes stashed, so it is pre-existing and unrelated to this PR.

title: gstack-config rejects every key containing the letter "i" under Turkish locale (a-z range is collation-dependent)
body:
## Summary

`bin/gstack-config` validates keys with `[a-zA-Z0-9_]`. Under a Turkish locale (`LANG=tr_TR.UTF-8`) the `a-z` range is resolved by **collation order**, and the letter `i` falls outside it (Turkish treats dotless `ı` and dotted `i` as separate letters). Every config key containing an `i` is rejected — which is most of them.

Worse, the failure is silent: skill preambles read config with `2>/dev/null || echo <default>`, so the error is swallowed and **every stored preference falls back to its default**.

## Environment

- gstack `1.61.0.0` (commit `94993f7`)
- `LANG=tr_TR.UTF-8`, `LC_ALL` and `LC_COLLATE` unset
- GNU grep 3.12, bash 5.x, Linux

## Reproduction

```bash
$ LANG=tr_TR.UTF-8 gstack-config get proactive
Error: key must contain only alphanumeric characters, underscores, and an optional @<endpoint-id> suffix

$ LANG=tr_TR.UTF-8 gstack-config get telemetry
anonymous
```

Minimal repro of the underlying cause — which ASCII lowercase letters fail `[a-z]` under `tr_TR`:

```bash
$ LANG=tr_TR.UTF-8 bash -c 'for ch in a b c d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x y z; do
    printf "%s" "$ch" | grep -qE "^[a-z]+$" || printf "%s " "$ch"; done; echo'
i
```

Exactly one letter: `i`.

## Which keys break

| Works | Rejected |
|---|---|
| `telemetry`, `auto_upgrade` — neither contains `i` | `proactive`, `question_tuning`, `explain_level`, `checkpoint_mode`, `codex_reviews`, `cross_project_learnings`, `skip_eng_review`, `artifacts_sync_mode`, `routing_declined`, `gstack_contributor`, `update_check`, `plan_tune_hooks`, `checkpoint_push`, `skill_prefix`, `workspace_root`, … |

Both the `get` and `set` paths are affected (`bin/gstack-config:267` and `:283`).

## Why this is worse than it looks

Skill preambles all use this pattern:

```bash
_PROACTIVE=$(~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-config get proactive 2>/dev/null || echo "true")
_QUESTION_TUNING=$(~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-config get question_tuning 2>/dev/null || echo "false")
```

stderr is discarded and the non-zero exit hits the `||` fallback, so a Turkish-locale user gets defaults everywhere and **no indication anything is wrong**. In a session on this machine the preamble reported `PROACTIVE: true`, `EXPLAIN_LEVEL: default`, `CHECKPOINT_MODE: explicit`, `QUESTION_TUNING: false` — none of which were the stored values; all were fallbacks. `gstack-config set` also fails, so the user cannot change them either. Silent both ways.

This likely affects any locale whose collation reorders ASCII letters, not just `tr_TR`.

## Root cause

`bin/gstack-config:267` and `:283`:

```bash
if ! printf '%s' "$KEY" | grep -qE '^[a-zA-Z0-9_]+(@[a-zA-Z0-9]+)?$'; then
```

Bracket **ranges** (`a-z`) are locale-collation dependent in POSIX. Bracket **classes** (`[:alnum:]`) are classification dependent and behave correctly.

## Proposed fix

```diff
-    if ! printf '%s' "$KEY" | grep -qE '^[a-zA-Z0-9_]+(@[a-zA-Z0-9]+)?$'; then
+    if ! printf '%s' "$KEY" | grep -qE '^[[:alnum:]_]+(@[[:alnum:]]+)?$'; then
```

Applied to both sites. Verified on this machine: all keys read and write correctly under `tr_TR.UTF-8` with no `LC_*` override.

One caveat worth a maintainer decision: `[[:alnum:]]` under a UTF-8 locale also accepts non-ASCII letters (e.g. `ü`, `ç`), so it is slightly more permissive than the original intent. If strict ASCII is required, `LC_ALL=C grep` or a `case` glob would be tighter:

```bash
case "$KEY" in
  *[!a-zA-Z0-9_@]*) ...reject... ;;
esac
```

(bash `case` globs are also collation-sensitive, so `LC_ALL=C` is the safer explicit form.)

## Suggested follow-up beyond this file

The silent-fallback pattern is the real amplifier. Even with the regex fixed, `2>/dev/null || echo <default>` means any future `gstack-config` failure disappears. This release notes a "silent failure" theme — this looks like the same class: a guard that reports success while doing nothing.

A quick `rg 'gstack-config get' --glob '*/SKILL.md'` will show how widespread the pattern is.

## Workaround for affected users

Until this lands, either apply the one-line patch above, or prefix calls with `LC_COLLATE=C`. Note that a shell-wide `LC_COLLATE=C` also changes sorting for every other tool, so the patch is the narrower fix.

title: /codex: five guard defects in codex/SKILL.md — review mode runs unsandboxed and its pass/fail gate cannot fail
body:
Auditing `/codex` on v1.61.0.0 turned up five defects in `codex/SKILL.md`, all in the class the v1.61.0.0 release notes call out: a guard that reports success while doing nothing. Two are one-line fixes. Ranked by severity, with the evidence for each.

Environment: gstack v1.61.0.0, codex-cli 0.145.0, Linux (WSL2), global-git install.

---

## 1. Review mode is the only codex call that sets no sandbox (P1)

`codex/SKILL.md:987`, the default review path:

```bash
_gstack_codex_timeout_wrapper 330 codex review "IMPORTANT: ..." -c 'model_reasoning_effort="high"' --enable web_search_cached
```

No `-s read-only`, no `-c sandbox_mode`. Every sibling path in the same file sets one: challenge at :1270 uses `-s read-only`, consult-new at :1425 uses `-s read-only`, consult-resume at :1479 uses `-c 'sandbox_mode="read-only"'`.

Top-level `codex review` has **no `--sandbox` flag**, so `-c sandbox_mode` is the only lever available:

```
$ codex review --help | grep -c -- '--sandbox'
0
```

Without it the call inherits the project default. On a project marked `trust_level = "trusted"` in `~/.codex/config.toml`, that default is write access. Asked directly, with no `-s` flag:

```
$ echo "Report ONLY your sandbox/write permissions for this workspace in one short sentence." | codex exec --json -
"I can read files and write only within /home/user/projects/<repo> and /tmp; approval escalation is unavailable."
```

This contradicts the skill's own Important Rules at :1585, "Never modify files. This skill is read-only. Codex runs in read-only sandbox mode." The prompt's "Do NOT modify agents/openai.yaml" is prose standing in for a flag.

**Fix:** add `-c 'sandbox_mode="read-only"'` to the `codex review` call, the same form :1479 already uses (which came out of #1258, where `exec resume` rejected `-s`).

---

## 2. The review pass/fail gate cannot fail on the default path (P1)

Step 4 at :1051:

> If the output contains `[P1]` the gate is **FAIL**. If no `[P1]` markers are found (only `[P2]` or no findings) the gate is **PASS**.

The custom-instructions prompt at :1022 explicitly demands those tags:

> "produce findings marked [P1] (critical) or [P2] (advisory)"

The default review prompt at :987 never does. It gets native `codex review` output, which uses its own severity vocabulary and no bracketed tags. So the substring search finds nothing and **a bare `/codex review` reports GATE: PASS regardless of what codex actually found.**

The same markers feed the findings count at :1101 (`findings (count of [P1] + [P2] markers)`), so `gstack-review-log` records `findings: 0` for those runs too, and the Review Readiness Dashboard inherits it.

This is the most consequential one, because `/codex review` is documented as the independent second opinion in the GSTACK REVIEW REPORT table.

**Fix:** two parts. Add the tagging contract to the default prompt. Then make the gate refuse to infer PASS from an untagged body: if the output carries no `[P1]` or `[P2]` tag at all but does describe findings, report `GATE: UNKNOWN` rather than PASS. "No `[P1]` substring" and "no critical findings" are different claims.

---

## 3. Challenge mode's hang detection is unreachable (P2)

Challenge at :1270 wraps in `timeout 600`, and its exit-124 branch at :1303 logs `codex_timeout` plus `_gstack_codex_log_hang` and prints "Codex stalled past 10 minutes."

But :1601 instructs "5-minute timeout on all Bash calls to codex (`timeout: 300000`)", and :1586 says "5 min for Review/Challenge". With a 300s Bash cap around a 600s inner wrapper, Bash always wins. The wrapper never fires, exit 124 never happens, and that whole block is dead code. The user gets a killed tool call with no diagnostic, which is the symptom #1327 was meant to prevent.

Review mode does this correctly and deliberately: 330s inner against a 300s Bash cap, with the comment at :985 explaining that Bash is meant to win there. Consult has the same 600s-inside-300s mismatch as challenge, and :1586 and :1601 also disagree with each other about consult (10 min vs 5 min).

**Fix:** make the Bash budget exceed the inner wrapper for challenge and consult (`timeout: 660000`), and reconcile :1586 and :1601.

---

## 4. Nothing stops codex running the toolchain in a read-only sandbox (P2)

The filesystem boundary keeps codex out of skill files. Nothing keeps it out of `npm run build` / `npm test`.

Given a review or sweep prompt, codex reasons that it needs a green baseline and runs them itself. In the read-only sandbox they fail on environment rather than on code (`tsx` cannot bind its IPC socket, `EPERM` on `/tmp/tsx-*/*.pipe`; Vitest cannot create its temp SSR dir, `ENOENT`). Codex then reports "cannot establish a green baseline" and exits having reviewed nothing.

Measured on our side: same prompt, one added prohibition, zero findings became 7 ranked findings of which 5 were real.

**Fix:** extend the boundary instruction with a prohibition on build/lint/test plus an explicit allowance for reading (`cat`, `rg`, `git diff`, `git show`). The boundary string is inlined in six places, so all of them need it.

---

## 5. Consult offers to resume a session without saying how old it is (P2)

:1371 asks:

```
You have an active Codex conversation from earlier. Continue it or start fresh?
```

No age, no size, no subject. A resumed session replays every prior turn into the model's window, so continuing an old one makes the "independent second opinion" answer with the context of unrelated earlier work, and the user has nothing to judge that on.

This one is a near miss rather than a hit, and only because the skill asks at all. We hit the same bug in our own helper, which resumed silently instead of asking: one session ran from 2026-07-10 to 2026-08-05, absorbed 31 turns across 29 unrelated features, and reached 18 MB before anyone noticed the reviews had gone strange. The `/codex` session on the same machine is 781 KB, and the confirm prompt is the entire reason for the difference.

**Fix:** read the rollout's mtime and size from `~/.codex/sessions` and put both in the question, defaulting to fresh past a day or a couple of MB.

---

I am running all five as a local patch against v1.61.0.0 and happy to open a PR if the approach looks right. Fixes 1 and 2 are the ones worth taking regardless of how you want the rest shaped.

title: fix(redact-prepush): six paths where the hook exits 0 on a real credential
body:
The pre-push credential scanner can be made to allow a push that carries a live key. Six separate paths, same outcome: `exit 0`, nothing scanned, secret on the remote.

| # | trigger | shipped | fixed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | credential on a line whose **content** starts with `++` | ALLOW | BLOCK |
| 2 | malformed stdin (unparseable ref update) | ALLOW | BLOCK(unscannable) |
| 3 | `diff.external` set | ALLOW | BLOCK |
| 4 | push to a remote other than `origin` | ALLOW | BLOCK |
| 5 | junk remote sha | ALLOW | BLOCK(unscannable) |
| 6 | `localSha="0"` read as a branch delete | ALLOW | BLOCK(unscannable) |

**#1** is the one I'd fix first even alone: added lines are filtered with `!line.startsWith("+++")`, which is meant to drop the `+++ b/file` header — but a genuine added line whose content begins with `++` renders as `+++…` too. A committed `.patch`/`.diff` carrying a key sails through unscanned.

**#3** needs no attacker: `diff.external` is ordinary user config. With it set, `git diff` emits no `+` lines, the scanner reads an empty diff, and everything is allowed. Silently.

## The false positive that teaches the bypass

Over the engine's 1 MiB cap the hook reports `engine.input_too_large` as HIGH and tells the user to **"Rotate the credential (a pushed secret is compromised)"** — for content it never scanned. On one machine that produced five entries in `~/.gstack/security/prepush-skip.jsonl`, including *"0 HIGH at 1.33 MB"* and *"synthetic credential-scrubbing fixture"*. None held a credential.

That matters beyond ergonomics: a gate that cries wolf trains its user to reach for `GSTACK_REDACT_PREPUSH=skip`, and the habit is then applied to the push where the gate was right. The fix scans in windows so large-but-clean input passes, and reserves blocking for content that genuinely could not be read.

## Fail-closed is preserved

An unreadable range still blocks (#1946 stands). What changed is the message: instead of `died of signal 9` with no explanation, it names the range, the reason, how many MB were read, and the concrete next step.

## Verification

`test/redact-prepush-fail-open-verify.sh` — 15 scenarios, each run against **both** the shipped and the fixed scanner, asserting an expected verdict per row and exiting non-zero on mismatch. Rows 2, 4, 5, 6, 9, 14 must agree between the two columns: that is the no-detection-regression check, including credentials straddling the window cut.

```
GATE: PASS (15/15)
```

I verified this independently of the change's author, against `bin/gstack-redact-prepush` and `lib/redact-engine.ts` that are **byte-identical** (sha256 `5c06f7de…` / `c1f5df32…`) to current `main` at v1.61.0.0, so the result applies to this base.

## Relationship to open PRs

Disjoint from #2398 (pushed range vs whole repo), #2328 (path-ignore) and #2358 (chained `pre-push.local` stdin newline) — I diffed all three and none touches these six paths. #2328 is motivated by the same false positive from the other direction; #2358 is a seventh fail-open path in the wrapper that this PR does not address.

Happy to rebase behind any of them if you'd rather land those first.

title: gbrain detection ignores project-scoped MCP registrations, then reports the result as "not detected"
body:
Two related defects in gbrain detection, both found on gstack **v1.61.0.0**. They
compound: the first makes a correctly-configured brain invisible, and the second
reports that invisibility with the wrong diagnosis, so the suggested fix cannot
work.

---

## 1. MCP detection reads only user-scope `mcpServers`, never project scope

Claude Code registers MCP servers at two scopes in `~/.claude.json`:

```jsonc
{
  "mcpServers": { ... },                  // user scope
  "projects": {
    "/path/to/some/repo": {
      "mcpServers": { "gbrain": { ... } } // project scope  <-- never read
    }
  }
}
```

Every gbrain detection site reads only the first. The shared skill preamble,
replicated across ~30 `SKILL.md` files (`context-restore/SKILL.md:510`,
`autoplan/SKILL.md:514`, `browse/SKILL.md:381`, `cso/SKILL.md:512`, and so on):

```bash
_GBRAIN_MCP_TYPE=$(jq -r '.mcpServers.gbrain.type // .mcpServers.gbrain.transport // empty' "$HOME/.claude.json" 2>/dev/null)
```

`bin/gstack-brain-cache:130-144`:

```js
const cfg = JSON.parse(readFileSync(claudeJsonPath, 'utf-8'));
const gbrainServer = cfg?.mcpServers?.gbrain;
const url = gbrainServer?.url || gbrainServer?.transport?.url;
```

and `gstack-upgrade/migrations/v1.37.0.0.sh:58-59` the same way.

**Effect.** Register gbrain per-project — which is the natural choice when only
some repos should reach a given brain, and what `claude mcp add` does without
`--scope user` — and gstack concludes there is no brain at all. Brain-aware
blocks get suppressed, `detectEndpointHash()` falls through to the `'local'`
literal, and remote-mode artifacts sync is never recognised. Nothing errors;
the features just quietly are not there.

`detectEndpointHash()` has a sharper consequence than the others: two different
project-scoped brains both hash to `'local'`, so switching between them does not
invalidate the cache — which is the exact scenario the function's own docstring
says it exists to catch.

**Suggested fix.** Fall back to project scope when user scope misses, preferring
the entry whose project key contains the current working directory:

```bash
jq -r --arg cwd "$PWD" '
  .mcpServers.gbrain
  // (.projects | to_entries
      | map(select($cwd | startswith(.key)))
      | sort_by(.key | length) | last
      | .value.mcpServers.gbrain)
  // empty
' "$HOME/.claude.json"
```

Nearest-ancestor rather than first-match matters for nested repos.

---

## 2. "gbrain not detected" is printed for states where gbrain *is* installed

`bin/gstack-config:446-449`:

```bash
      *)
        echo "gbrain not detected (local-status: $STATUS) → brain-aware blocks will be suppressed in planning-skill SKILL.md files."
        echo "Install gbrain (see /setup-gbrain) and re-run 'gstack-config gbrain-refresh'."
        ;;
```

The `case` handles `ok`, `timeout` and `thin-client` explicitly; **everything
else** falls into `*)` and is reported as "not detected", with advice to install
something that is already installed.

The message even prints the real status in parentheses and then contradicts it.
The common trigger is a healthy CLI whose **database is unreachable** — wrong
credentials, a paused hosted DB, a blocked port on a restrictive network. All
present as "not detected", which sends you to `/setup-gbrain` to reinstall a CLI
that was never the problem, while the actual fault is one layer down and
untouched.

**Suggested fix.** Split "absent" from "present but unhealthy":

```bash
      *)
        if command -v gbrain >/dev/null 2>&1; then
          echo "gbrain is installed but not healthy (local-status: $STATUS) → brain-aware blocks suppressed."
          echo "This is usually connectivity or credentials, not installation. Try 'gbrain doctor'."
        else
          echo "gbrain not detected → brain-aware blocks will be suppressed."
          echo "Install gbrain (see /setup-gbrain) and re-run 'gstack-config gbrain-refresh'."
        fi
        ;;
```

---

## Why they are worth fixing together

Defect 1 produces a status defect 2 then mislabels. A user with a working,
project-scoped, fully-healthy brain is told it is not installed and pointed at
the installer — and reinstalling changes nothing, because the registration was
never being read. The failure is silent in both directions, which is what makes
it cost real time to unpick.

Happy to send a PR for either or both if the suggested shapes look right.

title: Probe AGENTS.md for skill routing; resolve GSTACK_ROOT in team-init
body:
## What

Two small fixes to how gstack locates itself and detects routing, plus a regression test:

1. **The preamble's `HAS_ROUTING` probe now checks `AGENTS.md` as well as `CLAUDE.md`.** Every skill's preamble runs:

   ```bash
   _HAS_ROUTING="no"
   for _RF in CLAUDE.md AGENTS.md; do
     if [ -f "$_RF" ] && grep -q "## Skill routing" "$_RF" 2>/dev/null; then
       _HAS_ROUTING="yes"
     fi
   done
   ```

   Non-Claude hosts (Codex, Cursor, generic agent harnesses) route skills via `AGENTS.md` — the de-facto cross-harness convention file. Today a repo with `AGENTS.md` routing but no `CLAUDE.md` reports `HAS_ROUTING: no` and gets nagged to create `CLAUDE.md`. This fixes that, and the routing-injection prompt stops firing for repos that already route via `AGENTS.md`.

2. **`gstack-team-init` resolves `GSTACK_ROOT` instead of hardcoding `~/.claude/skills/gstack`.** Required-mode enforcement (the CLAUDE.md verification line and the generated `.claude/hooks/check-gstack.sh`) now resolves the install the same way skill preambles do: `$GSTACK_ROOT` env → `~/.codex/skills/gstack` → `~/.gstack/repos/gstack` → legacy `~/.claude/skills/gstack`. Install instructions point at the canonical global location throughout. This stops required mode from false-blocking on installs that keep the repo at `~/.gstack/repos/gstack` (the layout the setup produces on non-Claude hosts).

3. **Regression test for the probe** (`test/routing-probe.test.ts`): extracts the *live* generated block from `review/SKILL.md` and executes it across the three scenarios — both files routed, `AGENTS.md`-only, neither — plus a structural guard that the probe references `AGENTS.md`. The `AGENTS.md`-only case fails against the old probe, so a generator edit that breaks `AGENTS.md` detection is caught even when regeneration is clean.

## Why

- A repo routing via `AGENTS.md` should be treated as routed, not prompted to add `CLAUDE.md`.
- Required mode should enforce against the real install layout, not a path that only exists for Claude Code installs.
- The probe's behavior is now pinned by a test, so the AGENTS.md support can't silently regress.

## Testing

- `bun test test/routing-probe.test.ts` — 4 pass.
- Mutation check: the old CLAUDE.md-only probe returns `no` on an AGENTS-only repo, which the new test fails on.
- `gstack-team-init required` exercised in a throwaway repo: hook emits `{}` (allow) with the patched resolution on a global install, `deny` with a fake empty `HOME`.
- All skill docs regenerated via `bun run gen:skill-docs` (default + `--host codex`).

title: fix(version): read the version from a package.json, and accept 3-digit semver
body:
## The problem

`--version-path` / `.gstack/version-path` already let a repo point the version tooling anywhere, but two shapes still failed — and both failed **closed**, so instead of erroring they silently disabled `/ship`'s queue-collision check.

In a repo whose version lives in `frontend/package.json` as 3-digit semver:

```console
$ bun run bin/gstack-version-bump classify --base main
fatal: path 'VERSION' does not exist in 'origin/main'
{"state":"FRESH","baseVersion":"0.0.0.0","currentVersion":"0.0.0.0","pkgVersion":null,"pkgExists":false}

$ bun run bin/gstack-next-version --base main --bump patch --current-version 0.99.2
Error: could not parse base version '0.99.2'
```

Two independent causes:

1. **A `package.json` version source was read as raw text.** The pinned path was whitespace-stripped, so a JSON file became `{"name":"frontend","version":"0.99.2",...` — which `parseVersion` rejected, and every read fell back to the `0.0.0.0` default. This also silently discarded rival PRs' claims: the GitHub Contents API path base64-decodes the file and then parses it, so every competing claim was dropped as "malformed".
2. **`parseVersion` required exactly four components,** so `gstack-next-version` exited 2 on *every* invocation in a 3-digit repo.

The second one is the damaging half, because `gstack-next-version` **is** the queue-collision check. With it erroring, `/ship` takes its documented offline path — naive local patch arithmetic. Two branches cut from the same base then pick the same version, and **git merges that without a conflict**, because both sides set one line to identical text. The second PR's bump silently evaporates: two PRs ship as one version, and only one gets a CHANGELOG entry.

We hit that six times in one repo before working out why — the tests pass, the diff looks right in isolation, and `git merge` reports success, so there's nothing to notice.

## The fix

`lib/version-source.ts` holds the semantics so both CLIs agree by construction. Detection is by **shape, not new configuration** — no new flags or config keys:

- a version-path ending in `.json` is read and written as JSON via `.version`
- a version with three components stays three components through bumping and formatting

A repo with a root `VERSION` and 4-digit versions sees no behaviour change.

After:

```console
$ bun run bin/gstack-version-bump classify --base main
{"state":"FRESH","baseVersion":"0.99.2","currentVersion":"0.99.2","pkgVersion":"0.99.2","pkgExists":true}

$ bun run bin/gstack-next-version --base main --bump micro --current-version 0.99.2
{"version": "0.99.3", "base_version": "0.99.2", "version_path": "frontend/package.json",
 "host": "github", "offline": false,
 "warnings": ["--bump micro has no component to move in a 3-digit version; treated as patch"]}
```

## Decisions I'd most like a second opinion on

- **`MICRO` on a 3-digit version is carried out as a `PATCH`,** with a warning in the output. `/ship` auto-picks MICRO by default, so erroring would make it unusable in every 3-digit repo — and a silent no-op would be worse, since the caller would write back the version it started with and claim a slot already taken. A hard error with a "pin a 4-digit VERSION file instead" message is the other defensible option.
- **When the version-path IS a `package.json`, it's treated as the single source of truth:** the only file written, and the `DRIFT_*` states can't arise (no second file to drift from), so `classify` returns only `FRESH`/`ALREADY_BUMPED` and `repair` is a no-op. Also syncing a root `package.json` there would be guessing which of two JSON files the repo publishes from.

## Also fixes a pre-existing bug

`gstack-version-bump` derived `versionRel` from the CLI flag alone, ignoring the `.gstack/version-path` pin — so a pinned repo compared its local (pinned) version against the **base's root `VERSION`**: two different files. On a repo with no root `VERSION` the base then always read `0.0.0.0`, making every branch look `FRESH`.

## Tests

`test/gstack-next-version.test.ts` and `test/gstack-version-bump.test.ts`, in a clean clone of this branch:

```console
$ bun test test/gstack-version-bump.test.ts test/gstack-next-version.test.ts
 56 pass
 0 fail
Ran 56 tests across 2 files.
```

New coverage: 3-digit parsing/width, formatting narrowing, the MICRO→PATCH carry, slot-picking within a width, `extractVersion` for JSON vs plain-text paths, and an end-to-end temp-repo suite driving `classify` → `write` → `classify` → `repair` against a pinned `frontend/package.json` — asserting the values that used to be wrong (`baseVersion` was `0.0.0.0`, `pkgExists` was `false`).

I also ran the wider static tier. It has failures I could **not** attribute to this change, and I checked rather than assumed — stashing the change and re-running gives the same result: `swift build invariants > XCTest suite for StateServer` fails identically on unmodified `main` here (toolchain), and the 5 `gstack-gbrain-detect` failures pass in isolation and reference none of the changed modules (they look like cross-file interference over `HOME`/`GSTACK_HOME` in a concurrent full run). Happy to dig into either if they're not already known.

**Two existing assertions encoded the old contract** and are updated with the reasoning inline — `parseVersion('1.2.3')` was asserted null, and `VERSION_RE` was asserted to reject 3-digit. The garbage-rejection cases are kept and extended (`1.2`, `1.2.3.4.5`, `v1.2.3.4`, `1.2.3.x`).

## Deliberately not included

- **`ship/SKILL.md` prose.** Documenting the new shapes there breaks the byte-for-byte golden test, and fixing it properly means regenerating three host-variant copies and three golden fixtures — that reads like a release chore, and refreshing the goldens myself would make that test tautological. Happy to add the prose in a follow-up if you point me at the right regeneration path.
- **`CHANGELOG.md` / `VERSION`.** Those look maintainer-owned per the wave process in CONTRIBUTING.md. Say the word and I'll add an entry.

title: setup: link_codex_skill_dirs() never symlinks lib/, silently breaking 13 bin/ scripts on Codex/Copilot installs
body:
## Summary

`link_codex_skill_dirs()` symlinks `bin/` into the Codex/Copilot skill roots but never symlinks `lib/`. The 13 binaries in `bin/` that import `../lib/...` therefore fail at import time on any host installed that way, while the same binaries work fine under `~/.claude/skills/gstack`.

The failure is silent in the way that matters: the skill preamble calls these binaries with `2>/dev/null || true`, so nothing surfaces. Learnings, decisions, question-log and telemetry writes are simply dropped.

## Environment

- gstack `1.60.1.0`, macOS, bun 1.3.14
- Full install at `~/.claude/skills/gstack`; Codex root at `~/.codex/skills/gstack` (`~/.copilot/skills/gstack` is itself a symlink to the Codex root)

## Root cause

`setup`, in `link_codex_skill_dirs()`, links exactly these:

```
_link_or_copy "$agents_dir/gstack/SKILL.md"          "$codex_gstack/SKILL.md"
_link_or_copy "$gstack_dir/bin"                      "$codex_gstack/bin"
_link_or_copy "$gstack_dir/browse/dist"              "$codex_gstack/browse/dist"
_link_or_copy "$gstack_dir/browse/bin"               "$codex_gstack/browse/bin"
_link_or_copy "$agents_dir/gstack-upgrade/SKILL.md"  "$codex_gstack/gstack-upgrade/SKILL.md"
```

`lib/` is never linked. Note that linking `bin/` is not sufficient: bun resolves `../lib` against the **logical** path of the invoked script, not the resolved symlink target. So `$codex_gstack/bin/gstack-learnings-log` resolves `../lib` to `$codex_gstack/lib`, which does not exist.

## Reproduce

```
$ ~/.codex/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-learnings-log '{"skill":"x","type":"operational","key":"k","insight":"i","confidence":1}'
error: Cannot find module '/Users/me/.codex/skills/gstack/bin/../lib/jsonl-store.ts'
```

13 binaries import `../lib` (`grep -rlE '\.\./lib/' bin/ | wc -l`), including `gstack-learnings-log`, `gstack-decision-log`, `gstack-decision-search`, `gstack-question-log`, `gstack-brain-cache`, `gstack-gbrain-detect`, `gstack-gbrain-sync.ts`, `gstack-memory-ingest.ts`, `gstack-redact`, `gstack-telemetry-log`.

## Impact

Every skill preamble runs `gstack-learnings-search` and logs to `gstack-learnings-log`. On a Codex/Copilot install none of that persists, so the cross-session memory features look implemented but retain nothing. I only noticed because a learning I expected to be there was missing.

## Fix

Add `lib/` to the link list:

```
_link_or_copy "$gstack_dir/lib" "$codex_gstack/lib"
```

Worth auditing the other roots the same way: anything under `bin/` that reaches outside `bin/` needs its sibling linked too.

## Note on probing this

If you add a regression test, do not probe by running a binary with no arguments. `gstack-learnings-log` exits on `$1: unbound variable` (line 20) **before** reaching the import, so a missing `lib/` looks healthy. A probe that actually fails when it should:

```
bun -e "await import(process.argv[1])" "$root/bin/../lib/jsonl-store.ts"
```

title: /sync-gbrain capability check leaves _capability_check_<pid>.md in the user's repo (gbrain delete does not remove the file)
body:
## Summary

The Step 4 capability check in `/sync-gbrain` creates `_capability_check_<pid>.md` in the **user's repository working directory** and never removes it from disk. `gbrain delete` drops the page from the brain; the file stays.

So every `/sync-gbrain` run leaves an untracked file behind in whatever repo you happen to be in.

## Where

`sync-gbrain/SKILL.md`, lines 1062-1084 (gstack 1.60.1.0):

```bash
SLUG="_capability_check_$$"
...
  if echo "ping" | gbrain put "$SLUG" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
...
gbrain delete "$SLUG" 2>/dev/null || true
```

`gbrain put` writes the page file relative to cwd, and cwd during a skill run is the user's repo root.

## Impact

Minor but persistent, and it lands in the two places you least want stray files:

- It shows up as untracked in `git status`, so it can be swept into an unrelated commit by a `git add -A`.
- In an agent session it is noise the agent has to reason about — I removed one by hand this week after wondering what had written it.

## Suggested fix

Run the probe somewhere disposable rather than the user's repo:

```bash
_CAP_DIR=$(mktemp -d)
( cd "$_CAP_DIR" && echo "ping" | gbrain put "$SLUG" ... )
rm -rf "$_CAP_DIR"
```

Failing that, delete the file explicitly next to the `gbrain delete` call, since the two do different things:

```bash
gbrain delete "$SLUG" 2>/dev/null || true
rm -f "./$SLUG.md" 2>/dev/null || true
```

Happy to send a PR if you have a preference between the two.

title: fix(hooks): AskUserQuestion hooks are a silent no-op on Windows
body:
## The bug

On Windows, all three Claude Code `AskUserQuestion` hooks fire, exit 0, and write nothing. They have never captured a single event on my install. The only artifact is one line appended to `~/.gstack/hook-errors.log` per question:

```
2026-06-26T12:12:51.352Z question-log-hook: gstack-question-log exited undefined: null
...138 identical lines, one per question asked since install day...
```

`~/.gstack/projects/<slug>/question-log.jsonl` never got created. Everything downstream of it is dead on Windows: no `--derive` input, no developer profile, and `question-preference-hook` has no preferences to enforce because nothing was ever logged. `/plan-tune` inspects an empty store.

It fails silently by design (the hooks must never block a session), which is why it went unnoticed. `status: undefined` is the tell: the process never started.

## Root cause

Two Windows-only defects, both in path handling. Either one alone is fatal.

**1. `new URL(import.meta.url).pathname` is not a filesystem path on Windows.**

```js
new URL(import.meta.url).pathname        // "/C:/Users/me/.claude/skills/gstack/hosts/claude/hooks"
path.resolve(here, '..', '..', '..')     // "C:\C:\Users\me\.claude\skills\gstack"   ← doubled drive
```

The leading slash makes `path.resolve` treat the string as drive-root-relative and rebase it. Nothing under the result exists. `fileURLToPath` is the correct conversion.

This hit all four resolution sites, not just the spawn ones. `loadRegistry()` in `question-preference-hook.ts` resolves `scripts/question-registry.ts` the same way, so on Windows the registry silently failed to load and every question's `door_type` fell back to the default instead of the registered value.

**2. `bin/gstack-*` are extensionless bash scripts.**

Windows has no shebang support, so `spawnSync(bin, ...)` is ENOENT even with a correct path. The bins themselves are already Windows-aware (`gstack-question-log` has the `cygpath -m` handling from #1950) — they just never got invoked.

## The fix

One helper, `hosts/claude/hooks/spawn-bin.ts`, owns both:

- `repoRoot()` — `fileURLToPath`, so the install root resolves on every platform.
- `runBin(name, args, opts)` — resolves under `bin/` and routes through bash on `win32` only.

The three hooks call it and drop their duplicated path arithmetic (four copies of the same three lines, minus 19 lines net). **Unix behavior is unchanged**: same direct spawn, same resolved paths, the `win32` branch is the only new code path.

One more Windows quirk worth recording: Bun's `spawnSync` returns ENOENT for a backslash exe path containing spaces, so the Git Bash fallback is written with forward slashes. `GSTACK_BASH` overrides it if bash lives somewhere else.

## Tests

`test/hooks-windows-paths.test.ts`, in the style of `setup-windows-fallback.test.ts`:

- **Static tripwires** — fail CI if any hook re-introduces `new URL(import.meta.url).pathname` for self-location, or spawns a bin directly instead of through `runBin`.
- **Resolution check** — `repoRoot()` lands on a directory that actually contains `bin/` and `scripts/question-registry.ts`.
- **End-to-end** — drives `question-log-hook` with real hook stdin against an isolated `GSTACK_STATE_ROOT`, then asserts the event landed in `question-log.jsonl` with the right `source`, `user_choice`, `recommended`, and `followed_recommendation`, and that `hook-errors.log` is empty. This is the one that reproduces the actual user-visible symptom.

| | pre-fix tree | with fix |
|---|---|---|
| `bun test test/hooks-windows-paths.test.ts` | 0 pass, 5 fail | 5 pass, 0 fail |

Verified on Windows 11, Bun 1.3.14, against `main` at v1.61.0.0.

## Out of scope, but you should know

`test/skill-validation.test.ts` has 6 `gstack-slug` failures on Windows from the same bin-spawn class in the test harness:

```
error: Executable not found in $PATH: "...\gstack-fix\bin\gstack-slug"
```

Per the blame protocol in CLAUDE.md, I checked rather than assumed: the failure list is byte-identical with and without this change, so they are pre-existing and not caused by this PR. Left alone to keep the diff scoped. Happy to send a follow-up that routes the test harness through the same helper if you want it.

## Notes

- No `CHANGELOG` / `VERSION` edit — those are yours at ship time.
- No generated `SKILL.md` touched.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: fix(make-pdf): three bugs that break browse resolution and temp-file writes
body:
## Summary

`make-pdf` is unusable on a stock global install: `$P setup` fails at step 1 or 2 and `$P generate` fails at the write stage. Three independent bugs, each with a one-line-ish fix. All three still reproduce on `main` at v1.61.0.0.

Found while using make-pdf for real work (a multi-page letter), per the CONTRIBUTING "fix gstack while doing your real work" flow.

## The bugs

**1. `isExecutable()` resolves a directory as the browse binary**

`resolveBrowseBin()` tries `path.resolve(selfDir, "../browse")` as a sibling candidate. `./setup` creates a skill *directory* at `~/.claude/skills/browse` (holding a `SKILL.md` symlink). `isExecutable()` only called `fs.accessSync(p, X_OK)`, which succeeds on directories because they carry the traverse bit:

```
path:                /Users/me/.claude/skills/browse
exists:              true
accessSync(X_OK)  -> true    <- old isExecutable() said this IS the binary
statSync().isFile -> false   <- new guard correctly rejects it
```

So make-pdf "found" a directory and every later browse call died:

```
[1/5] Checking browse binary... OK (/Users/me/.claude/skills/browse)
[2/5] Launching Chromium... FAIL
```

Fix: guard with `statSync(p).isFile()`.

**2. Temp files land outside browse's safe-dirs allowlist**

`browseClient.ts` already documents this exactly, and already introduced `PAYLOAD_TMP_DIR` to solve it:

> v1.6.0.0 tightened `--from-file` validation to close a CLI/API parity gap (PR #1103), so `os.tmpdir()` on macOS (`/var/folders/...`) now fails `validateReadPath`.

But only `writePayloadFile()` ever used the constant. `orchestrator.ts` (default output, preview HTML, `tmpFile()`) and `setup.ts` (smoke fixture + output) still used `os.tmpdir()`, so browse rejects them:

```
[4/5] Generating smoke-test PDF...
      FAILED: browse pdf exited 1: Path must be within: /private/tmp, ...
```

Fix: export `PAYLOAD_TMP_DIR`, use it at those five sites. Side benefit: the default output path now matches what `SKILL.md` already documents (`$P generate letter.md` → `/tmp/letter.pdf`).

**3. Chromium smoke test uses a blocked URL scheme**

browse permits only `http:`, `https:`, `file:`. `setup.ts` opened `about:blank`:

```
[2/5] Launching Chromium... FAIL
Chromium failed to launch: browse newtab exited 1:
  Blocked: scheme "about:" is not allowed.
```

Fix: write a one-line blank HTML file under `PAYLOAD_TMP_DIR` and open that. Network-free, cleaned up in the existing `finally`.

## Verification

`bun test make-pdf/test/` → **185 pass, 0 fail**.

Built the branch and ran the flow that was broken:

```
[1/5] Checking browse binary... OK (.../gstack/browse/dist/browse)
[2/5] Launching Chromium... OK (tab 2)
[3/5] Checking pdftotext (optional)... OK
[4/5] Generating smoke-test PDF...
      PASSED.
[5/5] All checks passed.
```

Also rendered a real 2,212-word / 8-page document end to end.

## Notes

- Three commits, one per bug, so they can be taken or dropped independently.
- No VERSION bump or CHANGELOG entry: those are branch-scoped to your ship flow and would conflict across PRs. Happy to add one if you'd rather.
- Not fixed here, flagged only: `diagram-prepass.ts:294` now declares its own duplicate `PAYLOAD_TMP_DIR`. Worth collapsing onto the exported one, but that felt like separate scope.
- Found on macOS 27.0 (arm64), Bun 1.3.14. Bugs 1 and 3 are platform-independent; bug 2 is macOS-specific, since `os.tmpdir()` only diverges from `/tmp` there.

title: fix(config): make key validation locale-independent
body:
## Summary

- pin both gstack-config key validators to the C locale
- preserve the strict ASCII key contract instead of widening it with a locale-aware character class
- add a cross-platform regression tripwire plus get/set behavior coverage

Fixes #2494

## Why

POSIX bracket ranges follow locale collation. With GNU grep under tr_TR.UTF-8, the ASCII letter i can fall outside [a-z], so valid config keys are rejected and skill preambles silently fall back to their defaults.

## Tests

- fail-first: the new regression test failed on main because neither validator pinned LC_ALL
- `bun test test/gstack-config-key-locale.test.ts test/user-slug-fallback.test.ts test/docs-config-keys.test.ts test/explain-level-config.test.ts test/gstack-config-redact-keys.test.ts` — 35 pass, 0 fail
- `bash -n bin/gstack-config`
- `git diff --check`

## Full-suite note

I also attempted `bun test`, but it did not complete cleanly in my multi-repository macOS workspace: unrelated existing suites timed out or depended on unavailable local services and fixture assumptions (including global discovery, gbrain fixtures, and local server binding). The focused config suite above is green.

title: spec: inline `{{PREAMBLE}}` reference re-expands the whole preamble (~12k wasted tokens per /spec run)
body:
## Summary

`spec/SKILL.md.tmpl` mentions `{{PREAMBLE}}` inside a prose sentence. Substitution is
literal, so that inline mention expands the **entire preamble a second time**, mid-sentence,
into the generated `spec/SKILL.md`.

Cost: **48,519 bytes (~12,129 tokens) of pure duplication on every `/spec` invocation.**

Measured on `v1.60.2.0` (`960c3a8d`).

## Root cause

`spec/SKILL.md.tmpl:289`:

```
Read `GSTACK_PLAN_MODE` from the environment (emitted by `{{PREAMBLE}}`'s
preamble bash). Then:
```

The author clearly meant to *name* the preamble, not inline it. Every other template uses
`{{PREAMBLE}}` only as a standalone block on its own line.

## What it renders

Generated `spec/SKILL.md`, line 1100 — the sentence breaks off inside its own parenthesis
and roughly 1,100 lines of preamble are pasted in before it resumes:

```
Read `GSTACK_PLAN_MODE` from the environment (emitted by `## Preamble (run first)

```bash
_UPD=$(~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-update-check 2>/dev/null || ...)
...
```

Because the whole preamble re-renders, **21 sections appear twice** in `spec/SKILL.md`:

```
## Artifacts Sync (skill start)          ## Operational Self-Improvement
## AskUserQuestion Format                ## Plan Mode Safe Operations
## Completeness Principle — Boil the Ocean  ## Plan Status Footer
## Completion Status Protocol            ## Question Tuning
## Confusion Protocol                    ## Repo Ownership — See Something, Say Something
## Context Health (soft directive)       ## Search Before Building
## Context Recovery                      ## Skill Invocation During Plan Mode
## Continuous Checkpoint Mode            ## Skill routing
## First-run guidance (one-time)         ## Telemetry (run last)
## Model-Specific Behavioral Patch       ## Voice
                                         ## Writing Style
```

`spec/SKILL.md` is 2,359 lines / ~127 KB — the largest skill in the suite, and about a third
of that is this duplicate.

Beyond the token cost, the doubled copy includes `## Telemetry (run last)` and
`## Plan Status Footer`, so a model reading top-to-bottom encounters two "run last"
instructions and two closing footers.

## Reproduce

```bash
git show HEAD:spec/SKILL.md | grep '^## ' | sort | uniq -d
```

## Suggested fix

Reference it without the braces so the substitution doesn't fire, e.g.:

```
Read `GSTACK_PLAN_MODE` from the environment (emitted by the preamble bash). Then:
```

A guard in `gen-skill-docs.ts` would prevent the whole class — either treat a
backtick-wrapped `` `{{TOKEN}}` `` as literal, or fail generation when a token expands
somewhere other than at the start of a line. A cheap regression test would be the one-liner
above asserting no duplicate `^## ` headings in any generated skill.

## Scope

Only `spec` is affected by this bug. (`autoplan` and `setup-gbrain` each have one duplicated
heading, but those are their own content sections — `## Decision Audit Trail` and
`## GBrain Configuration` — not the preamble, so a different cause.)

## Related

#1572 covers the *runtime* cost of re-executing the preamble bash across sequential skill
invocations. This is the complementary *static* case: one skill carrying the preamble text
twice in a single file. Fixing this one is a one-line change.

---

Separately, and happy to open its own issue rather than muddy this one: `model-overlays/`
has no entry for the current Claude generation, so `claude-opus-5` and `claude-fable-5` both
resolve to the generic `claude.md` via `/^claude(-|$)/` in `scripts/models.ts`. That overlay
includes "Dedicated tools over Bash", which is close to text Anthropic removed from Claude
Code's own system prompt for these models, and the only versioned overlay (`opus-4-7.md`)
inherits it and adds three more directives. Worth a look if you're tracking model drift.

Thanks for gstack — the review and ship pipelines get heavy use here.

title: model-overlays: no entry for the current Claude generation; generic `claude.md` duplicates host system-prompt guidance
body:
Follow-up to the note at the bottom of #2508, filed separately as suggested there.

Observed on `v1.60.2.0` (`960c3a8d`).

## 1. No overlay exists for the current Claude generation

`model-overlays/` contains `claude`, `gemini`, `gpt`, `gpt-5.4`, `o-series`, `opus-4-7`.
The only version-specific Claude entry is `opus-4-7.md`.

`scripts/models.ts` resolves in this order:

```ts
if (/^claude-opus-4-7(-|$)/.test(s)) return 'opus-4-7';
if (/^claude(-|$)/.test(s))          return 'claude';
```

So `claude-opus-5` and `claude-fable-5` both fall through to the generic `claude` overlay.
That is reasonable as a default, but it means the model axis currently has no way to express
"this generation needs less steering than the last one" — the only direction available is
`opus-4-7.md`, which `{{INHERIT:claude}}`s and then adds three further directives
(effort-matching, one-question-per-turn pacing, literal-interpretation awareness) explicitly
tuned for Opus 4.7.

## 2. `claude.md` restates guidance the host already provides

Current contents are three directives. The third:

> **Dedicated tools over Bash.** Prefer Read, Edit, Write, Glob, Grep over shell
> equivalents (cat, sed, find, grep). The dedicated tools are cheaper and clearer.

Claude Code's own system prompt already instructs the model to prefer the dedicated
file/search tools over shell commands where one fits. So this bullet is not adding
information — it is a second, slightly-differently-worded copy of a rule the harness has
already stated, which is the kind of duplication gstack's own guidance elsewhere avoids.

"Todo-list discipline" is similar: the harness supplies task-tracking tooling and prompts for
its use.

## 3. The wrapper disclaims itself

`generateModelOverlay()` renders every overlay under:

> The following nudges are tuned for the {model} model family. They are **subordinate** to
> skill workflow, STOP points, AskUserQuestion gates, plan-mode safety, and /ship review
> gates. If a nudge below conflicts with skill instructions, the skill wins. Treat these as
> preferences, not rules.

An instruction block that opens by saying it may not apply still costs context on every skill
invocation, and it asks the model to hold a precedence question it would not otherwise have.

## Why this seems worth revisiting now

Anthropic's write-up on context engineering for the Claude 5 generation
(<https://claude.com/blog/the-new-rules-of-context-engineering-for-claude-5-generation-models>)
reports removing over 80% of Claude Code's system prompt for Opus 5 / Fable 5 with no
measurable loss on coding evals, and argues the failure mode is overconstraint — that
conflicting or redundant guidance makes a model spend reasoning deciding what to obey rather
than doing the work.

I am not claiming these three bullets are harmful. The narrower point is that the overlay
mechanism has no current-generation entry, so newer models silently inherit steering written
for older ones, and at least one bullet duplicates the host.

## Possible directions

Roughly in order of how much they'd need discussion:

1. Add `opus-5` / `fable` to `ALL_MODEL_NAMES` with lean (or empty) overlays, so the
   generation is at least addressable. `readOverlay()` already returns `''` for a missing or
   empty file and `generateModelOverlay()` drops the section entirely in that case, so the
   graceful-degradation path exists.
2. Drop the "Dedicated tools over Bash" bullet from `claude.md` as host-duplicated.
3. Consider whether the generic `claude.md` should be empty by default, with content living
   only in version-specific overlays — that keeps the mechanism while letting each generation
   opt in to the steering it actually needs.

Happy to send a PR for (1) or (2) if either direction appeals.

## Note on how this was measured

I run a small local script that empties `claude.md` and regenerates with
`--explain-level=terse`, re-applied after each upgrade since `/gstack-upgrade` does
`git reset --hard`. All figures and quotes above are read from `git show HEAD:...` rather
than my working tree, so they reflect stock `v1.60.2.0`.

title: fix(sync): run gstack-brain-sync through bash, not cmd.exe, on Windows
body:
## The bug

On Windows the `brain-sync` stage of `/sync-gbrain` fails on **every** run:

```
'C:\Users\...\.claude\skills\gstack\bin\gstack-brain-sync' is not recognized as an internal or external command,
operable program or batch file.

  ERR   brain-sync   gstack-brain-sync exited 1 (0.0s)
```

## Why the #1731 fix didn't cover it

#1731 added `shell: NEEDS_SHELL_ON_WINDOWS` to these spawns. That is correct for the `gbrain.cmd` shim and does nothing here: `shell: true` routes through **cmd.exe**, which resolves `.cmd`/`.bat` via PATHEXT but has no concept of a shebang, so an extension-less bash script is rejected outright.

A `.cmd` shim needs a **shell**. A shebang script needs an **interpreter**. The two cases look identical and are not, which is why one fix appeared to cover both.

## Why it matters more than one red line

`artifacts_sync_mode` defaults to pushing curated artifacts to git. With this stage dead, a Windows user's learnings accumulate in `~/.gstack` and are never committed, while the sync report shows one red line among otherwise green stages. It reads as a minor stage failure and is actually silent data stagnation.

## The change

New `bashScriptInvocation()` in `lib/gbrain-exec.ts`:

- Resolves Git for Windows' `bash.exe` and passes the script as `argv[0]`.
- Prefers Git bash over a bare `bash` on PATH: **WindowsApps ships a `bash.exe` that is the WSL launcher**, and if it wins PATH order it reads `C:\...` as a Linux path and the script never sees the repo.
- Forward-slashes the script path, since bash treats backslashes as escapes.
- `GSTACK_BASH` overrides for unusual installs.
- Returns `null` when no bash exists, so the stage reports `skipped (no bash found; set GSTACK_BASH to your Git bash.exe)` rather than an unactionable spawn error.

POSIX is unchanged: the script is exec'd directly, no interpreter, no shell.

## Tests

The #1731 tripwire asserted the shape that does not work (`spawnSync(brainSyncPath, ...)` + `shell: NEEDS_SHELL_ON_WINDOWS`), so it now asserts the opposite and fails if a raw spawn returns. Six unit tests cover the resolver: POSIX passthrough, Git-bash resolution, path slashing, `shell: false`, `GSTACK_BASH` override, and the no-bash `null`.

The `gbrain.cmd` assertions in that file are untouched — that part of #1731 is right and still enforced.

## Verification (Windows 11, gstack 1.61.0.0, bun 1.3.11)

Before: `ERR brain-sync   gstack-brain-sync exited 1 (0.0s)`
After: `OK    brain-sync   curated artifacts pushed (4.2s)` — and the artifacts repo committed and pushed on its own.

The suite is nondeterministic on Windows (the same tree gave 743 and 741 failures on back-to-back runs), so I compared the affected files rather than the whole run: **14 failures before, 14 after**, with 6 new passing tests. No behaviour change on POSIX, where the invocation is byte-identical to today's.

title: Back-compat aliases (_gstack-command, connect-chrome) ship duplicate name: fields, breaking Claude Code skill discovery
body:
## Summary

The two back-compat alias directories created by `setup` / `gstack-relink` — `_gstack-command` and `connect-chrome` — ship a `name:` field that is identical to their canonical skill. This produces **duplicate skill names** in `~/.claude/skills/`, which violates Claude Code's global unique-name requirement and causes Claude Code to drop the **entire** personal-skills set. The result: *none* of the gstack skills (`/gstack`, `/browse`, `/cso`, `/ship`, …) are discoverable, even after a full restart.

## Environment

- gstack `1.2.0`
- Claude Code `2.1.220` (host: `claude`)
- macOS (darwin), flat-name install (no `gstack-` prefix)

## Root cause

`setup` links two top-level alias dirs whose `SKILL.md` is a symlink into `gstack/`:

```
~/.claude/skills/_gstack-command/SKILL.md -> ~/.claude/skills/gstack/SKILL.md                 # name: gstack
~/.claude/skills/connect-chrome/SKILL.md  -> ~/.claude/skills/gstack/connect-chrome/SKILL.md  # name: open-gstack-browser
```

- `_gstack-command` (created by `link_claude_root_skill_alias`, setup ~L593) resolves to `name: gstack` — collides with `gstack/`.
- `connect-chrome` (back-compat alias, setup ~L1003–1010) resolves to `name: open-gstack-browser` — collides with `open-gstack-browser/`.

`gstack-relink` calls `gstack-patch-names <gstack_dir> <prefix>`, but that only patches `name:` fields for skills **inside** `gstack/`. The two top-level alias dirs are never patched, so they retain the canonical `name:` and collide.

## Reproduction

```bash
git clone --single-branch --depth 1 https://github.com/garrytan/gstack.git ~/.claude/skills/gstack
cd ~/.claude/skills/gstack && ./setup
```

Then check for duplicate `name:` fields across top-level skills:

```bash
cd ~/.claude/skills
for d in */; do [ -e "$d/SKILL.md" ] && awk -F': *' '/^name:/{print $2; exit}' "$d/SKILL.md"; done | sort | uniq -d
# => gstack
#    open-gstack-browser
```

Both collide → Claude Code refuses to load personal skills; all gstack commands disappear.

## Workaround

```bash
rm -rf ~/.claude/skills/_gstack-command ~/.claude/skills/connect-chrome
```

Restores discovery immediately (removing the symlink dirs doesn't touch their targets). But any subsequent `./setup` or `/gstack-upgrade` recreates them and re-breaks discovery.

## Suggested fix

Give the alias skills a distinct `name:` (matching their directory, e.g. `gstack-command` and `connect-chrome`) instead of symlinking the canonical `SKILL.md` verbatim — or extend `gstack-patch-names` to rewrite the `name:` field of the alias dirs so each skill name stays globally unique on the Claude Code host.
