title: fix(codex,review,ship): scope Codex review with --base — prompt-only review silently reviews the wrong diff
body:
## `/codex review` has been reviewing the wrong diff

On Codex CLI 0.144.x, `/codex review` returns a confident, well-formatted review of changes that are not the ones you asked about. There is no error, no warning, and no way to tell from the output that anything is wrong.

### The crash was the symptom. The fix for the crash was the bug.

Codex CLI 0.130.0 made the positional `[PROMPT]` mutually exclusive with the scope flags, so the old invocation started failing loudly:

```
error: the argument '[PROMPT]' cannot be used with '--base <BRANCH>'
```

That's #1428 and #1479. The resolution kept the prompt and dropped `--base`, then moved the scope into prompt text:

```bash
codex review "…Review the changes on this branch against the base branch <base>.
Run git diff origin/<base>...HEAD … to see the diff and review only those changes."
```

This parses cleanly, which is exactly why it survived. But `codex review --help` shows `[PROMPT]`, `--base`, `--commit`, and `--uncommitted` are all *scope selectors*, and a prompt-only `codex review` falls back to the **uncommitted working-tree** scope: it runs `git status --short; git diff` and reviews that.

Prompt text asking the model to "run git diff origin/main...HEAD" does not change what the CLI feeds the reviewer. The model gets the working-tree diff and reviews it, faithfully. So:

- On a dirty tree, you get a real review **of the wrong changes**.
- On a clean tree, you get "no changes" **on a branch full of them**.

Neither case produces an error, so the failure is invisible. A review tool that silently reviews the wrong thing is worse than one that crashes: the crash told you to look.

### The fix

Step 2A's default path now passes the scope flag and no prompt:

```bash
codex review --base <base> -c 'model_reasoning_effort="high"' --enable web_search_cached
```

Applied unconditionally, with no `codex --version` branch. `[PROMPT]` has always been optional, so the no-prompt form is valid on every version that supports `--base` — there is no version window this breaks.

Three supporting changes:

- **Filesystem Boundary** was scoped to the three `codex exec` paths. It claimed to govern Review mode's prompt argument, which no longer exists. Dropping it from the scoped path is acceptable: `--base` hands the model a pre-computed diff rather than turning it loose on the filesystem, so the rabbit-hole risk it guards against is much lower there.
- **Custom instructions** keep routing through `codex exec`. They cannot ride along with `--base` (that's the rejected combination) and cannot be smuggled in by dropping `--base` (that's the silent wrong scope). The rationale now says so explicitly.
- **Error Handling** documents both the argv error — carrying a "do not fix this by removing `--base`" warning, since that is the trap — and the silent-wrong-scope symptom. The second entry matters precisely because it has no error message anyone could search for.

### Tests that pinned the bug

Two tests asserted the broken shape as desired behavior, including one named *"codex review commands pass diff scope through prompt, not --base"*. Both worked by banning the substring:

```js
expect(content).not.toContain('--base <base> -c \'model_reasoning_effort="high"\'');
```

The correct bare form contains that substring too, so the assertion could not distinguish a scoped call from an unscoped one — it just banned `--base` outright. They now assert the real invariant for `codex/`: no positional prompt may precede a scope flag. That's the same line-level check `test/codex-hardening.test.ts` already uses, and those existing guards pass unchanged.

A stale comment in the boundary test instructed future contributors that the call "must be through `codex review "<prompt>"` not bare `codex review --base`" — i.e. it told the next person to reintroduce this. Corrected; the assertion itself was already passing and is untouched.

### `/review` and `/ship` had it too (second commit)

`scripts/resolvers/review.ts:559` carried the identical prompt-only invocation, and that resolver feeds both `/review` and `/ship`'s structured Codex pass — so those were reviewing the wrong diff as well, with the same absence of any error. Fixed the same way, with `review/SKILL.md`, `ship/sections/adversarial.md`, and the factory ship golden regenerated. The golden's only delta is this change.

**The adversarial pass a few lines above is deliberately left as-is.** It uses `codex exec`, which is agentic and genuinely runs the git command it's given, so scoping *that* one in prompt text is correct. The distinction is now written down next to both call sites, because the obvious "cleanup" is to unify them and that would reintroduce the bug on the wrong side.

With everything on the scoped form, both tests now assert the real invariant across all five files instead of pinning one shape per file: every `codex review` invocation carries a scope flag, and none puts a positional prompt in front of it. Prose mentions and `codex exec` calls are excluded.

### Dead fixture removed (third commit)

`test/fixtures/golden-ship-claude.md` has been unreferenced since v0.15.5.0 (#793) moved golden baselines into `test/fixtures/golden/`. Nothing reads it — not by name, not by the `**/SKILL.md` / `**/*.tmpl` globs in `gen-skill-docs.test.ts`, not by touchfiles, not by any workflow; the golden-file regression tests read only `test/fixtures/golden/`.

Removing it rather than leaving it: at 128KB it's the largest fixture in the tree, and it's a frozen snapshot of the *pre-#1428* invocation passing both a prompt and `--base` — the combination modern Codex CLI rejects outright. A stale fixture nobody runs is a plausible-looking template for whoever greps for `codex review` next, which is roughly how this whole bug propagated.

### Verification

- `codex review --base HEAD~2 -c 'model_reasoning_effort="high"' --enable web_search_cached` on a real repo returned a genuine review including a `[P2]` finding — the marker format Step 4's pass/fail gate parses, so the gate still works.
- `codex review --base HEAD~1` correctly reported an empty diff.
- `codex exec "<prompt>"` still accepts a prompt, so Challenge (2B) and Consult (2C) are unaffected.
- `codex review --help` on 0.144.1 confirms `[PROMPT]` is optional and the scope flags are what set scope.
- Full free suite (`bun test`): failure set is **identical** before and after — 840 failures on both, all pre-existing on this Windows checkout (`gstack-slug` executable-bit and `gtimeout` resolution). Verified by running the suite on `main` and diffing the failure lists, not by assertion.
- Two pre-existing flakes surfaced intermittently across the full-suite runs and are flagged rather than quietly dropped from the counts. Neither is caused by this diff:
  - `context-save-hardening.test.ts` → "50 .md files → only 20 returned". Appeared in some full runs, not others, including a run taken *before* the fixture deletion. It operates entirely inside a fresh `mkdtemp` directory and never reads the repo tree, so nothing here can reach it. Passes 3/3 in isolation.
  - `global-discover.test.ts` → "repos have required fields". Appeared once, passes 3/3 in isolation, and the file contains no reference to fixtures or goldens. It enumerates repos on the host machine, so it's sensitive to concurrent activity outside the test.
- `bun run gen:skill-docs` regenerated `codex/SKILL.md` against current `main`; regeneration is idempotent.

Tested on codex-cli 0.144.1.

Refs #1428, #1479

fix(browse): sidebar Terminal — duplicate WS subprotocol header + doubled CJK IME input
body:
Two independent bugs kept the sidebar Terminal pane unusable. Both verified end-to-end against a live agent in Chrome for Testing 145 / Bun 1.3.6.

## 1. Duplicate Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header breaks the WS handshake

**`/pty-session` mints fine, but `new WebSocket(url, ['gstack-pty.' + token])` never completes** — the pane sits at an empty cursor and typing does nothing.

Bun >= 1.3 auto-echoes the first offered subprotocol in the `server.upgrade()` 101 response. The agent *also* sets an explicit `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` header (needed back when Bun didn't auto-echo), producing a duplicate response header:

```
HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: gstack-pty.<token>   ← Bun auto-echo
Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: gstack-pty.<token>   ← manual echo
```

RFC 6455 allows at most one selected subprotocol, so strict clients reject the handshake — reproduced with python `websockets` (`InvalidHeader: multiple values`).

**Fix:** drop the manual echo; Bun's auto-echo selects the right protocol (the sidebar offers exactly one).

## 2. Korean/CJK IME input is sent twice

The local workaround for #1272 sent `e.data` manually on `compositionend`. But this xterm build's `_finalizeComposition` emits the same composed string through `onData` one macrotask later (`setTimeout(0)`), so every composed syllable went out twice (`안녕` → `안녕안녕`). ASCII was unaffected because it never goes through composition.

**Fix:** remove the custom composition listeners — this xterm version already suppresses partial jamo while composing and emits the final string exactly once through `onData`. Supersedes the #1272 workaround.

## Verification

- Raw-socket handshake: exactly one `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` header in the 101 (new regression test — `Headers.get()` normalizes duplicates away, so fetch-level assertions can't see this bug class).
- Full E2E: mint → WS upgrade with `gstack-pty.<token>` subprotocol → `{type:"start"}` → claude PTY boots and answers in the sidebar pane.
- `bun test` free suite green. A third commit fixes two stale static guards in `terminal-agent.test.ts` that were already failing on main (lazy-spawn guard still grepped `spawnClaude(` after the v1.44 `maybeSpawnPty(` refactor; the echo guard pinned the removed `acceptedProtocol`).

Note: fork PR, so paid eval/E2E workflows won't have secrets — the free suite covers these changes.

title: gbrain source worktree never advances after setup: artifacts push fine but brain silently stays at 0 pages
body:
## Summary

The gbrain federated-source worktree at `~/.gstack-brain-worktree` never advances after `/setup-gbrain` creates it. Artifacts keep getting committed and pushed to the artifacts repo on every skill run, so everything *looks* healthy, but the directory gbrain actually reads stays pinned at the init commit. Result: `gbrain sources list` reports `0 pages` indefinitely, and no warning is ever surfaced.

On this machine the worktree sat at the initial commit for 7 days before I noticed it by hand.

## Environment

- gstack `1.61.0.0`
- gbrain `0.44.0.0` (also reproduced on `0.42.52.0` before upgrading)
- `artifacts_sync_mode=full`, local-stdio MCP, Supabase engine
- Linux (WSL2)

## What I observed

`gbrain sources list` after a week of daily skill usage:

```
gstack-artifacts-way2joy  federated   0 pages  last sync 2026-08-04T04:30:50.720Z
                          /home/way2joy/.gstack-brain-worktree
```

The parent repo was current, the worktree was not:

```
$ git -C ~/.gstack worktree list
/home/way2joy/.gstack                 220111e [master]
/home/way2joy/.gstack-brain-worktree  83fe994 (detached HEAD)   # <- init commit, 2026-08-04

$ ls -a ~/.gstack-brain-worktree
.brain-allowlist  .brain-privacy-map.json  .git  .gitattributes  .gitignore
```

Only the five config files. No `projects/` directory at all, so there was nothing for gbrain to index — the `0 pages` was accurate, just not for the reason it appears.

Meanwhile the push side was working fine:

```
$ git -C ~/.gstack log --oneline -3
220111e sync: 2 file(s) | 2026-08-11T08:06:49Z
c1f625e sync: 2 file(s) | 2026-08-11T04:17:29Z
83fe994 chore: gstack-artifacts-init
```

## Why it happens

`ensure_worktree()` in `bin/gstack-gbrain-source-wireup` does advance the detached HEAD correctly (`git checkout --detach "$sha"`, around L186-189). The problem is that nothing routine calls it.

The end-of-skill hook present in every SKILL.md only runs:

```bash
bin/gstack-brain-sync --discover-new
bin/gstack-brain-sync --once
```

`gstack-brain-sync` has no wireup call and no worktree handling — its subcommands are `--status`, `--skip-file`, `--drop-queue`, `--discover-new`, plus the default queue drain. So the commit+push path runs constantly while the worktree advance never does.

The only callers of `gstack-gbrain-source-wireup` are:

- `setup-gbrain/SKILL.md` (one-time)
- `sync-gbrain/SKILL.md` (manual)
- `bin/gstack-brain-restore` (cross-machine restore)
- `gstack-upgrade/migrations/v1.17.0.0.sh` (one-time)

If a user sets gbrain up and then just uses gstack normally, none of those fire again.

## Why this reads as a bug rather than "you forgot to run /sync-gbrain"

`docs/gbrain-sync.md:158-162` says:

> ## Cross-machine pull cadence
>
> The preamble runs `git fetch` + `git merge --ff-only` once per 24 hours (cached via `~/.gstack/.brain-last-pull`). **You don't need to think about this — it happens automatically at the first skill invocation each day.**

That daily automatic step covers `~/.gstack` only. The worktree gbrain reads is not part of it, and the docs never say a separate manual step is required to make artifacts visible to the brain. The failure is also completely silent: sync mode reports healthy, pushes succeed, and `0 pages` looks like "nothing written yet" rather than "the reader is pinned to an empty commit."

## Workaround

Running the helper directly fixes it immediately:

```
$ bin/gstack-gbrain-source-wireup
Previous HEAD position was 83fe994 chore: gstack-artifacts-init
HEAD is now at 220111e sync: 2 file(s) | 2026-08-11T08:06:49Z
```

## Suggested fixes (maintainer's call)

Any one of these would close the gap:

1. Have `gstack-brain-sync --once` advance the worktree after a successful push (cheap: it's a `git checkout --detach` against a local repo).
2. Advance the worktree in the same once-per-24h preamble block that already does `git fetch` + `git merge --ff-only`.
3. If the manual `/sync-gbrain` cadence is the intended design, warn when the worktree HEAD is behind `~/.gstack` HEAD, and say so in `docs/gbrain-sync.md`.

## Secondary observation: `.jsonl` artifacts are never indexable

Possibly intended, but the pairing is confusing enough to mention.

`.brain-allowlist:5` publishes `projects/*/learnings.jsonl` as the first entry, and `projects/*/timeline.jsonl` further down. But gbrain only indexes markdown:

```
gbrain src/core/sync.ts:9    isSyncable()  →  filter to .md pages only
gbrain src/core/sync.ts:174  return path.endsWith('.md') || path.endsWith('.mdx');
```

So even with the worktree fully advanced, `/learn` output syncs to the artifacts repo (which does give cross-machine restore) but contributes 0 pages to the brain and is not reachable via `gbrain search`. After fixing the worktree on this machine the sync still reported:

```
0 file(s) imported, 0 chunks
```

If cross-machine transport is the whole intent for JSONL, a line in `docs/gbrain-sync.md` distinguishing "synced to the repo" from "indexed by the brain" would save people the hunt — the `0 pages` reading is easy to misdiagnose as a broken sync.

title: fix(upgrade): preserve local changes instead of reset hard
body: The gstack upgrade workflow runs git stash, git fetch, then git reset --hard origin/main. A failed or untracked-file collision can leave user-owned work outside the documented restore path. The reset also conflicts with repositories that prohibit destructive history or worktree rewrites. The safe update succeeded with git fetch followed by git merge --ff-only origin/main. Replace reset hard with a non-destructive fast-forward path. Preserve and report tracked and untracked local state. Add a regression test for dirty git installs.

title: fix(review): resolve checklist paths from installed skill root
body: The global review skill stops at Step 2 because it reads .claude/skills/review/checklist.md and greptile-triage.md relative to the target repository. A global gstack install stores both files under the installed gstack review directory. Repositories without a vendored copy cannot run review. Resolve references from the selected SKILL.md directory, with the target repository path only as an explicit vendored fallback. Add an end-to-end test that invokes global review from a repository with no local .claude/skills/review directory.

title: `/review` consumed 15M+ input tokens in a few minutes on Codex
body:
I hit extremely high Codex usage while running gstack `/review` on a ~422-line diff. I inspected the persisted Codex `token_count` events and can account for **at least 15.2M input tokens** from this single review: | Thread | Input tokens | |---|---:| | `/review` parent | 11.74M | | 5 spawned review agents | 2.83M | | nested `codex exec` | 0.62M | | **Observed total** | **15.19M+** | This accumulated very quickly. In the parent thread: 16:28:28 6,191,588 input tokens 16:33:58 10,490,863 input tokens That's **4.3M input tokens in 5m30s** (~782k/min), with one shorter interval reaching roughly **1M input tokens/minute**. The parent repeatedly made calls with ~170k–235k input tokens, mostly cached. It also spawned: testing_review maintainability_review security_api_review design_review adversarial_review and, while already running under Codex, invoked Codex again via: codex exec ... codex exec resume ... codex review ... One of those nested reviews was eventually detected by the parent itself as a: runaway nested Codex review process that is consuming tokens and terminated. I also noticed the parent reading large overlapping portions of `review/SKILL.md` more than once during the run. Parent thread: 019fe744-086c-7882-bf60-7a2cbad58146 I can provide the parent rollout, token-counter export, five child rollouts, and nested Codex rollout if useful. It looks like `/review` may be repeatedly reprocessing a very large parent context while also spawning subagents and nested Codex reviews. Is this expected behavior when gstack is running under Codex?

More context for the agent

 ## Context I observed unexpectedly high Codex usage while running gstack's `/review` on August 9, 2026. The review was for a relatively modest code change (~422 changed lines), but Codex usage dropped extremely quickly. I inspected Codex's local session data afterward to understand where the tokens went. The main Codex thread was: ```text 019fe744-086c-7882-bf60-7a2cbad58146 ``` Its rollout is: ```text ~/.codex/sessions/2026/08/09/rollout-2026-08-09T17-03-43-019fe744-086c-7882-bf60-7a2cbad58146.jsonl ``` The timestamps inside the rollout are UTC (`Z`). --- ## Parent thread usage The final persisted `token_count` for the parent reports: ```json { "input_tokens": 11742801, "cached_input_tokens": 11389184, "cache_write_input_tokens": 0 } ``` So the `/review` parent alone processed: * **11,742,801 input tokens** * **11,389,184 cached input tokens** Almost all of the input was cached, but Codex's persisted `total_token_usage.input_tokens` continued increasing on each model call. --- ## How quickly the usage accumulated This wasn't accumulated over hours. The parent's persisted counters show: ```text 16:28:28 6,191,588 total input tokens 16:33:58 10,490,863 total input tokens ``` That's: ```text 4,299,275 input tokens in 5m30s ≈ 782k input tokens/minute ``` A shorter interval: ```text 16:31:08 7,655,369 16:33:58 10,490,863 ``` is: ```text 2,835,494 input tokens in 2m50s ≈ 1.0M input tokens/minute ``` Individual model calls during this period became very large: ```text input cached input 168,319 167,680 175,709 168,704 178,081 174,848 180,804 177,920 181,520 179,968 182,402 182,016 194,426 182,016 194,806 194,304 206,348 194,304 218,035 205,568 218,546 217,856 230,244 217,856 231,471 229,120 231,602 231,168 232,938 231,168 233,326 232,192 233,877 233,216 235,354 233,216 ``` This looks like the parent context grew to >200k tokens and then continued making many model calls while carrying most of that context forward. That is an observation from the token counters, not yet a claim about what gstack should or should not be doing. --- ## Spawned review agents The parent made five `spawn_agent` calls: ```text testing_review maintainability_review security_api_review design_review adversarial_review ``` The corresponding child threads found in Codex's `thread_spawn_edges` table were: ```text 019fe749-4872-7790-80bb-bf225da2f59b 019fe749-6b4f-7c03-9fb5-74294310e346 019fe749-8423-7190-8507-ff9be0e19070 019fe755-fa73-7151-bb02-9b97a1faf434 019fe756-1e93-7cf3-9d92-aaa08ecb04b1 ``` The task → thread mapping below is inferred from spawn order / UUID timestamps: ```text testing_review 019fe749-4872-7790-80bb-bf225da2f59b input: 250,378 cached: 200,192 maintainability_review 019fe749-6b4f-7c03-9fb5-74294310e346 input: 330,165 cached: 242,688 security_api_review 019fe749-8423-7190-8507-ff9be0e19070 input: 406,393 cached: 355,328 design_review 019fe755-fa73-7151-bb02-9b97a1faf434 input: 515,028 cached: 455,936 adversarial_review 019fe756-1e93-7cf3-9d92-aaa08ecb04b1 input: 1,326,464 cached: 1,223,936 ``` Together: ```text 2,828,428 input tokens ``` This is important because the five spawned agents **do not explain the parent's 11.74M input-token count**. Their rollouts have their own counters. --- ## Nested Codex invocation The `/review` parent was itself already running in Codex, but it also executed Codex from inside the session. One command was essentially: ```bash codex exec \ 'Review the repository changes since commit 045bb8e. ...' \ -C /Users/daniel/projects/macos/Recadio \ -s read-only \ -c 'model_reasoning_effort="high"' \ --enable web_search_cached ``` It later resumed that nested session: ```bash codex exec resume \ 019fe75c-4b6f-78e2-bc66-eec14fac12f5 \ 'Return only the final findings from your review ...' ``` That nested Codex session has its own rollout: ```text ~/.codex/sessions/2026/08/09/rollout-2026-08-09T17-30-13-019fe75c-4b6f-78e2-bc66-eec14fac12f5.jsonl ``` Its final counter is: ```json { "input_tokens": 620864, "cached_input_tokens": 535808, "cache_write_input_tokens": 0, "output_tokens": 11035, "reasoning_output_tokens": 8093, "total_tokens": 631899 } ``` Later, the parent launched another nested command: ```bash codex review \ 'Review only git diff 045bb8e..HEAD. Do not inspect skill files. ...' \ -c 'model_reasoning_effort="high"' \ --enable web_search_cached ``` The parent subsequently attempted to interrupt it several times with `write_stdin(... "\^C" ...)`, inspected running Codex processes, and eventually sent `SIGTERM` to one nested Codex process. The parent-generated command justification described it as: ```text "the runaway nested Codex review process that is consuming tokens" ``` Important: that phrase is generated by the parent agent itself; it is **not evidence of an independent Codex mechanism detecting a runaway process**. I have not yet identified/added the separate token total for this second nested `codex review`, so the total below is a lower bound. --- ## Minimum observed token usage Known persisted input-token totals: ```text /review parent 11,742,801 five spawn_agent children 2,828,428 nested codex exec 620,864 ---------- minimum observed total 15,192,093 ``` So there are **at least 15.19M input tokens** directly visible in known rollouts associated with this one review. This is not necessarily equivalent 1:1 to ChatGPT subscription quota consumption. It is the sum of Codex's persisted `input_tokens` counters for the identified sessions. There may also be accounting/duplication semantics around forks that should be verified before treating this number as a billing total. --- ## Parent activity The parent rollout contains: ```text 75 custom_tool_call -> exec 19 function_call - 5 spawn_agent - 14 wait ``` One thing visible in the transcript is repeated loading of gstack's review instructions. It initially reads `review/SKILL.md` in chunks approximately covering: ```text 1-240 241-520 521-1040 1041-1560 1561-2080 ``` Later it reads large overlapping portions again: ```text 1-760 1-500 501-1000 1001-1500 1501-1900 ``` The parent also loads: ```text review/checklist.md review/greptile-triage.md review/design-checklist.md review/specialists/testing.md review/specialists/maintainability.md review/specialists/security.md review/specialists/performance.md review/specialists/api-contract.md ``` and substantial amounts of repository code/diffs. For example, before the parent reaches ~125k input tokens it has already: * read large parts of the gstack skill; * inspected multiple parts of the git diff; * read substantial portions of several Swift files; * loaded review specialist definitions. Afterward it continues running tests, builds, repository inspections, review agents and nested Codex reviews while its per-call context grows toward ~235k. This repeated skill loading might be relevant, but it should be verified whether it is expected behavior before treating it as the root cause. --- ## Example of context growth Some chronological parent model calls: ```text 16:04:14 20,539 input 16:04:21 24,077 16:04:26 29,045 16:04:30 37,425 16:04:39 43,484 16:06:01 49,804 16:06:19 53,083 16:06:39 65,954 16:06:58 69,015 16:07:06 80,235 16:07:17 90,927 16:07:23 91,749 16:07:27 96,721 16:07:46 100,241 16:08:18 106,301 16:08:40 116,529 16:09:14 124,685 16:09:51 130,225 16:10:30 144,471 16:10:59 148,538 16:11:46 164,573 16:21:30 167,029 16:23:19 168,319 16:23:49 168,995 16:24:18 175,709 16:28:40 178,081 16:28:50 180,804 16:29:09 181,729 16:30:29 182,402 16:31:08 194,426 16:31:56 206,348 16:32:32 218,035 16:32:49 218,546 16:33:26 230,244 16:33:30 231,471 16:33:38 231,602 16:33:48 232,938 16:33:54 233,326 16:35:40 233,877 16:41:09 235,354 ``` Most of the later calls are almost entirely cached input. This repeated processing of a ~170k–235k context appears to be where a large fraction of the parent's 11.74M input total comes from. --- ## Relevant chronology Approximate sequence: ```text 16:03 /review parent starts 16:04-16:07 large parts of gstack review/SKILL.md loaded 16:07-16:09 diff/repository inspection specialist/checklist instructions loaded 16:09:27 testing_review spawned 16:09:36 maintainability_review spawned 16:09:42 security_api_review spawned 16:10+ builds/tests/repository inspection continue 16:23:19 design_review spawned 16:23:28 adversarial_review spawned 16:24+ additional review/repository commands 16:29:09 nested `codex exec` started 16:30:58 nested `codex exec resume` used 16:32:40 another nested `codex review` started 16:33+ repeated attempts to interrupt nested Codex process list inspected nested Codex process terminated 16:33:58 parent has reached 10.49M accumulated input 16:41+ parent model calls are still ~235k input each final parent count: 11.74M input ``` --- ## Reproducing the parent counter ```bash FILE="$HOME/.codex/sessions/2026/08/09/rollout-2026-08-09T17-03-43-019fe744-086c-7882-bf60-7a2cbad58146.jsonl" jq -c ' select( .type == "event_msg" and .payload.type == "token_count" and .payload.info != null ) | .payload.info.total_token_usage ' "$FILE" | tail -1 ``` --- ## Finding spawned child threads ```bash PARENT="019fe744-086c-7882-bf60-7a2cbad58146" sqlite3 ~/.codex/state_5.sqlite " SELECT parent_thread_id, child_thread_id, status FROM thread_spawn_edges WHERE parent_thread_id = '$PARENT'; " ``` At the time of inspection all five edges were still reported as `open`. --- ## Questions worth investigating Please don't assume these are the causes; they're the areas that appear worth checking from the evidence above. 1. Why does the `/review` parent reach ~170k-235k context and continue making enough model calls to accumulate 11.74M input tokens? 2. Is loading overlapping portions of `review/SKILL.md` multiple times expected, or is instruction content unnecessarily entering the parent context more than once? 3. When gstack `/review` is already hosted by Codex, is it intentional to invoke additional `codex exec` / `codex review` processes? 4. Is the nested Codex behavior contributing materially to subscription usage beyond the parent and `spawn_agent` reviewers? 5. Could `/review` reduce the number of parent orchestration turns after the context becomes very large, move more work into isolated agents, compact/drop tool output, or otherwise avoid replaying ~200k+ context dozens of times? 6. Is there any duplication in Codex's persisted token counters for parent/child/forked sessions that means some of the numbers above should not be summed? The clearest issue regardless of the exact accounting semantics is the **rate** observed in the parent itself: approximately **4.3M additional input tokens in 5m30s**, including a ~2m50s interval at roughly **1M input tokens/minute**.

title: thin-client detection (#2051) misses bearer-token installs — brain blocks still silently suppressed
body:
### Summary

The v1.61.0.0 thin-client fix (#2051) keys detection on `remote_mcp` in `~/.gbrain/config.json`. That marker is only ever written by `gbrain init --mcp-only`, which is **OAuth-only**. Users onboarded through gbrain's **bearer-token** path — `gbrain connect <mcp-url> --token <bearer>` — never get the marker, so they remain structurally undetectable and keep hitting the exact silent-suppression this release set out to close.

### Environment

- gstack `1.61.0.0`
- gbrain `0.42.63.0` (local CLI), remote `gbrain serve --http` on another host
- macOS 26.x

### What happens

Brain reachable **only** over remote-HTTP MCP with a bearer token (registered in `~/.claude.json` as `type: "http"` + `Authorization: Bearer …`):

```
$ gstack-gbrain-detect
{
  "gbrain_mcp_mode": "remote-http",     <-- signal is right here
  "gbrain_engine": "pglite",
  "gbrain_local_status": "engine-locked",
  ...
}
$ gstack-gbrain-detect --is-ok; echo $?
1
```

and `./setup` prints:

```
gbrain not detected — brain-aware blocks suppressed in planning-skill SKILL.md files (zero token overhead).
```

The brain is fully working over MCP. The blocks are suppressed anyway, silently.

### Root cause

`lib/gbrain-local-status.ts` (the pre-probe check added in #2051) returns `thin-client` only when the config carries `remote_mcp`:

```ts
if (cfg && typeof cfg === "object" && cfg.remote_mcp) {
  return "thin-client";
}
```

That mirrors gbrain's own `isThinClient()`. The problem is upstream of it — **who writes the marker**:

| gbrain onboarding path | auth | writes `remote_mcp`? |
|---|---|---|
| `gbrain init --mcp-only` | OAuth client credentials | yes |
| `gbrain connect <url> --token <bearer>` | bearer | **no** |

`gbrain connect` only emits/runs the agent's MCP-add command; it never touches `~/.gbrain/config.json`. And gbrain's own `connect --help` presents bearer as the *default* and recommends it ("simple, long-lived, full-access — best local/personal"), so this is not a fringe path.

Net effect: every bearer thin client falls through to the probe, `gbrain sources list` fails against the dead/absent local engine, and the classifier lands on `engine-locked` / `broken-config` → blocks suppressed.

Note that `detectMcpMode()` **already** resolves `gbrain_mcp_mode: "remote-http"` for these users. The signal exists in the same JSON; the classifier just doesn't consider it.

### Reproduce

1. Have a remote `gbrain serve --http` with a bearer token; no working local engine.
2. `gbrain connect https://<host>/mcp --token <bearer> --install`
3. Confirm MCP tools work in Claude Code.
4. `gstack-gbrain-detect --is-ok; echo $?` → `1`, and `./setup` reports "gbrain not detected".

### Second-order issue

Fixing the classifier alone is not sufficient. Once un-suppressed, the rendered **Brain Context Load** block shells out to the CLI:

```
Extract 2-4 keywords from the user's request. Search the brain:
`gbrain search "<keywords>"`. Read the top 3 results with `gbrain get_page "<slug>"`.
```

The CLI's remote path (`core/mcp-client.ts` → `resolveSecret`) is OAuth-only and errors with `No client_secret available` for bearer users. It degrades gracefully (the block tells the agent to proceed without context on non-zero exit), so nothing breaks — but the block is dead weight rather than a feature.

A complete fix is probably one of:

- **(a)** teach the classifier to accept `gbrain_mcp_mode: "remote-http"` as thin-client evidence, **and** have the CLI remote path accept a bearer (e.g. `GBRAIN_REMOTE_TOKEN`); or
- **(b)** render an MCP-tool variant of the block for hosts that already expose gbrain MCP tools, so it never depends on the CLI at all. On such hosts the agent can call the tools directly and the CLI's auth mode stops mattering.

### Workaround (verified)

Register an OAuth client on the brain host and convert the install:

```
# on the host
gbrain auth register-client "<name>" --grant-types client_credentials --scopes "read write"
# on the client
gbrain init --mcp-only --issuer-url https://<host> --mcp-url https://<host>/mcp \
  --oauth-client-id <id> --oauth-client-secret <secret>
```

After this, `gstack-gbrain-detect` reports `thin-client`, `--is-ok` exits 0, blocks render, and `gbrain search` works from the shell. But that requires host-side admin access, which a "my agent already talks to the brain" user has no reason to expect they need.

title: GBRAIN_HOME resolved differently by gstack and gbrain (missing .gbrain segment)
body:
### Summary

gstack and gbrain resolve `GBRAIN_HOME` to **different config paths**. gstack treats it as the config directory; gbrain treats it as the *parent* and appends `.gbrain`. With `GBRAIN_HOME` set, gstack classifies engine status from a file gbrain never reads.

### The divergence

**gstack** — `lib/gbrain-local-status.ts:127`:

```ts
const gbrainHome = e.GBRAIN_HOME || join(userHome(e), ".gbrain");
// → $GBRAIN_HOME/config.json
```

Same convention in `bin/gstack-gbrain-detect`:

```ts
const GBRAIN_CONFIG = join(
  process.env.GBRAIN_HOME || join(userHome(), ".gbrain"),
  "config.json",
);
```

**gbrain** — `src/core/config.ts`, `configDir()`:

```ts
// GBRAIN_HOME is a parent dir; we always append '.gbrain' ourselves so
// setting GBRAIN_HOME=/tmp/x yields configDir() === '/tmp/x/.gbrain'.
return join(trimmed, '.gbrain');
// → $GBRAIN_HOME/.gbrain/config.json
```

The comment is explicit, so this is gbrain's intended contract; gstack is the one that deviates.

| `GBRAIN_HOME` | gstack reads | gbrain reads |
|---|---|---|
| unset | `~/.gbrain/config.json` | `~/.gbrain/config.json` ✅ |
| `/tmp/x` | `/tmp/x/config.json` | `/tmp/x/.gbrain/config.json` ❌ |

### Why it matters

`localEngineStatus()` reads the config **and** spawns `gbrain sources list` as the probe. With `GBRAIN_HOME` set, the two halves look at different installs: the file checks (`missing-config`, the `remote_mcp` thin-client pre-probe, `configuredEngine()` for the `engine-locked` branch) read gstack's path, while the spawned CLI reads gbrain's. Any resulting status is arbitrary.

Concretely, the `missing-config` / `broken-config` branches can fire against a perfectly healthy install, or — as I hit — a `remote_mcp` marker placed at gstack's path yields `thin-client` from `gstack-gbrain-detect` while `gbrain` itself reports `No brain configured. Run: gbrain init`.

The comment at `bin/gstack-gbrain-detect:51-53` says this must "stay consistent with lib/gbrain-local-status's config resolution" — the two gstack sites *are* consistent with each other, just not with gbrain.

### Reproduce

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/x && cp ~/.gbrain/config.json /tmp/x/config.json

GBRAIN_HOME=/tmp/x GSTACK_DETECT_NO_CACHE=1 gstack-gbrain-detect
# → reads /tmp/x/config.json, reports a status derived from it

GBRAIN_HOME=/tmp/x gbrain sources list --json
# → "No brain configured. Run: gbrain init"  (looked in /tmp/x/.gbrain/)
```

### Suggested fix

Append `.gbrain` to the override in both gstack sites, matching `configDir()`:

```ts
const gbrainHome = e.GBRAIN_HOME ? join(e.GBRAIN_HOME, ".gbrain") : join(userHome(e), ".gbrain");
```

Worth checking `buildGbrainEnv` in `lib/gbrain-exec.ts` for the same assumption, and the `gbrain_home` cache-invariant key at `lib/gbrain-local-status.ts:82` / `:212` (it stores the raw env value, which stays correct either way, but the cached *status* it guards would have been computed from the wrong file).

Low blast radius today — it only bites users who set `GBRAIN_HOME` (tests, Docker, multi-tenant, which is exactly what gbrain documents the override for).

### Environment

gstack `1.61.0.0`, gbrain `0.42.63.0`, macOS 26.x

title: fix(browse): pass windowsHide so the daemon stops popping console windows on Windows
body:
On Windows, `browse` leaves empty black console windows sitting on top of whatever you're doing. They arrive every few minutes for as long as any browser skill is alive, and they outlive the process that created them — so closing one isn't enough. I hit this mid-screen-share, which is how it earned a diagnosis.

## Cause

`browse/src/bun-polyfill.cjs` maps `Bun.spawn`/`Bun.spawnSync` onto node's `child_process`, and **node defaults `windowsHide` to `false`**. Bun never creates these windows, so nothing in the daemon's own code reads as wrong — the behaviour only exists on the node fallback path.

The one users actually notice is `spawnTerminalAgent()`, which launches `bun run terminal-agent.ts` through the shim. The daemon **respawns it on a watchdog**, so the window keeps coming back. Ten `bun.exe` processes were live on the machine I diagnosed this on, across two daemons.

Why the frames linger after the child exits: with *Default terminal application* set to "Let Windows decide", the console is brokered through Windows Terminal via `svchost`, and WT leaves the empty frame behind when its only child exits. The frame has **no child process at all** — which is why it looks like a dead terminal and is always safe to close.

## Fix

`windowsHide: true` on both wrappers. That covers every console child routed through the shim — the bun agent, plus the `tasklist` / `git` / `powershell` calls elsewhere in the daemon. No-op on macOS and Linux.

## Second commit: the tests couldn't run on Windows

While adding a regression test I found `bun test browse/test/bun-polyfill.test.ts` was **0 pass / 4 fail on Windows** — every test in the file, on the platform the polyfill exists for.

Each test interpolates the polyfill's absolute path into a *single-quoted* JS string for `node -e`. On Windows the backslashes are eaten as escapes:

```
'C:\Users\jwilk\dev\gstack-fork\browse\src\bun-polyfill.cjs'
  ->  C:Usersjwilkdevgstack-forkrowsesrcun-polyfill.cjs
```

`\b` is a real escape, so it deletes a character too. `require()` throws, the subprocess dies, stdout is empty, and every assertion compares against `""`. It passes on macOS/Linux only because those paths have no backslashes.

Fixed with `JSON.stringify(polyfillPath)`. Kept as a separate commit so you can take either half independently.

## Verification (Windows 11, bun 1.3.14, gstack 1.61.0.0)

| | pass | fail |
|---|---|---|
| pristine upstream | 0 | 4 |
| with both commits | **5** | **0** |
| with commit 2 only (fix reverted) | 4 | 1 — the new test, `VISIBLE` instead of `HIDDEN` |

The regression test stubs `child_process.spawn`/`spawnSync` *before* the polyfill destructures them and asserts the captured options, so it's deterministic, needs no window, and still verifies the contract on macOS/Linux where the option is a no-op.

End to end: restarted the daemon after patching and confirmed no bun window appeared, with the agent and Chromium still running normally.

## Not covered

`chromium.launch()` (`browse/src/…`, via playwright) goes through playwright's own process launcher, not this shim, so it still creates **one** window per daemon start rather than one every few minutes. Setting *Default terminal application* to "Windows Console Host" makes that one close with its process instead of being abandoned, but a `windowsHide` on the playwright launch would be the real answer. Happy to follow up if you'd like it in the same PR.

title: Two stated guarantees in the `codex` skill don't hold (v1.60.1.0)
body:
Both of these are cases where `SKILL.md` states a guarantee that the code beneath it doesn't provide. Filing together because they share that shape; happy to split if you'd rather.

Confirmed by reading the shipped file. Line numbers are v1.60.1.0 @ `a325940`; env is codex CLI v0.144.1 on macOS/zsh.

## 1. The gate rule ignores exit status, so failure output can be classified PASS

`SKILL.md:1049–1051`:

```
4. Determine gate verdict by checking the review output for critical findings.
   If the output contains `[P1]` — the gate is **FAIL**.
   If no `[P1]` markers are found (only `[P2]` or no findings) — the gate is **PASS**.
```

The verdict comes entirely from the presence of a substring; exit status is not part of the rule. Output from a run that failed — expired auth, invalid flag, timeout, empty result — contains no `[P1]`, and so satisfies the PASS branch as written.

Two qualifications in fairness:

- `:995–1000` does echo a non-zero exit, and `:1572` separately instructs the agent to surface auth/timeout/empty-response errors. The skill isn't silent on failure — but those are instructions to the agent, not part of the gate rule, and the rule still yields PASS.
- Codex's own v0.144.1 review rubric treats **P0** as blocking. The rule recognises only `[P1]`, so a P0-only result also lands in PASS.

**Suggested fix:** make the gate fail-closed — non-zero exit, empty output, or absent completion signal should yield FAIL (or UNKNOWN), never PASS — and recognise `[P0]` as blocking. Note a "completion signal" would have to be introduced deliberately; native human-readable review output doesn't currently emit a stable machine-checkable marker.

## 2. The default review path sets no explicit sandbox override

`SKILL.md:1585`, verbatim:

```
- **Never modify files.** This skill is read-only. Codex runs in read-only sandbox mode.
```

The default native path at `:987–989` invokes:

```
codex review "<prompt>" -c 'model_reasoning_effort="high"' --enable web_search_cached
```

No `-s read-only`, no sandbox override — so the effective sandbox resolves from the user's `~/.codex/config.toml` rather than from the skill. A user whose `sandbox_mode` is `workspace-write` or `danger-full-access` gets a review with write capability, and with `approval_policy = "never"`, without a prompt.

The custom-focus fallback at `:1027` does use `codex exec -s read-only`. Only the default path is affected — which arguably makes it the more misleading of the two, since a reader who checks one path and finds it correct has no reason to check the other.

**Suggested fix:** pass `-c 'sandbox_mode="read-only"'` on the native review path, or resolve and assert the effective sandbox before running.

---

Reported against the template/generator rather than the emitted file, since local edits to `SKILL.md` don't survive an upgrade.

title: `--enable web_search_cached` is deprecated in codex CLI v0.144.1
body:
Used at `SKILL.md:989, 1027, 1270, 1425, 1479` (v1.60.1.0 @ `a325940`).

Under codex CLI v0.144.1 the flag still parses, but every invocation emits:

```
deprecated: `[features].web_search_cached` is deprecated because web search is enabled by default.
Set `web_search` to `"live"`, `"indexed"`, `"cached"`, or `"disabled"` at the top level (or under a profile) in config.toml if you want to override it.
```

Replacement: `-c 'web_search="cached"'` — reproduced directly, and the notice disappears.

One caveat worth stating precisely: the two are **not** unconditionally equivalent. The legacy flag yields to an existing top-level `web_search = live|indexed|disabled`, whereas the `-c` form explicitly overrides it. For a user with no competing setting the behaviour matches; for a user with one, it does not.

Separately, and possibly worth a docs tweak: native `codex review` disables web search regardless of configuration, which makes the claim at `:1551` inaccurate for the default review path.

---

Minor/housekeeping — filed separately from the safety issues so it can be closed independently.

title: gstack-diff-scope: SCOPE_API misses top-level api/, and all-false is indistinguishable from no-match
body:
Two issues in `bin/gstack-diff-scope`, found while it was gating `/ship` reviews on a payments codebase. Tested against v1.61.0.0.

## 1. `SCOPE_API` misses top-level `api/`

The API pattern is:

```sh
*controller*|*route*|*endpoint*|*/api/*) API=true ;;
```

`*/api/*` requires a path segment **before** `api/`, so a project that puts its routes at the repository root — which is the convention for Vercel and Next.js `pages/api` at root, among others — never matches. Bash glob check:

| path | `SCOPE_API` |
|---|---|
| `api/ipospays/process-payment.ts` | **false** |
| `api/lib/chargeOnFile.ts` | **false** |
| `src/api/foo.ts` | true |

In our repo that is **63 serverless functions, none of them ever classified as API.** `SCOPE_API` gates the API-contract specialist in `/ship` Step 9.1, so that reviewer was silently skipped on every payment PR for as long as we have been using it. When we ran it by hand it returned a CRITICAL finding.

**Suggested fix** — add a leading-segment alternative:

```sh
api/*|*/api/*|*controller*|*route*|*endpoint*) API=true ;;
```

Same applies to `MIGRATIONS` (`*/migrations/*` misses a root-level `migrations/`) and to `TESTS` (`test/*|tests/*` are anchored, so those are fine).

## 2. All-false is indistinguishable from "nothing matched"

When the diff is non-empty but no pattern matches, the script prints nine `false` values and exits 0. That is byte-identical to the output for a diff that genuinely touches nothing sensitive.

The consequence is that a classifier bug, an unrecognised project layout, or a new top-level directory all present as "no reviewers needed" — and the skip is invisible. A tool that cannot distinguish "no matches" from "no input" cannot be trusted to gate a security review.

There is a third case worth folding in: if `BASE` is unreachable (a shallow CI checkout is the common one), `git diff` yields an empty file list and the script reports all-false with exit 0. That is a green meaning "we could not look".

**Suggested fix** — distinguish the three states:

```
exit 0   diff empty                       → all false, legitimately nothing
exit 0   diff non-empty, >=1 match        → flags
exit 2   diff non-empty, ZERO matches     → SCOPE_ERROR=unmatched + the paths
exit 2   base ref unusable                → SCOPE_ERROR=no_base
```

Printing the unmatched paths makes the fix obvious to whoever hits it, and it self-heals: a new top-level directory trips the error instead of quietly disabling reviewers.

## 3. Minor: non-ASCII paths are quoted

`git diff --name-only` escapes paths containing non-ASCII bytes (`"docs/M2 \342\200\224 Notes.md"`). The trailing quote defeats the `*.md` extension patterns, so a genuine docs file matches nothing. `git diff --name-only -z` with NUL splitting avoids it.

## What we did meanwhile

Rather than patch the binary — `gstack-upgrade` would overwrite it, and a fix that silently reverts is the same class of problem — we wrote an in-repo replacement with the corrected patterns and the exit codes above, enforced by a CI step so it cannot be skipped. Happy to open a PR against this repo with the pattern and exit-code changes if that is useful; the fixes are small and independent of our layout.

title: fix(gitattributes): pin *.txt to LF
body:
One line added to `.gitattributes`:

```
*.txt        text eol=lf
```

## Why

`.gitattributes` already pins LF for every other text format in the repo — `*.md`, `*.tmpl`, `*.yml`, `*.yaml`, `*.json`, `*.toml`, `*.sh`, `*.bash`, `setup`, `bin/*`, `**/scripts/*`, `*.ts/tsx/js/mjs/cjs`, and the hash-pinned `lib/diagram-render/dist/*`. `*.txt` is the one text format left out.

On Windows with `core.autocrlf=true`, the two tracked `.txt` files get rewritten to CRLF at checkout, so `git status` is never clean in a fresh clone.

## Repro

Fresh clone of `main`, `core.autocrlf=true`, comparing blob bytes to worktree bytes:

```
gstack/llms.txt                                    blob=12443  worktree=12617  +174
make-pdf/test/fixtures/combined-gate.expected.txt  blob=987    worktree=1007   +20
README.md                                          blob=45456  worktree=45456    0   <- pinned, unaffected
```

Exactly one byte per line, and `README.md` is the control: it is pinned by `*.md text eol=lf` and comes out clean. With this patch both `.txt` files also come out at delta 0.

## User-visible symptom

`git status` reports `gstack/llms.txt` as modified forever. Because `/gstack-upgrade` runs `git stash` before `git reset --hard`, every upgrade saves a phantom stash — one whose diff against its own parent is empty. The user is then told to `git stash pop` to recover changes that never existed.

## Scope

Only the two files above are affected today. I checked `make-pdf/test/fixtures/combined-gate.expected.txt` since it is an expected-output fixture, but `copyPasteGate` runs the text through `normalize()` and `collapseWhitespace()`, so I could not produce a test failure from the CRLF — this is a cleanliness fix, not a test fix.

## Note for existing checkouts

The attribute only affects future checkouts. Anyone with a dirty tree today needs a one-time renormalize:

```bash
git add --renormalize .
# or, per file:
rm gstack/llms.txt && git checkout -- gstack/llms.txt
```

Verified on Windows (Git for Windows, `core.autocrlf=true`) against `main` @ v1.61.0.0.

title: fix(setup-gbrain): support current gbrain installs
body:
## Summary

Fix `/setup-gbrain` against the current gbrain HEAD and unattended Linux/macOS environments.

- accept gbrain packages that intentionally omit top-level `version`, while preserving fail-closed PATH-shadow validation through resolved binary identity
- resolve package metadata and paths with Bun instead of requiring `jq` or GNU-specific tooling
- compare the minimum version floor without GNU `sort -V`, including gbrain's four-component version output
- fall back from unreachable SSH artifact remotes to canonical HTTPS without interactive credential prompts
- use SSH `BatchMode=yes` and fail before initializing local artifact state when neither transport is reachable
- invoke the actual TypeScript memory-ingest entrypoint through Bun in generated setup docs

## Why

A real `/setup-gbrain` run with gbrain `0.45.1.0` failed because current gbrain omits `package.json.version`. After restoring the CLI, artifact initialization also failed on a server where GitHub HTTPS auth worked but SSH did not. The setup docs referenced a shell wrapper that does not exist.

## Verification

- `bun test` — full Tier-1 suite passed
- `bun test test/gbrain-detect-install.test.ts test/gstack-artifacts-init.test.ts test/setup-gbrain-path4-structure.test.ts` — 53 passed
- `bash -n bin/gstack-gbrain-install bin/gstack-artifacts-init` — passed
- `bun run scripts/gen-skill-docs.ts --dry-run` — fresh
- live `gstack-gbrain-install` against gbrain `0.45.1.0` — passed
- live artifacts initialization against a private GitHub repository with SSH unavailable and HTTPS available — passed
- independent exact-candidate review at staged diff SHA-256 `3102158a012480b6ee6ce28397fe84287cf2e148c094bafba46deb18a58c80aa` — passed, no blocking findings

## Security / lifecycle

- credentials remain in Git credential helpers; no token is added to argv, logs, or committed configuration
- SSH and HTTPS connectivity probes are non-interactive
- artifact initialization remains fail-closed and does not write local repository state if both transports fail

title: Fix orphaned browse terminal agents after server exit
body:
## Summary

- Tie each detached terminal agent to the persistent browse server PID that owns it.
- Poll the owner PID and run the existing cleanup path when that server disappears.
- Add a process-boundary regression test that proves the agent exits and removes its state files after owner termination.

Detached terminal agents can otherwise be adopted by PID 1 after an interrupted browse session and remain alive indefinitely. On a machine with many agent sessions, those abandoned filesystem watchers can amplify FSEvents and Time Machine pressure.

title: fix(ship): version-bump skipped subdirectory manifests and wrote npm-invalid versions
body:
Two ways `gstack-version-bump` left a release half-done, both silent. Found while shipping two versions of a real project through `/ship`.

## 1. Subdirectory manifests were skipped entirely

The tool only ever looked at `./package.json`. A repo whose only Node package lives in `web/`, `app/`, or `frontend/` has no root manifest, so `classify` reported `pkgExists: false` and every bump wrote `VERSION` alone — leaving the manifest to be edited by hand. That's the exact drift this tool exists to prevent, in the one layout where it silently did nothing.

The path now resolves `--package-json-path` → `.gstack/package-json-path` → `./package.json`, mirroring the existing `resolveVersionPath`. A subdirectory package is covered by a one-line pin.

## 2. It wrote versions npm rejects

`VERSION` is 4-digit `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.MICRO`. npm's semver is 3-component and rejects the fourth, so mirroring 1:1 into an npm-managed manifest writes a version npm will not install.

When a `package-lock.json` sits beside the manifest — proof npm actually manages it — the MICRO is now dropped (`0.1.26.0` → `0.1.26`), and the lockfile's **two** version fields are mirrored as well: the document root and `packages[""]`, the entry describing the root package itself. npm keeps both in step and nothing else in a release does, so a lockfile left behind drifts one field per bump until someone runs npm. Pure JSON edit — no npm spawn, no dependency-tree churn.

**Without a lockfile nothing validates the field, so the historical 1:1 mirror is preserved.** gstack's own `package.json` carries `1.60.1.0` and keeps doing so.

This required an `expectedPkg` parameter on `classifyState`. It defaults to `VERSION` — but for an npm-managed manifest it's the 3-component truncation. Without that, a correctly-synced `0.1.27` reads as drift against `0.1.27.0` forever and every `classify` returns `DRIFT`.

## Tests

7 new cases in two blocks, covering the negatives as well as the happy paths:

```
subdirectory manifest (no root package.json)
  write finds a pinned manifest and bumps it
  --package-json-path overrides the pin
npm-managed manifest (lockfile present)
  write drops the MICRO and syncs BOTH lockfile version fields
  a correctly-synced 3-component manifest is NOT read as drift
  repair syncs manifest + lockfile to the 3-component form
  no lockfile keeps the historical 4-digit mirror (gstack itself)
```

- `bun test test/gstack-version-bump.test.ts` — 21/21
- Full Tier 1 free suite (`bun test browse/test/ test/ make-pdf/test/` with the `test` script's ignores) — exit 0, zero failures on a clean fork clone at `94993f7`
- **Not run:** Tier 2/3 (`test:e2e`, `test:evals`, ~$4). Per CONTRIBUTING they need `EVALS=1` and can't nest inside Claude Code. Flagging rather than letting silence imply coverage.

## Note on the golden fixtures

Step 12 of the ship skill documents the new behaviour, so all three ship-skill goldens are updated.

Heads-up for whoever reviews: on a **first** run in a fresh clone, `host-config.test.ts` reports the Codex and Factory goldens as failing. That's a test-ordering artifact, not a real failure — `.agents/` and `.factory/` are untracked generated files, and `gen-skill-docs.test.ts` regenerates them *after* `host-config.test.ts` has already compared them. A second run is green. Happy to file that separately if it's worth fixing.

I verified the updated fixtures are byte-identical to what a clean clone generates, so no local-environment rendering rode along.

title: test/host-config.test.ts golden tests fail in isolation: hidden cross-file dependency on gitignored .agents/ and .factory/
body:
`test/host-config.test.ts` can't be run on its own in a fresh clone. Its two golden-file tests read build artifacts that a *different* test file is responsible for creating, so running that one file gives 2 spurious failures.

## Reproduce (pristine `v1.61.0.0`, no modifications)

```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/garrytan/gstack.git && cd gstack
bun install
bun test test/host-config.test.ts
```

```
(fail) golden-file regression > Codex ship skill matches golden baseline
(fail) golden-file regression > Factory ship skill matches golden baseline
 75 pass
  2 fail
```

Now generate the artifacts and run the identical command again:

```bash
bun test test/gen-skill-docs.test.ts   # side effect: creates .agents/ and .factory/
bun test test/host-config.test.ts
```

```
 77 pass
  0 fail
```

Same command, same tree, opposite result. The only thing that changed is that another test file ran first.

## Cause

The two golden tests compare against generated host variants:

```ts
// test/host-config.test.ts
const current = fs.readFileSync(path.join(ROOT, '.agents',  'skills', 'gstack-ship', 'SKILL.md'), 'utf-8');
const current = fs.readFileSync(path.join(ROOT, '.factory', 'skills', 'gstack-ship', 'SKILL.md'), 'utf-8');
```

`.agents/` and `.factory/` are **gitignored** (`git check-ignore` confirms), so they don't exist in a fresh clone. Nothing in `host-config.test.ts` creates them — I deleted the directories and ran that file twice; it failed both times and never regenerated them.

What creates them is `test/gen-skill-docs.test.ts`, as a side effect of exercising the generator. Verified in isolation: `.agents` absent → run that file alone → `.agents` present.

So there's a hidden cross-file dependency, and since bun runs test files concurrently the golden tests are racing the generator.

## Why the full suite still looks fine

`bun test` (the documented Tier 1 gate) passes the golden tests — the generator wins the race in practice. So CI stays green and this only bites a contributor iterating on a single file, which is exactly how I hit it: I was changing `ship/SKILL.md.tmpl`, ran the golden test to check my fixture update, and spent a while assuming my own change had broken something upstream.

For what it's worth, the full gate on this pristine clone did have 3 unrelated failures, all environment-dependent rather than ordering-dependent — noting them only so they aren't mistaken for this issue:

```
(fail) --list > handles missing proposals file
(fail) gstack-community-dashboard > connects to Supabase when config exists
(fail) gstack-gbrain-install D5 detect-first > --dry-run falls through to fresh clone ...
```

## Possible fixes

Roughly in order of how much I'd trust them:

1. **Generate in a `beforeAll` in `host-config.test.ts`** — makes the dependency explicit and owned by the file that needs it.
2. **Skip when absent**, matching what `gen-skill-docs.test.ts` already does for the same directories (`if (!fs.existsSync(agentsDir)) return;`). Cheapest, but the golden check silently disappears in a fresh clone, which is where a regression is most likely to slip through.
3. **Generate to a temp dir inside the test** and compare that, so the test depends on nothing on disk.

Happy to send a PR for whichever you prefer — (1) unless you'd rather not have tests writing into the working tree.

Found while preparing #2531; that PR is unrelated to this and mentions the symptom in passing.

title: bun test is non-deterministic on a clean clone: 3 failures then 0, same command
body:
`bun test` — the documented Tier 1 gate — produces different results run to run on an unmodified clone. Same command, same tree, no changes in between: 3 failures, then 0.

## Reproduce (pristine `v1.61.0.0`, no modifications)

```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/garrytan/gstack.git && cd gstack
bun install
bun test browse/test/ test/ make-pdf/test/ \
  --ignore 'test/skill-e2e-*.test.ts' --ignore test/skill-llm-eval.test.ts \
  --ignore test/skill-routing-e2e.test.ts --ignore test/codex-e2e.test.ts \
  --ignore test/gemini-e2e.test.ts
```

(That's the `test` script from `package.json`, minus the trailing `slop:diff`.)

**Run 1 — 3 failures:**

```
(fail) --list > handles missing proposals file                                        [5006.61ms]
(fail) gstack-community-dashboard > connects to Supabase when config exists           [6887.86ms]
(fail) gstack-gbrain-install D5 detect-first > --dry-run falls through to fresh clone
       when no valid clone detected                                                   [7388.56ms]
```

**Run 2, identical command, nothing changed — 0 failures.**

A third run of just those three files together produced yet another failing set — only `gstack-gbrain-install D5 detect-first > rejects a pre-existing path that lacks a valid gbrain package.json`, with the other two green.

## Each file is deterministic in isolation

Two runs each, same clone:

```
test/distill-apply.test.ts          11 pass  0 fail   (x2)
test/telemetry.test.ts              40 pass  0 fail   (x2)
test/gbrain-detect-install.test.ts  16 pass  0 fail   (x2)
```

So the tests themselves are fine. Something about running the suite together isn't.

## What it isn't

**Not shared-state pollution** — at least not for `distill-apply`, which is hermetic:

```ts
beforeEach(() => {
  stateRoot = fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), 'gstack-apply-'));
  ...
});
afterEach(() => { fs.rmSync(stateRoot, { recursive: true, force: true }); });

// and in run():
env.GSTACK_STATE_ROOT = stateRoot;
delete env.GSTACK_HOME;
```

Fresh temp dir per test, state root redirected into it, `GSTACK_HOME` stripped from the child env. Another test writing to `~/.gstack` can't reach it.

**Not network or missing config** — `handles missing proposals file` asserts on a hermetic temp dir and touches nothing external.

## Hypothesis (not proven)

All three spawn subprocesses via `spawnSync`, and every failure carried a multi-second duration — 5.0s, 6.9s, 7.4s — against sub-second in isolation. Under bun's concurrent file execution, dozens of files each spawning children may be saturating the machine enough for these to time out or for a spawn to fail.

I'm flagging that as a guess. What I've established is the non-determinism and that it isn't state or environment; I haven't proven the contention mechanism.

Worth noting one failure was `Expected: 0, Received: 3` — a real exit code from the binary, not an obvious timeout artifact. So contention may not explain all of them.

## Why it matters

CONTRIBUTING lists `bun test` as the free gate that "runs on every commit." A gate that fails ~randomly trains people to re-run until green, which is how a real regression gets waved through. It also cost me a while on an unrelated PR (#2531) working out whether I'd broken something.

## Possible directions

- Run the subprocess-spawning files serially (bun's `--concurrency` or splitting them into their own pass)
- Give the `spawnSync` calls explicit generous timeouts so contention produces a clear timeout rather than a confusing assertion failure
- Capture `stderr`/`status` in the failure message on those assertions, so the next person sees *why* the child failed

Happy to take a crack at any of these if you have a preference.

Environment: macOS (Darwin 25.5.0), bun 1.3.13, pristine clone at `94993f7`.

Related: #2532 (a separate, deterministic isolation problem in `test/host-config.test.ts`).

title: fix(browse): allow about:blank so a restarted daemon can initialise
body:
## The bug

`validateNavigationUrl` rejects every scheme except http(s) and file — including `about:blank`. But the daemon opens its own first tab on about:blank, so once it restarts it can never come back:

```
$ browse newtab about:blank
Blocked: scheme "about:" is not allowed. Only http:, https:, and file: URLs are permitted.
```

## Why it shows up as a make-pdf failure

make-pdf's Chromium smoke test is exactly that command, so `make-pdf setup` reports:

```
[2/5] Launching Chromium... FAIL
Chromium failed to launch: browse newtab exited 1
```

against a completely healthy Chromium — and `generate` fails downstream with `page.pdf: Protocol error (IO.read): Read failed`, which is what talking to a half-started daemon looks like. Both symptoms point away from the cause, which is why this was slow to find.

**It only reproduces once the daemon restarts.** A daemon still holding its original tab keeps working, so the bug stays hidden until something recycles the process — and then make-pdf is dead until the tab gets recreated some other way.

## Scope

As narrow as it can be: `about:blank` **exactly**, matched on `href`, not the `about:` scheme.

| URL | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `about:blank` | blocked | **allowed** |
| `ABOUT:BLANK` | blocked | **allowed** |
| `about:config` | blocked | blocked |
| `about:net-internals` | blocked | blocked |
| `about:blankfoo` | blocked | blocked |
| `javascript:` / `data:` / `chrome://` | blocked | blocked |

about:blank has no origin, loads nothing and runs nothing. The rest of the scheme is a real surface and stays out.

Compared lower-cased because the URL parser normalises the protocol but not the opaque part, so `ABOUT:BLANK` parses to href `about:BLANK`. My first version used `===` and the test caught it.

## Tests

4 added to `browse/test/url-validation.test.ts` — about:blank resolves (and case-insensitively), about:config and about:net-internals still rejected, about:blankfoo still rejected.

Verified end to end on Windows: with the daemon killed, `make-pdf generate` on a 9-page document now goes cold start → PDF in 4.8s. Before, it failed every time.

## One note for reviewers on Windows

`browse/test/url-validation.test.ts` has **5 pre-existing failures** on this platform, all in the `file://` suites, which assume POSIX paths (`/tmp`, `/etc/passwd`). Unrelated to this change and unchanged by it — same 5 before and after. Happy to send a separate PR for those if useful.

title: fix(make-pdf): reject a directory when resolving the browse binary
body:
## The bug

`isExecutable()` tests `access(X_OK)` alone. That is **true for directories** — they carry the execute/traverse bit on POSIX and pass the check on Windows too — so binary discovery accepts a directory as the browse binary.

It bites on a stock global install. `~/.claude/skills/browse` is the skill's own docs folder, containing nothing but `SKILL.md`, but it sits on a probed path, passes `X_OK`, and wins.

## What the user sees

```
[1/5] Checking browse binary... OK (C:\Users\...\.claude\skills\browse)
[2/5] Launching Chromium... FAIL
Chromium failed to launch: browse newtab exited 1:
```

Two things make this hard to diagnose: the first line reports the **wrong path as OK**, and the error string is empty because what actually happened is that a directory was executed as a program. Setting `GSTACK_BROWSE_BIN` works around it, which makes it look like a discovery-*order* problem rather than a type-check problem.

## The fix

One `statSync(p).isFile()` before the access check.

## Tests

2 added to `make-pdf/test/browseClient.test.ts`, both failing before this change and passing after:

- **`rejects a DIRECTORY even though it passes access(X_OK)`** — asserts the precondition explicitly first, that the directory really does pass `access(X_OK)`, so the test documents *why* the bare check was wrong rather than only pinning the new behaviour.
- **`rejects a directory that shadows a real binary name`** — reproduces the exact shape: a directory named `browse` containing a `SKILL.md`.

```
WITH fix:     11 pass, 0 fail
WITHOUT fix:   9 pass, 2 fail   ← the two new ones
```

No pre-existing failures in this suite on Windows.

## Relationship to #2537

Found while fixing #2537 (`about:blank` blocked, which stops the daemon initialising). They're independent bugs in different packages — either can be merged alone — but on a Windows machine you need both before `make-pdf` works, so it's worth knowing they travel together.

title: fix(browse): forward windowsHide through the Bun polyfill spawn shims
body:
## The bug

On Windows, a `bun.exe` console window reopens by itself every so often, with no scheduled task, Run key, or startup shortcut behind it. I chased it down to the browse daemon and it turned out to be three things stacked, only the last of which is a defect:

1. A browse daemon left running from a headed session cannot self-terminate. The parent-process watchdog is disabled by design in headed mode (`browse/src/server.ts:686`), which is correct, but it means an orphaned daemon lives until killed.
2. That daemon runs a 60s ticker that respawns the terminal-agent whenever the recorded child PID is dead (`browse/src/server.ts:1493-1548`).
3. Each respawn opens a **visible console window**, because `browse/src/bun-polyfill.cjs` accepts a `Bun.spawn` options object and forwards only `stdio`, `env`, and `cwd` to `child_process.spawn`.

`windowsHide` is dropped in translation. Node defaults it to `false`; `Bun.spawn` hides the window. So the shim silently inverts the behavior on the one platform it exists to serve, per its own header comment ("Bun API polyfill for Node.js — Windows compatibility layer").

`stdio: 'ignore'` silences the child's output but does not suppress its console window, so the existing spawn options don't cover this.

## The fix

Both shims forward the option and default it to `true`, matching the Bun API being emulated. An explicit `windowsHide: false` still passes through, so nothing loses the escape hatch. `spawnTerminalAgent` also sets it explicitly at the call site, which is where the symptom surfaced.

## Tests

Three cases added to `browse/test/bun-polyfill.test.ts`, in the file's existing subprocess style: the default for `spawn`, the default for `spawnSync`, and that an explicit `false` is honored. They patch `child_process` before the polyfill is required, so they assert on what actually reaches Node rather than on the source text.

I verified each one goes red against the unpatched shim (3 fail) and green with it (7 pass), so they are known to detect the defect rather than merely passing.

## One drive-by, and why it was unavoidable

The suite could not run at all on Windows before this. The tests interpolate an absolute path into a JS string literal, so `C:\Users\...` had its backslashes consumed as escapes and every `require()` failed with MODULE_NOT_FOUND. All four tests failed for that reason alone, not on their assertions.

The path is now normalized to forward slashes, which Node accepts on Windows. This file goes from **0/4 to 7/7 on Windows**. I kept the change to the one line that builds the path plus the interpolations, so the existing tests are otherwise untouched.

## Verification

- `bun test browse/test/bun-polyfill.test.ts`: 7 pass, 0 fail (was 0 pass, 4 fail on Windows).
- `bun test browse/test/terminal-agent-pid-identity.test.ts browse/test/terminal-agent-integration.test.ts`: 9 pass, 6 fail, **identical to the clean baseline** on this machine. Those 6 are pre-existing Windows failures in that suite and are not touched by this change.
- I did not complete a full `bun test` run. It far exceeds the "<5s Tier 1" figure in CONTRIBUTING on Windows and timed out locally at 10 minutes. Happy to run anything specific you want covered.

Environment: Windows 10 Pro 19045, bun 1.3.14, branched from d078622 (v1.62.0.0).

title: fix(gbrain-install): --dry-run no longer requires the network (fixes flaky bun test)
body:
Fixes the `bun test` non-determinism in #2536. One-line guard, plus a comment explaining why it's there.

## The bug

`gstack-gbrain-install --dry-run` prints a plan and exits without cloning anything — but it makes a live request to github.com first:

```sh
if ! $VALIDATE_ONLY; then
  check_prereq bun ...
  check_prereq git ...
  if ! curl -s --head --max-time 10 https://github.com >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    fail "cannot reach https://github.com. Check your network and try again."
  fi
fi
```

The check is gated on `VALIDATE_ONLY`. `--dry-run` sets `DRY_RUN`. So the dry-run path hits the network for a result nothing downstream uses — both dry-run branches `exit 0` before any clone.

When that curl loses a race for sockets or DNS, `fail()` exits **3** and a dry run reports "cannot reach https://github.com" on a machine that is online.

## Direct proof, no test runner involved

60 concurrent `--dry-run` invocations against temp `HOME`/`GSTACK_HOME`:

| | Failures |
|---|---|
| before | **9 / 60** (~15%), all `cannot reach https://github.com` |
| after | **0 / 60** |

## Why this made the suite flaky

The three `gstack-gbrain-install D5 detect-first` tests each call `run(INSTALL, ['--dry-run'])` and assert `expect(r.status).toBe(0)`. A full `bun test` spawns many concurrent processes, the curl occasionally loses, and whichever D5 test was running goes red.

Every symptom lines up: green in isolation (16/16, repeatedly), a *different* one of the three failing each run, sub-second failures rather than timeouts, and the observed exit code of exactly 3.

## Validation

The documented Tier 1 gate, on a clean clone:

| | Runs | Failed |
|---|---|---|
| before (#2536) | 7 | **3 (43%)** |
| after | 10 | **0** |

Ten consecutive clean runs against a 43% per-run failure rate is roughly a 0.4% coincidence.

## Scope

Real installs are unchanged — they still get the fail-fast offline check rather than a hanging `git clone`. Only the path that never clones skips it.

I first blamed a `PATH` leak and proposed defaulting `SAFE_PATH` in the test helper. That was wrong, and I've retracted it in #2536 — it would also have broken these tests on any machine where bun lives at `~/.bun/bin`, which `SAFE_PATH` excludes.

## Not addressed here

`telemetry > connects to Supabase when config exists` appeared once in my first sample and looks like the same shape — a real network call inside the free suite. I haven't investigated it and make no claim about it; noting it in case it's worth a look.

Environment: macOS (Darwin 25.5.0), bun 1.3.13, clean clone at `94993f7`.

Full user-facing notes in `CHANGELOG.md`.

### What's in it (21 bisected commits + review fixes)

- **eval-store `_partial` fix** — `findPreviousRun` always picked the in-progress accumulator as the comparison baseline, so every historical "no regressions" line was a run graded against itself. Fixed with regression tests; **confirmed against the bug on the prior release before landing.**

A tripwire test enforces **zero un-wired off-machine sinks**.

- **Plan-eng-review:** 17 findings folded. **Plan-devex-review:** 4 user-facing requirements folded. **Codex (outside voice):** 14 findings folded.

The test times out because its terminal-scraping detector can't parse that AskUserQuestion out of a PTY buffer where spinner frames interleave char-by-char with the option text (a brittleness the test's own comments flag). `seedSkills` is what makes this test execute at all (the fork had deleted it). Not a shipped-code regression; P2 TODO filed to harden/re-tier the detector.

Three /health empirical checks that need a real headed browser (not verifiable by diff): the extension `POST` carries the pinned Origin under headed Playwright; the packaged GStack Browser.app picks up the new manifest key; the gbrowser/phoenix embedder's HealthMonitor doesn't consume the old `/health` token.
