title: fix(redact): scan large diffs in slices; stop digit-only UUIDs matching as cards/phones
body:
Two fixes to the redact guardrail, both found while using gstack on a real
monorepo — the workflow CONTRIBUTING.md recommends.

They're independent; happy to split into two PRs if you'd prefer.

## 1. `engine.input_too_large` blocks ordinary pushes

`gstack-redact-prepush` calls `scan()` once on the whole pushed diff, so any
diff over `DEFAULT_MAX_BYTES` (1 MiB) comes back as a single
`engine.input_too_large` HIGH finding and blocks the push.

That threshold is reached by ordinary work. A feature branch catching up to a
busy `main` produced **1,146,782 bytes** of added lines — only 9% over, and
only ~7% of it was the lockfile; the rest was genuine source.

The failure mode is worse than a noisy block:

- The message names no file, no line and no credential, so it reads as a bug.
- The documented remedy — "Rotate the credential" — doesn't apply.
- The documented escape hatch is `--no-verify`, which disables scanning
  **entirely**.

So a size cap that fires on normal branches actively trains people to bypass
the guard. It also silently discarded real findings: once actually scanned,
that same diff reported **21 MEDIUM** (PII/internal) that had never been
surfaced while the scan was aborting on size.

**Fix:** scan added lines in 768 KiB line-aligned slices and union the
findings.

No detection coverage is lost, because every pattern is single-line: none in
`redact-patterns.ts` carries the `m` or `s` flag, the `BEGIN PRIVATE KEY`
patterns capture only the header line rather than the key body, and the engine
already iterates line by line. A line boundary therefore cannot bisect a
detectable secret, so no inter-slice overlap is needed.

**Fail-closed is preserved.** A *single line* larger than the budget is still
handed to the engine intact, so a genuinely unscannable blob (minified bundle,
embedded base64) trips `input_too_large` and blocks exactly as before.

Kept in the hook rather than the engine on purpose: slice-relative `line`/`col`
are fine there (only `severity`, `id` and `preview` are read), but would break
engine callers that rely on absolute line numbers.

Verified by invoking the hook with real pre-push stdin:

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| 1.79 MiB benign diff | exit 0, scanned — previously blocked |
| secret in the **last** slice of 1.8 MiB | exit 1, `HIGH pem.private_key` |
| single 1.5 MiB line | exit 1, `input_too_large` (fail-closed intact) |
| the real diff that needed `--no-verify` | exit 0 |

## 2. Digit-only UUIDs match as credit cards and phone numbers

Placeholder UUIDs — `00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000`,
`11111111-1111-…`, `22222222-2222-…` — are the standard fixture shape in test
suites, and their digit runs collide with two MEDIUM patterns. A 13–19 digit
slice of one passes Luhn often enough to matter, so `pii.cc` fires; the hyphen
groups read as national phone formatting, so `pii.phone.e164` fires.

Of the 21 MEDIUM findings above, **14 were exactly this** — every one from a
test file, reported as "Credit-card number (Luhn-valid)" and "Phone number".
That volume is what stops people reading MEDIUM output at all.

**Fix:** add `insideUuid(match)` and gate both patterns on it. The same branch
now reports 7 findings, all genuine (a published contact address, a documented
support link, upstream lockfile maintainer emails, one migration filename), and
the three test files responsible for all 14 drop to zero.

**Containment must be TOTAL, deliberately.** A span merely adjacent to or
overlapping a UUID still reports, so suppression can only fire when the whole
match is demonstrably UUID interior. A real card sitting next to a fixture UUID
is still caught — pinned by a test, since that's how this change could quietly
become a hole.

It takes the match rather than the span because the decision needs surrounding
context; the span offset is derived exactly as `redact-engine.ts` derives it
(group 1 when present, else `match[0]`), so the two can't disagree about where a
span starts. The UUID scan is windowed to 40 chars either side to stay cheap on
a multi-megabyte buffer.

Scoped to cards and phones only. `pii.ssn` can't collide (its 3-2-4 grouping
never aligns with 8-4-4-4-12) and `pii.ip_public` needs dots, so widening the
gate there would add risk for no benefit.

## Verification

- `test/redact-engine.test.ts` — **78 pass** (2 new tests added)
- engine + pattern-lint + autoredact + CLI suites — **138 pass, 0 fail**
- `bun run build` — clean
- The new UUID test **fails against the pre-change patterns file** and passes
  after, so it's a real regression guard rather than a tautology.
- `redact-pattern-lint.test.ts` passes, so the added regex is linear-time.

One caveat on my environment, in the interest of not overclaiming: I'm on
Windows, and a full `bun test` here has failures I did **not** introduce —
`browse/test/batch.test.ts` (a `beforeEach`/`afterEach` hook timeout), an
`appendSemanticReview` POSIX file-mode `0600` assertion, and three
`gstack-config-redact-keys` round-trips. I confirmed each is identical against a
pristine checkout of the files I touched. Worth a CI run on Linux to be sure.

Separately, and not fixed here: `test/redact-prepush-hook.test.ts` builds `PATH`
with `:` as the separator, so on Windows its `git` stub never applies and the
"diff killed by a signal BLOCKS" case fails (14 pass / 1 fail, before and after
this PR). Happy to fix that in a follow-up if useful — it seemed out of scope
for these two.


---

title: fix(test): prepush hook test builds PATH with a POSIX-only separator
body:
The follow-up I offered in #2543. Independent of that PR — touches one test file
and no shipping code, so it can land in either order.

## The bug

`test/redact-prepush-hook.test.ts` shadows `git` with a stub by prepending a temp
dir to PATH, built as:

```js
PATH: `${stubDir}:${process.env.PATH}`
```

On Windows the separator is `;`, so `:` produces a single unparseable entry, the
stub is never found, and the **real** git runs. The diff then succeeds,
`gitStrict` never throws, and the hook exits 0 where the test expects 1.

It surfaces as a wrong assertion (`Expected: 1, Received: 0`) rather than as a
portability problem, which is what made it hard to place — I initially assumed it
was a regression from my own changes in #2543 and only found the real cause after
reproducing it against a pristine checkout.

## The fix

A `prependPath` helper mirroring the one already in
`test/gstack-brain-context-load.test.ts`, which handles both platform details:

- `path.delimiter` rather than a hardcoded `:`
- a case-insensitive lookup of the existing env key — Windows commonly spells it
  `Path`, and adding a second `PATH` alongside an inherited `Path` leaves which
  one wins up to the spawn implementation

On POSIX the helper resolves to `{ PATH: binDir + ":" + process.env.PATH }` —
byte-identical to the expression it replaces, so **behaviour there is
unchanged**.

## Why the test is also gated to POSIX

Fixing the separator alone does not make it pass on Windows, and it can't:

- The premise is that a signal-killed child yields `spawnSync` `status === null`.
  Windows has no equivalent — a force-killed process reports a non-zero exit
  code — so the branch the test names is unreachable there.
- The stub is a `#!/bin/sh` file named `git`, which Windows will not execute at
  all: process creation resolves commands through PATHEXT (.exe/.cmd/.bat) and
  ignores the shebang.

A Windows variant would have to assert the non-zero-exit path instead — a
different branch than the test name claims — so it's gated with
`test.skipIf(process.platform === "win32")`, matching
`test/session-runner-timeout.test.ts` and `test/setup-emoji-font.test.ts`.

The separator fix is still worth landing on its own: it's a latent trap for the
next test that copies this idiom, and the current form fails *silently* by
running the real binary rather than loudly.

## Verification

Windows, `bun test test/redact-prepush-hook.test.ts`:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| pass | 14 | 14 |
| skip | 0 | 1 |
| **fail** | **1** | **0** |

Three consecutive clean runs after the change.

Two caveats, since I can only verify one platform here:

- **POSIX is unverified by me.** The test should still run and pass there, by the
  byte-identical argument above, but it's worth a CI run.
- I saw the neighbouring `new branch (zero remote sha)` test fail once at
  ~6.8s under heavy parallel load, then pass 3/3 afterwards, and it also passes

title: v1.63.1.0 fix(ship): allocate from git when the PR queue is unreachable
body:
## Summary

`gstack-next-version` set `offline: true` whenever `gh pr list` failed and returned an **empty claim set**. `/ship`'s Step 12 then said *"fall back to local `BUMP_LEVEL` arithmetic"* — and local arithmetic cannot see a sibling's claim, so the fallback handed out a version another open PR already held.

Git already knows what the API was being asked for, so `offline` now degrades the queue **view**, not the **allocation**.

## Before / after

Fixture: base `0.1.66.0`, a sibling branch holding `0.1.67.0`, `gh` failing.

| | Allocated |
|---|---|
| old allocator | `0.1.67.0` — collides with the sibling |
| new allocator | `0.1.68.0` — bumps past it |

## What it reads when the host is down

- **Every remote-tracking branch's `VERSION` file** — those *are* the open PRs' branches, whether or not the API can enumerate them.
- **Versions already shipped in the base's commit subjects** — catches a number that merged and was then re-picked, which the `VERSION` file cannot see because it only holds the newest value. Bounded at 400 commits, and it warns when it truncates rather than implying it read all history.

New output field `fallback: "git" | null` so `/ship` can distinguish a git-derived pick from a host-derived one. **Additive** — the fallback only runs when the host query already returned nothing, so the online path is untouched (verified: `fallback: null`, same version as before).

## Why this mattered

Found while auditing a downstream repo that had **four duplicate version pairs** in `main` — `v0.1.6.0`, `v0.1.9.0`, `v0.1.32.0`, `v0.1.57.0` — spanning three weeks. The most recent was reproduced exactly: `gh pr list` failed mid-ship, the fallback allocated a number an open PR already held, and both merged. Two commits now claim one version there, so a version read off a running container no longer maps to a single commit.

## Test coverage

`test/gstack-next-version.test.ts`: **34 pass** (28 pre-existing + 6 new).

New tests cover: a sibling branch's claim found via remote-tracking refs; the pick landing past that sibling (`0.1.68.0`, not `0.1.67.0`); the shipped-subject scan; graceful degradation outside a git repo (warning, never a throw); and the `fallback` output contract in both directions (`"git"` when `gh` fails via a stub, `null` when online).

Adjacent suites unaffected: `gstack-version-bump` + `ship-version-sync` **35 pass**, `skill-validation` + `parity-suite` + `parity-sectioned` **340 pass** (13/13 skills parity).

## Self-review finding, fixed before commit

A comment claimed the 400-commit scan "says so" when it truncates. It didn't — the only warning in that block was the `git log` failure path, so a capped scan was silent. Made the comment true (warns when the log comes back exactly full), then verified by running a copy with the cap lowered to 5 against this repo's 118 commits: warning fires. At the real cap it correctly stays silent here.

## Not included, deliberately

`/ship`'s Step 12 instruction still tells the agent to use local arithmetic. That edit lives in `ship/SKILL.md.tmpl`, which currently also carries **unrelated in-flight work** in my working tree (the `--package-json-path` manifest resolution), and its regenerated artifacts collide with `d078622`. Rather than bundle someone else's unreviewed change, this PR ships the allocator only. **The allocator is safe on its own** — a git-derived pick is collision-safe whether or not the prose has caught up; the instruction just understates it. Happy to follow up with the prose change as a separate PR.

## Test plan

- `bun test gstack-next-version` — 34 pass
- `bun run bin/gstack-next-version --base main --bump patch --current-version <v>` — online: `fallback: null`
- Same command with a failing `gh` on `PATH` — `offline: true`, `fallback: "git"`, version still allocated, warning explains the degraded view

title: fix(setup): wire --host cursor through the install path
body:
## Summary

`./setup --host cursor` is documented in the README and `hosts/cursor.ts` already generates Cursor skills, but bash `setup` still rejected the flag:

```
Unknown --host value: cursor (expected claude, codex, kiro, factory, opencode, openclaw, hermes, gbrain, or auto)
```

This PR is the **installer slice only**: allowlist → generate → runtime root → skill links → sidecar → uninstall. It mirrors Factory/OpenCode. It does not try to be Cursor Cloud/CLI.

**Closes #1358.** Related: #1269.

### Why this shape (vs prior PRs)

Community PRs for this bug have been stuck in a deadlock:

| PR | What happened |
|---|---|
| #934 | Allowlist only — no generate/install/uninstall |
| #1184 | Cursor **and** Slate; copied OpenCode's fat runtime |
| #1326 | Closest, but raw `ln -snf` (fails the Windows `_link_or_copy` invariant) and no uninstall |
| #1526 | No sidecar / uninstall / `~/.cursor` detect; closed as superseded by #2142 |
| #2142 | IDE + CLI + Cloud, `VERSION`, `docs/CURSOR.md`, generator rewrites, `rm -rf` of existing skill dirs, unrelated `--local`/build side effects. Too big to land |

CONTRIBUTING's wave rule: if two PRs fix the same thing, keep the one that changes fewer lines. This is **6 files, +303/−7**, on current `main`. Fine to absorb into a wave.

This is **not** a replacement for #2142's Cloud/CLI work.

### What it does

- Accepts `--host cursor` (and `--host auto` via `command -v cursor` **or** `[ -d "$HOME/.cursor" ]` — the CLI is often not on PATH).
- Generates `.cursor/skills/`, plants a runtime root at `~/.cursor/skills/gstack` matching `hosts/cursor.ts` exactly (`bin`, `browse/dist`, `browse/bin`, `gstack-upgrade`, `ETHOS.md`, `review/checklist.md` + `TODOS-format.md`).
- Links `gstack-*` skill dirs **before** planting the sidecar (sidecar `mkdir` would skip the gen fallback). Skips `skill_name=gstack` so the runtime root is not double-discovered.
- Sidecar into repo-local `.cursor/skills/gstack` so in-repo `GSTACK_ROOT` has `bin/` (Codex already has `create_agents_sidecar` for this).
- Every link goes through `_link_or_copy` (no raw `ln`).
- Uninstall removes only `~/.cursor/skills/gstack*` (and project-local `.cursor/skills/gstack*`). Never `rmdir`s `.cursor`. Leaves unowned skills like `frontend-design`.

### What it deliberately does not do

- Slate (same missing-wiring bug; separate PR)
- Cursor `agent` CLI / Cloud Agents (`command -v agent` is too generic)
- Relocating runtime to `~/.cursor/gstack`
- OpenCode-fat extras (`design/dist`, `qa/templates`, `review/specialists`, …)
- `VERSION` / `CHANGELOG` / `README` / `docs/CURSOR.md` / ETHOS / voice
- Making `setup` call `host-config-export.ts` (docs claim this; practiced pattern is still copy-paste Factory bash)
- `rm -rf` of **unowned** skill dirs (the #2142 footgun). Per-skill links only replace a symlink or a missing path. The owned `~/.cursor/skills/gstack` runtime root still refresh-wipes, same as Factory/Codex/OpenCode.

### Credits

Installer ideas and live verification from @xidongc (#934), @BiyuHuang (#1184), @cropsgg (#1326), @mvanhorn (#1526), @its-vincentzhu (#2142). Thank you — this is the smallest complete path through that work.

AI was used for assistance.

## Test plan

- [x] `bash -n setup && bash -n bin/gstack-uninstall`
- [x] `bun test test/gen-skill-docs.test.ts test/uninstall.test.ts test/setup-windows-fallback.test.ts test/host-config.test.ts` → pass
- [x] `GSTACK_SKIP_COREUTILS=1 ./setup --host cursor` → `gstack ready (cursor).`
- [x] `~/.cursor/skills/gstack/bin` and repo-local `.cursor/skills/gstack/bin` exist
- [x] `gstack-diagram` and `gstack-spec` linked (were missing on a stale install)
- [x] `~/.cursor/skills/frontend-design` untouched
- [x] `./setup --host slate` still errors (out of scope)

Windows setup E2E will run in CI because `setup` changed. I did not run it locally.

Fork PRs do not get eval secrets; the free suite above is the gate.

title: macOS XProtect kills the Chromium that bun.lock pins, so browse cannot launch
body:
# macOS XProtect kills the Chromium that `bun.lock` pins, so `browse` cannot launch

**gstack version:** 1.62.0.0
**Platform:** macOS 15.5 (Darwin 25.5.0), Apple silicon

## What happens

`browse` fails to launch a browser. macOS XProtect (`xprotectd`) terminates
`chrome-headless-shell` on start — the process is killed by the OS, not by
Playwright, so the failure surfaces as a launch timeout rather than anything
naming XProtect.

The binary XProtect objects to is Playwright's **Chromium revision 1208**:

```
~/Library/Caches/ms-playwright/chromium_headless_shell-1208/
```

Not the `browse` binary itself — that was byte-identical to its 7 May build
throughout, before and after the failure started. Nothing in gstack changed. An
XProtect **definition** update changed, and revision 1208 fell inside it.

## The cause is the committed lockfile, not the semver range

`package.json` already permits a fix:

```json
"playwright": "^1.58.2"
```

`^1.58.2` allows any 1.x at or above 1.58.2, so a fresh resolve would pick up a
newer Chromium on its own. But the committed `bun.lock` pins it:

```
"playwright@1.58.2"
"playwright-core@1.58.2"
```

and `browse` is compiled with `bun build --compile`, which bakes the resolved
`playwright-core` into the binary. So the lockfile — not the declared range —
is what hands every macOS user Chromium 1208.

## What fixes it

Bumping to `playwright@1.62.1` (Chromium revision **1234**) and rebuilding
`browse` restores it. Playwright pruned 1208 itself on install, so there is no
leftover to clean up.

```
playwright 1.58.2 → chromium 1208   killed by xprotectd
playwright 1.62.1 → chromium 1234   launches normally
```

## Why this needs fixing upstream rather than locally

The obvious workaround — edit `package.json`/`bun.lock` and rebuild — does not
survive. `/gstack-upgrade` runs `git reset --hard origin/main`, which reverts
both files and puts `browse` back on the Chromium that XProtect kills. So every
user who fixes it locally loses the fix at their next upgrade, silently, and the
symptom returns looking like a fresh problem.

And it is not one machine's antivirus being unusual: XProtect is on by default
on every Mac, and the pin is the same for everyone. Anyone on gstack 1.62.0.0
running macOS should be hitting this.

## Suggested fix

Refresh `bun.lock` to a Playwright at or above 1.62.1 and rebuild the shipped
`browse` binary.

Two things that would make the next occurrence much cheaper to diagnose,
whichever Chromium is current:

1. **Surface the real cause.** A launch failure where the browser process is
   killed by the OS currently looks like a generic timeout. Checking
   `log show --predicate 'process == "xprotectd"'` after a launch failure, or
   simply naming XProtect as a possibility in the error text, would have saved
   the entire investigation here.
2. **Don't let a pin quietly outlive its Chromium.** Any pinned browser revision
   will eventually land in a definition update. Tracking Playwright more closely,
   or documenting how to bump it in a way that survives `/gstack-upgrade`, stops
   this being a recurring silent break.

## What I have not verified

Which XProtect definition version introduced it, and whether the detection is a
true positive against something in that Chromium build or a false one. I did not
disable, exclude, or re-run anything against XProtect — the diagnosis is from the
kill itself and from the version bump resolving it.

title: fix: stop eating the URL scheme when parsing Deploy Configuration
body:
## The bug

The deploy bootstrap parses the `## Deploy Configuration` block in `CLAUDE.md` with a greedy `sed 's/.*: *//'`. That cuts at the **last** colon on the line, so any URL with a scheme loses it:

```bash
$ echo "- Production URL: https://example.com" | sed 's/.*: *//'
//example.com
```

The last `:` belongs to `https:`, not to the key/value separator.

## Why it matters

That value becomes `PERSISTED_URL`, which `/land-and-deploy` and `/setup-deploy` use for the post-deploy health check. The check then hits a malformed URL and fails in a way that looks unrelated to the config, so the natural next move is to go debug the deploy instead of the parser.

It bit every project whose `Production URL` is written with a scheme, which is the normal way to write it. In my case `https://ismaelbriasco.com` silently became `//ismaelbriasco.com`.

## The fix

Anchor the pattern so it cuts at the **first** `": "`:

```bash
$ echo "- Production URL: https://example.com" | sed 's/^[^:]*: *//'
https://example.com
```

`PLATFORM` gets the same treatment. Its value has no colon today, so that line is a no-op, but it guards the same class of bug if a platform identifier ever grows one.

## Scope

Fixed in `scripts/resolvers/utility.ts` (the generator source) and regenerated with `bun run gen:skill-docs`, which is why `land-and-deploy/SKILL.md` moves in the same commit. No other generated host changed.

Verified against the real line that triggered it, before and after.

title: test(browse): de-flake the lease expiry assertion in ring-buffer runtime
body:
## The flake

`browse/test/terminal-agent-ring-buffer-runtime.test.ts` — the test `lease registry is independent of ring buffer state` ends by asserting that two back-to-back `mintLease()` calls produce **identical** `expiresAt` values:

```js
const a = mintLease();
const b = mintLease();
...
expect(va.expiresAt).toBe(vb.expiresAt);
```

`mintLease()` computes `expiresAt` as `Date.now() + LEASE_TTL_MS`, so this only holds if both calls land inside the same millisecond. Under full-suite load they sometimes straddle a tick and the test fails on a 1 ms difference. It passes reliably when the file is run on its own, which is what makes it read as noise rather than a real regression.

Observed failing roughly 1 run in 3 of `bun test browse/test/`.

## The fix

Assert closeness rather than equality:

```js
expect(Math.abs(va.expiresAt - vb.expiresAt)).toBeLessThanOrEqual(5);
```

The property this test exists to check is that both leases got the same TTL policy and that neither is coupled to ring-buffer state. Wall-clock coincidence was never part of that, so nothing is lost — a real coupling regression (say, one lease inheriting a ring-buffer-derived expiry) would still blow well past a 5 ms window.

I considered injecting a fixed clock into `browse/src/pty-session-lease.ts` to make `mintLease` deterministic and keep exact equality. That works, but it adds a test seam to production code for an assertion that doesn't need one, so I went with the smaller change. Happy to switch if you'd prefer the deterministic-clock version.

I did **not** delete the assertion — the independence property is worth keeping.

## Scope check

I swept the rest of `browse/test/` for the same shape. No other assertion compares two separately-sampled timestamps for exact equality:

- `cdp-inspector-history-cap.test.ts` timestamp equalities use synthetic counter values (`0`, `49`, `50`), not sampled clocks
- `pty-session-lease.test.ts` and `sse-session-cookie.test.ts` already use `toBeGreaterThan`
- the elapsed-duration budgets in `sanitize.test.ts` and `security-audit-r2.test.ts` are a different pattern and have order-of-magnitude headroom

## Verification

7 consecutive full `bun test browse/test/` runs (121 files, ~140 s each). The lease assertion did not fail in any of them.

One run showed 2 unrelated load flakes that passed in the others and are untouched by this change: `browser-skills-e2e.test.ts:89` (its nested `bun test` subprocess returned only its banner before a summary was captured) and `pair-agent-tunnel-eval.test.ts` (20 s timeout, `Unable to connect`). Both look like separate issues worth their own fix.

title: fix(browse): remove the dead security shield and its unfed /health status
body:
## Problem

The sidebar's SEC shield has been dead UI since the PTY terminal rewrite (ed1e4be2, #1216). That commit deleted `updateSecurityShield()` and both of its call sites along with the chat poll loop, but left the markup and CSS in place. Nothing has set the element's `data-status` since, and nothing unhides it — it ships `style="display:none"` and the only code that ever set `display: inline-flex` was the deleted function.

**Re-wiring it to `/health.security` is not viable, because that field is not live data either.** `getStatus()` reads `classifierStatus` out of `~/.gstack/security/session-state.json`, and the only writer of that file was `sidebar-agent.ts`, which the same rewrite deleted. `writeSessionState()` now has no production caller anywhere in the tree — its sole remaining caller is a unit test:

```
$ grep -rn "writeSessionState" browse/src browse/test
browse/src/security.ts:548:export function writeSessionState(...)   # definition
browse/test/security.test.ts:294:    writeSessionState(state);       # only caller
```

So `/health` reports either a permanent `inactive` (no file), or a stale `protected` wherever an old state file survived on disk. A single test run is enough to leave one behind — that unit test writes real fixture data (`sessionId: "test-session-123"`, classifiers `ok`) into `~/.gstack`, after which `/health` reports **`protected`** indefinitely.

That makes the shield worse than absent if it is ever unhidden: a green shield sourced from leftover state reads as *"no threats detected"* when the real state is *"not measured"*. Same fail-open class as #2026 (dashboard reporting "0 attacks" on backend error) and the project's own `9cc41b71` guards-failing-open wave.

## Fix

Remove the indicator and the status feed behind it, rather than wiring a needle to a gauge that measures nothing:

- shield markup in `sidepanel.html`, its CSS, and the stale comment in `sidepanel.js` that documented the indicator as "not driven yet"
- the `security` field from `/health` and the `getStatus` import
- `getStatus`, `SecurityStatus`, `StatusDetail`, and the now-unreachable `SessionState` / `readSessionState` / `writeSessionState`
- the tests covering them, including a `getStatus` shape assertion that passed on leftover fixture data and so never caught the false green

**The live defenses are untouched.** The canary, content-security L1-L3, and the L4 sidecar on `/pty-inject-scan` all report through their own call sites and never through `/health`. Per-tab decision files are unaffected.

## `browse/test/security-sidepanel-dom.test.ts`

Deleted outright, because every test in it is already dead:

- 2 assert the shield's `data-status` flips off `/health.security`
- 4 drive the security banner, whose markup `ed1e4be2` removed
- the whole suite stubs `/sidebar-chat`, an endpoint that no longer exists

The file looks healthy only because every case is `test.skipIf(!CHROMIUM_AVAILABLE)` and silently skips wherever Playwright is absent.

#2230 independently deletes this same file. If that lands first, this hunk drops out as a delete/delete; the change is otherwise standalone.

## On CI

`main` is currently red in these files — 75 failures across the security/sidebar suites, all of them testing the chat path `ed1e4be2` removed (`pollChat`, `stopAgent`, `/sidebar-agent/stop`, the browser tab bar). This branch has **the identical 75 failures, name-for-name**, with no regressions in either direction:

```
baseline (main):  298 pass, 75 fail
this branch:      296 pass, 75 fail    # -2 = the two tests removed above
comm -13 baseline mine  ->  (empty)
comm -23 baseline mine  ->  (empty)
```

#2230 is the PR that repairs that suite.

## Note

No regression test asserting the absence of the `security` key: it would fail on a correct future change that re-feeds the status from live signals (`isSidecarAvailable`, the content filters), punishing the fix rather than the regression. The reasoning is recorded in a comment where the field used to be.

title: mktemp templates with a suffix after the X-run break on BSD/macOS (breaks the 2nd /codex run in a session)
body:
## Summary

11 `mktemp` templates across the repo put the `X` placeholder run somewhere other than the end of the template (e.g. `codex-err-XXXXXX.txt`). That is a GNU-only construct. On BSD/macOS it silently disables randomization entirely, and the **second** call in a session fails outright.

The most visible symptom: **the second `/codex` run in a session aborts before Codex is ever invoked**, and the skill's own error handling reports it as a Codex/model stall — so it gets diagnosed as an OpenAI problem rather than a template bug.

## Root cause

GNU and BSD `mktemp` disagree about a template with trailing non-`X` characters.

GNU's man page states the behavior explicitly:

> `--suffix=SUFF`  append SUFF to TEMPLATE; SUFF must not contain a slash.
> **This option is implied if TEMPLATE does not end in X**

GNU quietly reinterprets the trailing `.txt` as a suffix and randomizes the `X`s anyway. BSD `mktemp` has no `--suffix` concept at all, so it uses the string **literally**.

Measured, same template, both binaries (macOS 15, coreutils 9.11 as `gmktemp`):

```
$ gmktemp "./codex-err-XXXXXX.txt"     # GNU — what CI runs
./codex-err-emiUQv.txt
$ gmktemp "./codex-err-XXXXXX.txt"
./codex-err-RWbt4Q.txt                 # randomizes fine

$ mktemp "./codex-err-XXXXXX.txt"      # BSD — every macOS dev laptop
./codex-err-XXXXXX.txt                 # literal X's, no randomization
$ mktemp "./codex-err-XXXXXX.txt"
mktemp: mkstemp failed on ./codex-err-XXXXXX.txt: File exists
```

The first call "succeeds" because the literal name happens to be free, which is exactly why this is invisible until it isn't.

## Reproduce

On macOS, run `/codex review` twice in one session. The second run dies at the `TMPERR=$(mktemp ...)` line in Step 2A before `codex` is executed. Because the skill's error handling maps a non-zero exit to the timeout/stall path, the user is told:

> Codex stalled past 5.5 minutes. Common causes: model API stall, long prompt, network issue.

## Why CI never caught it

`.github/workflows/` runs on `ubicloud-standard-8` (Linux) and `windows-latest`. Both get GNU semantics. There is no macOS runner — and macOS is the primary platform for the tool's users. Combined with the bug requiring a *second* invocation to surface, no first-run smoke test would ever see it.

## Affected sites — 11, in 4 source files

The generated `SKILL.md` files follow from the first three via `bun run gen:skill-docs`.

| File | Sites | Templates |
|---|---|---|
| `codex/SKILL.md.tmpl` | 5 | `codex-err-XXXXXX.txt`, `codex-prompt-XXXXXX.txt`, `codex-resp-XXXXXX.txt` |
| `claude/SKILL.md.tmpl` | 3 | `...-response-XXXXXX.json`, `...-error-XXXXXX.txt`, `...-diff-XXXXXX.patch` |
| `scripts/resolvers/review.ts` | 1 | `gstack-codex-oh-XXXXXXXX.txt` (emits the office-hours line) |
| `bin/gstack-developer-profile` | 2 | `developer-profile.json.XXXXXX.tmp` |

`bin/gstack-developer-profile` is worth separating out: it is a **live executable**, not a prompt, and the temp file is the atomic-rename target in the profile migration. A second migration attempt fails rather than merely inconveniencing an agent.

Note that templates ending in `X`s are fine regardless of length — `mktemp /tmp/codex-design-XXXXXXXX` and `mktemp -d` are unaffected. Only a suffix *after* the run is broken.

## Suggested fix

Move the extension ahead of the placeholder run so the `X`s stay terminal, which is valid on both implementations:

```diff
-TMPERR=$(mktemp "$TMP_ROOT/codex-err-XXXXXX.txt")
+TMPERR=$(mktemp "$TMP_ROOT/codex-err-txt-XXXXXX")
```

Nothing in the codebase keys off these extensions — the files are opened by path and read for diagnostics — so dropping the extension entirely would work too.

## Suggested guard

The broken form reads as correct to a reviewer, so it will come back without a test. A regex over the affected sources works (`mktemp[^|;&\n]*X{3,}[^X"'\s)]`), but it needs its own positive control: assert the detector matches `-XXXXXX.txt` and spares both `-txt-XXXXXX` and the legitimate 8-X templates, otherwise a zero-result scan proves nothing.

## The structural item

Fixing the 11 sites is containment. The reason a GNU-only assumption reached `main` and survived is that nothing ever executes this code on BSD. Other GNU-isms fail the same silent way — `sed -i`, `readlink -f`, `date -d` all differ between the implementations — and I have not audited the tree for them. A macOS CI runner is the actual fix, with the honest caveat that adding one will likely surface further existing failures and cost CI minutes.

## Offer

I have the fix implemented and verified locally against `main`: all 11 sites, regenerated skill docs, plus the regression test and its positive control described above. Mutation-verified — reintroducing the bug fails exactly the two expected tests (the template and its generated output) and no siblings. Full suite is unchanged before and after: the 5 `gstack-gbrain-detect` failures on this machine are environment-dependent and present on clean `main` too.

Happy to open a PR if that is useful.

title: fix(browse): capture skill subprocess output via temp files, not pipes
body:
## Problem

`$B skill test` is flaky under load. In a full `bun test browse/test/` run it intermittently returns only bun's version banner:

```
Expected substring or pattern: /13 pass|0 fail|tests passed/
Received: "bun test v1.3.12 (700fc117)\n"
```

The obvious reading is a read-ordering bug: `handleTest` awaited `proc.exited` before attaching readers, so it looked like it was reading a stream snapshot. That is not the cause. Fixing the ordering did not fix the flake.

## Root cause

Under a loaded parent, the **first piped spawn in a process** intermittently yields an empty stderr even though the child wrote it and exited 0. Instrumenting a full suite run, spawning the same child three times in a row:

```
pipe#0 exit=0 outLen=28 errLen=0    <- lost
pipe#1 exit=0 outLen=28 errLen=76
pipe#2 exit=0 outLen=28 errLen=76
```

Reproduced in 4 of 4 instrumented runs. Two candidate workarounds were measured losing the same bytes in the same position, so neither is a fix:

- attaching readers before awaiting `proc.exited` and settling with `Promise.all`
- a manual `stream.getReader()` drain loop (what `readCapped` did)

`Bun.spawnSync` captures reliably, but blocking is not an option in this module: a spawned skill calls back into the same daemon on `GSTACK_PORT`, so a synchronous wait would deadlock it.

It surfaced in `$B skill test` because `bun test` splits its report across streams (banner to stdout, pass/fail summary to stderr) and `handleTest` returned `stderr || stdout`, so a dropped stderr degraded silently to the banner. Worth noting the capture was lossy on *every* run, not just failing ones: the banner was missing from successful captures too.

## Fix

`runToFiles()` points the child's stdout/stderr at temp files via `Bun.file(path)`, awaits exit, then reads the files. The kernel has flushed everything by the time the child exits, so the post-exit read is always complete. It also removes the pipe-buffer stall risk on chatty children.

`spawnSkill` had the same defect and now shares the helper rather than carrying a second copy of the fix. There the loss is worse than a test flake: a dropped read blanks a skill's JSON result on `$B skill run` while still reporting success.

Uses `Bun.file(path)` rather than raw fds from `fs.openSync`. Opening descriptors and closing them around a spawn puts the caller into Bun's fd bookkeeping and produced an intermittent `EBADF: bad file descriptor, epoll_ctl` on a later spawn, observed once in a full-suite run.

The `tests passed for "<name>"` fallback is removed. A passing `bun test` always prints a summary, so exit 0 with no output means the run was not captured; it now throws rather than returning an unverifiable success string. The old assertion's `tests passed` alternative matched that string, so it would have passed vacuously on an empty capture.

## Tests

- The E2E assertion now checks both halves of the report (banner from stdout, summary from stderr) instead of a loose alternation.
- A static tripwire asserts `runToFiles` owns the module's only `Bun.spawn`, and that no site reads child output via `stdout: 'pipe'`, `new Response(proc.stdout)`, or `getReader()`. The data loss is load-dependent and silent, so a behavioural test cannot catch it reliably; the structure is what is pinned.

## Verification

5 consecutive full runs of `bun test browse/test/` (1970 tests each) with the target test passing in all five, and no `EBADF`.

The `terminal-agent: PTY round-trip via real WebSocket` failures in that suite are pre-existing and unrelated, confirmed by reproducing them on a clean tree (2 of 3 baseline runs).

## Not addressed here

14 other `stdout: 'pipe'` capture sites share this pattern across `browse/src/`. The highest-value one is `cookie-import-browser.ts`, where `getMacKeychainPassword` returns `stdout.trim()` as a keychain password and the DPAPI path base64-decodes stdout into a decryption key, so a lost read yields a silent empty credential rather than a loud error. Left out to keep this reviewable.

## Caveat

This establishes *that* the first piped spawn can drop a stream and that file-based capture is immune. It does not explain *why* Bun drops it. The fix is verified empirically against the reproduction, not derived from Bun internals.

title: fix(memory-ingest): pass --include-gitignored to gbrain import
body:
## The bug

`gstack-artifacts-init` writes an ignore-everything `.gitignore` at the root of `~/.gstack`:

```
# gstack-artifacts sync: ignore-everything base. Paths are included explicitly via
# .brain-allowlist and `git add -f` from gstack-brain-sync. Do not edit.
*
```

`gstack-memory-ingest` stages pages into `~/.gstack/.staging-ingest-<pid>-<ts>/`, which is inside that repo, and gbrain's markdown collector honours `.gitignore`. So the collector walks the staging directory, matches every staged file against `*`, and collects nothing.

**The failure is silent.** `gbrain import` exits 0 having imported nothing, while the ingest reports `written: N` from the *staged* count rather than the imported count. A run that indexes nothing is indistinguishable from a healthy one, and the memory corpus quietly stops growing.

## Reproduction

No gbrain or network needed. `git ls-files --others --exclude-standard` is the same view a gitignore-honouring collector takes:

```bash
git init .
mkdir -p .staging-ingest-12345/learnings
echo x > .staging-ingest-12345/learnings/page.md
printf '*\n' > .gitignore
git ls-files --others --exclude-standard   # -> empty
```

Observed on gstack 1.61.0.0 / 1.62.0.0 with gbrain 0.45.9.0 against a Supabase engine, but nothing here is engine or version specific.

## The fix

Pass `--include-gitignored` on the `gbrain import` call, so the import is independent of whatever `.gitignore` sits above the staging directory.

The alternative is adding a negation to the generated `.gitignore`:

```
!.staging-ingest-*/
!.staging-ingest-*/**
```

That does work (verified), but the file is gstack-owned and explicitly marked "Do not edit", so any regeneration silently reintroduces the bug. The flag fixes it at the call site instead, where the staging directory's location is actually known.

Staging dirs are created and deleted within a single ingest run and are never committed, so the `.brain-allowlist` plus `git add -f` path used by `gstack-brain-sync` is unaffected.

## Tests

`test/memory-ingest-include-gitignored.test.ts`, following the shape of the existing `memory-ingest-no-put_page.test.ts` source pin:

1. `--include-gitignored` is present in active code (comments stripped).
2. The flag sits on the same `spawnGbrainAsync` call as the `import` subcommand, so it cannot drift onto another call.
3. A behavioural test for the collision itself, so the reason for the flag survives even if the call site is refactored.

Both source pins fail against the unpatched file; the behavioural test documents the collision and passes either way. The three sibling memory-ingest suites (`gstack-memory-ingest`, `memory-ingest-no-put_page`, `memory-ingest-timeout`, 28 tests) still pass.

title: fix(windows): decisions are filed under a project named "unknown", and never sync
body:
On Windows, every decision logged by `gstack-decision-log` is filed under a project literally named
`unknown`, and the Context Recovery block that should read it back never fires. Separately — and on
every platform — the decision store is not in the sync allowlist, so it never leaves the machine
even with `artifacts_sync_mode` on.

Measured on one machine before the fix: **62 decisions accumulated across 10 days and 170 gstack
skill runs, and were surfaced zero times.** Two of them were owner decisions that existed in no
other store, in a directory outside git and outside backup.

---

## 1. `resolveSlug` returns the literal string `"unknown"` on Windows

`bin/gstack-slug` is a `#!/usr/bin/env bash` script with no file extension. Windows honors neither
the shebang nor PATHEXT for an explicit path, so `CreateProcess` fails **ENOENT** and `r.stdout` is
`undefined`. `lib/bin-context.ts:12` never inspected `r.error`:

```js
const r = spawnSync(slugBinPath, { encoding: "utf-8" });
const m = (r.stdout || "").match(/^SLUG=(.+)$/m);
return m ? m[1].trim() : "unknown";   // ← every Windows call lands here
```

Reproduced directly:

```
spawn error : ENOENT / spawnSync C:\...\bin/gstack-slug ENOENT
resolveSlug : unknown
```

`decisionPaths()` then writes to `~/.gstack/projects/unknown/` — **one bucket shared by every
project on the machine**. Mine mixed three.

### Why it is silent

Three things had to line up, and they did:

1. **Both** decision bins (`gstack-decision-log` and `gstack-decision-search`) call the same
   `resolveSlug`, so they miss *identically*. Writes and searches agree with each other and the
   store is internally consistent — just in the wrong place.
2. The **read** path is bash (`generate-context-recovery.ts` → `eval "$(gstack-slug)"`), which
   resolves the slug **correctly** to the real project directory.
3. That block then guards on `[ -f "$_PROJ/decisions.active.json" ]` with **no `else`**. The file
   isn't there, so the whole ACTIVE DECISIONS section is skipped and prints nothing.

A missing file and a working store produce identical output. Nothing logs, nothing exits non-zero.

### Why `shell: true` is not the fix here

Unlike #1731, this is not a PATHEXT/shim-resolution problem — `cmd.exe` cannot run a bash script
either. And re-spawning through `bash` is worse than it looks: on Windows `bash` frequently resolves
to `C:\WINDOWS\system32\bash.exe`, i.e. **WSL**, whose `$HOME` and `/mnt/c/...` paths produce a
*different* slug **and** a *different* `slug-cache` directory. That trades one split store for
another, silently.

So this ports `gstack-slug`'s own three steps natively — cache → git remote → basename — keeping its
`[a-zA-Z0-9._-]` alphabet (`tr -cd` deletes, it does not substitute) and, critically, its **MSYS-form
cache key** (`C:\Users\j\foo` → `/c/Users/j/foo` → `_c_Users_j_foo`). Reproducing that key is what
keeps the native path and the shell path on the same answer; getting it wrong would re-derive instead
of reusing, and could drift.

**The fallback is win32-gated, so POSIX behaviour is byte-identical.**

## 2. No allowlist glob matches the decision store

`gstack-decision-log:40` enqueues `projects/<slug>/decisions.jsonl` after every write. None of the
16 managed globs in `.brain-allowlist` match it, so `compute_paths_to_stage` rejects every one at its
*"must match at least one allowlist glob"* check.

The writer and the syncer disagree, silently: enabling artifacts sync backs up learnings, plans,
designs and timelines — everything **except** the durable decision ledger. A dropped path prints
exactly what a synced one does when the queue is otherwise empty.

Fixed by adding the three `decisions.*` globs and classing them `artifact` so they also sync under
`artifacts-only`.

## Tests

`test/bin-context-windows-slug.test.ts` (9) exercises the fallback **on every platform** — only the
*gating* is win32-specific — so POSIX CI catches a regression that would otherwise surface only on a
Windows user's disk. Covers the MSYS cache-key derivation, all three resolution steps, https/ssh
remote forms, `tr -cd` deletion semantics, cache write-back with no trailing newline, plus a static
gate pinning the platform check in the style of `gbrain-spawn-windows-shell.test.ts`.

`test/artifacts-allowlist-decisions.test.ts` (3) reads the heredocs out of `gstack-artifacts-init`
rather than executing it, because `gstack-artifacts-init.test.ts` drives the real script through
`#!/bin/bash` shims and a colon-separated `PATH` and therefore cannot run on Windows — the platform
where the companion bug bites. (I confirmed that file already fails on Windows unmodified, so I left
it alone.) It applies `fnmatch.fnmatchcase` semantics, matching what `compute_paths_to_stage` uses.

Both files added to `windows-free-tests.yml`.

**Verified by planted negative, not just by passing:**

| Change reverted | Result |
|---|---|
| `resolveSlug` body only (exports kept) | 2 fail, incl. *"a spawn that cannot run resolves to a real slug, not 'unknown'"* |
| `gstack-artifacts-init` allowlist | 2 fail, marker test correctly still passes |
| Nothing | 12 pass |

Windows CI subset, run locally on Windows 11 / bun 1.3.14: **39 pass, 6 skip, 0 fail**.

## Not changed here

`docs/gbrain-sync.md:34` still says `gstack-brain-init`, renamed to `gstack-artifacts-init` in
v1.27.0.0 — `test/no-stale-gstack-brain-refs.test.ts` exists but doesn't catch this one. Left out to
keep the diff focused; happy to send it separately.

Also worth a look, though out of scope: `gstack-artifacts-init` creates the repo with `gh`/`glab`
and then verifies it via `git ls-remote` over **SSH**. On a machine where the CLI and the SSH key
authenticate as *different* accounts, that aborts at line 188 before writing anything, even though
`gstack-brain-sync` only ever does `git push origin HEAD` and works fine over HTTPS. And `git init`
there could use `core.autocrlf=false` — it stores JSONL that must round-trip byte-exactly.

title: gstack-uninstall leaves ~52 per-skill directories behind on Windows (exit 0, reports success)
body:
## Summary

On Windows (Git Bash / MSYS2, no Developer Mode), `gstack-uninstall --force`
exits `0` and prints `gstack uninstalled.`, but leaves **~52 `gstack-*`
directories plus `_gstack-command/`** in `~/.claude/skills/`.

The root cause is a mismatch between how `setup` installs and how
`gstack-uninstall` removes:

| Script | Behavior on Windows |
|---|---|
| `setup` | creates **real directory copies** via `cp -R` (`_link_or_copy`) |
| `bin/gstack-uninstall` | only removes **symlinks** |

`setup` is explicit about this in its own output:

> `note: Windows install uses file copies (no Developer Mode required).`
> `Re-run ./setup after every 'git pull' to refresh skill files.`

But `bin/gstack-uninstall` filters per-skill entries by symlink:

```sh
# bin/gstack-uninstall
for _LINK in "$CLAUDE_SKILLS"/*; do
  [ -L "$_LINK" ] || continue     # <-- real directories are skipped
  ...
done
```

So on Windows every per-skill entry is skipped, and only
`~/.claude/skills/gstack` + `~/.gstack/` get removed.

The issue was reproduced on Windows copy installs; symlink-based installs
were not tested in this report.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| OS | Windows 11 (`MINGW64_NT-10.0-26100`, x86_64), Git Bash |
| Developer Mode | off (so `ln -s` falls back to copies) |
| bun | 1.3.14 |
| gstack | `d078622b73539fc1a7a27e709861e9b6b058ae98` (VERSION `1.62.0.0`) |

## Steps to reproduce

Run in an isolated `HOME` so your real config is untouched:

```sh
export HOME=/tmp/gstack-repro
export CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR="$HOME/.claude"
mkdir -p "$HOME/.claude/skills"
echo '{}' > "$HOME/.claude/settings.json"

git clone https://github.com/garrytan/gstack.git
cd gstack
git checkout d078622b73539fc1a7a27e709861e9b6b058ae98

./setup --host claude --prefix --no-plan-tune-hooks --no-team
ls "$HOME/.claude/skills" | wc -l          # => 55

"$HOME/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-uninstall" --force
echo "exit code: $?"                       # => 0
ls "$HOME/.claude/skills" | wc -l          # => 53  (expected: 0)
ls "$HOME/.claude/skills" | head -5        # => gstack-autoplan, gstack-benchmark, ...
```

Confirm the entries are real directories rather than symlinks:

```sh
[ -L "$HOME/.claude/skills/gstack-qa" ] && echo symlink || echo "real directory"
# => real directory
```

## Expected

`gstack-uninstall` removes all per-skill entries it created, regardless of
whether they are symlinks or copies — matching what `setup` actually produced
on this platform.

## Actual

Exit code `0`, output `gstack uninstalled.`, but 53 entries remain.
A user following the documented uninstall path is left with a
partially-removed install and no indication that anything was skipped.

## Suggested fix

The copy-install path currently has no corresponding removal path. Rather than
matching on the `gstack-*` name alone (which could delete unrelated user skills
that happen to share the prefix), it would be safer to give the uninstaller a
reliable ownership signal, for example:

- have `setup` record an install manifest listing exactly what it created, and
  have `gstack-uninstall` remove only what that manifest lists; or
- write an unambiguous ownership marker into each installed entry and key the
  removal off that.

The general principle: **the removal logic should be symmetric with whichever
install path was actually taken** (symlink or copy), rather than assuming one
of them.

The exact mechanism is yours to choose — this report only establishes that
copies created on Windows are never removed.

## Notes

- `--force` was used to keep the run non-interactive; the interactive path
  should behave the same.

title: fix(browse): cancel the parent watchdog when handoff promotes a daemon to headed
body:
## The bug

`handoff` destroys the thing it just created.

It exists so a human can take over a headless session — log in, solve a CAPTCHA, clear an MFA prompt. In a Claude Code session the browser disappears roughly fifteen seconds later and takes the session with it. Driving two registrar control panels last week that cost **five daemon deaths and three logins**, each one discarding the authenticated session.

## Why

The parent-process watchdog (`server.ts`) assumes connection mode is fixed at boot: headless daemons outlive their parent, headed ones do not. Its comment says so, and it is right for the boot case — the env guards (`BROWSE_PARENT_PID=0`, `BROWSE_HEADED=1`) cover daemons that *start* headed.

`handoff` breaks the assumption. `browser-manager.ts` swaps in a headed context on a **running** daemon and sets `connectionMode = 'headed'` with no restart, so a daemon that legitimately registered a watchdog is suddenly on the fatal side of the branch:

```js
const headed = activeBrowserManager.getConnectionMode() === 'headed';
if (headed || tunnelActive) { activeShutdown?.(); }
```

The parent is typically a short-lived shell, and Claude Code's Bash tool kills one after every invocation — a case the watchdog's own comment already calls out. So the next poll fires and shuts the daemon down.

`browse connect` is unaffected: it cold-restarts with the watchdog disabled and detaches into its own process group.

## The fix

`BrowserManager` exposes `onHeadedPromotion`, fired **only** on runtime promotion, not on a headed boot. The server binds it to a canceller for the interval it already owned but previously discarded.

Bound on both the module-level manager and any embedder-supplied one, since the watchdog reads `activeBrowserManager` — binding only the default would let embedders (gbrowser) promote silently.

One placement note worth keeping: the binding sits beside the `browserManager` declaration rather than beside `clearParentWatchdog`. Putting it with the function reads better, since the function lives with the watchdog it cancels, but that touches `browserManager` in its temporal dead zone, which aborts module evaluation and leaves every later `const` uninitialized. `findport.test.ts` catches it instantly, which is how I found it.

## Tests

`watchdog.test.ts` already noted in its header that all three of its cases fix mode via env at spawn time, so none reaches the headed branch — the gap this PR closes.

Driving a real `handoff` needs a headed Chromium, which does not belong in the free tier, so the wiring is pinned with static tripwires instead, matching `cdp-session-cleanup.test.ts` and `server-auth.test.ts`. Verified in both directions: removing the notification call fails them, restoring it passes.

`cli.ts:1093` is untouched, so the `BROWSE_PARENT_PID: '0'` literal that `server-auth.test.ts` pins is intact.

## Suite status

Full `bun test`: the same **6 pre-existing failures on this branch and on `main`** (`gstack-gbrain-detect`, `gstack-artifacts-init`). They pass in isolation on both branches, so it is test-order pollution rather than anything from this change. `findport.test.ts` — the one my first attempt broke — is 9/9 on both.

## Note

There is a second, separate path that shares the same predicate: the SIGTERM handler also quits when runtime mode is headed, gated by neither env var. It does not bite `connect`-launched daemons because they are detached, and I have left it alone rather than widen this PR. Happy to follow up if you want it addressed.

title: session-update: pull --ff-only can never succeed on a default install — 308 consecutive failures, and the reason is discarded
body:
## Summary

On a default install, `bin/gstack-session-update` can **never** fast-forward, and the reason is thrown away. Two independent bugs, the second hiding the first.

My install logged **308 consecutive `PULL_FAILED exit=1` since 2026-06-22 with zero successes**, silently frozen at `1.60.1.0` while upstream was at `1.62.0.0` — 34 commits behind. Nothing surfaced this; the log is written every session and never read, because a bare `exit=1` says nothing.

Related but distinct: #2517 covers the `/upgrade` path using `git reset --hard`. This is the automatic session-start updater, a different code path.

---

## Bug 1 — the install dirties tracked files, so `pull --ff-only` always aborts

Every top-level `SKILL.md` is locally modified, each by exactly one line:

```diff
-name: browse
+name: gstack-browse
```

On my install that is **52 files, 52 × (1 insertion, 1 deletion), and 0 changed lines that are not `name:`** — a uniform, mechanical namespace prefix.

`git pull --ff-only` therefore aborts every time:

```
error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by merge:
	autoplan/SKILL.md
	benchmark/SKILL.md
	browse/SKILL.md
	... (52 files)
Please commit your changes or stash them before you merge. Aborting
```

**The prefixes cannot simply be discarded.** When I removed them to test, the host's skill list collapsed from ~30 individually-invocable `gstack-*` skills to a single `gstack` entry. They are load-bearing for skill resolution — so the updater is deadlocked against a state the install itself requires.

## Bug 2 — the failure reason is discarded

`bin/gstack-session-update` (v1.60.1.0, line 79):

```bash
git -C "$GSTACK_DIR" pull --ff-only -q 2>/dev/null
PULL_EXIT=$?
...
if [ "$PULL_EXIT" -ne 0 ]; then
  log_entry "PULL_FAILED exit=$PULL_EXIT"
```

`2>/dev/null` drops the only useful diagnostic. `~/.gstack/analytics/session-update.log` accumulates identical `exit=1` lines indefinitely. Mine has 308 of them and not one says why.

---

## Reproduce

```bash
cd ~/.claude/skills/gstack            # or your install dir
git status --porcelain | wc -l        # non-zero on a default install
git pull --ff-only                    # aborts: local changes would be overwritten
grep -c PULL_FAILED ~/.gstack/analytics/session-update.log
grep -c SUCCESS   ~/.gstack/analytics/session-update.log   # 0
```

## Suggested fixes

**Bug 2 is a one-liner and worth doing regardless** — capture stderr and log it:

```bash
PULL_ERR=$(git -C "$GSTACK_DIR" pull --ff-only -q 2>&1)
PULL_EXIT=$?
...
log_entry "PULL_FAILED exit=$PULL_EXIT reason=$(printf '%s' "$PULL_ERR" | tr '\n\t' '  ' | cut -c1-300)"
```

**Bug 1** — options, roughly in order of preference:

1. **Stop prefixing tracked files.** If `gstack-` must be prepended for host skill resolution, apply it at install/generation time to a file the repo does not track (there is already a `SKILL.md.tmpl` alongside each generated `SKILL.md`), or register the prefixed name without rewriting the checked-in source.
2. **Ship the prefixed names upstream**, so the working tree matches HEAD and nothing is dirty.
3. **Make the updater tolerate it** — `git pull --ff-only --autostash`, or stash/pull/pop with a failure path. Weakest option: it treats the symptom, and a conflict on pop is a new failure mode.

## Environment

- gstack `1.60.1.0` → manually updated to `1.62.0.0`
- Windows 11, Git Bash (MSYS2), Claude Code as host
- Install at `~/.claude/skills/gstack`, remote `origin/main`, clean upstream tracking

## Workaround, for anyone else stuck

```bash
cd ~/.claude/skills/gstack
# save the prefixes so they can be reapplied
git status --porcelain | awk '$1=="M"{print $2}' | while read -r f; do
  echo "$f|$(grep -m1 '^name: ' "$f")"
done > /tmp/gstack-names.txt
git stash push -u -m "gstack prefixes"
git pull --ff-only
# reapply: for each line, restore its `name:` value, then verify all are gstack-*
```

After reapplying, confirm the host still lists the `gstack-*` skills individually — if it shows one `gstack` entry, the prefixes did not take.

title: gstack-version-bump write/repair leave package-lock.json stale — every /ship bump dirties the tree in npm repos
body:
## Symptom

In any repo with a committed `package-lock.json`, every `/ship` version bump leaves the lockfile carrying the previous version (top-level `version` and `packages[""].version`). The tree goes dirty on the next `npm install`, and downstream clean-tree asserts (e.g. a gate/measure step) reject the work several steps later — nowhere near the cause.

## Root cause

`bin/gstack-version-bump` is explicit about it — the header contract reads: *"write/repair mutate VERSION + package.json only."* The lockfile also carries the version (twice, in lockfileVersion >= 2), so the contract itself omits a file it logically must own. The binary contains zero references to `package-lock`.

## Evidence

One consumer repo patched this at the symptom **six times** before tracing it upstream (commits `ea47287`, `1668025`, `b1afdb0`, `b9c462b`, `eda8276`, `15ac158`, each a `chore(lock): sync package-lock`). Repeated identical chore commits after every ship are the fingerprint.

## Fix

PR incoming: `write` and `repair` also sync both lockfile fields when the file exists, under the same exit-3 half-write semantics as the package.json write. `classify` stays read-only and unchanged (a hand-edited-lockfile drift state is out of scope, same philosophy as DRIFT_UNEXPECTED for package.json).

title: fix(version-bump): write/repair sync package-lock.json alongside package.json
body:
Fixes #2567.

## What

`gstack-version-bump write` and `repair` now also sync `package-lock.json` when it exists — both its top-level `version` and `packages[""].version` (lockfileVersion >= 2). Same exit-3 half-write semantics as the existing package.json write, so `classify` → `repair` still converge after a partial failure.

The lockfile carries the version too, so the current contract ("VERSION + package.json only") guarantees a stale lockfile after every bump in npm repos. The tree goes dirty on the next `npm install` and downstream clean-tree asserts fail far from the cause. One consumer repo accumulated six identical `chore(lock): sync package-lock` symptom commits before tracing it here (details in #2567).

title: Global-git installs stay permanently dirty: the claude :user render happens in-place, so every upgrade leaves a stash
body:
## Summary

On a **global-git install**, `./setup`'s gbrain render writes into **tracked** files, so the
checkout is permanently dirty. The upgrade flow's `git stash` therefore fires on every single
upgrade and saves content `./setup` regenerates seconds later. They accumulate silently.

I found **four** on one machine — one per upgrade since 1.58.5 — each `16 files changed,
326 insertions(+), 0 deletions(-)`, and each byte-for-byte identical to what the next
`./setup` produced.

## Why it happens

A global-git install is simultaneously the git checkout **and** the deployed skill tree:

```
~/.claude/skills/cso/SKILL.md -> ~/.claude/skills/gstack/cso/SKILL.md   (symlink onto a TRACKED file)
```

So the brain-aware blocks have to land in the tracked file for the host to read them, and
`setup` renders them in place:

```
gbrain detected — regenerating Claude SKILL.md with brain-aware blocks (~250 token overhead per planning skill)...
```

`gstack-config gbrain-refresh` already acknowledges the consequence:

> Note: this dirties the install's git tree (generated blocks differ from main, by design).
> A 'git reset --hard origin/main' there reverts them; re-run 'gstack-config gbrain-refresh' to restore.

`setup` also already has the escape hatch, but it is scoped to dev trees only:

```sh
if [ -n "${GSTACK_SKIP_GBRAIN_REGEN:-}" ]; then
  # Dev/source tree (set by bin/dev-setup): never regenerate tracked
  # SKILL.md in place — that dirties checked-in source.
```

A user-facing global install has no equivalent, so it takes the in-place path and stays dirty.

## Reproduce

1. Install gstack globally (git install at `~/.claude/skills/gstack`) with `gbrain` on PATH.
2. `./setup` -> 16 tracked `SKILL.md` are modified.
3. Upgrade (`git stash; git fetch; git reset --hard origin/main; ./setup`).
4. `./setup` regenerates the same 16 files; the stash is now redundant.
5. Repeat on the next release. `git stash list` grows by one each time.

## Why the leftovers are worse than clutter

`git stash list` showing four entries reads as unsaved work. The obvious reaction —
`git stash pop` — lays generated instruction markdown from an **older gstack** over the
current version. Nothing breaks loudly; the skills just run on stale rules. That is a quiet
failure mode, and the stash entries are the only thing inviting it.

## Suggested fix — every piece already exists

The repo already has all the machinery; it just is not wired for the global-install path:

| Piece | Status |
|---|---|
| `gen-skill-docs --out-dir` | exists, with `test/gen-skill-docs-out-dir.test.ts` |
| The "B2 contract" | already asserts *"the worktree SKILL.md is byte-unchanged (source stays canonical)"* |
| A gitignored render tree | `.agents/` exists and is ignored |
| Symlink indirection | already how skills are deployed |

So: render the claude `:user` variant into an untracked out-dir and point
`~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` at **that** instead of at the checkout. The symlink layer
means no new mechanism is needed, and a global install would then stay clean, never stash on
upgrade, and let `gbrain-refresh` drop its "this dirties your tree" caveat.

## A workaround worth warning users away from

`git update-index --skip-worktree` on the generated files silences `git status`, but its
interaction with `git reset --hard` is git-version-dependent — an upgrade could then silently
fail to land the new `SKILL.md`. That trades a noisy stash for an upgrade that quietly does
nothing, which is strictly worse.

The safe workaround today is `git checkout -- .` in the install dir **before** upgrading, since
`./setup` reproduces the render exactly.

## Environment

- gstack 1.62.0.0 -> 1.63.0.0 (observed across 1.58.5 / 1.61 / 1.62 / 1.63)
- global-git install at `~/.claude/skills/gstack`, host `claude`, `gbrain` on PATH
- Linux

title: pre-push: force-pushing a rebased branch scans upstream commits too, blocking on engine.input_too_large
body:
## Summary

`gstack-redact-prepush` blocks any force-push of a **rebased** branch with `HIGH engine.input_too_large`, on repos where main is moderately active. The scanned range silently becomes `your commits + upstream's commits` instead of just your new content, and blows the 1 MiB engine cap.

The block is not a finding — it is the engine reporting it never ran. But it is emitted as HIGH, so it stops the push, and the only documented escape is `--no-verify`, which disables the guard entirely for that push.

gstack `1.62.0.0`.

## Mechanism

`bin/gstack-redact-prepush` picks the range in `addedLinesFor()`:

```ts
if (ZERO.test(remoteSha)) {            // :86  new branch  -> merge-base..local
} else if (!objectExists(remoteSha)) { // :92  tip missing -> merge-base..local
} else {
  range = `${remoteSha}..${localSha}`; // :101 existing branch, "incl. force-push"
}
```

After a rebase, `remoteSha` still **exists locally** — it is your own pre-rebase tip — so `objectExists()` is true and the third branch is taken. But it is no longer an ancestor of `localSha`. `remoteSha..localSha` therefore includes every upstream commit rebased onto, because relative to the orphaned remote tip those are new too.

`lib/redact-engine.ts:82` caps input at 1 MiB and emits `engine.input_too_large` (`:271`) above it.

## Measured on a real repo

Branch of 23 commits rebased onto a main that had advanced 23 commits:

| range | added-line bytes | |
|---|---|---|
| `remoteSha..localSha` — what the hook used | **1,195,772** (1.14 MiB) | over cap → blocked |
| `merge-base..localSha` — actual new content | **283,311** (0.27 MiB) | would scan fine |

Scanning the 1.14 MiB in three sub-cap chunks by hand: `HIGH=0` in all three. The push was clean; the guard just could not see it.

Note the payload is only 14% over the cap, not orders of magnitude — so this fires on ordinary branches, not just large ones. It also gets *worse* the longer a branch lives, since more upstream commits accumulate to be swept in.

## Reproduce

```bash
git checkout -b feature main && git commit --allow-empty -m x && git push -u origin feature
# let main advance enough that (your commits + main's commits) > 1 MiB of added lines
git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main
git push --force-with-lease     # HIGH engine.input_too_large
```

## Why the existing fallbacks do not catch it

Both non-default branches already resolve to `merge-base..local` — the correct range. The gap is that the guard for "remote tip unusable" only tests **existence**, not **reachability**. A rebased tip exists and is useless.

## Suggested fix

Extend the `:92` condition to also catch a non-ancestor tip:

```ts
} else if (!objectExists(remoteSha) || !isAncestor(remoteSha, localSha)) {
```

with

```ts
function isAncestor(a: string, b: string): boolean {
  return spawnSync("git", ["merge-base", "--is-ancestor", a, b]).status === 0;
}
```

This keeps the stated "scans MORE, never less" posture — `merge-base..local` is a superset of the genuinely-new content — while dropping the upstream commits that are already on the remote and were already scanned when they were pushed there.

Two smaller things worth considering alongside it:

1. **Chunk instead of refusing.** The engine could scan `ceil(n / cap)` slices and union the findings. A size cap that converts to a hard block means the guard is weakest on exactly the largest diffs.
2. **Distinguish "did not scan" from "found a credential"** in the output. The current message is `credential(s) in the pushed diff:` followed by `engine.input_too_large`, which reads as a detection. In our case it sent someone hunting for a leaked secret that did not exist, and the honest remedy (`--no-verify`) looks identical to ignoring a real finding.

title: Windows: terminal-agent spawns a visible console window that steals keyboard focus
body:
## Symptom

While the `browse` daemon is alive, a console window titled `C:\Users\<user>\.bun\bin\bun.exe`
appears repeatedly and **takes foreground focus**. On Windows a newly created console window
steals keyboard input, so it interrupts whatever the user is typing in another application.
It recurs rather than happening once, which makes `browse` effectively unusable on an
attended desktop.

**Environment**

- Windows 11 Pro (26200), Git Bash / MSYS2
- `browse` build `11de390be1be6849eb9a15f91ff4922dd16c589a`
- Headless (`launched`) mode — not `--headed`

## Root cause

`src/terminal-agent-control.ts`, in `spawnTerminalAgent()`:

```ts
const proc = (Bun as any).spawn(['bun', 'run', script], {
  cwd: opts.cwd || process.cwd(),
  env: { ...process.env, BROWSE_STATE_FILE: opts.stateFile, /* ... */ },
  stdio: ['ignore', 'ignore', 'ignore'],
});
proc.unref?.();
```

The call already passes `stdio: ['ignore','ignore','ignore']` and calls `unref()`, but there
is **no `windowsHide` option** — and on Windows, redirecting stdio does not stop the OS from
allocating a console window for the child. The watchdog then respawns the agent whenever it
exits, which reproduces the window each time and is why closing it doesn't help.

Confirmed by process inspection — the window belongs to a direct child of the daemon, not to
the daemon itself:

```
ProcessId       : 55380
ParentProcessId : 51412
CommandLine     : bun run <...>\browse\src\terminal-agent.ts

ProcessId       : 51412
Name            : node.exe
CommandLine     : node.exe <...>\browse\dist\server-node.mjs
```

This matters for anyone debugging it: killing the visible `bun.exe` by name leaves the real
`node.exe` daemon alive to spawn another within seconds, which looks exactly like "it keeps
popping back up no matter how many times I close it."

## Why this looks like an oversight rather than a design choice

`src/cli.ts` already handles precisely this class of problem for the server launch, with a
comment saying so (~lines 318–328): it notes that `Bun.spawn()` + `proc.unref()` doesn't
truly detach on Windows, and routes the launch through Node's `child_process.spawn` with
`{detached: true, stdio: ['ignore','ignore','ignore']}` instead. The terminal-agent spawn
never got the same treatment.

## Suggested fix

Add `windowsHide: true` to the spawn options. If `Bun.spawn` does not honour `windowsHide`
on Windows, route this spawn through Node's `child_process.spawn` the same way `cli.ts`
already does for the server:

```ts
import { spawn as nodeSpawn } from 'child_process';

nodeSpawn(process.execPath, [script], {
  detached: true,
  stdio: ['ignore', 'ignore', 'ignore'],
  windowsHide: true,   // <-- suppresses the console window
  env: { /* ... */ },
}).unref();
```

Two other `Bun.spawn` call sites spawn `bun` as a child and look like they'd have the same
behaviour on Windows, worth auditing in the same pass:

- `src/browser-skill-commands.ts:188` — `Bun.spawn(['bun', 'test', testFile], …)`
- `src/browser-skill-commands.ts:266` — `Bun.spawn(['bun', 'run', scriptPath, …], …)`

## Workaround

`browse stop` tears down both the daemon and the `bun` child, which stops the popups.

## Secondary, minor

`browse stop` prints:

```
[browse] Unable to connect. Is the computer able to access the url?
```

and **still succeeds** — both processes do exit (verified by checking for the `server-node.mjs`
and `bun.exe` processes immediately afterward; nothing matched). The message reads like a
failure and invites a pointless retry or a manual hunt for surviving processes. It looks like
`stop` is being routed through the `goto` path and treated as a URL. Suggest suppressing that
line, or printing an explicit `stopped` confirmation instead.

Updates `playwright` from 1.58.2 to 1.62.1
Release notes

Sourced from playwright's releases.

v1.62.1

Bug Fixes

  • #41989 [Regression]: tsconfig "extends" bare specifier isn't resolved via node_modules walk-up like tsc (fatal since 1.62)
  • #41998 [Regression]: directory-form tsconfig project references ("path": "../pkg") fail to resolve (fatal since 1.62)
  • #41985 Accessibility snapshot drops button name when text is nested inside spans with aria-hidden SVG
  • #42000 [Regression]: page.evaluate() arg of a branded primitive type (string & { brand }) no longer type-checks since 1.62
  • #42013 [BUG]Image-type actionable elements are not presented in the snapshot.

v1.62.0

🧱 New component testing model

Component testing moves to a stories and galleries model. A story wraps your component in one specific scenario — hard-coded props, mock data, providers — and a gallery page that you serve renders stories on demand. The new fixtures.mount() fixture navigates to the gallery, mounts a story by id, and returns a Locator scoped to the story's root element:

test('click should expand', async ({ mount }) => {
  const component = await mount('components/Expandable/Stateful');
  await component.getByRole('button').click();
  await expect(component.getByTestId('expanded')).toHaveValue('true');
});

Pass a story type as a template argument to type-check its props, and use update(props) / unmount() on the returned locator to re-render or tear down within a test.

🛑 Cancel operations with AbortSignal

Most operations and web-first assertions now accept a signal option that takes an AbortSignal, letting you cancel long-running actions, navigations, waits, and assertions:

const controller = new AbortController();
setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 1000);

await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click({ signal: controller.signal });
await expect(page.getByText('Done')).toBeVisible({ signal: controller.signal });

Providing a signal does not disable the default timeout; pass timeout: 0 to disable it.

🖼️ WebP screenshots

expect(page).toHaveScreenshot() and expect(locator).toHaveScreenshot() can now store snapshots in the WebP format — just give the snapshot a .webp name:

// Visual comparisons store the golden snapshot as lossless WebP.
await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('homepage.webp');

// Standalone screenshots can trade quality for size with lossy WebP.
await page.screenshot({ path: 'homepage.webp', quality: 50 });

Release notes

Sourced from actions/upload-artifact's releases.

v7.0.0

v7 What's new

Direct Uploads

Adds support for uploading single files directly (unzipped). Callers can set the new archive parameter to false to skip zipping the file during upload. Right now, we only support single files. The action will fail if the glob passed resolves to multiple files. The name parameter is also ignored with this setting. Instead, the name of the artifact will be the name of the uploaded file.

ESM

To support new versions of the @actions/* packages, we've upgraded the package to ESM.

Updates `actions/download-artifact` from 4 to 8
Release notes

Sourced from actions/download-artifact's releases.

v8.0.0

v8 - What's new

[!IMPORTANT] actions/download-artifact@v8 has been migrated to an ESM module. This should be transparent to the caller but forks might need to make significant changes.

[!IMPORTANT] Hash mismatches will now error by default. Users can override this behavior with a setting change (see below).

Direct downloads

To support direct uploads in actions/upload-artifact, the action will no longer attempt to unzip all downloaded files. Instead, the action checks the Content-Type header ahead of unzipping and skips non-zipped files. Callers wishing to download a zipped file as-is can also set the new skip-decompress parameter to true.

Enforced checks (breaking)

A previous release introduced digest checks on the download. If a download hash didn't match the expected hash from the server, the action would log a warning. Callers can now configure the behavior on mismatch with the digest-mismatch parameter. To be secure by default, we are now defaulting the behavior to error which will fail the workflow run.

ESM

To support new versions of the @actions/* packages, we've upgraded the package to ESM.

What's Changed

  • Don't attempt to un-zip non-zipped downloads by @​danwkennedy in actions/download-artifact#460
  • Add a setting to specify what to do on hash mismatch and default it to error by @​danwkennedy in actions/download-artifact#461

Full Changelog: https://github.com/actions/download-artifact/compare/v7...v8.0.0

Node.js 24

This release updates the runtime to Node.js 24. v6 had preliminary support for Node 24, however this action was by default still running on Node.js 20. Now this action by default will run on Node.js 24.
