title: Reviews stay valid after merging main when a stacked parent was already on main (GST-3315)
body:
/ship keeps a PR's review when the PR merges main and its stacked parent had already landed before the review. It used to refuse over the parent's files. Why: yc-software/qm#3457 was asked to re-review files it never changed. Nothing for readers to do.
What changed A stacked PR whose parent had already squash-merged into main before the review would later merge main again, and /ship then asked for a fresh review that blamed the parent's files, which the PR never touched. On qm's real commits (7e790c7d to 2c777efc), /ship used to blame parent 635834740 even though the reviewed base 91716d50 already held it. Now it compares from the merge base, so an unchanged PR keeps its review, and context that main moved next to the PR's own lines gets one scoped review of just that file (there, src/mcp/mcp-client.ts). - The stacked-parent finder skips a parent commit that the reviewed base already contains. - Step 11.5's base-merge check uses the same parent rule, and patch IDs are taken with `--unified=3`, so a user's `diff.context` can't shrink the context that gets compared. - `docs/ship-policy.md` gets one paragraph on the rule, and `changelog.d/` gets the release note. - New tests cover the qm#3457 shape, negative controls (the PR's own edit still refuses; a parent not yet on the base still counts), Step 11.5 using the same rule, and `diff.context=0`. The qm#3457, Step 11.5 and `diff.context=0` tests failed before their fixes; the two controls pass before and after.
Why "Asked to re-review files it never changed" (yc-software/qm#3457). A PR that only merged main should keep the review it already passed, and only lines that actually moved next to its own changes should be read again.
Blast radius The parent finder is also used by the squash commit message at land time (`lib/squash-message.ts:64`); see review note 1. Every other change can only make /ship compare more of the branch, never less, so a mismatch still refuses (walked failure path in both reviews, plus the new negative-control tests).
Pre-Landing Review One full review pass of the whole diff: a batched specialist reader (testing, security, state machines), a red-team reader, a native adversarial reader and a second-model review (GPT-6.1 Sol). No blocking findings. The specialists found nothing, the second-model review was clean, the red-team reader's one finding is recorded privately (security-category details stay out of the body), and the adversarial reader's three findings are the review notes below. No fixes were applied.
Review notes 1. (Medium, not blocking) For a stacked child that merges main after its parent's squash lands, the squash commit body now repeats the landed parent's Co-authored-by and trailer lines. Before this change it pulled in main's trailers instead, so it was wrong both ways. No test covers that case yet. A follow-up can apply the new skip only to the review-reuse check and Step 11.5, with a squash-message test where the child merges main. 2. (Low) `--unified=3` pins only `diff.context`. `diff.algorithm`, `diff.interHunkContext` and the indent heuristic can still change patch IDs between machines; that can only cause a wrong refusal, never a wrong acceptance. 3. (Low) A review recorded by an older gstack under a non-default `diff.context` refuses once after this change and needs a fresh /ship.
Exploratory QA Functional smoke, 2 probes through the repository's own tests: an unrelated main change keeps the review (pass) and an own edit after the base merge refuses (pass). Verdict: pass. The squash-message case in note 1 was reproduced by the reviewers in a scratch repository, not here.
Scope Drift Scope Check: CLEAN. Intent: keep a review valid when a stacked parent was already on the reviewed base. Delivered: that rule in the parent finder and Step 11.5, the patch ID context pin, docs, a release note and tests.
TODOS No TODO items completed in this PR.

title: The weekly test-time recording can land again on its own (GST-3303)
body:
The weekly job that re-records how long each test file takes can land its update again without someone fixing it by hand. Free Tests uses those times to split the suite evenly. It had not landed an update since 11-09: the Windows half kept failing, and its pull request waited for a maintainer whenever a new file ran past 60 seconds. Nothing to do. The bot's commit and pull-request step runs for real only on the weekly schedule, so the next Monday run is its first live test.
What changed - **Windows recording, two at a time.** It used to time four files at once on a four-core runner. Under that load, tests that pass in the nightly Windows run failed. Today's file count no longer fits the 30-minute job either: a run on main this evening stopped at the limit after 838 of 921 files, with several red files. The recording now runs two files at a time with a 60-minute limit. A trial on this branch timed all 921 files cleanly in 38 minutes. - **Slow files no longer stall the seed pull request.** The seed check refuses a file over 60 seconds unless the allowlist names it, and the bot never touched the allowlist, so each weekly pull request waited for a hand edit. Now the bot lists each new file over 60 seconds with the run that measured it and a follow-up to split it, and drops entries for files back under 60 seconds. It does this with `scripts/free-seed-allowlist.ts --reconcile`, the same kind of entry a maintainer added by hand on 11-09 and 11-20. The pull request description names every file it adds or drops.
Evidence - Four at a time, on main: Windows Free Tests run 44830554276 stopped at its 30-minute limit after 838 of 921 files, with red files including ceo-review-gate and the two gstack-doctor test files. All of these pass in the nightly Windows run. - Two at a time, on this branch: run 44830546810 timed all 921 files, none red, in 38 minutes. - The 11-16 weekly run had four red Windows files of the same kind, and every weekly recording since 10-26 has ended red on Windows. That's one run of each setting, so it's a strong signal rather than a rate.
Review Five reviewers read the whole change, then read the wording fix again. They were a batched specialist (testing, security, state machines), a red team, a native adversarial reader, a second-model review (GPT-6.1 Sol) and a targeted reader for the test-gate change. None found a defect that would fail a test, break production or lose data. The Windows recording job's time limit, raised from 30 to 60 minutes, was approved by the maintainer on the two runs under Evidence.
Review notes Below the blocking floor (advisory, informational, test-gap or wording items); recorded here and not fixed in this PR. - INFORMATIONAL `scripts/lib/free-ci-health.ts:164` auto-admission is unbounded (count and duration); deliberate loosening of the seed ratchet on the bot's PR - INFORMATIONAL `scripts/lib/free-ci-health.ts:157` growth gate becomes automatic on the seed PR (same as targeted#1) - INFORMATIONAL `scripts/free-seed-allowlist.ts:29` reconcile ignores record-failures.txt, so a timed-out or crashed file can be admitted or pruned on a bad duration - INFORMATIONAL `scripts/test-pr-profile.ts:241` comment says only the ratchet reads the allowlist; new scripts not in FREE_ONLY_PR_FILES - INFORMATIONAL `scripts/lib/free-ci-health.ts:169` formatSeedAllowlist reserializes every entry; a hand-formatted file would diff whole on first change - INFORMATIONAL `scripts/free-seed-allowlist.ts:29` auto-admission is unbounded (same as p1/targeted#1); bound it per run
Exploratory QA The new allowlist command was run three times on a copied tree with made-up timings. It admitted a new 65-second file with the run link and a follow-up, dropped a file back at 59 seconds, kept a listed slow file, changed nothing on a second run, and refused a missing run link with exit 2 before writing anything. The workflow's own commit step was not exercised here.
Documentation **Status:** updated. One stale wording fix was made in `docs/TESTING_INTERNALS.md`. **Scope:** 8 files changed across 4 commits (14a84980..4732d5f): the weekly seed recorder workflow, the Windows recording job (two workers, 60-minute limit), the `scripts/free-seed-allowlist.ts --reconcile` command and its library helpers, tests, a changelog fragment and `docs/TESTING_INTERNALS.md`. There was no uncommitted content before the audit. **Documentation health:** - `docs/TESTING_INTERNALS.md`: Updated. The Free suite duration seed section now says files at four workers failed under load, not that they timed out. This matches the corrected workflow comment and changelog. - `CONTRIBUTING.md`: Current. The manual Windows seed refresh command is unchanged. - `TODOS.md`: Not changed (outside this audit's scope). Its seed items stay accurate. - `changelog.d/ci-seed-recorder-unstuck.md`: Reviewed and current. It was not edited because it is outside this audit's scope. **Coverage debt:** `scripts/free-seed-allowlist.ts` has a reference entry and a usage header but no how-to page. It is an internal CI tool, so this is low-priority debt. **Diagram drift:** none.

title: Capy threads use halved token limits and follow three new rules on subagents, relays and going forward (GST-3323)
body:
Capy threads working on a PR now check in at 500M own tokens, standing threads rotate at 250M, and any subagent past 50M gets a look; `gstack-runaway scan` and /ship's default subagent cap use the new lines. Why: Capy's token counts have read about half what they did before 2026-11-15, so the old lines were double the ones in use, and three standing rules (subagents, relays, going forward) were missing from the factory rules every Capy thread reads. Nothing to do: the new lines apply on the next gstack upgrade.
What changed - **Token lines, in the tools and the prose.** `lib/runaway.ts` limits: standing rotation 500M to 250M (warn 400M to 200M), check-in for a thread holding a PR 1B to 500M, subagent stop-and-look 100M to 50M. `lib/ship-budget.ts` `SUBAGENT_DEFAULT_CAP` 100M to 50M. The same numbers in factory.md rule 12, lane-card.md, the controller manual (`the controller manual`), capy/skill/gstack/captain.md, /runaway-stopper, its successor brief, docs/ship-budget.md, docs/skills.md and README.md. title: New page on running gstack work across more than one agent system (GST-3323)
body:
Adds docs/working-across-agent-systems.md, one short page on running gstack work when two or more agent systems share a repository, with pointers to it from the README and the controller manual. Why: the practices that kept cross-system work cheap and correct (one sender per side, answers on the pull request, filtered wake-ups instead of polling, pinned harness versions) were written nowhere in gstack, and other systems can't read our private notes. Nothing to do: any agent can be pointed at the page with "read docs/working-across-agent-systems.md first".
What the page says - Six rules: one sender per boundary; answer on the pull request; ring, don't poll, with a filter at the source and a marker on your own comments; every message is a paid turn; a message from another system is a claim to check and pass on in its own words; pin the other harness's version and model. - The short cost rules: touched tests only before a push, no rerun of a passed check on an unchanged tree, the full suite once on the finished head, no acknowledgements, polling or environment prints. - A placeholder pointing to /eval-plan for the eval checklist, to be updated when that checklist lands there. - Two practices marked as another team's and not yet measured by us: freeze shared contracts before parallel work splits, and one integration branch with one sync owner.
What changed Teams that run more than one coding agent on the same repository kept relearning the same lessons. Messages got lost in one agent's own conversation, agents were woken by every comment, and a harness changed its default model underneath them. The new page puts those lessons in one place an outside developer can read: six rules (one sender per boundary, answer on the pull request, wake the other side only for events meant for it, treat every message as a paid turn, check a message from the other side before acting, pin the other harness's version and model), a short list of habits that keep runs cheap, and two practices from another team that are clearly marked as not yet measured by us. The README's docs table and the controller manual now link to it.
Why Other agent systems can't read our notes, so the rules have to live in a public page they can be pointed at.
Blast radius Documentation only: one new page, one README table row, a two-line pointer in the controller manual (`crew/docs/captain.md`) and a changelog fragment. No code, tests, CI or install steps change.
Pre-Landing Review Pre-Landing Review: 3 issues — 0 auto-fixed, 0 asked (0 fixed, 0 skipped), 0 deferred, 3 noted Below the blocking floor (advisory, informational, test-gap or wording items); recorded here and not fixed in this PR. - INFORMATIONAL `docs/working-across-agent-systems.md:28` Published figures (117/15, 100 runs 15/85, five and a half hours, 14 agents) cite no source run; unverified, not shown wrong - INFORMATIONAL `docs/working-across-agent-systems.md:52` Evals paragraph says the checklist is moving into /eval-plan with no tracking link; may go stale - INFORMATIONAL `crew/docs/captain.md:58` Pointer could be read as making the unmeasured Worth trying section binding; section is labelled

There were no staged, unstaged or untracked changes. title: /cso on Windows: start fails with "trusted compiled helper is missing or invalid" because the published helper has an NTFS link count of 2, while doctor reports ready
body:
gstack version 1.101.0.0 (b7022438597e), installed under `~/.claude/skills/gstack` and built by `setup` on 2026-11-18. `bin/.gstack-cso-build-result` reads `result=ok stage=publish reason=committed launcher=yes`.

Platform: Windows 11 (build 26300) with Git Bash. There is no Linux Docker, so the scanners show as missing, which is expected.

## What happens

`gstack-cso-launcher.exe doctor --repo <repo>` exits 0 and lists only the scanner capabilities as missing.

`gstack-cso-launcher.exe start --repo <repo> --diff --base <ref> --budget 900` exits 69 with `gstack-cso: trusted compiled helper is missing or invalid; run gstack setup/build`. Retrying gives the same result. In an earlier run, `start` returned a run ID and then every `inspect` failed with that message.

## Likely cause

`lib/cso/launcher-windows.c` (around line 182) refuses the core helper when `core_info.nNumberOfLinks != 1`. Both published binaries have a link count of 2:

```
-rwxr-xr-x 2 ... 116077056 Nov 18 23:01 gstack-cso-core.exe
-rwxr-xr-x 2 ...    155648 Nov 18 23:01 gstack-cso-launcher.exe
```

I searched `~/.claude`, `~/.gstack`, and my own config repo by file ID and found no second name for either file. Calling `FindFirstFileNameW` on them as the user returns ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED (5), so I couldn't list the other name. `scripts/build-cso.sh` moves the staged files into `bin/` with `mv`, so I suspect the second name comes from the Windows staging or publish step, perhaps a staged copy or a lock holder that keeps a link. I haven't confirmed that.

## Expected

`setup` should leave the helper with exactly one link so that `start` works, or the launcher should accept the second link if it is intentional on Windows.

`doctor` should run the same integrity checks as `start` (link count, generation manifest, and lock), so it can't report ready when `start` will refuse to run.

## Workaround

I haven't found one that keeps the integrity check intact, so I used a different security reviewer for this change.

title: Teach agents nine habits that several teams learned the hard way (GST-3336)
body:
Agents using gstack now get nine working habits that three or four teams each reached on their own: don't write a file back from a cut-off read, change the design when reviews keep finding the same kind of bug, narrow a safety guard only with a tested exemption, prove a change on the real path, move timers and automations with a handoff, land base-branch settings first, and check that a check can see your change. Why: each habit cost one of those teams a lost file, a leaked key, an outage or extra review rounds. Nothing to do as a reader.
Where each habit lives, with its evidence | Habit | Where | Evidence (teams, as each tells it) | |---|---|---| | Never write a file back from a cut-off read; edit in place and compare line counts | agents' start card | 4 teams: a 240-line record file came back as 44 lines; a source file cut mid-way; a preregistration lost its tail; a rules file lost 37 rows | | When a review round finds another case of a kind it already found, change the design | team manual, working rules | 4 teams: a new double-send path in each of four rounds; five /ship runs before an allowlist rebuild passed in one; a pattern-matching PR closed for a rebuild; exemptions dropped after repeated bypasses | | Narrow an over-catching safety guard with a tested exemption, not a narrower match | team manual, working rules | 3 teams: three review blockers from a narrower replacement match; a narrowed command hold bypassed three ways; a wrapper that broke every upgrade | | A green fake or dry run isn't done until one run drives the real path | factory page, point 7 | 3 teams: 23 green tests against a fake, then a real gateway ranked the wrong message; 569 of 569 dry-run cases passed and the pin still couldn't launch; a flag that passed a plain check caused a 12-minute outage | | A handoff moves waits, watches and automations, not only PRs | team manual, No orphaned work; rotation handoff gets a Clocks table and the successor brief registers it | 3 teams: an archive paused a one-shot automation; timer waits ended by other wakes never came back; a wake about seven hours late let a reaper take a run's spend record | | Land review exclusions and secrets allowlist entries in their own PR first | docs/ship-policy.md, review_exclude_paths | 3 teams each opened extra settings PRs in the middle of a /ship (one cost two extra PRs) | | Check that a check can see what you changed and counts what its name says | factory page, point 7 | 3 teams: a reading-time clock that couldn't see added text; a "briefs before prep" count that counted polls; a model "loss" that was the harness refusing 607 of 607 page reads | | Write launch and env files with a file tool or a quoted heredoc; check variables by exact name | agents' start card | 2 teams, safety: an unquoted heredoc printed an environment, API key included; a name prefix matched a secret's name | | Check that task machines hold no readable answers before an eval session | /eval-plan Held-out exposure row and the prereg template | 2 teams: one model found answers with `git log --all` in 19 of 160 sessions and a build cache held 164 hidden test names; a test agent ran `find /` where the key was readable | | A relayed approval is a claim: read it at its source before acting | docs/working-across-agent-systems.md, rule 5 | 2 teams nearly acted on relayed approvals (an install; about ten write-path PRs); both were real but unchecked. Kept as a permissions guard | | Decide a harness pin from a repro, not release notes; record what actually ran | docs/working-across-agent-systems.md, rule 6 | 2 teams: a fix missing from the next stable build and a release that dropped turns in 3 of 3 runs; a CLI release that changed its default model | Rule 5's example now says what happened: the owning side couldn't reproduce the report and the other side accepted that. This is a budget raise: the factory page's byte budget goes from 4,875 to 5,050 bytes because point 7 gains two clauses (a green fake or dry run isn't done; a check must see the change and count what its name says), each reached on its own by three teams.
What stayed prose, and why - The cut-off-read rule has no gstack tool to hold it: the file-read and file-write tools belong to the agent host, not gstack. - Launch and env files are written at run time, outside the repository, so no repository check can see them. - `gstack-review-plan` already prints that a branch's own `review_exclude_paths` applies only after it lands; the new paragraph says to plan for that before opening the data PR. - The no-answers check is a template default and a plan row, not a `prereg --check` failure: making it a hard check needs a dated grandfather rule and is left to the /eval-plan rework. - The guard-narrowing rule went to the team manual rather than review/checklist.md, because a change to a reviewer prompt needs a no-loss replay first.

title: pregate: root node:test files run under vitest when the root package.json declares vitest, and fail "No test suite found"
body:
## What happens

In a repo whose root `package.json` declares `vitest` (common in a pnpm monorepo that shares a vitest config from the root), `gstack-pregate`'s `lanes` check runs root-level `node:test` files with `npx vitest run`. Vitest finds no suites in a `node:test` file and fails it, so `lanes` reds on files that pass under `node --test`. `/ship` Step 16 (`gstack-ship-release finish`) then stops on `pregate fail on the stamped tree`, on every PR whose selection includes such a file.

Workspace tests in the same repo are fine: they route per package (`pnpm exec vitest run` from each package root). Only the root group is affected.

## Repro (vitest 4.1.10, node 24)

`package.json`:

```json
{ "name": "repro", "private": true, "devDependencies": { "vitest": "4.1.10" } }
```

`scripts/sum.test.mjs`:

```js
import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";

test("adds", () => {
  assert.equal(1 + 1, 2);
});
```

- `npx vitest run scripts/sum.test.mjs` exits 1: `FAIL scripts/sum.test.mjs`, `Error: No test suite found in file …/scripts/sum.test.mjs`, `Tests no tests`.
- `node --test scripts/sum.test.mjs` exits 0: `pass 1`, `fail 0`.

In a pregate run, the lanes log shows the `node:test` cases executing and passing inside vitest's process, each file followed by `❯ scripts/<file>.test.mjs (0 test)` and then `FAIL … No test suite found`.

## Cause

`detectRunner` in `lib/pregate/checks/lanes.ts` (1.102.1.0, lines 53-67) checks `deps.vitest` (line 61) before the `.mjs`/`.js` → `node --test` branch (line 64). It never looks at what the file imports, so any root JS test in a vitest-declaring repo gets vitest.

A declared `runner` doesn't work as a workaround in a monorepo: it disables per-package routing (`planRuns`, line 226), so every workspace's vitest tests would go to that one command too.

## Suggested fix

Do what `importsPlaywright` already does for `@playwright/test`: a root `.js`/`.mjs`/`.cjs` test file that loads `node:test` (an `import … from "node:test"` or `'node:test'`, a bare `import "node:test"`, or a `require("node:test")` anywhere on a line, since `const { test } = require(…)` never starts one) gets `node --test {files}`, whatever the root unit runner is. The 1.93.15.0 CHANGELOG entry *"Playwright specs in a vitest repo went to vitest, which found no tests and failed"* is the same failure shape.

A regression fixture: a root `package.json` declaring vitest, one root `node:test` `.mjs` and one root vitest `.test.ts`. Expect two root groups, `node --test` and `npx vitest run`.

title: Pilot every arm of the /ship conductor trial and add one planned halfway look (GST-3003)
body:
The /ship conductor trial plan now runs an uncounted pilot in every arm and checks its judge on those outputs before any counted trial, and takes one planned look at half the cases. Why: two rules adopted on 2026-11-19 (an uncounted pilot per arm, and one halfway look for runs over $500) apply to plans whose counted runs have not started, and this one has not. Nothing to do: no bar, arm or decision changes; no paid call has run.
What changed The trial plan let its first round of trials count toward the result, took its judge's labels from outside pull requests, and had no planned interim look. It now runs one uncounted pilot trial per arm on cases 1 to 3 with four checks (the part under test ran, the no-gstack arm saw no gstack, every case can be supplied), labels the judge on this run's own uncounted outputs, and takes one look after cases 1 to 5 with fixed O'Brien-Fleming stop bounds. An early stop at that look can only keep the conductor. It stops for harm (F clearly costs more or catches less) or for futility, and a crossing in F's favour never stops the run, because removing the conductor needs the evidence of all 10 cases. The budget estimate moves from $2,785 to $3,073, with a worst case of $3,181 if the judge stage needs its extra C and F trials; the $3,250 cap is unchanged.
Why The 2026-11-19 rules cover plans whose counted runs have not started. Meeting them before the first paid call keeps the trial's numbers countable. The last change keeps an early stop from deciding the trial's question on half the data.

A futility stop can only keep the conductor, so this cannot retire it early; freezing the simulation's model and inputs before the counted trials would close it. - `docs/evals/ship-conductor-fold-prereg.md:233` (core checklist, informational): "near $2,773" is $3,073 minus $10 for each of the 30 counted F trials; the 3 uncounted pilot F trials would save about $30 more (about $2,743). title: Split the slowest free test file so no shard waits on it (GST-3303)
body:
Free Tests no longer waits on one 263-second test file. Its 79 tests (80 cases) now run as six files of 25 to 40 seconds, so the shard planner can spread them out. This is part of making pull request CI faster: a file that big puts a floor under one shard, and that floor matters most on bigger runners. Nothing to do.
What changed - `test/review-pass.test.ts` is split by topic into six files: the manifest and small units (it keeps the name), the pass program's core flow, the Step 11 second-model reviews, failed second-model reviews and cyber-policy retries, the later steps, and readers on a shared machine. - Their shared fixtures (the manifest builder, a feature-branch repo, the fake host, the pass runner) moved unchanged into `test/helpers/review-pass-harness.ts`. Every test and its comments moved word for word, and the count is the same: 79 tests, 80 cases. The fixtures moved with two edits: ROOT now resolves two levels up, and the repo fixture uses mkdir -p. - The duration seed lists the six files. Their values are the per-case times from Free Tests run 44840566118 on CI (estimates; the next weekly recording replaces them), scaled up to the old file's recorded 263 s so they match the rest of the seed. Each is under the 60-second limit, so the allowlist entry for the old file is gone. - Windows never ran the old file, because it checks POSIX file modes. The five new files that lost that check are listed as Windows-incompatible, so Windows coverage doesn't change. - `test/helpers/free-fixtures-data.ts` points the cyber-policy fixture at the file that reads it now, and `docs/review-policy.md` names the new files.
Evidence - Locally, one process: the old file took 216 s with all 79 passing. The new files, all six run at once on four cores, all pass. - On CI (run 44840566118), after the split, the six files took 24.7 to 40.0 seconds each (run 44875106601). - Recent PR runs on the 8-core runner: the shard that holds this file was the slowest in 7 of 28. So the gain on today's runners is a few seconds at most. The point is to let a 16-core trial pay off, which the earlier trial couldn't because this one file set the floor.

title: Job-log tree.json step now recommends a 5-second sleep so slow-stamping runners still reuse CI results (GST-3339)
body:
When a repository's artifact storage is full, gstack's reuse of CI test results reads tree.json from one log line, and the docs' `sleep 2` after that line was too short on a Ubicloud runner, so gstack refused the run and fell back to running tests locally. The docs, the troubleshooting entry and the refusal's fix line now say `sleep 5`, and a new test checks the documented sleeps against GitHub's whole-second step times. Repositories that copied the old step should change `sleep 2` to `sleep 5`.
Diagnosis from the two real runs Run 44845717681 (harness-evals, `sleep 1` / `sleep 2`): the line was logged at 00:57:39.338 and the next step's header 00:57:40.987, which the jobs API reports as 00:57:40. The check keeps the line at least a second before every later step's reported start, so the window ended at 00:57:39 and the line was refused. The API times match the floor of the runner's own log times at every step boundary in both runs, so there is no clock lag between the two; the gap is the runner logging output about 0.37 s after `echo` runs, plus the whole-second cut. Run 44857547577 (`sleep 3` / `sleep 5`) bound with tree_source=job-log. The binding check itself is unchanged, because loosening its margins would let a line a test prints near the end of the test step bind on a runner with no stamping delay. The new test replays both runs and fails on the old docs (`sleep 2` with the line logged 1.5 s late).
What changed docs/pregate.md and docs/troubleshooting.md now recommend `sleep 5` after the `GSTACK_TREE_JSON` line, and the CI_CARRY_TREE_LOG_UNBOUND fix line says the same. test/run-evidence-job-log.test.ts replays runs 44845717681 and 44857547577 and checks the documented sleeps at every sub-second offset with the runner logging the line up to 2.5 s late.
Why Runners record a log line's time a fraction of a second or more after the echo runs, and the jobs API cuts step times to the whole second, so `sleep 2` left too little room and a real run was refused.
Blast radius Docs, one fix string and one test. The binding check in lib/run-evidence.ts is unchanged.
Review and test coverage
Review notes Below the blocking floor (advisory, informational, test-gap or wording items); recorded here and not fixed in this PR. - INFORMATIONAL `changelog.d/ci-tree-log-sleep-after.md:4` documented sleep 1 / sleep 5 step is proven by the synthetic sweep, not a real run - INFORMATIONAL `lib/result-codes-release.ts:431` repos already on sleep 2 fail once before the fix line points them at sleep 5; detail could name the measured gap - INFORMATIONAL `test/run-evidence-job-log.test.ts:244` headroom bounded at about 3 s; sweep stops at 2.5 s Pre-Landing Review: No issues found. Gate edits: none detected (0 tagged). Coverage: 2 of 4 changed paths tested. Two informational gaps: nothing ties the result-code fix line or the troubleshooting fix text to the documented sleep. Exploratory QA: both required smoke checks passed (the fix line names sleep 5; all three places agree). Overall evidence verdict inconclusive because one extra grep probe was too narrow and was replaced. Tests: free-tests run 44876265116 at 0a9962e6, 1722 files passed.

title: Skipped quarantined tests fail the run, and the upgrade snooze sticks for git installs (GST-3344)
body:
A quarantined test that the runner skipped now fails the run, and "Not now" on the upgrade prompt now lasts its full snooze on git installs. Why: four outside reports showed a false pass, a snooze that came back after two hours, a model check that ignored `config.toml`, and two `$B` rules missing from /browse. Nothing to do.
What changed - **gstack-flaky (#4550).** A quarantined test still has to run, so a skip on the attempt that decided the run is now a `quarantined-fail`: the run is red, the flaky log records the skip, and the quarantine report no longer counts it toward the clean streak. A test skipped first and passing on the whole-command retry still passes, and an ordinary skip still follows the runner's verdict. Thanks to @DananjayaNadun for the report and @Huyvux12, whose #4551 found the fix; this is a rewrite on main, not their branch. - **Upgrade snooze (#4561).** The "Not now" snippet in `gstack-upgrade/SKILL.md` took one hand-picked field, and agents sometimes picked the third field of a four-field `UPGRADE_AVAILABLE` line, so the snooze never matched. It now takes the whole line and keys on the same field `gstack-update-check` reads. That is the SHA on a four-field line, else the new version. The note under it was shortened so the skill stays inside its size budget. - **gstack-models (#4491 follow-up).** `gstack-models resolve --role plan-review` and `list` now read a custom Codex provider's `config.toml` model through the same reader `gstack-codex-probe role-ready` uses, so they accept `gpt-6-astra` and refuse any other name with `custom_provider_model_not_tier`, instead of always saying `custom_provider_requires_model`. A `config.toml` it cannot read, or whose model is not a string, is reported as a `native_provider_unresolved` error instead of crashing the command. The reader moved from `scripts/resolve-codex-generation-model.ts` into `lib/model-policy.ts` unchanged, because the installed Claude Code runtime ships `lib/` but not `scripts/`. `docs/model-policy.md` now lists these commands. - **/browse (#4557, #4558).** The fallback command reference now says that `$B eval ` reads only files under the temp directory or the daemon's working directory, and that each git root gets its own daemon, so a `cd` into another repository starts a new one without the session.
Tests - [x] `bun --no-env-file test --timeout=30000 test/quarantine.test.ts test/skill-positional-literals.test.ts test/update-check-main-moved.test.ts test/skill-size-budget.test.ts test/parity-suite.test.ts`: 77 pass, 0 fail - [x] Free Tests CI at d1f36f4 (https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/actions/runs/44879023867): green - [x] `bun run typecheck`: clean
Why Each item is a reported bug where gstack said something that was not true. A run reported green with a test that never ran, a reminder that came back early, a model check that said no model was set when one was, and /browse leaving out two rules that make `$B` fail.
Blast radius `lib/flaky-run.ts` only changes the verdict for quarantined tests whose deciding attempt was a skip; non-quarantined tests and quarantined tests that ran are unchanged (quarantine.test.ts, 32 pass). The model-policy change touches `gstack-models` only when custom Codex routing is detected (lib/model-policy.ts:569), and the other caller in `scripts/resolve-codex-generation-model.ts` keeps its own behavior; the generated `browse/SKILL.md` and `gstack-upgrade/SKILL.md` were regenerated and pass the size budget and parity checks.
Test Coverage All new code paths have test coverage (7 of 7). Tests: 1841 → 1842 (+1 new, the malformed `config.toml` case). The 4-field snooze test runs in CI only; it times out on the 4-core ship machine, as the rest of its file does on clean main. Tests ran: focused 77 Tests ran: free 1722 files (CI run 44879023867)
Pre-Landing Review One finding, fixed before merge (security finding, details recorded privately). The fix check, the adversarial read and the second-model review found nothing at the blocking floor; their notes are below. Second-model review (GPT-6.1 Sol): clean.
Review notes Below the blocking floor (advisory, informational, test-gap or wording items); recorded here and not fixed in this PR. - INFORMATIONAL `lib/model-policy-cli.ts:331` The wrapped error's cause already ends with CODEX_MODEL_REPAIR and repair repeats it, so text output prints the repair sentence twice. Output is correct, only duplicated. - INFORMATIONAL `lib/flaky-run.ts:301` A quarantined test that Bun filtered out with -t (or a skipIf(win32) quarantined test on Windows) now counts as quarantined-fail: gstack-flaky exits 1 and the recorded failure resets its clean streak. No CI job runs gstack-flaky; matches the existing missing-test rule. Medium, Blocks: no, INVESTIGATE (policy call). - INFORMATIONAL `gstack-upgrade/SKILL.md.tmpl:60` If an agent pastes only the version instead of the whole line, awk $(3) is empty and the snooze file is unreadable, so the reminder keeps returning (the old {new} habit). Low, Blocks: no. - INFORMATIONAL `lib/model-policy-cli.ts:325` gstack-models resolve uses kind exec, so with review_model set in config.toml it displays model where gstack-codex-probe role-ready review would pick review_model. Display only. Low, Blocks: no.
Issues Refs #4491 Refs #4550 Refs #4557 Refs #4558 Refs #4561
Documentation **Status:** updated. One factual doc fix; no blockers. **Scope:** base 41729a0 to head 797e3d4 (3 commits, 14 files); no staged, unstaged or new files. Changes: quarantined tests skipped on the final attempt now fail (`lib/flaky-run.ts`), the upgrade snooze keys on the whole `UPGRADE_AVAILABLE` line, `gstack-models` reads a custom Codex provider's `config.toml` model, and /browse notes on `$B eval` and per-git-root daemons. **Documentation health** - `docs/model-policy.md`: Updated (added `gstack-models resolve` and `list` to the commands that share the custom-provider plan-review selection). - `docs/flaky.md`: Current (already updated on this branch for skipped quarantined tests). - `docs/troubleshooting.md`: Current. - `browse/SKILL.md.tmpl`: Current (edited on this branch). - `gstack-upgrade/SKILL.md.tmpl`: Current (edited on this branch). **Coverage debt:** no new public surface without reference docs. **Diagram drift:** none.

title: Eval plans now pilot every arm, check the judge per arm, state their cost and take one planned look above 500 dollars (GST-3218)
body:
`/eval-plan` now refuses an eval plan that would waste money: every arm gets a small uncounted pilot, the judge is checked on each arm's outputs, the plan carries a cost line, and a run above 500 dollars takes one planned look at half its units. Small questions get a 100-dollar quick look that publishes no number. Why: 23.7% of the 28,836 dollars spent on our last 30 evals settled nothing, mostly through arms and judges that broke after the full run. Nothing to do as a reader; plans frozen before 2026-11-21 keep their old rules.
What the plan check now asks for | Rule | Where it's held | |---|---| | Name the decision each outcome changes | `## Decisions` (already checked); Step 0 of the skill says don't run an eval that changes nothing | | Uncounted pilot per arm, at most a tenth of its budget, showing the part ran, the judge passes on that arm's outputs, and the units can be supplied | `## Pilot`: `share:` (10% or less), `counted: no`, `ran:`, `judge:`, `supply:` | | The pilot draws every unit type, in a seeded order that doesn't depend on concurrency | `## Pilot`: `units:`, `seed:` | | Judge checked per arm, at a stated reasoning effort | `## Scoring`: `per-arm: yes`, `effort:`; `judge --check` prints a `JUDGE_ARM:` line per arm and fails an arm below the bar | | A cost line | `## Cost`: `paid:`, `meter:`, `ledger:` (the private file that gets the actual cost and the decision it settled) | | One look at half the units above 500 dollars paid | `## Interim look`: `at: 50%`, `looks: 1`, O'Brien-Fleming `bounds:`, `futility:` | | A "smaller change" arm is scored with tests | a `regression test` bar is required beside it | | No answers readable on the task machine | an `answers:` line under held-out exposure, now a hard check for plans frozen on or after 2026-11-21 | | Quick look first for a small question | `prereg --init --quick` writes a three-line plan capped at 100 dollars; `results --check` refuses it with `EVAL_QUICK_LOOK_NO_NUMBER` | New plans name GPT-6.2 Sol as the frontier Sol (judges GPT-6 or GPT-6.2 Astra for Claude arms), and GPT-6.2 Sol and Astra are in the price table. Plans frozen earlier keep their models. The cross-agent page's eval placeholder now points at /eval-plan.
Evidence and how we'll measure it The rules come from our audit of the last 30 evals: 23.7% of 28,836 dollars settled nothing, the biggest single loss (2,033 dollars) was a judge that failed its check after the whole grid ran, a pilot that drew one unit type planned a 77% yield and got 9%, a "smaller change" instruction cut code to 0.44x and wrote fewer tests (28 of 100 sessions against 79), and a reader that inherited its parent's highest effort cost about four times the default. Cost per decision (1,922 dollars today) gets recounted over plans written under these checks on Monday 2026-12-07.

title: /cso never looks through a symlinked folder, and Capy release and triage steps stop writing to GitHub as the owner (GST-3344)
body:
/cso now checks every folder above a source file before it looks at the file, and on Capy the release PR and /ship's triage issue no longer go through gh as the owner. Why: /cso could stat a path through a symlinked folder before failing closed, and on Capy gh signs in as the owner's own GitHub account. Nothing to do; whoever opens release PRs on Capy publishes the `HOST_PUBLISH:` files with the PR tool, as other /ship steps already do.
What changed - **/cso capture.** A tracked file such as `d/f` whose folder `d` was replaced by a symlink used to be stat-ed through the link (`lstat repo/d/f` follows `d`) before a later read failed closed, and if the link's target lacked `f` the file was quietly recorded as deleted. Capture now walks the folders above each path from the root down first: a symlinked or non-folder ancestor fails with `UNSAFE_PATH` before any lstat of the path, and a missing ancestor still means the file is absent. The source-cap message's size count skips such paths the same way instead of measuring through the link. - **Release PR on Capy.** With `GSTACK_CAPY=1`, the command that opens release PRs still writes the new version and pushes `release/`, then prints a `HOST_PUBLISH: pr-create` line (repo, base, head, title and body files) instead of running `gh pr create`. An already open release PR is still reused. Off Capy nothing changes. - **Test-failure triage on Capy.** The "Blame + assign GitHub issue" block in /ship keeps its title and body files and prints where they are, instead of running `gh issue create`. - **REVIEW_DIFF_TOO_LARGE.** A file or folder name holding a newline or another control character is quoted in `top=` and in the fix text, so the line stays one line. Names with spaces print as before. - **Wording.** `docs/ship-policy.md` says 11.3 MB (11,320,357 bytes) for harness-evals#494's 25 transcripts, and `lib/review-secret-excerpt.ts` and its test comment say 12.26 MB was main's whole reader diff.
Tests - `test/cso-snapshot-state.test.ts`: a tracked file under a folder swapped for a symlink (target holds a folder of that name, or nothing) fails with `UNSAFE_PATH` and no lstat touches a path under the link; the source-cap error measures nothing through it. title: /verify hides Claude Code's built-in verify skill, and the name alone triggers its run-before-every-commit line
body:
## What happened

gstack installs its build-and-check skill as `~/.claude/skills/verify` (`name: verify`). Claude Code ships a **built-in** skill with the same name, and a user skill with a given name hides the bundled one. So with gstack installed, `/verify` is never Claude Code's built-in again, and nothing says so.

The built-in is a different tool. Its description in Claude Code 2.1.296:

> "Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. …"

A second effect comes from the same name. Since Claude Code **2.1.286** (2026-09-30, CHANGELOG: "when your project or user skills include one named `verify`, Claude is now told to run it right before committing"), the Bash tool description gets `Always run /verify right before the commit command (never for docs or tests).` In 2.1.296 the check matches on the name only (`verify: e.some(n => n.name === "verify")`), so gstack's skill gets that line on every commit.

#4508 made that pre-commit call cheap (the quick pass, plus `verify_before_commit`). It says the skill keeps its name "as asked", and it does not fix the hidden built-in:

- `gstack-config set verify_before_commit off` makes the quick pass skip. The skill is still named `verify`, so Claude Code still adds the commit line, and the agent still loads gstack's 12 KB SKILL.md to read `skipped` (the cost #4508 measured: ~2.4x a commit with no gstack).
- The built-in `verify` stays hidden whatever the setting is.

Seen here: an agent committing code ran gstack's `/verify` because of the commit line. It got `VERIFY skipped: the repo's check commands are not trusted yet`, after it had already run the repo's own check command on the same tree. The user did not know `/verify` was gstack's, and did not know a built-in existed.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Install gstack on Claude Code ≥ 2.1.286 (here: gstack 1.102.0.0, Claude Code 2.1.296).
2. Start a session. The skill list shows `verify: … (gstack)` and no built-in `verify`. The Bash tool description has `Always run /verify right before the commit command`.
3. Make a code change and ask the agent to commit: it invokes gstack's `/verify` first.
4. `mv ~/.claude/skills/verify` out of the way and start a new session: the commit line now points at the built-in `verify`, which is listed again.

## Proposal

Install the skill under a name that does not collide with a Claude Code built-in, for example `gstack-verify` (only this one skill, not the whole `--prefix` mode), keeping `verify` as an opt-in alias for users who want gstack's loop on every commit. Setup could also warn when a gstack skill name shadows a Claude Code bundled skill (today: `verify`).

Local workaround in use: after each upgrade, remove the gstack-owned `skills/verify` and write `skills/gstack-verify/SKILL.md` as a copy with `name: gstack-verify` (the same rewrite `_install_alias_skill_md` does for aliases). It has to be re-run after every `./setup`, which re-creates `skills/verify`.

## Readiness report

Run after the local workaround above.

```text
gstack doctor 1.102.0.0
ok              install root    ~/.claude/skills/gstack: claude global current (1.102.0.0)
ok              rescue refs     none in ~/.claude/skills/gstack
ok              state root      ~/.gstack durable=yes (selected by default)
warn            bun             1.3.11 at ~/.local/share/mise/shims/bun is below the tested 1.4.2
                                fix: bun upgrade (https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md#bun-too-old)
ok              hooks           19 hook(s) parse
not configured  codex           codex_reviews disabled; outside reviews in /review, /ship, /autoplan and /codex skip Codex
not configured  artifacts sync  off; cross-machine artifacts sync is unavailable
ok              browse bundle   browse/dist built
ok              binaries        find-browse, design, pdf, gstack-global-discover launch (4 of 4)
ok              cso             native helper 1.102.0.0 (a529769efd98)
ok              claude code     2.1.296 (Claude Code) at ~/.local/bin/claude
ok              session journal largest of 1: 3.4 MiB
ok              guard log       no guard decisions logged
ok              CLAUDE.md       no gstack section lists skills
11 ok, 1 warn, 2 not configured, 0 fail
```

## Environment

- Host and version: Claude Code 2.1.296 (the commit line is absent in 2.1.280, present in 2.1.296)
- OS: macOS (Darwin 25.6.0, arm64)

title: Destructive-command check catches abbreviated --no-dry-run, stops over-blocking /dev/shm, and the redactor keeps regex literals with a slash in brackets
body:
The destructive-command check now denies `git push -fn --no-dry origin main`, and stops hard-denying a `--no-dry-run` that git reads as a push-option value and redirects into /dev/shm or /dev/fd. The secret redactor stops redacting regex literals like `/token=[A-Za-z0-9/]+/g`, and an escaped `\/` no longer ends a regex, which was leaking `/token=\/x`. Nothing to do; each change sits on top of the existing catches, with tests that dangerous neighbours still deny.
What changed, file by file - careful/bin/check-careful.sh: the push parser resets dry-run on `--no-dr`…`--no-dry-run` (checked against real git: `--no-d` is ambiguous and git refuses it), and skips one `--no-dry*` word right after `-o`, `--push-option` or a short flag group ending in `o`. Still denied: no `-n`, `-o` taking another value, a value attached in the group (`-fnox`), a second `--no-dry`. - careful/bin/check-careful.sh: the /dev redirect pre-scan skips `>/dev/shm/` and `>/dev/fd/` lines only; those still go through the on-disk folder lookup. Still denied: /dev/sda, /dev/shm/../sda, /dev/shm/sda/../../sdb, /dev/./sda, /dev//sda, a real disk beside a shm redirect, and /dev/./sda behind 70 decoy redirects. - lib/redact-patterns.ts: `isRegexLiteralBody` finds the closing slash outside character classes and escapes. - test/helpers/native-auto-decide.ts: a skill load whose output holds the loader's own `SKILL_START:` line (a start that timed out partway) is no longer credited as the session's start.

title: Fix /ship review counting, cleared reviewer notes and security findings in the posted PR description (GST-3343)
body:
/ship no longer stalls on summary notes a reviewer already cleared, counts only full review passes as rounds, records a round approval relayed during a stopped run, and keeps security findings out of the ship record it posts in the PR description. These four bugs each stopped a real /ship run until someone edited a record by hand; the goal is unattended shipping that finishes on its own. Nothing to do as a reader.
What changed Four things made unattended /ship runs stop and wait for someone to edit a record by hand. Each now works on its own: - When a reviewer reports no blocking findings, bullets such as "noted P2 findings", "deferred P1" or "P0 or P1" are read as notes the lead lowers with a reason, instead of findings nobody can clear. A bullet that names a real open finding still blocks until judged. - The scoped re-read after the one fix round no longer counts as a review round in the review loop, the PR history, the pre-push check or the ship record. docs/review-policy.md says the same. - `gstack-approvals round-grant` accepts `--owner-ref :` with the owner's words while a /ship run is stopped, and records the grant as relayed from that message. - The ship record's list of round grants shows a security finding as its ruled public form ("README.md:515 (red-team, ruled not security class)") or as an opaque id. When a security finding stays hidden, the grant's free-text reason is hidden too, so posting the PR body no longer stops on the finding and no longer publishes a description of it.

Each of these bugs stopped a real run (a reviewer note that could not be lowered, a round count that read a re-check as a second round, a grant that could not be recorded while a stopped run still held its checkout, and a ship record the PR-description scanner refused), and each needed a hand edit to get past.

title: Fix ready notes, landing decisions, release PR descriptions and squash messages (GST-3343)
body:
Landing a ready PR now reads its gate decisions from the PR's ready note, and the ready note, a reopened release PR and a stacked PR's squash message now say the right thing. Each of these stopped a landing or left a wrong public record until someone fixed it by hand; the goal is unattended shipping that lands on its own. Nothing to do as a reader.
What changed - `gstack-ship-queue ready` writes the signed, applied, non-security gate decisions into the ready note, and landing reads them from there beside its own approval store, under the same checks. When both hold a decision for the same finding, the newer one wins. `--accept-gate-disposition` still decides what lands. Security decisions stay private and are never written to the public note. - The ready note shows the decision trail's flags from its trail-read row instead of a placeholder line, and calls a PR from a fork an outside PR that was not trial-merged, rather than a sibling. - Reopening a release PR rewrites its description with the new release notes. Off Capy it edits the PR with gh and fails if GitHub refuses; on Capy it hands the new description to the host's PR tool instead of writing to GitHub as the owner. - When /ship's finish step left no plan line, the ready note writes the plan's public form without the plan record's row. - A stacked PR's squash message no longer repeats its parent's trailers. - docs/ship-budget.md says how to restart the budget meter for a stopped run whose spending record was already closed, and docs/troubleshooting.md says landing also reads the ready note's decisions.
Tests Each code fix has a test that failed first: test/ship-queue-land-direct.test.ts (including a newer store decision beating an older ready-note one), test/ship-queue-ready-tail.test.ts, test/release-stamp.test.ts (including the reopen hand-off on Capy), test/plan-record.test.ts and test/squash-message.test.ts. The nine focused test files passed locally at f78d2f73 (227 tests), and the full free suite passed in CI at the same tree (run 44885071384).
Why Landing, release and squash records should be right without a person copying files or fixing text by hand.
Blast radius Only gstack's own shipping tools change: `gstack-ship-queue ready`, `land` and `verify`, `gstack-release-stamp open` on a reopen, and the squash message land writes. A ready note written before this change has no decisions in it, so landing reads only the local store, as before.
Documentation **Status:** updated. One factual fix in docs/troubleshooting.md; no blockers. Scope: 6 commits (6cac5ab..ebdab82), 17 files changed. Covers the gate decisions that land now reads from the READY note, the trail-read flags line, how fork PRs are labelled in trial merges, the release PR body being rewritten on reopen, the plan line taken from /ship finish, trailers in a stacked PR's squash message, and restarting the budget meter for a stopped run whose spending record was already closed. title: Reader subagents on Capy stop sending telemetry, error runs report their error class, and test fixtures stop reading the owner's settings
body:
On a Capy machine, a shell that never loaded gstack's launch file (such as a review subagent's) now sends no usage data instead of falling back to the machine setting, as the privacy doc already promised. Error runs now fill the existing error_class field from their exit reason, and each setup step and outcome is reported at most once a day per install, so a loop rerunning setup no longer floods the counts. Tests no longer inherit the owner's preferences file, skill loadout or plugin state, which caused false failures.
Details - bin/gstack-telemetry-tier: a checkout with the Capy installer's state file reports `off` unless the Capy opt-in applies, also when reached through a host directory that links only `bin/` (Codex and the other linked hosts). A shell that did load the launch file (the main agent itself, or a subagent that runs the install check) still sends under the owner's opt-in; telling those apart needs a variable set by the review dispatcher, which is a reviewer-prompt change and is not in this PR. - bin/gstack-skill-end passes `--error-class` from exit_reason's fixed list (blocked, tool_error, test_failed, context_limit, gave_up) on error runs. No new field. - bin/gstack-telemetry-log: an onboarding event is recorded once per step and outcome per install per UTC day, using a marker file in the analytics folder. - scripts/lib/shard-engine.ts adds GSTACK_PREFERENCES_FILE and GSTACK_LOADOUT_SKILL_ROOT to the launch markers the test sandbox and preload strip; test-setup.ts also drops CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA; test/helpers/ship-bin-fixture.ts drops every marker itself, so it holds when the preload does not load. - test/launch-env-echo-ratchet.test.ts: its installer regex was anchored to the line start and missed the two exports written by conditional lines; it now finds every `echo "export …"` line, so the check is stricter.

Deferred: 4b upgrade_completed (real upgrades go through /gstack-upgrade and session-update, which never send it; fix needs a template change and regeneration), 4c channel (no such field; needs ingest), the sourced-launch-file half of item 2 (reviewer brief change, needs the no-loss replay). title: README and docs no longer say gstack makes your agent fix more bugs (GST-3261)
body:
The README now says plainly that gstack doesn't make a coding agent fix more everyday bugs, and describes `/review` and `/ship` by what they check and record. Why: our own test on 100 GitHub bugs and features found no gain (Claude Opus 5.5 fixed 58 with gstack, 61 of 99 without), so the README shouldn't promise one. Nothing to do: docs only.
What changed ![README: 'What gstack is for' now says what /review and /ship check and record, and a new paragraph says gstack doesn't make the agent fix more bugs](https://api.capy.ai/pr-assets/dSFQAB_XUBfS10gTEqcdNwuKq2r-6KH6_4jzd3omGqM.png) README: "What gstack is for" now says what `/review` and `/ship` check and record, and a new paragraph says gstack doesn't make the agent fix more bugs. - README: a new "What it doesn't do" paragraph with the result and links. Five lines that promised fewer bugs ("Catch what CI misses", "AI-written changes you can trust", "/review finds the bugs…", "Nothing falls through the cracks") now say what the tool does. - docs/skills.md: the `/review` row and the Greptile triage line, kept in step with the README. - docs/why-gstack.md and docs/ON_THE_LOC_CONTROVERSY.md: Garry's numbers stay, credited to AI coding agents plus his workflow, with a note linking the test. The Karpathy section says gstack has a step for each failure mode, not that it enforces them.
Why A reader of the README was told gstack would "catch what CI misses" and make "AI-written changes you can trust". The skill-pack head-to-head (garrytan/gstack-evals#352, corrected by #387) found no difference in the fix rate with gstack on Claude Opus 5.5: -4.0 points, 95% interval -11.0 to +2.2, and security fixes tied at 29 of 60. So the docs now say what the tools do instead of promising a higher fix rate.

The review checklist found no blockers, and a second-model review (openai/gpt-6.1-sol) came back clean. Every number in the added lines was checked against the results page and its correction, and each one matches.

title: Destructive-command check catches more force pushes and outside deletes, stops over-blocking /dev/shm, and the redactor keeps regex literals intact
body:
The destructive-command check now catches force pushes to main hidden behind abbreviated or misplaced dry-run flags, and asks before deletes that reach outside the project through a `cd` into a system folder or a device node under /dev. It also stops hard-blocking two safe cases (a `--no-dry-run` that is really a push-option value, and files under /dev/shm and /dev/fd), and the secret redactor stops mangling regex literals with a slash in brackets. Nothing to do; every change sits on top of the existing catches, with tests that dangerous neighbours still deny.
Changes, with the commands they cover careful/bin/check-careful.sh, toward denying or asking more: - `git push -fn --no-dry origin main`: any unambiguous prefix of `--no-dry-run` (`--no-dr` and longer, checked against real git) undoes `-n`. - `git push -f -o -n origin main`, `-fo -n`, `--push -n`, `--push-opt --dry-run`: the value of `-o`/`--push-option` (abbreviations included) keeps the dry-run state before it, while its other effects still count. - `git push -f4`, `-4f`, `-fo-n`, `-f -4o -n`: a short flag group with a digit still forces; it never starts a dry run. - `cd /etc/nginx && rm -f sites-enabled/default`, `cd /usr/local/lib && rm -f libdemo.so`: a relative delete after a `cd` into a system folder asks, like the absolute path already did. After `;` the folder is unknown to the check, so that form is unchanged. - `rm -f /dev/loop0`, `for i in 0 1 2 3; do rm -f /dev/loop$i; done`, `rm /dev/nvme0n1`: removing a device node asks. careful/bin/check-careful.sh, two over-catches removed by exemptions on top of the existing catch: - `git push -fn -o --no-dry-run origin main`: a `--no-dry*` word that git reads as the push-option value no longer undoes `-n`. - `echo x > /dev/shm/sda`, `printf x > /dev/fd/disk1`: a disk-like name directly inside /dev/shm or /dev/fd skips the /dev pre-scan and is still looked up on disk. Still denied: /dev/sda, /dev/shm/../sda, /dev/./sda, /dev//sda, and a disk redirect right after one (`>/dev/shm/sda>/dev/mmcblk0`). Elsewhere: - lib/redact-patterns.ts: a regex literal's closing slash is found outside character classes and escapes, so `/token=[A-Za-z0-9/]+/g` stays readable and an escaped slash no longer ends the literal (that case was leaking a URL-path secret). - test/helpers/native-auto-decide.ts: a skill load whose output holds the loader's own `SKILL_START:` line (a start that timed out partway) is not credited as the session's start.
Agent notes Lane GSTA-685, small-fix batch B items 6, 7(a)(d)(e), 8(a) and 9. Successor to #4594, closed unmerged after its round-2 review found the redirect-terminator blocker (Captain GSTA-36 ruling C: split, not an exception). Also fixes the three force-push gaps #4594's first review found on main. Item 5 dropped (not reproducible: the export-subst ratchet already catches `export $(` in heredoc bodies). Deferred: 7(b) slow-probe timeout, 7(c) warn vs refuse past the probe cap (behavior design), 8(b) skill-load degrade (resolver change regenerating 56 SKILL.md files). Pre-existing, not changed: `echo x >/tmp/sda>/dev/mmcblk0` (same terminator cause, outside this PR's exemption). Redactor fix carried from the second-model patch in handoffs/GSTA-675. Every fixed item has a test that failed before the fix. title: Run Free Tests shards on 16-core runners to cut about a minute (GST-3303)
body:
Free Tests now runs its shards on 16-core Ubicloud runners with eight test workers each, up from 8-core runners with four. In two trial runs this took about a minute off the slowest shard; the first five pull request runs after it lands are the real check. This is part of making pull request CI faster. title: careful: force-push check fires on a plain git push when a later command in the same line has a +token or -f (e.g. date +%F)
body:
gstack 1.101.0.0 (b7022438597e), `careful/bin/check-careful.sh`.

## What happens

The destructive-command check asks for confirmation ("Destructive: git force-push rewrites remote history") on an ordinary push when the same Bash command contains a `+` token or `-f` somewhere else. This command triggered it:

```bash
git add .planning/STATE.md && git commit -q -m "docs(state): ..." && git push -q 2>&1 | grep -v "^remote:"; git log --oneline -1; echo "$(date +%F) checkpoint" >> notes.log
```

Nothing in it force-pushes. The `+%F` belongs to `date`.

## Cause

Lines 340 to 345 run two independent greps over the whole command string:

```bash
if [ -z "$WARN" ] && grep -qE 'git\s+push\s' <<< "$CMD_MEDIUM" 2>/dev/null \
  && grep -qE '(-f\b|--force|(^|[[:space:]])\+[^[:space:]])' <<< "$CMD_MEDIUM" 2>/dev/null; then
```

The first finds `git push`, and the second finds `+%F` from `date`. The second grep isn't limited to the push's own arguments, so any later `+token` or `-f` anywhere in the line counts. That includes `date +%F`, `chmod +x`, `rm -f`, `tail -f`, and `sort -f`. Since the check is a PreToolUse hook, it prompts even in bypass-permissions mode.

## Expected

Match force flags only among the arguments of the `git push` itself, stopping at the first `;`, `&&`, `||`, `|`, newline, or redirect. A rough version:

```bash
push_args=$(grep -oE 'git\s+push\b[^;&|<>]*' <<< "$CMD_MEDIUM")
grep -qE '(^|\s)(-f|--force(-with-lease)?)(\s|$)|(^|\s)\+[^[:space:]]' <<< "$push_args"
```

A real `git push origin +main`, `git push -f`, or `git push --force` should still warn.

title: Destructive-command check catches more force pushes and outside deletes, and stops asking about quoted spellings
body:
The destructive-command check now catches force pushes to main hidden behind abbreviated or misplaced dry-run flags, and asks before deletes that reach a system folder through a `cd` (including `cd ../../etc`) or a device node under /dev. Quoting no longer changes its decision: a quoted build-folder delete or a quoted `gh` title or body gets the same answer as its unquoted spelling, which was already allowed. Fixes #4628, fixes #4601. Nothing to do; no command that main asks about or blocks becomes allowed except those same-command spellings.
Changes, with the commands they cover careful/bin/check-careful.sh, toward asking or blocking more: - `git push -fn --no-dry origin main`: any unambiguous prefix of `--no-dry-run` undoes `-n`. - `git push -f -o -n origin main`, `-fo -n`, `--push -n`: the value of `-o`/`--push-option` keeps the dry-run state before it and never takes a value itself. - `git push -f4`, `-4f`, `-fo-n`: a short flag group with a digit still forces. `-fn4` and `-4fn` stay dry runs, as main reads them. - `git push -f -o ci.skip origin` on main: the push is read both with and without the push-option value as an operand, so it is blocked like `git push -f origin`. - `cd /etc/nginx && rm -f sites-enabled/default`, `cd ../../../etc && rm -f hosts`, `cd /dev && rm -f sda`: a relative delete after a `cd` into a system folder asks; `..` is folded the way `cd` reads it. - `rm -f /dev/loop0`, `/dev/sg0`, `/dev/zram0`, `/dev/ram0`, `/dev/mtd0`, `/dev/ubi0`, `/dev//sdb1`: removing a device node asks. Spelling-independent decisions, each with negative controls in test/careful-replay.test.ts: - `rm -rf "/home/me/app/dist"` is allowed like `rm -rf /home/me/app/dist` when nothing in the quotes differs from the unquoted spelling (no `$`, backtick, glob, `~`, space or `..`). - `gh issue create --title "… git push … -f"` and the quoted `--title`/`--body` (`-t`/`-b`) of `gh issue`/`gh pr` create, comment and edit are masked like a commit message, matching their backslashed spelling. A double-quoted value with `$(` or a backtick, a later statement, a pipe, `echo`, `bash -c` and other `gh` subcommands are still read. - `git push -fn > -o --no-dry-run origin main`, `git push -n -f --receive-pack -o --no-dry-run origin main`: a push-option value never makes a push safer. It can't start a dry run, and a `--no-dry-run` after `-o` still undoes `-n`, since a redirect or another option can take `-o` itself. - `git push -fn4 --no-dry-run origin main`: a later `--no-dry-run` undoes the `-n` in a digit group. test/helpers/native-auto-decide.ts: a skill load whose output holds the loader's own `SKILL_START:` line is not credited as the session's start.
Main-vs-head comparison 5,920 push, redirect and cd-then-delete commands: 5,281 same, 639 stricter, 0 looser. 18,346 more commands covering quoted deletes, `gh` titles and bodies, `cd ..`, /dev nodes and push flag groups: 17,411 same, 467 stricter, 468 looser (unchanged by the last two commits, which only add asks or denies). Of the 468, 216 were asks on main and 252 were blocks (quoted `gh` text such as `--title 'git push -f origin main'`); main allows the backslashed spelling of every one. title: Let the /ship conductor trial end at the remote gate when a case's base isn't main (GST-3003)
body:
The /ship conductor trial plan now ends a trial at the remote gate when the case base isn't main, gives the no-gstack arm bun and its dependencies, and audits every counted trial for exposure to the plan.
Why: in the uncounted pilot no trial could finish shipping, because the remote test gate can't pass on a non-main base; one arm also read the plan on main.
Nothing to do: no bar, arm, decision or catch rule changes, and no counted trial has run.

<details><summary>What changed</summary>

In the uncounted pilot, no trial could reach the end of /ship: on a case whose base branch isn't main, the final check refuses the remote test gate (`base_mismatch` on the CI route, `paid_only` on the VM route). The plan now treats that refusal as the end of a trial, and the shared brief tells each arm to stop there and report it.

- A C or F trial ends when /ship finishes, when its final check refuses the remote test gate, or wherever else /ship stops. Cost, wall time and `calls=` are measured to that end, and any work to get around the refusal is counted and reported.
- The no-gstack arm is recorded as it ran (a container on the runner's machine, no drive mounted) and gains bun and the installed dependencies, so it can run tests the way the other arms' CI does.
- A new exposure audit runs on every counted C and F trial (reads of team notes or handoffs that name the trial, and diffs or history against main on the planted path), with a sensitivity analysis that repeats each comparison without the flagged trials.
- Budget: the pilot row becomes its measured $83 and a second pilot adds $85; the estimate moves from $3,073 to $2,995 and the worst case from $3,181 to $3,103, and the $3,250 cap is unchanged.

</details>

<details><summary>Why</summary>

In the pilot, every trial stopped at the same remote-gate refusal, so the plan as written could never produce a counted trial. With this change, trials end at a point every arm can reach, and the comparison stays fair because the same wall applies to both gstack arms.

</details>

<details><summary>Blast radius</summary>

Only the preregistration and one changelog fragment change; no code, prompt or skill file is touched. The budget figures were recomputed from the table by the review and by the documentation audit (file read), and the targeted tests for eval plans and docs passed (88 tests ran).

</details>

title: /ship's review no longer stops when Capy's drive sync database grows past 100 MB (GST-3359)
body:
The review's download sweep now ignores Capy's own drive sync database (`state.db` and its SQLite side files under `~/.capy/drive-engine`). Why: that database grew past 100 MB during a review stage on a Capy machine, the sweep took it for a reader's download, and the pass blocked every later stage while the file existed. Nothing to do: any other download of 100 MB or more, under `~/.capy/drive-engine` or `~/.capy/work` included, still counts.
What changed and how it was tested - `lib/review-sweep.ts`: the inventory skips only files named `state.db`, `state.db-wal`, `state.db-shm` or `state.db-journal` below `~/.capy/drive-engine`. That folder is still walked, so any other big file or repository there still counts; the old check is otherwise untouched. - Why a path exemption and not "only files missing from the start snapshot": the snapshot option would let a stage overwrite an existing small file with a large download, and that must stay a violation. Nothing but Capy's sync engine writes its database files. - `test/review-sweep.test.ts`: two tests through the real `gstack-review-dispatch sweep` command with `HOME` set as on Capy. The first (written first, failed on main with `FETCH_VIOLATION … drive-engine/loc/state.db`) grows a state.db present at stage start past the line and expects a clean sweep. The second is the deny control: a new large file under `~/.capy/work` or `~/.capy/drive-engine`, and an existing file written past the line, are all still violations. - Docs: `docs/review-policy.md#what-readers-may-fetch` and `docs/troubleshooting.md#fetch-violation` name both skipped folders.
Documentation Scope: the diff from 7fe1900f to HEAD on review-sweep-skips-capy-drive-engine, which changes lib/review-sweep.ts and its test, docs/review-policy.md, docs/troubleshooting.md and one changelog.d fragment. The working tree has no staged, unstaged or untracked changes. Result: current. The review-policy and troubleshooting docs already describe the new behavior. The per-stage fetch sweep ignores only the Capy drive sync database files under ~/.capy/drive-engine (state.db and its -wal, -shm and -journal files). Every other file there, and anything under ~/.capy/work, still counts as a violation when it is 100 MB or more. That matches the code, and no other doc needed an update. Debt: none found.

title: Tell /ship review readers never to kill processes they didn't start (GST-3360)
body:
/ship's review readers are now told, in every brief, never to stop or signal a process they didn't start: no `pkill`, `killall` or kill by name. Why: a reader on a machine shared by several /ship runs ran `pkill -x sleep` and ended other runs' processes. Nothing to do: the rule rides in the workspace paragraph that closes every dispatched brief.
What changed - `lib/review-brief.ts`: a `PROCESS_RULE` sentence inside the workspace paragraph. Both review-pass dispatch sites call `withWorkspace`, so every blocking and audit brief now carries it. - `test/review-brief-process-rule.test.ts`: fails on main, passes here. - `docs/review-policy.md`: the reader-brief contract now mentions the rule. - A `changelog.d` fragment.
Why A reader on a shared machine ran `pkill -x sleep` and ended processes that other review runs had started. Readers dispatched on Capy run no Claude Code hooks, so the brief is where the rule can hold today.
Blast radius Only the text of dispatched reader briefs changes. Brief hashes are computed after rendering and checked against the file on disk, so briefs already in flight stay valid (read in `bin/gstack-review-dispatch`). The full free suite passed in CI run 44897535257 at this head.

No hook or sandbox enforces it, so a reader that ignores its brief could still run pkill. - `lib/review-brief.ts:229`: a team rule asks for a no-loss replay before reviewer-prompt changes merge. Whether it applies to this process-safety sentence is the owner's call. - `lib/review-pass.ts:213`: reader prompts built outside `withWorkspace`, such as outside-voice runs from skill templates, don't get the rule. - `test/review-brief-process-rule.test.ts:8`: the test's regex pins the rule's exact wording.

title: Install gstack into Gemini CLI, and slim older installs down to the packages they run on (#1247)
body:
`./setup --host gemini` now installs every gstack skill into Gemini CLI, and installs made before v1.91.231.0 drop about 510 MB of test and eval packages they never used (#1247, #3447).
Why: you can run gstack from the agent you already use, and an older install takes half the disk space.
Nothing to do: the next `./setup` slims an older install on its own; contributors keep the full toolchain with `bin/dev-setup`.

<details><summary>What changed</summary>

![docs/hosts.md now says how Gemini CLI finds and loads gstack skills](https://api.capy.ai/pr-assets/ibQ9eAaNirmuVjAG8dIAMFd3g-rf4KyMVRs5BNyj8mc.png)

docs/hosts.md now says how Gemini CLI finds and loads gstack skills.

<details><summary>Before/after as text: docs/hosts.md now says how Gemini CLI finds and loads gstack skills</summary>

~~~diff
--- Before · docs/hosts.md § Per-host notes at 6049245 · source text
+++ After · docs/hosts.md § Per-host notes on this branch · source text
@@ ⋯ 10 unchanged ⋯ @@
 never for a Gemini-CLI-only `~/.gemini`. The Antigravity 2.0 app and IDE read
 `~/.gemini/config/skills`, which this host does not install.
 
+Gemini CLI loads gstack skills itself when a task matches (`activate_skill`,
+after you approve); ask for `gstack-office-hours`, or list them with
+`/skills list`. Setup writes only `~/.gemini/skills/gstack*` and never
+`~/.agents/skills`, and `--host auto` selects Gemini CLI only when `gemini` is on
+`PATH`. Inside a repo with a project-local Codex install, Gemini CLI uses the
+Codex skills in `.agents/skills` (the workspace tier wins), and workspace skills
+load only in trusted folders (`/trust`).
+
~~~

</details>

People asked for gstack in Gemini CLI (#1247, #2309), and there was no way to get it. `./setup --host gemini` (or `gemini-cli`) now links every skill into `~/.gemini/skills` as `gstack-<skill>`, where Gemini CLI lists them and loads one when you ask for it by name. `--host auto` picks Gemini CLI only when `gemini` is on your PATH, and `gstack-uninstall` removes only what gstack put there, so your own skills stay.

Separately, `./setup` used to treat any checkout with TypeScript installed as a contributor's, so every install made before v1.91.231.0 kept about 510 MB of test and eval packages forever (#3447). A clone now counts as a contributor's only when it is marked (`git config gstack.contributor true`, which `bin/dev-setup` sets, or `GSTACK_CONTRIBUTOR=1` for one run). An unmarked clone that still has the dev toolchain moves to production dependencies once. Setup sets the old `node_modules` aside, installs, checks every runtime package resolves, and only then deletes the old copy. If anything fails, the old copy goes back. A second `./setup` started during that move now stops with a message instead of installing over it.

</details>

<details><summary>Why</summary>

"Gemini CLI support" (#1247) was one of the longest-open requests, and the dev-package bloat (#3447) cost every long-time user about half a gigabyte. Both serve the README's goal of gstack working in the agent you already run, without setup getting in your way.

</details>

<details><summary>Blast radius</summary>

The change touches `setup`, `gstack-uninstall`, the host registry (`hosts/index.ts`) and the generated skill size allowlist, so every host's install runs through the new contributor check. That is safe because a marked or CI checkout never migrates, a failed install restores the full `node_modules`, and `test/setup-production-deps.test.ts` runs both paths, including an interrupted move and a held lock, against a real Bun fixture (script ran).

</details>

<details><summary>Test Coverage</summary>

Coverage: 86% value-weighted (91% including weakly covered paths).
Test value: 0 tests written by the coverage step, 2 existing tests extended (`test/setup-production-deps.test.ts`: an offline-recovery case and a live-lock case).
Two paths have no test yet, listed as proposals:
- A migration lock file that holds an empty process id. Proposed test: write an empty lock and check that setup reclaims it.
- A `~/.gemini/skills/gstack` folder the user owns (not a link). Proposed test: check that setup leaves it alone and reports it skipped.

Tests ran: free 1681 (CI run 44903728230 at this head).
