title: Give the /ship conductor trial's judge one more attempt on fresh labels (GST-3003)
body:
The /ship conductor trial plan gives its real-problem judge one more attempt, checked once on fresh labels, and stops the trial incomplete if it misses its bar again. Why: the judge agreed with the hand labels at kappa 0.20, then 0.48 after one revision, against a 0.6 bar, while a second blind labeller matched the first at 0.84. Nothing to do: no bar, arm, decision or catch rule changes, and no counted trial has run.
What changed ![The plan's new Second judge attempt step makes the old labels development data and checks the revised judge once on fresh labels](https://api.capy.ai/pr-assets/l1LzwW9PwAWjVTc7mjuIT1Q4vcjIUD1uZv0YmX8PIPE.png) The plan's new Second judge attempt step makes the old labels development data and checks the revised judge once on fresh labels.
Before/after as text: The plan's new Second judge attempt step: the old labels become development data and the revised judge is checked once on fresh labels ~~~diff --- Before · docs/evals/ship-conductor-fold-prereg.md § Procedure at df4d0bd · source text +++ After · docs/evals/ship-conductor-fold-prereg.md § Procedure on this branch · source text @@ ⋯ 20 unchanged ⋯ @@ case 4, then case 5, until both counts are met or this stage reaches $150. These trials never enter a counted comparison. +**Second judge attempt (uncounted), added 2026-11-21.** The judge stage's 207 labels have now been used for two +checks, so they become development data. The judge prompt is revised against them once more: it carries the +labellers' rubric word for word, runs at reasoning high, and sees each changed file at the case head beside the diff, +because the labellers read the code at the head. The judge model stays GPT-6 Astra. The script, prompt and input +hashes are posted on GST-3003 before any new finding exists. Then C and F each run one uncounted trial on case 4 and +one on case 5, and N one uncounted trial on each of cases 1 to 10, under the same briefs and end rule. If these hold +fewer than 48 findings, or fewer than 24 from C and F, C and F each add one uncounted trial on case 6. Every finding +these runs list is labelled by the same blind procedure (one labeller, the same brief, no access to the earlier labels +or any judge output) and frozen with a SHA-256 before the judge sees any. `gstack-eval-plan judge --check` runs once +on those labels, and that line is the judge check. These trials and labels never enter a counted comparison. + **End of a trial.** A C or F trial ends at `SHIP_RECEIPT:`, at finish's Step 16 refusal of `pregate.json/remote_gate` with `base_mismatch` or `paid_only` (the case bases are not main, so that gate cannot clear; it is the same wall for both arms and is not a harness failure), or wherever else /ship stops. Cost, wall time and `calls=` are measured to that ~~~
The judge that decides which review findings are real problems missed its agreement bar twice, so its counts could not be used. The plan now treats the 207 existing labels as development data, revises and freezes the judge against them, and checks it once on fresh labels from new trials that never count. If it misses again, the trial stops incomplete instead of trying a third time. - The dated amendment note says the 0.84 agreement comes from two Opus 5.5 labellers given one brief, so it shows the brief gives the same labels twice, not that two people would agree. - Scoring now says the judge also sees the changed files at the case head, and that the check that counts is the one on the fresh labels. The held-out table says the same about what the judge may read. - Stop rules: a miss on the fresh labels stops the run incomplete; the first judge stage and the second attempt together share the $150 limit. - Budget: the second attempt adds $80, and a second labeller plus this amendment's review adds $35. The estimate is now $3,173 (worst case $3,200), under the unchanged $3,250 cap.
Why "The judge failed its bar twice." Without a judge that agrees with the labels, the trial cannot count real problems found beyond the planted bug. This gives the judge one honest, preregistered retry on labels it has never seen, and ends the trial if that fails.
Blast radius Only the preregistration and one changelog line change; no code, prompt or test reads this file. `gstack-eval-plan prereg --check` still passes on it (script ran), and every budget row sums to the stated $3,173 (script ran).
Pre-Landing Review Pre-Landing Review: No issues found. One advisory note: the older Stop rules bullet ("fix the script or the judge prompt and relabel") can be read beside the new "no further attempt" bullet; the newer, more specific bullet governs, and the plan's rules were left as the owner wrote them. A second-model review (GPT-6.1 Sol) read the whole diff and found nothing blocking.
Eval Results No evals affected: the selector picked no behavioral probes and no quality judges for these two files.
Documentation **Status:** updated. One factual correction in the preregistration; no blockers. **Scope:** base df4d0bd..9993e1e on g1-judge-gets-one-more-attempt: one commit touching `docs/evals/ship-conductor-fold-prereg.md` (fourth amendment: a second judge attempt on fresh labels, a new stop rule and budget rows) and the new changelog fragment `changelog.d/capy-g1-judge-second-attempt.md`. Nothing staged, unstaged or untracked. No skill templates, generated docs or code changed. **Documentation health:** - `docs/evals/ship-conductor-fold-prereg.md`: Updated. The Held-out exposure row now says the judge also reads the changed files at the case head, matching the amended Real problems section. The amendment's numbers check out: 103+104=207 labels, estimate $3,173, worst case $3,200 under the $3,250 cap, expected total $2,873. - `changelog.d/capy-g1-judge-second-attempt.md`: Current. One plain line that matches the change. **Coverage debt:** none. This adds no new public surface (commands, flags, skills or environment variables), only eval-plan procedure. **Diagram drift:** none. The changed docs contain no diagrams.

title: Codex skills no longer stop on temp-file cleanup, which Codex refuses as rm -f (GST-3364)
body:
Skills that clean up temp files now run on Codex: Codex CLI refuses any `rm` with a force flag, and 67 of the 1,239 shell blocks in gstack's Codex skills used one. This unblocks gstack on Codex (office-hours, review, ship, the plan reviews, spec and gstack-upgrade all hit it). Nothing to do after merging.
What Codex refuses, and where it comes from Codex 0.170's `codex-rs/shell-command/src/command_safety/is_dangerous_command.rs` (`rm_args_include_force_option`) flags any literal `rm` whose arguments before `--` include `--force` or a single-dash cluster containing `f` (`-f`, `-rf`, `-fr`, `-Rf`). It parses the whole script with tree-sitter, so text inside `trap '...'`, `$(...)` and `bash -c` counts too. `codex-rs/core/src/exec_policy.rs` then returns `Forbidden` when approvals are off ("rm -f style commands are not permitted. Use a safer approach") and `Prompt` otherwise. Both files are unchanged at tag `rust-v0.170.0`. The rule has been in place since the forced-rm hardening in 0.145 (openai/codex#33464).
What changed - The templates and shared resolvers that render into the Codex skills now use plain `rm ` where the file is known to exist, `rm 2>/dev/null || true` (or `[ ! -e ] || rm -- `) where it may already be gone, and `rm -r ` for folders. /ship's leftover-worktree cleanup adds `

title: The spawnSync overflow test no longer fails about once an hour on CI (GSTA-712)
body:
The raw-Bun overflow test in test/spawn-sync.test.ts stops failing at random on CI: its child process now writes 32 KiB instead of 200,000 bytes. Why: the old write sat 13 KB under Linux's 212,992-byte socket send buffer. When it didn't fit, the child hit a broken pipe and exited 1, so the test saw status 1 instead of 0. Trunk flagged it 22 times in one day, and every time it passed on retry. Nothing to do: this changes tests only.
Evidence - Trunk test cba2aa0b (quick tier, bun-default variant): 21 failed runs from 2026-11-21 00:18Z to 11:04Z, 6 of them on main pushes. Each failed in 10 to 15 ms with `Expected: 0, Received: 1` and passed on the serial retry (Free Tests 44842411894, 44886887009 and 19 more). - Local sweep on Bun 1.4.4 (one write, `maxBuffer` 1024): 200,000 and 210,000 bytes gave status 0 in 6 of 6 runs (about 320 ms each). 230,000 bytes gave status 1 in 4 of 6, the fast runs. 400,000 and 1,000,000 bytes gave status 1 in 6 of 6, in about 10 ms, with the child's `EPIPE: broken pipe, write`. That matches the CI failures. - strace: Bun's spawnSync reads one 66,560-byte chunk, sends SIGTERM (which the child ignores) and stops reading. The child's 200,000-byte `sendto` only succeeds when the whole write fits the send buffer. - After the change: 32 KiB gave status 0 with ENOBUFS in 600 of 600 runs (24 parallel processes). `bun test test/spawn-sync.test.ts test/script-invocation.test.ts test/spawnsync-timeout-tripwire.test.ts`: 47 pass, 0 fail, and 8 parallel copies of the first two files also passed. - test/script-invocation.test.ts used the same 200,000-byte child. Its wrapper test passed either way, but now the child really exits 0, which is the case that test is about.
What changed ![The overflow test's child now writes 32 KiB, which fits the socket send buffer, so it exits 0 every time](https://api.capy.ai/pr-assets/7jGETBJqcpw2K0q0CGd4ktRiYiYkJlQe5HwdD5d91Gc.png) The overflow test's child now writes 32 KiB, which fits the socket send buffer, so it exits 0 every time.
Before/after as text: The overflow test's child now writes 32 KiB, which fits the socket send buffer, so it exits 0 every time ~~~diff --- Before · before.txt · captured output +++ After · after.txt · captured output +const OVERFLOW = "process.on('SIGTERM', () => {}); process.stdout.write('x'.repeat(32768)); setTimeout(() => {}, 300);"; -const OVERFLOW = "process.on('SIGTERM', () => {}); process.stdout.write('x'.repeat(200000)); setTimeout(() => {}, 300);"; ~~~ The free test suite kept failing for no reason about once an hour. The spawnSync overflow check expected exit status 0 and sometimes got 1. Its child process now writes 32 KiB, which still runs far past the test's 1 KiB output limit but always fits the socket buffer, so the child really exits 0 and the check tests what it says. The same child in test/script-invocation.test.ts gets the same size.
Why "Trunk flagged it 21 times on 2026-11-21": a red free suite on main and on pull requests that went green on retry. A 200,000-byte write only succeeds when the whole write fits the 212,992-byte send buffer, so the test passed or failed on timing. With 32 KiB the outcome no longer depends on timing.
Blast radius Only two test files and a changelog fragment change; no product code, helper or assertion changes. The assertions still require status null with ENOBUFS from the wrappers, and both files passed 44 of 44 in five local runs on Bun 1.4.4 (script ran), with CI's free suite green at this head.
Pre-Landing Review No issues found. A testing reviewer and a second-model review (GPT-6.1 Sol) each read the whole diff and returned no findings. The second-model review saw one timeout in the unchanged wtreeFingerprint fixture (test/script-invocation.test.ts:223) while it ran tests alongside other work; five local runs of both files passed 44 of 44 each, and CI's free suite passed at this head.
Documentation **Status:** current. The test-only fix needs no doc changes. **Scope:** the diff from 27e5db99 to 0e0925d (2 commits): `test/spawn-sync.test.ts`, `test/script-invocation.test.ts` and `changelog.d/flaky-spawn-overflow-fixture-fits-send-buffer.md`. Nothing was staged, unstaged or new. I searched tracked Markdown and templates for references to the overflow fixture. **Documentation health:** - changelog.d/flaky-spawn-overflow-fixture-fits-send-buffer.md: current. It matches the diff and was reviewed only, not edited. - docs/, README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, AGENTS.md: current. None of them references the fixture. **Coverage debt:** none. No public surface changed. **Diagram drift:** none.
Tests - [x] bun test test/spawn-sync.test.ts test/script-invocation.test.ts: 44 pass, 0 fail (and 44 of 44 in each of five repeat runs) - [x] bun run test, carried from CI Free Tests run 44914101831 at this tree: green, 1,731 test files

title: gstack: gstack-brain-context-load is documented as running at every skill start, but nothing calls it
body:
GBrain retrieval at skill start appears to be unwired.
The docs and the helper both say the preamble runs `gstack-brain-context-load` at every skill start, but no runtime file calls it.

What the docs say:

> At every gstack skill start, the preamble runs
> `gstack-brain-context-load` which:

https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/blob/41729a023ecf4c8c41d95ad69c666f2fd619c8fb/setup-gbrain/memory.md?plain=1#L263-L271

> Called from the gstack preamble at every skill start. Reads the active skill's
> `gbrain.context_queries:` frontmatter (Layer 2) or falls back to a generic

https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/blob/41729a023ecf4c8c41d95ad69c666f2fd619c8fb/bin/gstack-brain-context-load.ts?plain=1#L3-L8

What the code does:
A search of `bin/`, `lib/`, `scripts/` and every `SKILL.md` finds no caller outside tests and the CHANGELOG.
`gstack-skill-start` wires `gstack-brain-sync`, not the context loader:
https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/blob/41729a023ecf4c8c41d95ad69c666f2fd619c8fb/bin/gstack-skill-start?plain=1#L392

Cost to users:
Skills that declare `gbrain.context_queries` (office-hours, plan-ceo-review and others) never get the "Prior office-hours sessions" or similar sections, so users who set up GBrain get less context than the docs promise.
`gstack-config set gbrain_context_load off` also suggests a working feature.

Possible fixes (your call which matches the intent):
1. Call the loader from `gstack-skill-start` (or `gstack-skill-load`) when GBrain is configured, under its 2 s budget.
2. If retrieval moved elsewhere on purpose, update `setup-gbrain/memory.md` and the helper header, and drop the unused `context_queries` blocks.

A related detail: office-hours' "Prior office-hours sessions" query filters `type: ceo-plan`, while office-hours saves pages tagged `design-doc`, so it would not match even once wired.

title: gstack: /design-review audit summaries match gstack-design-doc-find's design-doc pattern
body:
A `/design-review` audit summary can be picked up as the branch's design doc.

office-hours writes the design doc as `{user}-{branch}-design-{datetime}.md`:
https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/blob/41729a023ecf4c8c41d95ad69c666f2fd619c8fb/office-hours/sections/design-and-handoff.md.tmpl?plain=1#L19

/design-review writes its summary into the same folder as:
> Write a one-line summary to `<PROJECT_DIR>/{user}-{branch}-design-audit-{datetime}.md`
https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/blob/41729a023ecf4c8c41d95ad69c666f2fd619c8fb/design-review/SKILL.md.tmpl?plain=1#L289

`gstack-design-doc-find` picks the newest file matching `*-<branch>-design-*.md`, which matches both:
> #   1. newest $GSTACK_STATE_ROOT/projects/<slug>/*-<branch>-design-*.md
https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/blob/41729a023ecf4c8c41d95ad69c666f2fd619c8fb/bin/gstack-design-doc-find?plain=1#L10-L11

Cost to users:
After a design review, `/plan-ceo-review`, `/plan-eng-review` and `/autoplan` on that branch treat a one-line audit pointer as the design doc they review against.

Possible fixes (your call which matches the intent):
1. Rename the audit summary so it does not contain `-design-` after the branch (for example `{user}-{branch}-ui-audit-{datetime}.md`).
2. Exclude `*-design-audit-*` in `gstack-design-doc-find`.

title: gstack: /spec --execute PRs never auto-close the source issue
body:
The README says `/ship` auto-closes the source issue on merge, but this cannot happen for `/spec --execute` runs.

The archive records the branch `/spec` ran on:
> printf 'spec_branch: %s\n' "$(git branch --show-current 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)"
https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/blob/41729a023ecf4c8c41d95ad69c666f2fd619c8fb/spec/sections/gate-and-file.md.tmpl?plain=1#L199

`--execute` then spawns the work on a new branch:
> SPAWN_BRANCH="spec/${SLUG_TITLE}-$$"
https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/blob/41729a023ecf4c8c41d95ad69c666f2fd619c8fb/spec/sections/gate-and-file.md.tmpl?plain=1#L266

`/ship` selects an archive only by an exact `spec_branch` match with the current branch:
https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/blob/41729a023ecf4c8c41d95ad69c666f2fd619c8fb/ship/sections/pr-body.md.tmpl?plain=1#L45-L52

So the spawned session's `/ship` finds no matching archive and omits `Closes #N`, contrary to:
https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/blob/41729a023ecf4c8c41d95ad69c666f2fd619c8fb/spec/SKILL.md.tmpl?plain=1#L482-L487

Cost to users:
Issues filed by `/spec --execute` stay open after their PR merges, and the spec-to-PR link is lost.

Possible fixes (your call which matches the intent):
1. Rewrite `spec_branch` to `$SPAWN_BRANCH` in the archive (or a copy in the worktree) before spawning.
2. Let `/ship` match on a `spec_spawn_branch` field as well.

Found by reading the files at `41729a0`, not by a live run.

title: gstack: gstack-distill-free-text sends to the Anthropic API without an egress receipt
body:
One off-machine send skips the egress ledger.

The README:
> Every off-machine send writes a receipt you can audit with `gstack-egress list`.
https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/blob/41729a023ecf4c8c41d95ad69c666f2fd619c8fb/README.md?plain=1#L291

`gstack-distill-free-text`, which `/plan-tune` runs, posts the user's free-text answers to the Anthropic API through the SDK:
https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/blob/41729a023ecf4c8c41d95ad69c666f2fd619c8fb/bin/gstack-distill-free-text?plain=1#L195-L206

The script has no call into the egress library, so the send never appears in `gstack-egress list`.
The egress header describes the ledger as written at every enumerated sink:
https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/blob/41729a023ecf4c8c41d95ad69c666f2fd619c8fb/bin/gstack-egress?plain=1#L20-L21

Cost to users:
Users who audit what left the machine with `gstack-egress list` do not see that their typed question answers were sent to Anthropic.

Possible fix: route the call through the same receipt step the other sinks use (fail-closed like the brain-sync and telemetry sinks), and extend the egress wiring test to cover SDK calls, not only curl, fetch and git.

Found by reading the files at `41729a0`, not by a live run.

title: gstack: /design-shotgun never passes --reason, so taste memory never learns preferences
body:
The README says design-shotgun's "Taste memory learns what you like", but the preference fields are never written.

design-shotgun calls the updater with only a path:
> call `{{BIN_DIR}}/gstack-taste-update approved <approved image path>` (the
https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/blob/41729a023ecf4c8c41d95ad69c666f2fd619c8fb/design-shotgun/SKILL.md.tmpl?plain=1#L180-L184

The updater only extracts preferences from a reason string:
> that mentions fonts/colors/layouts/aesthetics. If the reason is missing,
> the session is recorded but dimensions don't get updated.
https://github.com/garrytan/gstack/blob/41729a023ecf4c8c41d95ad69c666f2fd619c8fb/bin/gstack-taste-update?plain=1#L163-L185

Cost to users:
The taste profile that design-shotgun and design-consultation rank against stays empty, so repeated sessions do not converge on the user's style.

1. Have design-shotgun pass `--reason "fonts: ...; colors: ...; layouts: ...; aesthetics: ..."` built from the approved variant's brief.
2. Have the updater read the variant brief or approved.json directly, as its own "v2" comment suggests.

+open=0
+open_after_release=1

A workflow's start used to renew one shared lease on the installation, and nothing released it when the workflow ended, so `gstack upgrade` stayed blocked until the lease was 120 minutes old. title: A finished /ship no longer blocks gstack-upgrade for two hours (GST-1205)

What changed - `gstack-skill-start` records each run on the install's workflow lease under its session id, and `gstack-skill-end` releases that run. A lease whose runs have all finished is `idle`, and `gstack-lease live` (what gstack-upgrade reads) skips it. A run that is still open, or a sibling run on the same harness, still holds the upgrade back. - `gstack-lease` gains `release` and `open` (exit 0 while a named run is open, 1 otherwise), `touch --run `, and an `idle` state in `list`. - The session id no longer loses its random part when urandom is unavailable, so two starts in the same second never share a lease run. - Review fix: `open` was missing from the verb list, so every `gstack-lease open` call exited 2; it is now accepted and tested, and `--help` prints the full usage.

title: /plan-tune's dream cycle now logs each send of your typed answers to Anthropic (#4617)
body:
`gstack-distill-free-text`, which /plan-tune's dream cycle runs, now writes an entry to gstack's send log (`gstack-egress list`) before it sends your typed answers to Anthropic, and sends nothing if it can't write that entry. Why: the README promises that every off-machine send is logged, and this was the one sender that skipped it. Reported by @robbiesierra in #4617. Nothing to do: these sends now show up in `gstack-egress list`.
What changed - **The fix.** Right before the Anthropic call, the script records the destination host (honoring `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`), how many answers went and the prompt size, using the same shared helper as every other sender. The entry never holds your answer text or your key. A second entry records whether the call succeeded. If the entry can't be written, the script stops with exit 3 before any request, and your answers wait for the next run. - The off-machine send test now fails when code calls a model provider (through an SDK, inside a shell script's inline Bun step, or over HTTP) without logging the send first. A new case proves that made-up unlogged senders fail, a logged one passes, and the senders that already log (the second-model review API runner, `context-bill --exact`, the design image calls and the fixed distill script) still pass. - **What the sweep found.** Besides the distill script, the stricter test flags two developer-only eval scripts, `scripts/judge-calibration.ts` and `scripts/preflight-agent-sdk.ts`. Both run only by hand with the developer's own key, import test helpers and send fixed test data, never user data, so they are listed as exempt with that reason. - **Docs.** ARCHITECTURE.md and docs/CONTRIBUTOR_REFERENCE.md now name this send among the ones that stop when they can't be logged, say the test also catches model-provider calls, and list developer-run test and eval tools among its exemptions. - **Tests.** Two new cases run the real script against a local stand-in for the Anthropic API: the log entry must exist when the request arrives and must not contain the answer text or key; with an unwritable log the script must fail, send nothing and leave the answers for later. Both fail on main. What is sent, consent prompts and telemetry stay as they were.
Why "`gstack-distill-free-text` sends my typed /plan-tune answers to Anthropic, but nothing shows up in `gstack-egress list`" (#4617). Every other off-machine send writes a log entry first; now this one does too, and the test that guards the send log catches the next model-provider call that forgets.
Blast radius Only `bin/gstack-distill-free-text` changes behavior. It gains one log write before its one API call and refuses to send when that write fails, which costs nothing because the answers stay queued for the next run. Evidence: script ran against a local stand-in API for success, refused-log and API-500 cases (exit 0, exit 3 with zero requests, exit 1 with an `error:500` outcome), and the full free test suite passed in CI at this head.

title: /review on Codex with OpenAI models no longer blocks a review that ran its adversarial pass (GST-3375)
body:
/review on Codex no longer blocks or logs a miss for sessions that really ran the adversarial review, when the model is an OpenAI one. Why: Codex encrypts the message it sends a new subagent for OpenAI models, so the check never saw the review brief's text; it now accepts a started subagent named `adversarial` whose message is encrypted. Nothing to do: Claude Code's check is unchanged, and a plaintext, missing, failed or differently named subagent still counts as missing.
What changed Codex users running /review on an OpenAI model hit an end-of-session block that said the adversarial pass never ran, even when it had, and the session then logged a miss. The check read the spawned agent's message for the brief's text, but Codex encrypts that message for OpenAI models (openai/codex#26210). Now a started `spawn_agent` named `adversarial` whose message is encrypted counts as the pass, so those sessions finish cleanly. On Codex, /review's Done means list asks for that name, and the block text names it too. A plaintext message is still held to the brief's text, and Claude Code's check doesn't change. The Codex wording was kept short so the generated Codex /review skill stays at its size limit.
Tests - [x] Full free suite in CI at 0f0f27a (run 44924286621): 1732 test files passed. - [x] macOS and Windows checks at 0f0f27a: cso-macos-launcher, macos-named-regressions (run 44924286621) and windows-smoke (run 44924286587) passed. - [x] `bun test test/skill-contract-codex.test.ts test/skill-contract.test.ts test/skill-descriptions.test.ts test/skill-md-size-guard.test.ts`: 189 tests passed. The new encrypted-spawn tests failed on main (3 of 10).
Why "The adversarial pass ran, but the check blocked the session anyway." With OpenAI models on Codex the brief's text is encrypted, so the check could never see it. It now trusts the agent's name when the message is encrypted, and still reads the text when it isn't.
Blast radius The change touches the Codex session reader, the contract checker, the /review contract and its generated Done means text on every host. Claude Code's path only gains an unused optional field, because its check reads `sealed` only on the Codex branch (lib/skill-contract.ts:379, file read). The generated Claude Done means text is byte-identical to main, and the Codex /review skill is 104,052 characters, exactly at its size pin (size guard test ran).
Pre-Landing Review Pre-Landing Review: 2 issues — 0 auto-fixed, 1 asked (0 fixed, 1 skipped), 0 deferred, 1 noted. Neither blocks: both are below the blocking floor. The second-model review (GPT-6.1 Sol) found nothing and recommended merging. The adversarial pass found five low-severity notes and recommended shipping as is; none blocks.

Exploratory QA Functional smoke on the contract checker CLI, two probes on the changed path, both pass: `gstack-skill-contract check` on the encrypted-spawn fixture meets the adversarial pass (exit 0), and the same fixture with the agent renamed `adversarial_review` is reported missing (exit 1) with a fix line that names `task_name "adversarial"`. Not probed: a plaintext message shaped like an encrypted token (listed in Review notes).
Eval Results Not run. The eval selector picked more than 100 behavioral probes, because the contract checker is used by every skill session, which is far over this PR's $10 paid-run budget. Coverage of the prompt change is left to the scheduled release eval run.

title: Plan reviews no longer read a /design-review audit summary as the design doc (#4615)
body:
After a /design-review run, /autoplan, /plan-ceo-review and /plan-eng-review now read the branch's real design doc instead of the one-line audit summary that /design-review saves next to it. Plan reviews are only useful when they review the actual design, so picking up a pointer file silently gave them nothing to work with. Nothing to do.
What changed ![With a design doc and a newer audit summary on the branch, the finder used to return the audit summary; now it returns the design doc](https://api.capy.ai/pr-assets/7H8xXvFmFc3iIppqSq8IZjPUtWvNGPm9FGvrwuHRumE.png) With a design doc and a newer audit summary on the branch, the finder used to return the audit summary; now it returns the design doc.
Before/after as text: With a design doc and a newer audit summary on the branch, the finder used to return the audit summary; now it returns the design doc ~~~diff --- Before · before.txt · captured output +++ After · after.txt · captured output $ gstack-design-doc-find proj feat-x +~/.gstack/projects/proj/user-feat-x-design-20261101-0900.md -~/.gstack/projects/proj/user-feat-x-design-audit-20261121-1000.md ~~~
/design-review writes a one-line summary named `{user}-{branch}-design-audit-{datetime}.md` into the same project folder as the design docs. `gstack-design-doc-find` picks the newest `*-design-*.md` file there, so right after a design review it handed the plan reviews that summary instead of the design doc. The finder now skips audit summaries the same way it already skips office-hours decision memos, falls back to the next-newest real doc, and still finds the right doc on a branch whose own name contains "design-audit".
Why Reported by @robbiesierra in #4615: after running /design-review, the next plan review read the audit pointer as the design doc. Plan reviews now get the design they are meant to review.
Blast radius Only `bin/gstack-design-doc-find` changed, in the loop that filters candidate files; the precedence between the private state folder and `docs/designs/`, and the plan-copy warnings, are untouched (file read, and the existing 22 tests in the two finder test files pass). Its callers are the Design Doc Check blocks in the plan-review skills, which only read the printed path, so a file that is no longer returned can only change which doc they read, never break them (two new tests and two isolated CLI runs).
Pre-Landing Review No issues found. The batched specialist reader (testing, security, state machines, red team) and the separate adversarial reader both returned no findings. The core checklist found nothing either.
Exploratory QA Two isolated command-line runs, both passing: with a design doc and a newer audit summary on branch `feat-x`, the finder returns the design doc; on a branch named `fix-design-audit`, it returns that branch's design doc, not its newer audit summary. Not re-run: the `docs/designs/` precedence and the plan-copy warnings, which this change does not touch.

Eval Results No prompt-related files changed, so evals were skipped.
Verification Results No plan file for this bug fix, so there were no plan-specific checks; the two QA runs above are the automatic checks.

There were no staged, unstaged or new files outside those three. I also searched `docs/`, `README.md`, `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` for references to the design-doc finder and to `design-audit` file names. **Result:** The docs are current. The fix updates the finder's own precedence comment to say it skips `/design-review` audit summaries the same way it skips decision memos. The changelog fragment explains the change to users. title: Keep Ubicloud test VMs and their results safe when the machine that started them dies (GST-1220)
body:
When the machine that started a Ubicloud test VM dies, another machine can now take the VM over with `ubi-runner.sh recover`, and the VM can upload its own results as it runs.
Why: long eval runs on Ubicloud no longer strand a billing VM or lose results when their controller machine goes away.
Nothing to do: the recovery bundle and results upload are off unless `UBI_RECOVERY_DIR` or `--sink` is set.

<details><summary>What changed</summary>

A controller that died mid-run used to leave its Ubicloud VM behind with no way for another machine to reach it. The ssh key and settings lived only on the dead machine, and results the VM had produced were lost unless something pulled them first. Now `up` can write an encrypted recovery bundle of the VM's key and settings to a shared folder (`UBI_RECOVERY_DIR`), and `recover` on another machine rebuilds that state so `pull`, `ssh` and `down` work from there. `recover` takes a VM over only after the bundle's own key opens it, so a VM another caller started under the same name is never adopted (`RECOVER_UNPROVEN`). With `--sink https-put:<presigned URL>`, the VM uploads a heartbeat and its result files on a timer, so results survive the controller. A counted run (`--counted`) refuses to start without a working recovery bundle.

</details>

<details><summary>Why</summary>

"A dead controller strands nothing" was the goal of GST-1220. A Capy machine that sleeps or is replaced in the middle of an eval used to leave its VM billing until its time limit ran out, with its results stuck on it. Another machine can now take over the VM and finish or tear it down, and the results reach the caller even if nobody is left to pull them.

</details>

<details><summary>Blast radius</summary>

Only `scripts/ubicloud/ubi-runner.sh` changes behavior, and every new path is opt-in. With neither `UBI_RECOVERY_DIR` nor `--sink` set, `up`, `run` and `down` take their existing paths (the existing runner tests in test/ubicloud-runner*.test.ts pass unchanged, 97 tests in the targeted run). The bundle is authenticated before it is decrypted, and the runner's own secrets never reach the VM (red team read of `--pass` and the sink URL, both test-covered).

</details>

All new code paths have test coverage (each changed runtime file has a changed test naming it). The new test `recover refuses a VM the bundle's key does not open` fails before the review fix and passes after it.

title: Ubicloud runs keep their results and VMs when the machine that started them dies (GST-1220)
body:
Ubicloud test runs no longer lose their VM or their results when the Capy machine that started them sleeps or dies: another machine can take the VM over with `recover`, and the VM can push its own results on a timer. This serves gstack's goal of tests that finish on cheap remote machines without babysitting. Nothing to do.
What changed ![ubi-runner usage: up gains --sink, --tag and --counted, and a new recover command rebuilds a VM's state on another machine](https://api.capy.ai/pr-assets/V6aHJpRQqm3qN5z_bPsfTJwEj3xndkkrvxxL3Or-l-s.png) ubi-runner usage: up gains --sink, --tag and --counted, and a new recover command rebuilds a VM's state on another machine.
Before/after as text: ubi-runner usage: up gains --sink, --tag and --counted, and a new recover command rebuilds a VM's state on another machine ~~~diff --- Before · before.txt · captured output +++ After · after.txt · captured output + up [-s SIZE] [-l LOCATION] [-n NAME] [-S STORAGE_GIB] [-b IMAGE] [--tag K=V]... + [--sink https-put:URL] [--sink-path PATH]... [--counted] - up [-s SIZE] [-l LOCATION] [-n NAME] [-S STORAGE_GIB] [-b IMAGE] create a VM and wait for SSH; prints its name + (STORAGE_GIB: one of $ALLOWED_STORAGE). --tag is kept in the VM's + state and recovery bundle; --sink starts a pusher on the VM that + uploads heartbeat.json and the PATH entries under ~ as results.tgz; + --counted (or UBI_COUNTED=1) refuses without a recovery bundle + (UBI_RECOVERY_REQUIRED, UBI_RECOVERY_UNAVAILABLE). run and verify + take the same four options + recover [--owner OLD] [--dir DIR] + rebuild this machine's state for the VMs with a bundle under + DIR/OLD (UBI_RECOVERY_DIR, this owner); prints RECOVERED, RECOVER_GONE + or RECOVER_FAILED per VM. Run it only once the creating machine is dead - (STORAGE_GIB: one of $ALLOWED_STORAGE) ssh NAME [COMMAND] shell or login-shell command on the VM (user ubi, passwordless sudo) ~~~
When the machine running `scripts/ubicloud/ubi-runner.sh` went away, its VM kept billing until its TTL ran out and nobody could pull its results, because the ssh key and state lived only on that machine. Now `up` writes an encrypted recovery bundle for each VM to `UBI_RECOVERY_DIR` (a drive folder on Capy), and `recover` on another machine rebuilds the state so `pull`, `ssh` and `down` work there. `recover` adopts a VM only after the bundle's key opens it, so it can never take over a VM that another caller created under the same name. `up --sink https-put: --sink-path PATH` starts a pusher on the VM that uploads its results every few minutes and once more at `down`, so results land even when no machine survives. `--counted` refuses to start a run that has no recovery bundle. `--pass` now forwards only variables the caller exported, never the runner's own (the recovery secret and the sink URL included).
Why "A dead controller strands the VM and its results" (GST-1220). Paid and long runs on Ubicloud now survive a Capy machine sleeping or being replaced. The next machine recovers the VM, or the results are already in the sink.
Blast radius Only `scripts/ubicloud/ubi-runner.sh` and its docs change. Every new behavior is off unless `UBI_RECOVERY_DIR`, `--sink` or `--counted` is set; the one change on the default path is that `--pass` reads the caller's exported value, which the existing `--pass` tests and 32 new or extended cases in `test/ubicloud-runner-recovery.test.ts` cover against the fake Ubicloud API (script ran: 32 pass, 0 fail at d23508b5).
Pre-Landing Review Two full review passes ran on this change (pass 1 on the whole branch, pass 2 on the fix range), each with a batched testing, security and state-machine reader, a red-team reader and a targeted secrets reader; pass 1 also had a native adversarial reader and a second-model review (openai/gpt-6.1-sol). The second-model review found two blocking problems in `recover` and the adversarial reader found one more; all three are fixed in d23508b5 with a test each that fails before the fix: - `recover` now proves the bundle's ssh key opens the VM before adopting it (`RECOVER_UNPROVEN` otherwise). - `recover` accepts owner tags up to the 31 characters the runner issues (it stopped at 12). - A rerun checks its sink spec before teardown is armed, so a bad `UBI_SINK` no longer destroys the VM it meant to resume. Two smaller fixes rode along: the pusher keeps the last results snapshot when its paths disappear, and `--sink-path` refuses a leading dash. Everything else was below the blocking floor and is listed under Review notes.
Review notes Below the blocking floor (advisory, informational, test-gap or wording items); recorded here and not fixed in this PR. - INFORMATIONAL `scripts/ubicloud/ubi-runner.sh:1182` The new keep-last-results behavior of the sink pusher (~/.ubirun-sink.had) has no test. - INFORMATIONAL `scripts/ubicloud/ubi-runner.sh:1444` The new --sink-path leading-dash rejection has no negative test. - INFORMATIONAL `sf-65c51570e840` security finding, details recorded privately - INFORMATIONAL `sf-78c73c4eb8c1` security finding, details recorded privately - Pass 1's remaining adversarial and red-team notes (four, all below the floor: archive size on the VM, a final push to a VM that is already gone, a leftover directory from two concurrent recovers, and the default bundle secret) are recorded privately in the review log.
Exploratory QA Smoke (bounded 300 s): the recovery test file passed end to end against the fake VM API (29 of 29 at 727bbaf5), and `recover` with no recovery directory refused with `UBI_RECOVERY_REQUIRED` before any API call. `usage` could not be probed: it lists the project's VMs through the live Ubicloud API, and no real key was used, so it is recorded as a setup limit (the evidence tool's verdict for that run is `blocked` for this reason). After the fix commit both required checks were rerun and passed (32 of 32; refusal intact). No real VM, presigned URL or drive folder was exercised.
Eval Results No paid cases selected: `bun run eval:select` chose no behavioral probes or quality judges for this diff (the ubicloud skill's broad checks run with release coverage).
Scope Drift Scope Check: DRIFT DETECTED (informational). Intent: recovery bundles, recover and a results sink (GST-1220). Delivered: that, plus a rewrite of how `up` reads the create answer (HTTP status instead of the CLI exit code) and its money-path tests, which the bundle cleanup on a refused create depends on.

The docs already match this branch's ubi-runner recovery bundles, the recover command and the results sink (GST-1220), so no edits were needed. **Scope:** base 2df1b8b3 to HEAD d23508b5 (2 commits, 8 files) plus the untracked changelog fragment. Nothing was staged or unstaged. **Documentation health** - `docs/troubleshooting.md`: Current. A new section covers UBI_RECOVERY_REQUIRED/UNAVAILABLE, the RECOVER_* codes, UBI_SINK_INVALID, SINK_FLUSH_FAILED, UBI_CREATE_UNKNOWN and UBI_ATTACH_UNKNOWN, and it matches the script. - `docs/TESTING_INTERNALS.md`: Current. It documents the machine-swap `recover` step and `--sink`. - `ubicloud/SKILL.md.tmpl` / `ubicloud/SKILL.md`: Current. They document the `--pass` exclusions and `$U recover`, and the generated output matches the template. - `changelog.d/...c080.md`: Reviewed only (the parent owns it). **Coverage debt:** `--sink`/`--sink-path`/`--counted` have reference coverage only (script header, troubleshooting, changelog) and no how-to step in the ubicloud skill. This is a common gap; `/document-generate` could fill it. **Diagram drift:** none, because no changed docs contain diagrams.

title: Node test files run with node --test in repos that use vitest (#4586)
body:
Test files that use Node's built-in test runner (`node:test`) now run with `node --test` in repos whose package.json declares vitest or jest, so /ship's pre-merge test check stops failing on them. Before, a root `.js`, `.mjs` or `.cjs` file that loads `node:test` was handed to vitest, which found no tests and failed every PR that touched one. Reported by @eoin-obrien in #4586. Nothing to do.
What changed ![A node:test file in a vitest repo now gets node --test instead of vitest](https://api.capy.ai/pr-assets/JztmBPzB4VNDlw409jMUvnH7CJNnnTNTjac9191UXQo.png) A node:test file in a vitest repo now gets `node --test` instead of vitest. In a pnpm monorepo whose root package.json declares vitest, /ship stopped at its finish step on every PR that touched a root `node:test` script test: the check ran that file under vitest, vitest found no suite, and the run failed. The runner detection now looks at the file itself. A `.js`, `.mjs` or `.cjs` test that loads `node:test` at the start of a line (an `import`, a bare import or a `require`) runs as its own `node --test` group from the repo root, while vitest and jest files keep their runner. A file that also loads vitest or `@jest/globals` stays with that runner, and import text inside comments, strings or template literals doesn't count. Bun repos are unchanged because `bun test` runs `node:test` files itself, and a runner declared in `.gstack/pregate.json` still takes every file. One existing assertion changed on purpose. The "negative controls … keep today's plan" test pinned the fixture file `test/util.test.js`, which requires `node:test`, to vitest in a root-vitest repo. That expectation was the #4586 bug itself, so it now expects vitest for the vitest file and `node --test` for the node:test file. No outside code was carried over. The issue's fixture was rebuilt from scratch in the new test.
Why /ship should only fail for a real test failure. A repo mixing vitest with Node's own test runner is common in pnpm monorepos, and today every PR in such a repo that touches one of those files stops at the finish step for a reason that has nothing to do with the change.
Blast radius Only runner detection for JS test files changes: `detectRunner` and `planRuns` in `lib/pregate/checks/lanes.ts` (read at lines 53-66 and 233-300). Repos that declare a runner, bun repos, and files that don't load `node:test` get the same plan as before; the existing bun-repo and declared-runner tests pin that, and the 93 focused tests in the selection, Dart and Rust suites pass.
Pre-Landing Review Two full review passes, one fix round, and one granted follow-up check. The first pass found that a `.js` file importing both vitest and `node:test` went to `node --test`; that was fixed. A second-model review then found the fix misread import text inside template literals; that was fixed under one granted follow-up check, which came back clean. Remaining items are below the blocking floor and listed under Review notes.
Review notes Below the blocking floor (advisory, informational, test-gap or wording items); recorded here and not fixed in this PR. - INFORMATIONAL `sf-89c56ae1f58f` security finding, details recorded privately - INFORMATIONAL `lib/pregate/checks/lanes.ts:205` A jest-globals or mocha file that imports node:test helpers is still routed to node --test; pre-existing before the fix. - INFORMATIONAL `lib/pregate/checks/lanes.ts:203` Dynamic import('vitest') is not seen by the exclusion; rare and fails loudly. - INFORMATIONAL `lib/pregate/checks/lanes.ts:203` The template-literal strip does not handle nested templates: a node:test file whose template holds a nested template with line-start vitest import text still goes to vitest.
Exploratory QA Five probes against a scratch repo (root package.json declaring vitest), run through the real `planRuns`: a `node:test` `.mjs` file gets `node --test` and a `.ts` vitest file keeps vitest; `node --test` then runs that file and passes (1 test); a `.js` file importing both vitest and `node:test` went to `node --test` before the first fix and stays on vitest after it; a `node:test` file holding generated vitest text in a template literal gets `node --test` at the first commit and after the second fix, and went to vitest only at the head between them. No probe was blocked or skipped.

One factual edit, no blockers. **Scope:** committed diff bd77c8cc..9ae8c3a5 on fix/pregate-node-test-files-run-with-node (`lib/pregate/checks/lanes.ts`, `test/pregate-selection.test.ts`, `changelog.d/fix-pregate-node-test-files-run-with-node.md`); no staged, unstaged or untracked changes. **Documentation health:** - `docs/pregate.md`: Updated. The `runner` row now says `.js`/`.mjs`/`.cjs` tests that load `node:test` (and not vitest or `@jest/globals`) run through `node --test` from the repo root even in vitest or jest repos, while bun repos keep `bun test`. - `changelog.d/fix-pregate-node-test-files-run-with-node.md`: Current. **Coverage debt:** the new node:test runner detection is covered by reference docs only (the `docs/pregate.md` runner row); there is no how-to, which is fine for internal detection behavior. No diagram drift.

title: Install gstack for Gemini CLI, and move older installs off the dev toolchain (GSTA-732)
body:
`./setup --host gemini` now installs every gstack skill for Google's Gemini CLI, and older installs drop the ~520 MB test toolchain on their next `./setup`. This serves gstack's goal of working in the coding agent you already use, and keeps everyday installs small. Nothing to do. Contributors keep the toolchain with `bin/dev-setup` or `git config gstack.contributor true`.
What changed ![./setup --host gemini now installs every gstack skill where Gemini CLI finds it](https://api.capy.ai/pr-assets/XJggAPeS4tT5d0QuyfutvpGg1-vjzkilq0SsM3krWHQ.png) `./setup --host gemini` now installs every gstack skill where Gemini CLI finds it.
Before/after as text: ./setup --host gemini now installs every gstack skill where Gemini CLI finds it ~~~diff --- Before · before.txt · captured output +++ After · after.txt · captured output +$ ./setup --host gemini # this change +gstack ready (gemini) + gemini skills: ~/.gemini/skills (ask for gstack-; + Gemini CLI activates it with activate_skill) +$ gemini skills list # Gemini CLI 0.66.0 +gstack [Enabled] +gstack-autoplan [Enabled] +gstack-office-hours [Enabled] +gstack-review [Enabled] +gstack-ship [Enabled] +... 63 gstack skills; the user's own my-own-skill stays [Enabled] -$ ./setup --host gemini # before this change -Unknown --host value: gemini — nothing was installed or changed. Expected one of: -claude (default), codex, kiro, factory, opencode, cursor, copilot, agy (alias -antigravity), slate, openclaw, hermes, gbrain, or auto. Tiers: ./setup --help -$ gemini skills list -(no gstack skills) ~~~
Gemini CLI users ran `./setup --host gemini` and got "Unknown --host value". Now setup links every gstack skill into `~/.gemini/skills`, where `gemini skills list` shows them and Gemini CLI loads one with `activate_skill`. Skills you put there yourself are left alone, and `gstack-uninstall` (and the manual steps in docs/uninstall.md) remove only the entries gstack made. `--host auto` picks Gemini CLI only when the `gemini` command is installed, never for a bare `~/.gemini` folder. Installs made before v1.91.231.0 still hold about 520 MB of test-only packages. The next `./setup` moves them to production-only dependencies once, puts the full install back if that move fails, and waits when another `./setup` is already moving them. A contributor clone keeps everything: `bin/dev-setup` marks it, or set `git config gstack.contributor true`.
Why "Add Gemini CLI as a host" (TODOS #1247, #2309) had sat open while Gemini CLI shipped native skill loading. Gemini CLI users now get gstack with one command, and everyone on an older install gets a smaller one without reinstalling.
Blast radius The new host touches the host registry (hosts/index.ts), skill generation, setup's install and uninstall paths, and the shared `~/.gemini` folder that Antigravity also reads. It is safe because setup only creates and removes its own symlinks and banner folders there, which the new uninstall tests and the install-registry tests check (script ran). The dependency move is one-shot, guarded by a lock and a backup that is restored on any failure, with tests for the failure, the restore and the wait (script ran, red without the fix).
Test Coverage Coverage: 13 of 16 new paths (81%) covered. Test value: 0 tests written, 0 rejected by the authoring gate, 0 existing tests extended, 0 paths weakly covered. Proposed tests for the 3 gaps: - setup leaves a `~/.gemini/skills/gstack` folder that the user owns untouched. - a skill you disabled is removed from `~/.gemini/skills` on the next setup. - `gstack-team-init` finds the Gemini skills folder.
Pre-Landing Review Two full review passes, one fix round and one fix check. Four blocking findings, all fixed in 5a2660a6: - docs/uninstall.md: the manual Gemini uninstall step would have deleted the user's own `gstack*` skills. It now removes only symlinks and gstack's banner folders. - setup: a second `./setup` could start while another was moving dependencies. It now waits for the running move. - setup: a failed dependency move could delete the backup. The backup is now always restored. - test/codex-e2e-multiblock-live.test.ts: the test ran setup without the contributor setting, so it would prune the toolchain it needs. One more finding was fixed in bf6f4721 (security finding, details recorded privately). Two first-pass findings and three second-model findings were below the blocking floor and are left as notes (one of them is a security finding, details recorded privately). The fix check found nothing. Second-model review: ran, 2 findings, both fixed above.
Review notes Below the blocking floor (advisory, informational, test-gap or wording items); recorded here and not fixed in this PR. - INFORMATIONAL `test/setup-production-deps.test.ts:404` The recovery test's 'finished' case does not assert the restored backup was migrated again, so the old keep-the-partial-install branch would still pass. - INFORMATIONAL `test/setup-production-deps.test.ts:438` The new wait test's holder releases the lock after a fixed 2 s sleep; a very slow runner could miss the waiting line. - INFORMATIONAL `setup:1876` _deps_wait_migration falls through after 10 minutes with the holder still alive, so a migration slower than that can still be clobbered. - INFORMATIONAL `sf-8b77b714e67e` security finding, details recorded privately - INFORMATIONAL `sf-2cb119aa8ab7` security finding, details recorded privately
Exploratory QA Surface: command line. 2 probes, both pass: - `bun run scripts/gen-skill-docs.ts --host gemini` renders 64 skill folders, and the review skill's name matches its folder. No tracked file changed. - `./setup --host gemini --local` in a test home exits 1 with the --local refusal and the Gemini trusted-folder note, and writes nothing under `~/.gemini`. Not probed here: uninstall and a full `./setup --host gemini`, which would touch the real state folder. The uninstall and install-registry tests cover both.

title: careful: the build-folder delete exception fails when the path is quoted
body:
The build-folder exception in `careful/bin/check-careful.sh` (the regex near line 216) lets an unquoted recursive delete of a build folder through, but the same command with the path in quotes asks for permission. Quoting a path is ordinary shell hygiene, and agents do it by default, so on projects whose path contains a space the exception never applies.

Each command below was fed to the hook as a Bash tool payload on Windows (Git Bash):

| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `rm -rf dist` | allowed |
| `rm -rf /tmp/a/dist` | allowed |
| `rm -rf "dist"` | ask |
| `rm -rf "/tmp/a b/dist"` | ask |

`rm -rf "dist"` and `rm -rf dist` delete the same folder, so the quoted form should get the same decision. An absolute path with a space, such as `"/c/Users/me/Github Projects/app/dist"`, can only be written quoted, so it always asks.

Why it matters: the prompt waits for a person even in bypass mode. An agent in a long unattended run quoted its build folder path and sat on the prompt for about six hours overnight.

A possible fix: before matching, strip one pair of matching quotes around each target and allow spaces inside the quoted part, while still rejecting `$`, backticks, globs, and `..` in it so nothing that expands can slip through.

Related: #4601 (another false positive in the same hook).

title: gstack stops offering to add skill routing rules to your project's CLAUDE.md (GST-3382)
body:
gstack no longer asks to append a `## Skill routing` section to your project's CLAUDE.md; its prompt-routing hook, on by default, now starts the right skill by itself.
Why: in a preregistered test on Opus 5.5 the hook loaded the bug-fix skill in 45 of 60 and 48 of 60 sessions, past the section's 39 of 60 ([results](https://github.com/garrytan/gstack-evals/tree/main/wiki/board/2026-11-21-capy-b1e-matcher-fix-results)).
Nothing to do: a section an older gstack added stays as you left it and keeps working; delete it if you like.

<details><summary>What changed</summary>

![Skill start in a project without a routing section: main offered to add one to CLAUDE.md; this branch no longer does](https://api.capy.ai/pr-assets/_J3QZkhV1zMYWWi2EmaHDJJl0QtipHxM6Geh3bCygcs.png)

When a skill starts in a project without a routing section, main offered to add one to CLAUDE.md, and this branch no longer does.

<details><summary>Before/after as text</summary>

~~~diff
--- Before · before.txt · captured output
+++ After · after.txt · captured output
 $ gstack-skill-start --skill testskill   # project without a routing section
 HAS_ROUTING: no
+(no routing offer)
-ROUTING_DECLINED: false
-GSTACK_INSTRUCTION_BEGIN: routing-injection <nonce>
-> gstack works best when your project's CLAUDE.md includes skill routing rules.
-Options: A) Add routing rules to CLAUDE.md (recommended)  B) No thanks, I'll invoke skills manually
-## Skill routing
~~~

</details>

People starting a skill in a project without a routing section used to get a one-time question asking to append one to CLAUDE.md and commit it. That question is gone, because the prompt-routing hook already names the matching skill.

- `bin/gstack-skill-start` no longer emits the routing offer (the question, the section to append and the commit). It still reports `HAS_ROUTING`, which says whether a project already carries a section.
- The `routing_declined` setting, which only answered that offer, is gone from `gstack-config`, along with the `ROUTING_DECLINED` status line and the offer's question-registry entry.
- Existing CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md files are never edited. gstack's offered section had no begin or end marker, and people edit it, so gstack can't tell its own text from yours; it stops writing the section and leaves existing ones alone.
- The section's exact bytes now live in `test/fixtures/claude-md-skill-routing.md`, so the E2E tests that put it in a fixture project's CLAUDE.md send the model the same text as before.
- Docs: docs/proactive.md, docs/skill-routing-and-contracts.md, docs/uninstall.md and docs/OPENCLAW.md say the offer is gone and what to do with an old section.
- Two test fixes: the /design-review build-loop test no longer expects the removed offer's text, and its single-source check now compares paths with forward slashes so it passes on Windows.

</details>

<details><summary>Why</summary>

This follows a decision written down before the test ran ([preregistration](https://github.com/garrytan/gstack-evals/tree/main/wiki/plans/2026-11-20-capy-b1e-matcher-fix-prereg), results merged in garrytan/gstack-evals#415). Its decision row said that if the hook alone reaches 39 of 60 on both task sets, gstack cuts the CLAUDE.md routing offer and relies on the hook.

- On B1's 60 bug-fix tasks the hook got Claude Opus 5.5 to load the skill in 45 of 60 (75.0%, 95% interval 62.8 to 84.2).
- On 60 fresh tasks no earlier run had used, it loaded in 48 of 60 (80.0%, 68.2 to 88.2). With no gstack installed, the skill loaded in 0 of 60.
- The bar, 39 of 60, is what the CLAUDE.md section managed on the same 60 tasks. Against the previous hook (B1d), the fixed matcher gained 13 loads and lost none.

The run measured gstack main at 5df6b5a8 (#4539, the bug-report matcher fix). Main has one later matcher change, #4566, which ignores words inside backticks. Replaying the hook's matcher at 5df6b5a8 and at this branch's base over the test's own prompts gives the same skill and the same hook line on all 60 in-sample prompts (they live in test/fixtures/skill-route-b1-in-sample.json) and on the 55 fresh prompts rebuilt byte for byte from SWE-rebench (each matched the preregistration's prompt sha256). The other 5 fresh prompts could not be rebuilt exactly; 2 near-copies route the same, and 3 interface tasks were not checked.

</details>

<details><summary>Blast radius</summary>

The removal touches every skill start, `gstack-config` and the question registry. It is safe because nothing outside the tests read the removed key, status line or question id (a repo-wide search by four reviewers), and a config.yaml that still holds `routing_declined: true` keeps working: `gstack-config get`, `list` and `defaults` all exit 0 (script ran, QA probe 002).

</details>

<details><summary>Pre-Landing Review</summary>

No blocking issues. Five reviewers read the change (two of them read the test files in summary only). They were a batched testing, security and state-machines specialist, a red-team reader, an adversarial reader, a second-model review on GPT-6.1 Sol and a targeted reader for the config change. Four found nothing and the adversarial reader raised two low notes below.

</details>

<details><summary>Review notes</summary>

Below the blocking floor (advisory, informational, test-gap or wording items); recorded here and not fixed in this PR.

- INFORMATIONAL `docs/OPENCLAW.md:121` docs/OPENCLAW.md still lists 'routing injection' among the onboarding blocks spawned sessions suppress; the block no longer exists after this PR. Nothing breaks.
- INFORMATIONAL `bin/gstack-config:64` A routing_declined line left in an upgraded user's config.yaml now does nothing and the header no longer explains it; gstack-config get still prints it. No wrong behavior.
- INFORMATIONAL [ADVISORY] `bin/gstack-skill-start:322` HAS_ROUTING is still computed and printed but no gate reads it now; kept for older installed skill files.

The first note was later fixed by the documentation audit (see Documentation).

</details>

<details><summary>Exploratory QA</summary>

Three smoke probes on isolated fixtures (own HOME and state root, a fresh git project with no CLAUDE.md), all passing:
- With `routing_declined` unset and the one-time prompt already answered (the case where main offered the section), skill start exits 0, prints no routing offer and no `ROUTING_DECLINED` line, and creates no CLAUDE.md.
- The same with a stale `routing_declined: true` in config.yaml.
- `gstack-config get`, `list` and `defaults` all exit 0 with that stale key, and the key is absent from active values and defaults.

Not probed here: `proactive: all` and `off` (covered by test/proactive-skill-start.test.ts).

</details>

title: /eval-plan refuses gpt-4o and older-generation models in every role, and asks for 100 judge labels from 2026-11-22 (GST-3384)
body:
/eval-plan now refuses gpt-4o and older-generation models in every role a plan picks (arms, judge, readers, simulators) and names the replacement; a competitor tested as its vendor ships it keeps its built-in model on its own arm.
Why: eval numbers should come from current frontier models, and from 2026-11-22 a model judge must agree with 100 hand labels, not 40.
Nothing to do.

<details><summary>What changed</summary>

![A plan that names gpt-4o as an arm used to pass; now prereg --check refuses it and names the replacement](https://api.capy.ai/pr-assets/MOK0YTnrGixpthzrEFYAnyAQEJ-XeFbOqYunm4uBEFE.png)

A plan that names gpt-4o as an arm used to pass; now prereg --check refuses it and names the replacement.

<details><summary>Before/after as text: A plan that names gpt-4o as an arm used to pass; now prereg --check refuses it and names the replacement</summary>

~~~diff
--- Before · before.txt · captured output
+++ After · after.txt · captured output
 $ gstack-eval-plan prereg --check prereg.md   # arms: gpt-4o, gpt-4o#plain
+PREREG: incomplete present=10/10 stack=none models=refused file=prereg.md
+MODEL_GENERATION: refused gpt-4o role=arm replacement=gpt-6.2-sol (R116, docs/TESTING_INTERNALS.md#frontier-models-under-test)
+gstack-eval-plan prereg: an arm, judge, reader or simulator is gpt-4o or a model lib/pricing.ts marks superseded_by (R116), or an arm is not the newest id of a family the eval model rules order newest first (gpt-4o as arm is an older generation; use gpt-6.2-sol (R116)); fix: use the replacement the MODEL_GENERATION or EVAL_MODEL line names; a competitor system tested as its vendor ships it declares its built-in model with a vendor-default: line in ## Models; or reorder families in .gstack/eval-models.json in a reviewed PR (EVAL_MODEL_OLD_GENERATION)
+exit 1
-PREREG: ok present=10/10 stack=none file=prereg.md
-exit 0
 
~~~

</details>

An eval plan could pick gpt-4o, or a model a newer generation has replaced, as an arm, a judge or a helper model, and nothing stopped it. Now `gstack-eval-plan prereg --check` refuses gpt-4o (any variant) and every model `lib/pricing.ts` marks with the new `superseded_by` field (11 rows), in each role: arms, the Scoring judge, and `reader:` and `simulator:` lines in a new optional `## Models` section. `dry-run` and `pilot start` refuse such arms too. Each refusal prints the model, its role and the current replacement.

A competitor system tested as its vendor ships it declares its built-in model on a `vendor-default: <model> <system>` line. That exempts only the arm whose loadout names the system (`gpt-4o-mini#mem0`), never a plain or `#no-gstack` arm on the same model; `results --check` then wants the results to name the model. Plans frozen before 2026-11-21 keep their models.

Plans frozen on or after 2026-11-22, or with no frozen date, need 100 hand labels behind a model judge instead of 40; the agreement bar stays at kappa 0.6.

gstack's own eval warmup and distill defaults, the recommendation judge and five canary tests move from Claude Haiku 4.5 to Haiku 5.5, and the eval harness version moves from 6 to 7 because judge behaviour changed.

</details>

<details><summary>Why</summary>

"No gpt-4o or older-generation model sits in a role we choose; a competitor's vendor defaults and plans frozen earlier keep theirs." A published eval number is only useful if it was measured on the models people use today, and a judge checked against 40 labels was too thin a check, so the label bar rises for new plans.

</details>

<details><summary>Blast radius</summary>

The refusal only runs inside `gstack-eval-plan` (prereg, dry-run, pilot start, results) and in the shared eval defaults; plans frozen before 2026-11-21 skip it and older plans keep the 40-label bar (tests on both sides of each date in `test/eval-plan-model-generations.test.ts` and `test/eval-plan-result-checks.test.ts`, script ran). No preregistration in this repository names a refused arm (scanned every `## Arms` section with `checkModelGenerations`, script ran).

</details>

<details><summary>Test Coverage</summary>

16 changed behaviours traced; 15 have value-level tests and one is weakly covered (the dry-run command-line message names the rule only in the library test). One regression test added in review: a `vendor-default` line no longer exempts a plain or `#no-gstack` arm on the same model; it failed before the fix and passes after.

</details>

<details><summary>Pre-Landing Review</summary>

Two full passes over the whole branch, then the second-model review and a focused money/auth reader on the final code. Pass 1 found one blocking problem, confirmed by running the CLI: a `vendor-default` line exempted every arm on that model, including gstack's own plain arm, against the documented rule. Fixed in this PR with a test. Pass 2 and the final readers found nothing blocking. The second-model review (GPT-6.1 Sol) and the focused reader returned clean.

</details>

<details><summary>Review notes</summary>

Below the blocking floor; recorded here and not fixed in this PR.

- INFORMATIONAL `lib/eval-plan-checks.ts:155` The arm exemption matches any loadout that is a prefix of the vendor-default system text; no test pins a different-system or too-short loadout (#zep, #m).
- INFORMATIONAL `sf-23c1f0362417` security finding, details recorded privately

- INFORMATIONAL `lib/eval-plan.ts:456` dry-run and pilot start check arms without the plan's frozen date, so a plan frozen before 2026-11-21 that names an older arm passes prereg --check but is refused at dry-run (no plan in this repository is affected).
- INFORMATIONAL two more pass-1 findings: security finding, details recorded privately.

</details>

<details><summary>Exploratory QA</summary>

Command-line probes of `gstack-eval-plan` on synthetic plans, no network and no paid calls. The required checks pass on the final code: a current plan passes; gpt-4o arms, an older judge, and older reader and simulator lines are refused with their replacements; a plan frozen 2026-11-20 keeps its models; the 100-label bar applies from 2026-11-22 and 40 still passes before; dry-run refuses a gpt-4o arm. The probes found the `vendor-default` problem above (failed, replayed, fixed, then passed). Two optional probes stay open: one used a bad fixture, and one showed dry-run cannot see a plan's `vendor-default` line (listed in Review notes). Overall status: inconclusive on those two, required checks passing.

</details>

**Scope:** the 3 commits on `eval-plan-refuses-older-models` (base 6263e0ef, head 97a6ae09). /eval-plan now refuses gpt-4o and any model `lib/pricing.ts` marks `superseded_by` in every role (R116). Judges now need 100 labels for plans frozen on or after 2026-11-22. Eval warmup and distill defaults move to Haiku 5.5.

title: v1.102.2.0 release
body:
v1.102.2.0 ships 38 user-visible changes, listed one per line under Release notes with the pull request that made each. It changes only the version, the CHANGELOG and the files generated from them, so it needs no review: merge it once its checks are green.
Release notes - Habits from nine teams, written into gstack. (#4585) - Three more habits from teams that run evals. (#4602) - The /ship conductor trial plan gives its real-problem judge one more attempt on fresh labels after it missed its agreement bar twice, and stops the trial incomplete if it misses again (GST-3003). (#4611) - The /ship conductor trial plan now stops a trial only at the final remote-gate refusal, gives both arms the same note that the brief overrides team rules, and counts every report the no-gstack arm returns (GST-3003). (#4609) - The /ship conductor trial plan now ends a trial at the remote gate when its case base isn't main, gives the no-gstack arm a test runner, and audits every trial for exposure to the plan (GST-3003). (#4605) - The /ship conductor trial plan now runs an uncounted pilot in every arm before its counted trials and takes one planned look at half the cases (GST-3003). (#4587) - gstack's own use on Capy can be counted, and is kept out of real-use numbers. (#4576) - Free Tests shards finish closer together. (#4578) - The weekly test-time recording can land again on its own. (#4581) - The job-log tree.json step's recommended sleep is long enough for real runners. (#4589) - Pull requests no longer wait on the Trunk flaky-test upload, and the quick tier's flaky passes now reach Trunk. (#4579) - Windows Setup E2E finishes sooner on install changes. (#4575) - Skills no longer stop on Codex when they clean up temp files. (#4612) - /review on Codex with OpenAI models no longer holds back a review that ran its adversarial pass. (#4622) - Crew threads on Capy now check in at 500M own tokens, standing threads rotate at 250M and any subagent past 50M gets a look, half the old lines, because Capy's token counts read about half what they did before 2026-11-15. (#4582) - gstack no longer offers to add a `## Skill routing` section to your project's CLAUDE.md. (#4629) - The README and docs no longer say gstack makes your agent fix more bugs. (#4598) - `/eval-plan` now writes eval plans that waste less money. (#4591) - /cso checks every folder above a source file before it looks at the file, so it never looks through a symlinked folder. (#4592) - Plan reviews no longer read a /design-review audit summary as the branch's design doc. (#4623) - Node's built-in test files now run with `node --test` in repos that use vitest or jest. (#4626) - A quarantined test that the runner skipped now fails the run instead of passing it. (#4590) - A flaky free test is fixed: the spawnSync overflow check no longer fails about once an hour on CI. (#4613) - Free Tests runs its shards on 16-core runners. (#4600) - /office-hours asks for ground truth first. (#4468) - Every startup session ends with a dated test. (#4468) - /plan-tune's dream cycle now logs each send of your typed answers to Anthropic. (#4621) - Landing a ready PR no longer depends on a hand-copied gate decision, and the ready note, release PR and squash message say the right thing. (#4596) - /ship no longer asks for a fresh review because of a stacked parent that main already had. (#4580) - Results PRs with large captured agent sessions can be reviewed. (#4574) - /ship no longer stalls on review notes a reviewer already cleared, counts review rounds the way the review policy reads them, and keeps security findings out of the PR body. (#4595) - /ship's review readers are now told never to stop processes they didn't start. (#4607) - /ship's review no longer stops when Capy's own drive sync database grows past 100 MB. (#4606) - /ship's preflight now honors your repository's time limit for rerunning CI-skipped tests, and tells you when a fresh worktree needs its packages installed. (#4608) - The slowest free test file is now six files. (#4588) - Step 11.5 keeps a reviewed head current across base-only merges. (#4577) - On a Capy install, only the owner's opt-in sends telemetry. (#4597) - New page: working across agent systems. (#4583)

title: Large repos can raise the review-plan time limit for every /ship step (GST-3398)
body:
`GSTACK_REVIEW_PLAN_TIMEOUT_MS` now raises the review-plan time limit in every place /ship runs the plan, not just two of them. Why: on a 301,669-file repository the plan takes 255 to 316 s on a 2-core machine; the plan and the review pass read the variable, but render and preflight still cut it off at 180 s. Nothing to do unless your repository is large; then set the variable (docs/troubleshooting.md#review-plan-stopped).
What changed ![With GSTACK_REVIEW_PLAN_TIMEOUT_MS=1, render used to ignore the limit and finish; now it stops at the limit like the review pass does](https://api.capy.ai/pr-assets/b7t2AqM6qpkm_6XClyrhK176xU5qXFoWjrlvxRo3fgs.png) With GSTACK_REVIEW_PLAN_TIMEOUT_MS=1, render used to ignore the limit and finish; now it stops at the limit like the review pass does.
Before/after as text: With GSTACK_REVIEW_PLAN_TIMEOUT_MS=1, render used to ignore the limit and finish; now it stops at the limit like the review pass does ~~~diff --- Before · before.txt · captured output +++ After · after.txt · captured output $ GSTACK_REVIEW_PLAN_TIMEOUT_MS=1 gstack-review-dispatch render --role outside-voice --base main ... +gstack-review-dispatch render: gstack-review-plan did not finish inside the pass (reason=timeout after timeout_ms, reason=signal when something killed it, reason=spawn when it could not start), so the review stopped before any reader ran: gstack-review-dispatch pass writes no manifest, and a plan run by itself prints no plan (step="gstack-review-plan --base main --json" reason=timeout timeout_ms=1 signal=SIGTERM); fix: … (REVIEW_PLAN_STOPPED) +BRIEF_RENDER_FAILED: gstack-review-plan --base main --json did not finish, so the base policy's review selection is unknown and no brief is rendered without it +exit=1 -BRIEF: reader=outside-voice sha256=d54fec8eb844af700cd43e5fccea7d3048992a9a1419e8776902fac5bf76fd40 bytes=4587 file=/b-one/outside-voice.prompt.md -exit=0 ~~~
A large repository that raised the limit still had /ship cut off at 180 seconds, because `gstack-review-dispatch render` (which runs the plan when the base policy has `review_exclude_paths`) and `gstack-ship-preflight` passed a fixed 180,000 ms to `gstack-review-plan`. Both now read the limit through `reviewPlanTimeoutMs()` in `lib/review-collect.ts`, the parser the plan and `gstack-review-dispatch pass` already used. A whole number of at least 1 ms sets it, a fraction rounds down, and an empty, zero, negative or non-numeric value keeps 180,000 ms. Render and pass now share one plan runner, so a render that runs out of time prints the same `REVIEW_PLAN_STOPPED` line instead of `exited SIGTERM`. docs/troubleshooting.md documents the variable and which commands read it.
Why harness-evals#548 stopped twice at `timeout_ms=180000` even though the variable was set. Large repositories can now raise one limit and have every /ship step honor it.
Blast radius Only the two callers that launch `gstack-review-plan` change, and the default stays 180 s, so repositories that never set the variable behave exactly as before. A whole-tree read found no other hard-coded plan timeout (bin/gstack-review-dispatch and lib/ship-preflight.ts read; render and preflight walked at limits of 1 ms, 600,000 ms and unset in a fixture repository).
Test Coverage All new code paths have test coverage. One path is weakly covered: preflight's use of the shared limit has only a source check; a fixture probe in Exploratory QA exercised it. Tests: 1851 → 1851 (+0 new; the PR's own tests were written before this run) Coverage: 83% value-weighted (100% including 1 weakly covered path) Test value: 0 tests written, 0 rejected by the authoring gate, 0 existing tests extended, 1 path weakly covered (weak = ★, gate-failing or unrated). Tests ran: targeted 34 Tests ran: test 1732
Pre-Landing Review No blocking issues. Four review passes (a batched specialist read, a red-team read, a native adversarial read and a second-model review) found three items below the blocking floor, listed under Review notes; none was fixed in this PR. The second-model review returned clean.
Review notes Below the blocking floor (advisory, informational, test-gap or wording items); recorded here and not fixed in this PR. - INFORMATIONAL `sf-6650a61b0584` security finding, details recorded privately - INFORMATIONAL `lib/ship-preflight.ts:195` Preflight runs gstack-review-plan without GSTACK_REVIEW_PLAN_BOUNDED=1 under the same limit as the plan's own wrapper, so on timeout the wrapper is killed and the inner plan keeps running; RUNTIME_LINES prints unknown with no stop line. Same behaviour on main. - INFORMATIONAL `lib/review-collect.ts:152` reviewPlanTimeoutMs accepts values of 2^31 ms or more, which Bun's spawnSync wraps to a short timeout.
Exploratory QA Functional smoke on an owned two-commit fixture repository, 5 probes, all pass: render finishes with the variable unset; stops with `REVIEW_PLAN_STOPPED timeout_ms=1` and writes no diff at 1 ms; finishes at 600,000 ms; preflight prints `RUNTIME_LINES: unknown` at 1 ms and a count when unset. Not measured: plan speed on a large repository.
Eval Results No prompt-related files changed — evals skipped.
Review bot comments No review bot comments.
