title: A finished /ship no longer blocks gstack-upgrade for two hours (GST-1205)
body:
A gstack upgrade no longer waits up to two hours after a /ship (or any gstack workflow) has already finished. Why: keeping gstack current between runs without forcing the upgrade. Nothing to do.
What changed "I finished /ship but gstack-upgrade still says UPGRADE_BUSY." Each workflow used to renew a lease on the install that counted for 120 minutes no matter whether the workflow had ended. Now `gstack-skill-start` records its session as an open run on the lease and `gstack-skill-end` closes it, so once every run on a lease is closed the lease is idle and blocks nothing. A run still open counts for 120 minutes from its own start; a lease written without a run, or by an older gstack, counts exactly as before. ![gstack-lease now answers whether a run is still open, and a released run leaves the lease idle](https://api.capy.ai/pr-assets/HV9G1KP8Tjf1axtnRQQ-vI6GjwF_YnBL_uVadmQRgOk.png) Before: the branch head before review (4630d318), where `open` was rejected. After: this head.
Before/after as text: gstack-lease now answers whether a run is still open, and a released run leaves the lease idle ~~~diff --- Before · before.txt · captured output +++ After · after.txt · captured output $ gstack-lease touch --run ; gstack-lease open --run ; gstack-lease release --run ; gstack-lease open --run +open_while_open=0 +open_after_release=1 +$ gstack-lease list (after the run is released) + 0m idle -gstack-lease: unknown verb 'open' -open_while_open=2 -gstack-lease: unknown verb 'open' -open_after_release=2 ~~~
`gstack-lease` gains `release --pid

--run ` and `open --run `, and `list` shows `idle`. `open` is what `gstack-ship-preflight` uses to refuse a base merge in the middle of a /ship and what gate dispositions use to stop counting a parked run once its lease ends; review found it was documented but missing from the verb list, so both callers got exit 2, and this PR adds it with a test.

Why "A finished /ship's workflow lease blocks gstack-upgrade" (GST-1205). Upgrades are supposed to wait only while a workflow is actually running; now they do.
Blast radius It touches the lease file format (run entries after the identity line), `gstack-skill-start`, `gstack-skill-end`, `gstack-upgrade`'s live check, `gstack-ship-preflight` and gate dispositions. Older lease files without run entries are never idle, so they keep blocking as before (read at bin/gstack-lease `idle()`; tested in test/gstack-lease.test.ts), and `test/ship-gate-dispositions.test.ts`, which failed in CI run 44949884082 before the fix, passes after it (13 pass, script ran).
Pre-Landing Review Pass 1 (testing, security, state-machine and red-team checklists in one reader) found one blocker: `gstack-lease open` was rejected as an unknown verb, which left the /ship mid-run merge guard unable to fire and made every parked run count as open forever. Fixed in fa60eb70 with a test that fails without the fix. A second pass over just the fix (a red-team reader plus a reader checking the fix itself) found nothing blocking. Step 11: the Claude adversarial reader found 0 blocking and 3 notes (below); the second-model review (openai/gpt-6.1-sol) returned CLEAN.
Review notes Below the blocking floor (advisory, informational, test-gap or wording items); recorded here and not fixed in this PR. - Medium `bin/gstack-lease:270` a run counts 120 minutes from its own start, so a live non-Capy /ship past 120 minutes no longer blocks gstack-upgrade or gstack-session-update; documented trade-off, GST-1677 covers Capy - Low `bin/gstack-skill-end:62` release trusts the pid prefix of whatever --session-id it is given; a nested skill passing its parent's SESSION_ID would close the parent's run early - Low `sf-0dd7c164abca` security finding, details recorded privately
Exploratory QA Functional smoke on `bin/gstack-lease` in an owned temp checkout: captures 002 and 003 reproduced `open` exiting 2 before the fix; captures 004 and 005 pass on the fixed source (open answers 0 then 1; release leaves the lease idle and `live` exits 1). Verdict: pass. Not probed: `open` against a dead or reused-pid holder (it shares `live`'s state rules).

It covers run-scoped leases, `idle`, and `open --run`, and links to the troubleshooting anchor. - docs/troubleshooting.md: current. The lease, idle and run-open text matches bin/gstack-lease and lib/ship-preflight.ts. - changelog.d fragment: current (read only). - bin/gstack-lease help text: current for `release`, `open`, `--run` and `list` showing `idle`. **Coverage debt:** `gstack-lease release`, `open`, `--run` and the `idle` state have reference and how-to coverage. title: A finished /ship no longer blocks gstack upgrades (GST-1205)
body:
A /ship run that has finished no longer stops gstack from upgrading on the same machine. Upgrades now wait only for workflows that are still running, so machines shared by several agents stay current without waiting two hours after every /ship. Nothing to do.
What changed ![gstack-lease open now answers 0 while a run is open and 1 after it is released, instead of failing as an unknown command](https://api.capy.ai/pr-assets/bDZJfSowrfwNQOZWO-pbzEbMsYEcag_YQGkThSHN8fU.png) gstack-lease open now answers 0 while a run is open and 1 after it is released, instead of failing as an unknown command.
Before/after as text: gstack-lease open now answers 0 while a run is open and 1 after it is released, instead of failing as an unknown command ~~~diff --- Before · before.txt · captured output +++ After · after.txt · captured output touch exit=0 live-after-touch exit=0 +open-while-open exit=0 -open-while-open exit=2 release exit=0 live-after-release exit=1 +open-after-release exit=1 -open-after-release exit=2 HOLDER 0m idle ~~~
Every workflow start already took a lease on the shared install, and nothing gave it back, so a finished /ship kept blocking upgrades until the lease aged out. Each start now records its run on the lease and each workflow end closes that run. A lease whose runs have all closed is idle and blocks nothing; a run that never closes stops counting 120 minutes after it started. `gstack-lease list` shows idle leases, and `gstack-lease open --run ` answers whether one run is still open, which the /ship preflight and the gate-disposition check already call.
Why A finished /ship held the upgrade back: installs reported "a gstack run in this session holds a workflow lease" long after the run ended. Now only workflows still running hold it back.
Blast radius The lease file format gains run lines; a lease written by an older gstack, or without a run, counts exactly as before (bin/gstack-lease `idle()` treats a lease with no entries as never idle, read at file:line). The two existing callers of `open`, lib/ship-preflight.ts:64 and lib/gate-dispositions.ts:118, now get the 0/1 answer they expect instead of exit 2 (script ran: QA capture, and test/ship-gate-dispositions.test.ts plus test/ship-preflight.test.ts, 45 pass).
Pre-Landing Review Two review passes. Pass 1 found that the new `open` command was never accepted by the script's command list, so it always failed; that is fixed, with a new test, and `--help` now prints the whole usage text. Pass 2 (a check of the fix plus a second-model review) found nothing in the fix. Three low or medium edge cases are noted and not fixed: a run longer than 120 minutes stops counting (as documented), run ids are not validated, and a clock that jumps backwards keeps a run open longer.
Deferred findings Blocking findings in code this PR did not change (review scope: frozen). They stay on this PR and are not filed as issues. - Deferred: CRITICAL `sf-257601a61acf` security finding, details recorded privately
Exploratory QA One CLI smoke probe on an isolated lease directory: before the fix `open` exited 2 both while the run was open and after release (captured twice); after the fix it exits 0 then 1. Verdict: pass on current inputs. The skill start and end round trip is covered by the existing test, not probed.
Scope Drift Scope Check: CLEAN. Intent: a finished /ship stops blocking gstack-upgrade. Delivered: run entries on the lease, released by workflow end, plus the `open` query and docs.
Verification Results No plan file (bug fix): no plan checks. Automatic QA: 1 contract, pass.
TODOS No TODO items completed in this PR.
Documentation Scope: the lease change in two commits, across 7 files (`bin/gstack-lease`, `bin/gstack-skill-start`, `bin/gstack-skill-end`, `docs/capy-install.md`, `docs/troubleshooting.md` and two test files), plus the new changelog fragment. Nothing was staged or unstaged. Result: the docs are current. `docs/capy-install.md` and `docs/troubleshooting.md` already cover `gstack-lease touch --run`, the new `release` and `open` verbs, the `idle` state in `list`, the 120-minute run window and how leases with no recorded run are handled. These match the script's usage text and the calls in `gstack-skill-start`, `gstack-skill-end` and `lib/gate-dispositions.ts`. No edits were needed. Debt: `gstack-lease open` and `release` are explained only in the script's usage text and these reference docs, with no how-to. This is minor and does not block.

title: Second-model review defaults to GPT-6.2 Sol instead of GPT-6.1 Sol (GST-3384)
body:
When you don't name a second-model reviewer, the review step in /ship and /review on Capy now uses GPT-6.2 Sol instead of GPT-6.1 Sol, still at medium reasoning. A reviewer you name yourself is used exactly as given.
Why: reviews should run on the current frontier model, not an older generation.
Nothing to do.

<details><summary>What changed</summary>

A Claude-run /ship or /review on Capy that named no second-model reviewer used to start `openai/gpt-6.1-sol`. It now starts `openai/gpt-6.2-sol` at medium reasoning. The status line the review prints for that reviewer now says "default configuration" instead of "certified configuration", because the earlier no-loss measurement ran on GPT-6.1 Sol, not on 6.2. `docs/unattended.md` says which model that measurement used, and that you can still name GPT-6.1 Sol yourself.

Before: `openai/gpt-6.1-sol reasoning=medium … (certified configuration)`
After: `openai/gpt-6.2-sol reasoning=medium … (default configuration)`

</details>

<details><summary>Why</summary>

Our tooling should run on current frontier models, and GPT-6.1 Sol is the previous generation. With this change the default second-model review uses the current Sol, with no extra setup.

</details>

<details><summary>Blast radius</summary>

Only the default model for the second-model review changes, in `lib/capy-review-pass.js`. An explicitly named reviewer, the family-conflict stop and the fallback after a `cyber_policy` refusal (GPT-6 Astra read-only, then Gemini 4 Carbon) are unchanged. Nothing in `lib/`, `bin/`, `scripts/` or the skill templates parses the old "certified configuration" text (repo-wide search). The Sol family alias in `lib/agent-model.ts` and the smart tier in `lib/model-catalog.ts` still name GPT-6.1 Sol; they are separate settings and this PR does not touch them.

</details>

<details><summary>Test Coverage</summary>

All 4 changed code paths are covered by updated tests in `test/review-pass-step11.test.ts` and `test/review-pass-voice-failures.test.ts` (default model chosen, default note, non-default note, resume). No tests were added.

</details>

<details><summary>Pre-Landing Review</summary>

No blocking findings. One review round with three readers (a batched specialist, a Claude adversarial read and a second-model read); the second-model read was clean. Low-severity notes, none fixed:
- `lib/capy-review-pass.js:107`: the new default has no recall measurement of its own; the earlier measurement ran on GPT-6.1 Sol.
- `test/review-pass-step11.test.ts:187`: a test comment reads "the undefault configuration's recall", a leftover from a word swap.
- `lib/agent-model.ts:28`, `lib/model-catalog.ts:28`: these still map Sol to GPT-6.1, so the Sol a review uses depends on how it was chosen.
- `lib/capy-review-pass.js:111`: a review resumed across a gstack upgrade could run its retry on a different Sol than its first read; each status line prints the real model.

</details>

<details><summary>Exploratory QA</summary>

Smoke checks passed: no consumer reads the old "certified configuration" text, and the updated review-pass tests pass at this tree. No plan checks (no plan file).

</details>

<details><summary>Scope Drift</summary>

Scope Check: CLEAN. The diff changes the default reviewer model, its status wording, one docs paragraph, a changelog fragment and the matching tests.

</details>

<details><summary>Eval Results</summary>

No paid evals ran. No prompt, template, judge or eval harness changed. The eval selector picks 81 gate shards for this diff only because many cases reference `lib/capy-review-pass.js`; the change only affects Capy runs, and those cases run in Claude Code.

</details>

<details><summary>Documentation</summary>

**What was checked:** the five files this change touches, including the developer guide `docs/unattended.md` and the release-note fragment, plus a repo-wide search of docs and skill templates for older mentions of GPT-6.1 Sol.

**Result:** the docs are up to date and nothing needed editing. The guide already says that a Claude-run review with no second reviewer named now uses GPT-6.2 Sol at medium reasoning, that the earlier recall measurement ran on GPT-6.1 Sol, and that you can still choose GPT-6.1 Sol yourself. The release note says the same thing.

**Remaining doc debt:** `ETHOS.md` still lists GPT-6.1 Sol as one of the frontier models gstack is tested on. That setting is separate from this change and should be updated in its own PR.

title: A base branch with too many review_exclude_paths patterns no longer stops every /ship (GST-3399)
body:
When the base branch's ship policy fails only because of its `review_exclude_paths` or `review_content_patterns` list (for example 65 patterns, one over the limit of 64), /ship now reviews every file instead of stopping. Why: harness-evals main went to 65 patterns, and every /ship there stopped with POLICY_INVALID, including the PR that shortens the list. Nothing to do: the plan prints a `REVIEW_EXCLUDE: fallback (WARNING: ...)` line naming the error and the fix, and `gstack-ship-policy validate` still reports the list.
What changed ![On a base whose exclusion list has 65 patterns, the review plan used to refuse; it now reviews every file and prints the fallback warning](https://api.capy.ai/pr-assets/b9Z5a8A_HCoziHVqI6p-Dtn-QPdC1-Q_3PIwzNE5TVs.png) On a base whose exclusion list has 65 patterns, the review plan used to refuse; it now reviews every file and prints the fallback warning.
Before/after as text: On a base whose exclusion list has 65 patterns, the review plan used to refuse; it now reviews every file and prints the fallback warning ~~~diff --- Before · before.txt · captured output +++ After · after.txt · captured output +REVIEW_EXCLUDE: fallback (WARNING: the base policy origin/main@3a2e7aa45d0c does not validate: review_exclude_paths: more than 64 patterns; its review_exclude_paths and review_content_patterns are set aside and every file is reviewed, as with no exclusion; every other key applies as committed; fix: correct the list on main with its own PR, which this plan reviews in full; docs/ship-policy.md#review-exclude-paths) +READERS: forbid_fetch=0 forbid_paths=1 note=no head_added=0 digest=83d07b9ac5e4 +REVIEW_PLAN: class=code pass=1 next=full dispatches=3 numbers=yes(1) fingerprint=1009b849049384d2 reason="pass 1 reviews the whole diff" +after_exit=0 -READERS: refused: origin/main@3a2e7aa45d0c:.gstack/ship-policy.json review_exclude_paths: more than 64 patterns; fix the base branch's .gstack/ship-policy.json (POLICY_INVALID) -before_exit=3 ~~~
A repository whose base policy had one pattern too many could not ship anything, not even the fix for the list. Now, when every error in the base's `.gstack/ship-policy.json` is in `review_exclude_paths` or `review_content_patterns`, the policy loader drops both keys and applies the rest of the committed policy, so every file is reviewed and the readers' `forbid_paths`, `forbid_fetch` and `review` settings still apply. Falling back to the built-in defaults would have dropped those, which would be looser. Any other error, invalid JSON or an unreadable base still refuses, and a branch's own policy never counts before it lands. - `gstack-review-plan` prints the fallback line on stdout and stderr, and `--json` carries `review_exclude: { state: "fallback", source, errors }`. - The record /ship writes for the merge step stores the fallback as `review_exclude_fallback`, and the merge step and pre-merge checks read the base the same way. - `gstack-ship-policy show-effective` (the /ship policy line and the version check in /land-and-deploy) now reports such a base as valid with its other keys and prints the same warning; only `validate` still reports the list as invalid. - The limit of 64 is unchanged: it is the shared cap on every list in the policy (`MAX_LIST`, #3118), which `review_exclude_paths` adopted in #3852. - `REVIEW_PLAN_STOPPED`'s fix text now tells large repositories to set `GSTACK_REVIEW_PLAN_TIMEOUT_MS` (the follow-up from #4632's review).
Why "Every plan there refused POLICY_INVALID, the PR that shortens the list included." A bad exclusion list on the base deadlocked the repository. Now the list is set aside loudly, review gets wider rather than narrower, and the PR that fixes the list can be reviewed and land.
Blast radius The change reaches every reader of the base policy. That means the review plan, the record /ship writes, the merge step, the pre-merge checks and `show-effective`. It is safe because only the two exclusion keys are dropped and both only remove files from review, so the fallback can never review less than the committed policy. A /ship record from a review that left a PR file out is also refused when it is re-checked after a base merge (walked in tests: `test/review-exclude-base-fallback.test.ts`, `test/review-exclude.test.ts`, and a QA run on a 65-pattern repository).
Test Coverage Coverage audit (audit-only): 9 of 14 changed paths tested before the fix round. The two gaps that mattered, the `review_exclude_fallback` record /ship writes and its re-check after a base merge, and `show-effective` on a set-aside base, now have tests. Remaining gaps: the REVIEW_DIFF_TOO_LARGE fix text under a set-aside list, and the `REVIEW_PLAN_STOPPED` fix sentence (static text). Tests ran: targeted 107 Tests ran: free 1734 (files, taken from CI run 44959954725)
Pre-Landing Review Two full passes and one fix round. Pass 1 (specialists, a second reader for missed issues) found three informational items and one stale comment: two were fixed in 83611fd (one security-category finding, details recorded privately; the missing test for the merge-step record), the comment was moved back, and one wording item (security-category finding, details recorded privately) was left as a note. Pass 2 on the fix range found nothing. The adversarial reader found three low notes below; the second-model review returned CLEAN.

title: Installs leave gstack's test fixtures out of the user's home (GST-3402)
body:
A fresh `./setup` install, and the next update of an existing one, no longer puts `test/fixtures/` (gstack's test and eval data) on disk. Why: those files hold eval task material (real issues from other repos, held-out prompts) that every agent session and eval run in that home could read; nothing installed reads them. Nothing to do: contributor clones (`git config gstack.contributor true`), CI and clones with the dev toolchain keep the full tree.
How it works - Every install path is a shallow git clone of the whole repository followed by `./setup`: the README command, the Capy installer, `/gstack-upgrade` (fast-forward, reset or fresh clone) and the session auto-updater. Codex, Gemini and the other hosts get generated skill folders that link back into that checkout, so the checkout is the only place `test/` lives. - `setup` now runs `_trim_install_fixtures` after the build succeeds. For a user install (the same signal that already picks production-only dependencies: unmarked, not CI, no dev toolchain) it sets a git sparse checkout of `/*` and `!/test/fixtures/`. Git applies it on every later pull, `reset` and `gstack-ff-update`, so new fixtures never reach disk. - It changes only the top of gstack's own checkout (a vendored copy inside a project is left alone), leaves sparse patterns someone else set, keeps a fixture the person edited, and never fails setup. - Marking a trimmed clone as a contributor's and running `./setup` again brings the fixtures back. - Only `test/fixtures/` is left out. The runtime imports 24 files under `test/helpers/`, and the browse cookie integrity check hashes files under `browse/test/`, so those stay.
What still carries the data The working tree no longer has the files, but a shallow clone's git object store still holds them, compressed, for the checked-out commit: `git show HEAD:test/fixtures/...` inside the install would print them. Removing that needs the eval material out of this repository's tree.
Tests - `test/setup-install-fixtures.test.ts` (new; 7 of its 9 cases fail on main): a fresh shallow install has no `test/fixtures/` and keeps `test/helpers/`; fixtures stay out across `bin/gstack-ff-update` and `git pull --ff-only` while other files move; an edited fixture is kept; contributor, CI, `GSTACK_CONTRIBUTOR=1` and dev-toolchain clones keep the tree; marking a clone restores it; a vendored copy and foreign sparse patterns are untouched; setup calls it once, after the build; the static import closure of `bin/`, `lib/`, `hosts/`, the binaries' sources and the doc generator never reaches `test/fixtures/`, with a negative control. - By hand on a fresh shallow clone of this branch in an isolated home: `./setup --host claude` left `test/fixtures/` out with a clean `git status`; a forced rebuild on the trimmed tree passed; `gstack-skill-start` started ship, review, qa-only and browse; the Capy installer (`install.sh --for ship`) ended `gstack: ok` on the trimmed tree.
Agent notes GSTA-759 for GST-3402 (from GEVA-568 via GEVA-2). The /ship receipt is added here when /ship finishes. ```gstack-receipt-runs {"head":"793d137543b74908b15ffb2171c437bb101f164b","run":"ship-4638","status":"started","review_loop":{"passes":1,"blocking_found":0,"deferred":0,"noted":0,"fixed":1,"scope":"frozen","rounds":1,"dispatches":{"specialist":3,"red-team":1}}} {"head":"ba7b197004b7232a539447cda0ea9e8bd87ad130","run":"ship-4638b","mark":"stop","tree":"a9a370a4b2d7cb8f5f3f249e150fdc03562fc8a2"} ```

title: The release gate's live /autoplan guard test runs its actor on Haiku 4.5 again (GST-3407)
body:
The live /autoplan publication guard test goes back to a Claude Haiku 4.5 actor; the four other canaries and the eval defaults stay on Haiku 5.5.
Why: since #4630 moved the actor to Haiku 5.5, the test failed 8 of 8 tries and holds the stable release, because the new actor runs ahead of the background reviewer's notice and never reaches the path the test checks.
Nothing to do.

<details><summary>What changed</summary>

The release gate's live /autoplan guard test failed every try after #4630 moved its scripted actor to Haiku 5.5. The test now pins its actor to `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` again, and its header comment records why and which runs showed it. This fix adds its own changelog fragment; the fragment #4630 landed stays as it is.

| Actor | Commits | Tries | Result |

| Haiku 5.5 | 5db285c1, 3c1c22e6, c8641cc4 | 8 (runs 44952328945, 44955253712, 44956497475) | 8 fail: 7 time out at 488 s with all four guarded steps done before the first notice (`afterNotice: []`), 1 skipped its Phase 1 publication and was refused `publication_missing` |
| Haiku 4.5 | bisect prefixes up to 79eea6d5 | 11 (runs 44954167348, 44956497475) | 11 pass in 68 to 80 s, notice before the close packet Read |

</details>

<details><summary>Why</summary>

"The release gate failed autoplan-guard-pty 8 of 8 tries." The test asserts that the close packet Read, the Phase 2 entry and the Phase 2 dispatch happen in the turn the CEO reviewer's completion notice starts (`closePacketReadAfterNotice`). Haiku 5.5 does all four steps before the notice arrives, so the test never reaches the path it checks. The actor acts out a scripted turn and is not a model under test, so Haiku 4.5 keeps it.

</details>

Only this one live test reads the changed `MODEL` constant, and no threshold, trial count or assertion changes. The guard itself made the right call on every try (no wrong allow, no permission card). Run 44954167348 is a bisect over earlier commits, not a rerun of 5db285c1, so this is not a flaky case (file read: test/skill-e2e-autoplan-guard-pty.test.ts:34; runs read).

title: gstack-uninstall no longer deletes nested worktrees, locked worktrees or a .gstack repo (GST-2268)
body:
Uninstalling gstack no longer deletes work that exists nowhere else: a worktree nested inside another `.gstack-worktrees/` checkout, a locked worktree, unpushed submodule commits, or a project `.gstack/` that is its own git repository. This serves the install goal: removing gstack must never take a user's unsaved work with it. Nothing to do as a user; a clean worktree on a branch is still removed by a plain `--force`.
What changed People running `gstack-uninstall` could still lose work that #4241 meant to protect: a worktree nested inside another `.gstack-worktrees/` checkout was never looked at, a locked worktree went with `--force-worktrees`, a submodule's local-only commits went with the worktree holding it, and a `.gstack/` folder holding its own git repository was deleted with the install. The uninstall now finds every checkout under `.gstack-worktrees/`, nested ones included, and stops before removing anything when one has uncommitted changes or unshared commits, when a worktree is locked (even with `--force-worktrees`), or when a submodule inside one of those worktrees has commits no remote-tracking branch holds. A `.gstack/` that is its own repository is kept and named. Every check runs again after the confirmation prompt, so a checkout edited while the prompt waits is still kept. A locked worktree now stops a plain `--force` with a clear reason (output from this branch, fixture paths shortened): ```text gstack-uninstall: refusing to delete r/.gstack-worktrees/run-1/wt: it is locked (git worktree lock) fix: commit the work to a branch or stash it, unlock a locked worktree with git worktree unlock , re-run with --keep-state to keep every worktree, or re-run with --force-worktrees to delete the unlocked ones anyway ``` Review caught one regression in the first version. The list of registered worktrees became a bash array, but one check still read it as a single value, so every clean worktree on a branch was refused and a plain `--force` removed nothing. That line now reads the whole list, and a new test proves a clean worktree is removed again.
Why "`gstack-uninstall` still loses work #4241 was meant to save" (GST-2268). Removing gstack should take gstack's files and nothing a person cannot get back.
Blast radius Only `bin/gstack-uninstall`, its doc and its tests change; nothing else calls the script. The new checks only add refusals before the first removal (read in `_check_project_keep` and `_check_deletion_targets`, both called before the prompt and again after it), and the one path that now removes more, a clean registered worktree, is covered by a test that fails without the fix (script ran: 63 of 63 tests pass).
Pre-Landing Review Pass 1 found one blocking regression (every clean registered worktree refused as unregistered) and one test-isolation note (two git-shim tests could loop through a wrapper `git`); both were fixed. Pass 2, the second-model review (GPT-6.1 Sol) and the adversarial read found nothing. The test-isolation note did not reproduce on this machine; the fix falls back to the old lookup when git's own binary is not found.
Exploratory QA Four smoke contracts on throwaway repositories, each run before and after the review fix: no worktrees (exit 0), a dirty worktree nested in another (exit 2, both kept), a locked worktree (exit 2, kept) and a clean worktree on a branch (exit 2 before the fix, the regression; exit 0 and removed after it). All four pass on the final code.
Scope Drift Scope Check: CLEAN
Issues Refs #4241
Verification Results No plan file, so no plan checks; automatic QA above.
TODOS No TODO items completed in this PR.
Documentation **Scope.** Base d615415, head d71e678. Committed files: `bin/gstack-uninstall`, `docs/uninstall.md`, `test/uninstall.test.ts`, plus one untracked changelog fragment. Nothing staged or unstaged; the banned-terms check found nothing. **Result.** Current, with no edits. `docs/uninstall.md` already describes the new behavior: nested worktrees, locked worktrees (even with `--force-worktrees`), the submodule check, the check that runs again after the prompt, keeping a `.gstack/` that is its own git repository, and the safer manual removal loop. The changelog fragment, README.md and docs/install.md agree with it. No diagrams changed and no generated docs needed regenerating. **Debt.** `docs/troubleshooting.md#uninstall` has no entry for two project-level refusals: `refusing to delete : it is locked (git worktree lock)` and `refusing to uninstall: /.gstack/ holds its own git repository...`. These were reported and not filled, as the audit rules require. title: Router tests use synthetic prompts instead of real benchmark tasks (GST-3402)
body:
gstack's current files no longer contain real benchmark tasks: the router tests' 63 SWE-rebench prompts are replaced with synthetic ones covering the same routes. Why: every install is a clone of this repository, so those tasks sat in each user's home and in every eval run that installed gstack, contaminating any eval that uses them. Nothing to do; a new check fails if a SWE-bench-style task id appears under `test/` or `browse/test/` again.
What changed Eval runs install gstack, and an install is a clone, so the router tests' real SWE-rebench prompts were sitting next to the agents being measured. Those prompts are gone from the current tree, the router tests run on made-up projects and issues instead, and a free test now stops any SWE-bench-style task id from coming back. - Deleted `test/fixtures/skill-route-b1-in-sample.json` (60 B1 in-sample prompts built from SWE-rebench tasks) and `test/fixtures/skill-route-bug-reports.json` (3 SWE-rebench bug reports), and removed the three real task ids from `test/skill-route.test.ts`. - Added `test/fixtures/skill-route-synthetic-prompts.json`: made-up projects and issues only. The B1 wrapper around each task is kept, since that is the text the router sees in those runs. - `test/free-fixtures.test.ts` now scans every file under `test/` and `browse/test/` for an id shaped like a SWE-bench or SWE-rebench task, with a negative control that uses invented ids. A file too large to scan is reported instead of skipped. - `docs/skill-routing-and-contracts.md` points at the new fixture, and `docs/TESTING_INTERNALS.md` describes the new check. - Older commits still hold the original prompts, so an install with full git history, such as one pinned to a commit, can still reach them through `git log`. Removing them from history would need a rewrite, which this PR does not do.
Coverage, before and after | Router test | Before | After | |---|---|---| | B1-shaped prompts: every bug report names prove-it alone, never /verify first; plain prompts name nothing; a feature task is not a bug report | 60 real prompts (46 bug, 14 feature) | 60 synthetic prompts (46 bug, 14 feature), same assertions; the prompt hash check against the eval plan is dropped because there is no plan to match | | GST-3123: words a long bug report shares with a /qa trigger don't route it to /qa; with a bug-fix skill it routes there | 3 real reports, the longest 17,470 characters | 4 synthetic reports, the longest 14,118 characters, with a new assertion that one is longer than the router's head and tail windows | The task-id check fails on main, naming both deleted fixtures and `test/skill-route.test.ts`.
Router gaps the first draft found My first draft of the synthetic reports was written without looking at the detector. 14 of the 46 bug reports did not read as bug reports, and one routed to /verify first. Three of the 4 long reports routed to /qa, because a long report containing "find", a defect word and "site" anywhere matches the "find bugs on site" trigger, and one contained the phrase "test the site". I reworded those prompts to state their symptom plainly, so this PR keeps the router's behavior and its tests as they were. The gaps are recorded for a follow-up.
Why Real benchmark tasks in the repository meant every gstack install carried them into the user's home and into every eval arm that installed gstack. An agent under test could find the very task it was being scored on. Now the current tree holds only synthetic prompts, and a free test keeps it that way.
Blast radius Only tests, test fixtures, one changelog entry and two docs change; no product code, skill text, setup or install path is touched. The deleted fixtures had no other readers (a tree-wide search for both file names finds none), and CI's full free suite passed at this tree (run 44964526303).
Pre-Landing Review Two review rounds, plus one quick recheck of the first fix. The first round's Red Team found the changelog overclaimed (full-history installs still hold the old prompts), and that wording was fixed. The second-model review (GPT-6.2 Astra) found two real problems in the new check, both fixed and rechecked by the second round: the negative control spelled two real task ids in pieces (it now uses invented ids), and files over 8 MB were skipped silently (they are now reported). Nothing above the blocking floor is open.
Review notes Below the blocking floor (advisory, informational, test-gap or wording items); recorded here and not fixed in this PR. - INFORMATIONAL `sf-0f9be970b67d` security finding, details recorded privately - INFORMATIONAL `test/free-fixtures.test.ts:178` The task-id scan checks file contents but not file paths, so a task stored under a folder named after its id with no id in the text would pass. - INFORMATIONAL `test/fixtures/skill-route-synthetic-prompts.json:1` The synthetic fixture's about text says no text comes from a real task, but every prompt keeps B1's prompt wrapper (task content is all synthetic). - INFORMATIONAL `test/free-fixtures.test.ts:159` The scan's pattern misses an id glued to a word character, such as one prefixed with instance_. - INFORMATIONAL `changelog.d/synthetic-skill-route-fixtures.md:4` Clones made before this change keep the old prompts in their git history after upgrading; only a fresh shallow install is clean. - INFORMATIONAL `test/skill-route.test.ts:77` The bug-report-is-not-a-QA-request router test never produces a /qa candidate with these prompts (also true on main), so it passes without exercising the overlap. - INFORMATIONAL `test/free-fixtures.test.ts:177` No test covers the new branch that reports a file over 8 MB as too large to scan.
Exploratory QA No runtime surface changed: this PR touches tests, fixtures and docs only. The reviewers ran the two affected test files themselves (44 pass, 0 fail at the reviewed tree), and the new check's negative control proves it catches a planted id.
Design Review No frontend files changed — design review skipped.
Eval Results No prompt-related files changed — evals skipped.
Plan Completion Plan completion audit: not run (no plan is bound to this branch; bug fixes need no plan).
TODOS No TODO items completed in this PR.
Documentation **Status:** updated. One factual doc edit; no blockers. **Scope:** base c8641cc to HEAD 78a1c6c (4 commits, 8 files), with no staged, unstaged or untracked changes. The changes swap the real SWE-rebench router fixtures for synthetic prompts and add a free test that scans for task ids. **Documentation health:** - `docs/skill-routing-and-contracts.md`: current (the branch already points it at the synthetic fixture; 60 prompts, 46 bug reports, checked against the file) - `docs/TESTING_INTERNALS.md`: updated (documents the task-id scan in `test/free-fixtures.test.ts`) - `changelog.d/fix-synthetic-skill-route-fixtures.md`: reviewed, owned by ship **Coverage debt:** the task-id scan now has reference coverage only. There is no how-to for contributors on adding router fixtures safely (common gap). No architecture diagram drift.

title: Hash manifests no longer keep excluded results files in review, and the data-file scan cap can be raised (HARN-64)
body:
A results PR whose `pins.sha256` lists its data files now gets `review_exclude_paths` instead of a refused 13.3 MB review, and hash-manifest lines no longer read as money, auth or data for review depth. Why: harness-evals #538 kept all 2,140 excluded result files in review because the name scan timed out on a 2,140-path manifest and would have counted that manifest as code anyway. Nothing to do; `GSTACK_REVIEW_CONSUMER_SCAN_CAP` is a new optional override.
What changed - **Name scan** (`lib/review-exclude.ts`): `git grep -F -o` with thousands of strings grew with the string count (2,140 paths: 176 s, past git's 120 s bound, so every candidate was kept as `consumer-scan-unavailable`). It now lists hit files with `git grep -F -l --no-color`, reads them (worktree files directly, blobs through one `git cat-file --batch`), and checks each path with a substring test. A file whose every non-blank line is a hex digest and a path (as `sha256sum` writes) names nothing; any other line makes it a consumer again. - **Risk classes** (`lib/review-risk.ts`): the same manifest rule skips the money, security, data and eval line checks. Path checks still run, and the secret line check still reads manifest lines. The manifest path may only hold letters, digits and `. / _ - + @ ~`, so no assignment, call or quoted string fits. - **Consumer-scan cap** (`lib/review-collect.ts`, `bin/gstack-review-plan`): `GSTACK_REVIEW_CONSUMER_SCAN_CAP` raises the 2,000-file cap through the same bounded parser as the other review-plan limits. A tripped cap prints a `CONSUMER_SCAN: skipped:` line that names both remedies, raising the cap or moving the data into its own PR. The cap is read from the environment, so a raised cap must also be set where a finished review is checked again (docs/review-policy.md). - Docs: docs/ship-policy.md (review_exclude_paths name scan) and docs/review-policy.md (consumer scan). Changelog fragment added.
Why harness-evals #538 at 2072d985 (303,971 files): the plan took 163 s before and 48 s after, with `active excluded 2140 kept 0`. Risk classes went from money, security, data and eval to security, data and eval, so the depth stays full.
Blast radius Only the review-depth and review-exclusion planning that /ship and the merge checks read. A manifest with any non-digest line is read exactly as before. With `color.grep=always` set in git config, the scan still reads plain file names (new test).
Tests - CI: free-tests.yml run 44972050629 at 4277b6a2 (green, 1,736 test files). macOS named regressions from that run and windows-smoke run 44971605277 at the same head. - Review-depth check with no paid run: the risk rules change was repinned under replay HARN-64. Planning the last 460 main commits of gstack, harness-evals and gstack-evals with the old and the new rules gave the same class and risk classes on all 460, including the 13 commits that touch a hash manifest. - Failing-first: on main, the manifest risk case and two exclusion cases fail; the new `color.grep=always` case failed before the `--no-color` fix and passes after.
Agent notes ## Agent notes Lane GSTA-757 for HARN-64. The cause was the exclusion's name scan, not CONSUMER_SCAN_CAP. Documentation audit (Step 14.5): **Status:** current. The docs already match the change, and no edits were needed. **Scope:** the committed range from dd611038 to 4277b6a2 (11 files, no staged, unstaged or new files): the consumer-scan cap override in lib/review-collect.ts and bin/gstack-review-plan, the `git grep -l` name scan and hash-manifest skip in lib/review-exclude.ts, the `HASH_MANIFEST_LINE` risk exemption in lib/review-risk.ts, plus tests and fixtures. I inventoried the docs tree and grepped every doc for consumer-scan, cap and manifest references. **Documentation health:** - docs/review-policy.md: current (the branch already documents `GSTACK_REVIEW_CONSUMER_SCAN_CAP`, the `CONSUMER_SCAN: skipped:` line and the warning that carry and the merge queue need the same cap) - docs/ship-policy.md: current (the branch already documents the hash/pin manifest rule and the `git grep -F -l` scan) - Other docs: no stale references found **Coverage debt:** the risk-class table in docs/review-policy.md doesn't say that a hash or pin manifest's lines skip the money, security and data classes but still count for secret; ship-policy.md covers it. `GSTACK_REVIEW_CONSUMER_SCAN_CAP` has reference coverage only, with no troubleshooting entry for the `CONSUMER_SCAN:` line. No diagram drift. Pre-Landing Review: 2 issues — 1 auto-fixed, 1 asked (0 fixed, 1 skipped), 0 deferred, 0 noted. title: Stop gstack-uninstall deleting a repo's committed .gstack files and unsaved worktrees (GST-2197)
body:
`gstack-uninstall` no longer deletes a project's committed `.gstack/` files, a `.gstack/` that is its own git repository, or unsaved work in `.gstack-worktrees/` checkouts.
Uninstalling gstack should never cost you work that exists nowhere else.
Nothing to do.

<details><summary>What changed</summary>

![Before, uninstall deleted a .gstack folder holding its own git repo and its unpushed commit; now it keeps it and says why](https://api.capy.ai/pr-assets/pVavVnfOwv5qg3Hdl4IRNFAj88nbNTDbtMdASwzjLek.png)

Before, uninstall deleted a .gstack folder holding its own git repo and its unpushed commit; now it keeps it and says why.

<details><summary>Before/after as text: Before, uninstall deleted a .gstack folder holding its own git repo and its unpushed commit; now it keeps it and says why</summary>

~~~diff
--- Before · before.txt · captured output
+++ After · after.txt · captured output
 $ gstack-uninstall --force   # in a repo whose .gstack/ is its own git repo with one unpushed commit
 exit=0
 --- stderr
+kept /tmp/demo/proj/.gstack/: it holds its own git repository, whose commits may exist nowhere else; check it, then remove it by hand
 --- after
+.git
+notes.md
+unpushed
-ls: cannot access '/tmp/demo/proj/.gstack': No such file or directory
-fatal: cannot change to '/tmp/demo/proj/.gstack': No such file or directory
 
~~~

</details>

Running `gstack-uninstall` inside a project used to delete the whole `.gstack/` folder and every checkout under `.gstack-worktrees/`, including committed ship policy, uncommitted edits and commits no branch held. A plain uninstall now removes only the files git ignores under `.gstack/` and keeps a `.gstack/` that is its own repository. A checkout under `.gstack-worktrees/` with uncommitted changes, unsaved commits, a lock or no registration stops the uninstall with exit 2 before anything is removed; `--force-worktrees` deletes those anyway, except a locked one. Every folder uninstall is about to delete (each gstack install, the per-skill folders and `~/.gstack`) is checked the same way first. `--keep-state` keeps both project folders.

</details>

<details><summary>Why</summary>

Uninstalling gstack took a project's checked-in `.gstack/ship-policy.json` and a worktree's unsaved edits with it, and neither can be rebuilt. Now uninstall only removes what gstack can rebuild, and it stops and names the checkout when something there is unsaved.

</details>

<details><summary>Blast radius</summary>

Only `bin/gstack-uninstall`, its docs page and its tests change. The new checks run before any deletion and only add refusals or kept folders, so the worst new outcome is an uninstall that stops with exit 2 and a fix line; 73 tests in `test/uninstall.test.ts` cover the kept, refused and still-deleted cases (script ran), and two hand probes reproduced and then confirmed the `.gstack` repository case.

</details>

<details><summary>Review notes</summary>

Below the blocking floor; recorded here and not fixed in this PR.

- INFORMATIONAL `bin/gstack-uninstall:425` The unsaved-work check runs `git status` inside checkouts under project-local skill folders, so a crafted `.git` config clean filter there would run. A `git clone` cannot deliver one; refusing every `.git` there would block uninstalling project-local git-clone installs.
- INFORMATIONAL `bin/gstack-uninstall:429` On git older than 2.36 every git-clone install now makes uninstall exit 2. Intended, documented and tested; the refusal already says it needs git 2.36 or later.
- INFORMATIONAL `bin/gstack-uninstall:783` When `$HOME` is itself a git repo, the project `.gstack` is `~/.gstack`: uninstall prints "kept" and the global state step then deletes it anyway (no new loss versus before; misleading message).
- INFORMATIONAL `test/uninstall.test.ts:923` The new test checks the kept message and the commit log, but not that `notes.md` survives, and no deeper nested `.git` case.
- INFORMATIONAL `bin/gstack-uninstall:783` The guard keeps any nested `.git`, including fully pushed clones and orphaned gitlink files; no data loss, a product call.

</details>

<details><summary>Exploratory QA</summary>

Functional smoke on the CLI in isolated temporary homes and repositories: a repo with tracked `.gstack` policy kept it and removed the ignored state (pass); a `.gstack/` holding its own repository was deleted before the review fix (failed, replayed) and kept after it (pass). Final verdict: pass, 7 probes.

</details>

<details><summary>Scope Drift</summary>

Scope Check: CLEAN. Intent: stop uninstall deleting committed `.gstack` files and unsaved worktrees. Delivered: that, plus the same unsaved-work check on every folder uninstall deletes.

</details>

<details><summary>Documentation</summary>

**Status:** current. No doc edits were needed.

Scope: base 9178cace to head 7b369cdb, plus the untracked changelog.d fragment. Changed files: bin/gstack-uninstall, docs/uninstall.md and test/uninstall.test.ts. I also read the docs that mention gstack-uninstall.

| File | Status |
|---|---|
| docs/uninstall.md | Current. The branch already describes the protection for tracked .gstack files, the worktree checks and --force-worktrees, and the text matches the script's --help. |
| docs/troubleshooting.md | Current. The #uninstall messages and fixes match. |
| docs/install.md, docs/state-root.md, docs/hosts.md | Current. Their mentions don't conflict with the new behavior. |
| changelog.d fragment | Current. It matches the behavior. |

Coverage debt: none. Diagram drift: none.

</details>

- [x] `bun test test/uninstall.test.ts`: 73 pass, 0 fail (tests_ran=73)
- [ ] `bun run test` (full free suite): runs in CI on this head

</details>

title: Pull requests get a Test changes summary of deleted or skipped tests and edits to their own checks (GST-3386)
body:
Every gstack pull request now gets a flag-only Test changes check listing removed or skipped tests, loosened limits and edits to the files that run its own checks.
Why: agents write most of our tests, and a pull request shouldn't be able to quietly weaken them or grade itself with an edited checker; this two-week trial measures how often that happens.
Nothing to do: the check isn't required, and a flag never turns it red.

<details><summary>What changed</summary>

![Pull requests now get a Test changes summary; main had none](https://api.capy.ai/pr-assets/NPUIJRAdMqg2vONxRidrdRSE7ZdlBApwPbEC-ics1Z4.png)

Pull requests now get a Test changes summary; main had none.

<details><summary>Before/after as text: Pull requests now get a Test changes summary; main had none</summary>

~~~diff
--- Before · before.txt · captured output
+++ After · after.txt · captured output
+$ bun scripts/test-changes-report.ts --base dd611038 --head f362224b --summary-file summary.md
+TEST_CHANGES: tagged={} tests_added=14 tests_removed=0 gate_files=1 unread=0 candidate=dd611038ca41..f362224be5d2
+
+## Test changes (flags never fail this check)
+
+Tests added: 14. Tests removed: 0. Hunks that remove or skip a test (RH-1), add a suppression (RH-13), bypass a gate (RH-14) or relax a gate value (RH-15): 0.
+
+**This pull request edits files that run or define its own checks:**
+
+- `.github/workflows/test-changes.yml`
+
+Each flag needs a reason in the pull request, or a reviewer ruling. See docs/ship-policy.md#test-changes.
-$ git cat-file -e origin/main:.github/workflows/test-changes.yml
-fatal: path '.github/workflows/test-changes.yml' exists on disk, but not in 'origin/main'
-(main has no Test changes check: a pull request that deletes or skips tests gets no summary)
 
~~~

</details>

A pull request could delete or skip a test, or edit the workflow that grades it, and nothing on the pull request said so. Now a check on every pull request lists hunks that remove or skip a test, add a suppression, bypass a check or loosen a limit, counts test declarations added and removed, and names edits to the files that run this repository's own checks. It runs main's copy of the scan on `pull_request_target`, reads the pull request's commits as git objects without checking them out, and exits 0 on any flag. `gstack-gate-diff` gains `--head <sha>` to scan merge-base to a fetched commit without touching the working tree.

</details>

<details><summary>Why</summary>

"A pull request shouldn't be able to grade itself." Agents write most of our tests, so this trial shows reviewers, on every pull request, where tests or checks got weaker, and measures how often that happens before anything is made blocking.

</details>

<details><summary>Blast radius</summary>

The new workflow is not a required check and never checks out or runs pull request code. It checks out main only with a read-only, non-persisted token, and pull request fields reach the shell only through `env:` (test/test-changes-workflow-safety.test.ts, read and run). `gstack-gate-diff` keeps its working-tree path unchanged unless `--head` is passed (bin/gstack-gate-diff, file:line read; 141 focused tests and the full free suite passed at this head).

</details>

<details><summary>Test Coverage</summary>

Coverage: 67% of 15 changed code paths have a test at two stars or better; 0 regressions found. Tests: 1855 → 1855 (audit only, the head was frozen).
Leftover gaps, proposed but not written: declarations in .md/.json hunks not counted; RH-13/14/15 counts (only RH-1 exercised); `--base` without `--head` rejected; `gstack-gate-diff --head` with no sha; the partial-read line.
Tests ran: focused 141
Tests ran: free 1736 files (from the CI run at this head)

</details>

<details><summary>Pre-Landing Review</summary>

No blocking issues. This was a read-only final review of this head: six readers (a batched testing, security and state-machine reader, a red team, an adversarial reader, a second-model review on gpt-6.1-sol, and a targeted reader for check-editing code) all returned no blockers. The second-model review's verdict was clean.

Below-floor notes, shipped as notes:
- A `[skip ci]` commit whose subject looks like a test declaration can raise the "tests added" count by one.
- The "Partial read … were not tagged" summary line is worded too strongly: hunks past the reading cap are still tagged.
- Unpaired loosened limits (gate-diff's `RH-15?` tag) aren't reported; the doc doesn't say so.
- The workflow has not run on GitHub yet; the blobless fetch without stored credentials is proven only by the first run after merge.

title: Repos can prove copied open-source files match their upstream byte for byte (GST-3298)
body:
New `gstack-vendored-verify` checks that every file a repo copies from an open-source project is byte-for-byte that project's file, at a commit on its default branch, a tag or a branch the base names, from a repository the base branch trusts. Why: harness-evals copies 1,056 upstream test files into its eval tasks and today hides them from review in tar archives; this proves the claim the archives only assert (1,054 of 1,056 verify on #504 in 19 seconds; 2 are upstream executables). Nothing to do unless you vendor code: the new `review_vendored` policy key is off by default.
What changed - `lib/review-vendored.ts`: the `review_vendored` key's validation, the `gstack-vendored/v1` manifest, and the check. Fetches go anonymously to each upstream over https with no ambient git config, prompt or redirect, and a timeout; commit history and each pin's file listing are cached under the state root, so `--offline` answers from the cache. - `bin/gstack-vendored-verify --base [--all] [--offline] [--json]`: one line per pin, one line per failure with its reason code and fix, exit 1 when a manifest claims something untrue. Meant as a required CI check. - A commit only a fork, a pull request ref or a merge-queue branch holds fails (`VENDORED_UNREACHABLE`), even when the base's branch glob is `*`; so does a force-pushed one. A named branch the upstream lacks is skipped instead of failing the other pins. Executables, symlinks, submodules, renamed files, local edits and unlisted upstreams fail with their own codes. - `lib/ship-policy.ts` registers the key (validation lives in the new module; ship-policy.ts stays at its 800-line cap). Eight result codes with troubleshooting entries; docs/vendored-code.md; a ship-policy.md key row; a changelog fragment. - /ship's review does not read the key yet; that is the follow-up PR.
Tests `test/review-vendored.test.ts` (18 cases) builds local upstream repositories and runs the command against them: verified files; a one-byte edit; pull-ref, merge-queue and force-pushed pins; a base-named `release/*` branch; a deleted upstream; an upstream the head tries to trust for itself; a `*` glob that must still refuse a merge-queue commit; a named branch the upstream lacks; an upstream submodule; `--json` keeping its pin count; executable and renamed files; bad manifests; changed-only versus `--all` scope; `--offline` reusing the cache; and a 401 server and a hanging server, both failing without prompting or hanging. Every consumer repo's global git config rewrites the upstream root to a missing folder, so a fetch that read ambient config would fail. Real run on harness-evals#504 (24a377ab with its tars unpacked and a generated manifest, 11 GitHub upstreams, 71 pins): checked=1056 verified=1054 failed=2, 19 s cold, 15 MB cache. The 2 failures are `tests/test_rr.py` in cachetools, executable upstream too (VENDORED_MODE).
Agent notes
Documentation **Status:** blocked. One factual correction is needed, and read-only mode can't make it. **Scope:** 7 commits (dd611038ca41..b6d4150) that add `gstack-vendored-verify`, the `review_vendored` policy key, 8 `VENDORED_*` result codes and their doctor anchors. Docs audited: docs/vendored-code.md (new), docs/troubleshooting.md, docs/ship-policy.md and the changelog.d fragment, checked against bin/gstack-vendored-verify and lib/review-vendored.ts. AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and README.md are unaffected. **Documentation health:** - docs/vendored-code.md: current (flags, exit codes 0 to 3, timeout env var and manifest rules all match the code) - docs/troubleshooting.md: current (all 8 anchors match the result codes) - changelog.d/vendored-files-verified-against-upstream-pins.md: current - docs/ship-policy.md: needs a fix. The `review_vendored` row leaves out pins from branches the base policy names (`{ url, branches }`) **Coverage debt:** `gstack-vendored-verify` has reference, how-to and explanation coverage in docs/vendored-code.md but no tutorial. That's a common gap and doesn't block. No architecture diagram drift was found. Documentation exception: accepted by GSTA-674 lane 2026-11-22 via GSTA-674 lane message to its /ship subagent, 2026-11-22 (option A): docs/ship-policy.md's review_vendored row leaves out base-named branches; the one-line fix ships in PR 2 (GST-3298)

title: Stop gstack-uninstall from deleting a repo's committed .gstack files and unsaved worktrees (GST-2197)
body:
`gstack-uninstall` no longer deletes a repo's committed `.gstack/` files, worktrees with unsaved work, or a `.gstack/` that is its own git repository.
Why: uninstalling gstack should never cost a user their own work.
Nothing to do.

<details><summary>What changed</summary>

Running `gstack-uninstall` in a repo used to remove the whole `.gstack/` and `.gstack-worktrees/` folders, including files the repo commits there (such as ship policy) and checkouts with uncommitted changes or unpushed commits. Now a plain uninstall keeps git-tracked `.gstack/` files and removes only the ones git ignores, keeps a `.gstack/` that holds its own git repository (with a message saying so), and stops with exit 2 before removing anything when a checkout under `.gstack-worktrees/` holds unsaved work. `--force-worktrees` deletes those checkouts anyway, and the check runs again after you confirm.

![A .gstack folder that is its own git repository: deleted before the fix, kept with a message after](https://api.capy.ai/pr-assets/ICmmqPN49NPBJpIPWskJ76dQSTnEeRXvp3qcxUHIb9c.png)

<details><summary>Why</summary>

"Stop gstack-uninstall deleting a repo's committed .gstack files and unsaved worktrees" (GST-2197). Uninstall is the last thing someone runs, so it must leave every file it did not create, and every commit that exists nowhere else, where it found it.

</details>

<details><summary>Blast radius</summary>

Only `bin/gstack-uninstall`'s per-project cleanup and its docs change; the global `~/.gstack` removal and host cleanup are untouched. Every new path fails toward keeping data, and `test/uninstall.test.ts` (73 tests, run here and in CI) walks each refusal and keep case (script ran).

</details>

<details><summary>Pre-Landing Review</summary>

Two review passes. Pass 1 found one blocker: a `.gstack/` that is its own git repository was still deleted when the project tracks nothing there. It was reproduced with a failing test, fixed (the folder is now kept with a message) and the test restored. Pass 2 and the second-model review found nothing blocking.

</details>

- INFORMATIONAL `test/uninstall.test.ts:923` No test for a .git left in .gstack-worktrees after its checkouts are removed. Severity Low, Blocks: no.

title: /ship can finish again when a docs check ran before a base merge (GST-3260)
body:
Pull requests that merged their base after /ship's docs check can finish /ship again, instead of being refused with no way out. Before this, a docs check that edited a file, followed by a base merge and a re-check with no edits, made /ship's final record refuse with a `field=review_exclude` error. Nothing for readers to do.
What changed - `writeExcludeBinds` no longer counts files under `review_exclude_paths` that only the merged base changed. A file the PR itself touches still counts. - When the latest docs check made no edits, the earlier checks it builds on are still tried, instead of an immediate refusal. - The rebuilt file selection is compared with the reviewed one the same way /ship already compares them across a base merge, so a base policy change by itself doesn't void it. - A docs file the PR changes after the last check still refuses (new negative test).
Why gbrain#9975 hit this on gstack 1.102.1.0: docs check A1 edited docs/guides/setup.md, a base merge added docs files and a sixth review_exclude pattern, and re-check A2 at the merged head made no edits. /ship refused with both checks, and no documented route cleared it.
Agent notes - Failing-first: `test/review-exclude.test.ts` "the #9975 shape …" failed on main with the GBRA-712 refusal (receipt write, RECEIPT_INVALID field=review_exclude) and passes here; 51/51 in that file. Code: lib/ship-receipt-depth.ts. The fix also binds through carryExcludeBinds/reviewedRecord. - Part of GST-3260 (PR 4 of 4, independent of the others). title: Land checks a PR whose base moved in a separate clone, then with full CI, before merging (GST-1766)
body:
When main has moved since a PR's last CI run, `gstack-ship-queue land` now runs its local merge checks in a throwaway clone and can then run the full CI suite on the merged code before it merges. Why: the old checks shared the checkout's git directory, so a PR's own test commands could plant a hook that later ran with land's tokens, and a PR could reach main on a base its full suite never saw. Nothing to do: gstack's own policy turns the CI run on; other repos opt in with `land.merged_ci`.
What changed - **Separate clone.** `land.merged_checks` run in a fresh clone outside the checkout (`git clone --no-hardlinks`, its remote removed) with a copy of `node_modules`, so writes to its `.git`, hooks, config or modules are deleted with it. About 2.5 s extra per stale-base land on this repo (0.5 s clone, 2.2 s module copy). - **Pinned tools.** Land resolves the absolute `git` and `gh` at its first call (`lib/tool-path.ts`) and, before the checks, puts their directories first on its own `PATH`, so a `git` a check drops earlier on `PATH` never runs. gh's child `PATH` starts with the pinned git's directory. - **Fail closed on writes outside the clone.** Besides the checkout's git config, hooks, `commondir`/`gitdir` and their symlink hops (from #4119, carried here), land now also records every config file git loads in the checkout (includes and the global file), the global and XDG config paths when absent, gh's `config.yml` and `hosts.yml`, and the pinned binaries. A change refuses with `QUEUE_LAND_MERGED_CHECKS`, makes no further git or gh call, keeps the land lock held, and the fix text now says hold and inspect instead of "merge main and push". - **Pre-push guard decision.** Only land turns hooks off for its git calls (queueHooksOff() in crew/lib/ship-queue-gate.ts, called first in landDirect), which skips the managed pre-push redaction hook on its lock, notes and scratch-branch pushes: land pushes only records it writes and a merge of commits that were already pushed (and scanned) on their own branches, and running a checkout hook after repo commands is the hole being closed. Other queue pushes keep the hook. - **`land.merged_ci` (`{ workflow, profile }`).** After any local checks pass, land pushes the merged commit to `gstack-land/`, dispatches the workflow there, waits up to 45 minutes, and lands only when `lib/run-evidence.ts` `verifyRun` accepts the run under the named profile with the merged commit and tree. Red run: `QUEUE_LAND_MERGED_CHECKS`. Can't push, dispatch, finish or prove: `QUEUE_NOT_READY`. The branch is deleted either way. gstack's policy sets `{ "workflow": "free-tests.yml", "profile": "ci-reuse/free-tests" }` and keeps its local checks as the fast first step.
Things a reviewer should look at - Network and permissions: land now pushes and deletes a branch named `gstack-land/` and runs `gh workflow run` with its own credentials. The pushed commit can include workflow file changes from the PR, so the token needs the workflow scope it already uses for branch pushes. - Workflows: no workflow file changes. Pushing `gstack-land/*` may start other workflows that trigger on any branch push. - No dependency, install script or secret handling changes. `lib/gh-poll.ts` (every gh call through it) now runs the pinned gh with the pinned git's directory first on `PATH`. - Not sandboxed: a check can still read anything the user can and write the checkout's other files; bwrap/unshare was left out because it isn't available on every land machine (macOS has no equivalent). - Not covered by a land-level test: the dispatch wiring in `ship-queue-land-direct.ts` (the fixture's gh shim can't serve run artifacts); `test/land-merged-ci.test.ts` covers every verdict with fake dependencies. - Follow-up, not here: main's push run can't reuse the dispatch run (the push reuse looks up the PR head's tree, not the merged tree), so a stale-base land still runs Free Tests twice.
Agent notes Base: #4119's branch `capy/keep-lands-merged-checks` (closed PR, parked at 59b7b262), merged with main at dd611038 (three conflicts resolved: docs/captain.md took main's rewrite, which no longer holds the refusal table; lib/land-merged-checks.ts and lib/ship-queue-land-direct.ts kept both sides). GST-3303 change 7 and GST-1766 in one PR on the Captain's ruling. #4119's four tests were rewritten for the clone: relative writes now land in the clone (test asserts the checkout is untouched and land merges), absolute writes still refuse. Local checks at 9b287181: `bun run typecheck` clean, `bun run typecheck:test` no new diagnostics, `gen:skill-docs --host all` left no diff; `bun test` on test/ship-queue-land-direct, land-merged-ci, gstack-ship-policy, module-size-ratchet, free-seed-ratchet, spawnsync-timeout-tripwire, bun-entry-isolation, changelog-fragments, gh-poll, gh-poll-tripwire, ship-policy-compat: all pass. title: Stop gstack-uninstall deleting a repo's committed .gstack files and unsaved worktrees (GST-2197)
body:
`gstack-uninstall` no longer deletes the files your repo commits under `.gstack/` (ship policy and the like), a `.gstack/` folder that is its own git repo, or checkouts under `.gstack-worktrees/` that hold unsaved work. Uninstalling gstack should never cost you work it did not create. Nothing to do.
What changed ![Before: uninstall deleted a .gstack/ folder that was its own git repo, local commits included. After: it keeps the folder and says why.](https://api.capy.ai/pr-assets/EmDDxTXKVQEOO6L6ufWPiASMt0Zt-WuFocW0AsO29NU.png) Before: uninstall deleted a `.gstack/` folder that was its own git repo, local commits included. After: it keeps the folder and says why. Both outputs were captured from the same throwaway fixture before and after the fix.
Why Uninstall deleted a repo's committed `.gstack/` files and checkouts with unsaved edits, work that gstack never created. People who uninstall, or reinstall to fix a broken setup, now keep that work, and uninstall stops and names the checkout instead of guessing.
Blast radius Only `bin/gstack-uninstall` and its docs change. Every new keep path either refuses before anything is removed (exit 2) or keeps a folder that used to be deleted, so nothing that was kept before is removed now. Evidence: `test/uninstall.test.ts` (73 tests) passed locally and on CI run 44965912410, and QA reran the uninstall on a throwaway fixture before and after the fix.
Pre-Landing Review Two review passes, plus an adversarial reader and a second-model review on the final range. - Fixed: a `.gstack/` that is its own git repository was deleted outright, local commits included, when uninstall ran from an ordinary project, even though the header and docs said it is kept. The fix keeps it and prints why, with a regression test that failed before the fix. - Not changed: on git older than 2.36, uninstalling a git-cloned install refuses because `git worktree list -z` is unavailable. The branch asserts this fail-closed behavior on purpose (`test/uninstall.test.ts`), and the error names the fix. - Second-model review (openai/gpt-6.1-sol): clean.
Review notes Below the blocking floor (advisory, informational, test-gap or wording items); recorded here and not fixed in this PR. - `bin/gstack-uninstall:783` When the project git root is $HOME, the new guard prints 'kept $HOME/.gstack/' and the global-state block then removes STATE_DIR anyway; message only, unpushed work is refused earlier by _repo_risk. - `bin/gstack-uninstall:783` The guard keeps any nested repo (even clean and pushed) at deletion time with exit 0, unlike _repo_risk's up-front refusal for other targets; conservative by design, a one-line stderr note.
Exploratory QA Surface: the `gstack-uninstall --force` CLI in a throwaway fake HOME and two throwaway repos. - Tracked files under `.gstack/` kept, ignored files removed: pass. - A `.gstack/` that is its own git repo with a local commit: failed before the fix (folder and commit deleted; reproduced twice), passes after the fix (folder and commit kept). - Not probed by QA: the `.gstack-worktrees/` refusal paths, which `test/uninstall.test.ts` covers.
Design Review No frontend files changed, so design review was skipped.
Eval Results No prompt-related files changed, so evals were skipped.
TODOS No TODO items completed in this PR.
Documentation **Status:** current. The branch's uninstall docs already match the new gstack-uninstall behavior; no edits were made. **Scope:** committed diff from 9178cace (bin/gstack-uninstall, docs/uninstall.md, test/uninstall.test.ts) plus the new changelog.d fragment. I read every doc that mentions gstack-uninstall and found no stale statements. **Documentation health** - docs/uninstall.md: current. It already documents --force-worktrees, the worktree, submodule and locked-worktree checks, the install-folder checkout checks and the --keep-state behavior. - docs/troubleshooting.md: current. Its Uninstall section covers the install-folder refusals and links back to uninstall.md. - docs/state-root.md, docs/hosts.md, docs/install.md: current, no change needed. - changelog.d fragment: current, and it agrees with uninstall.md. **Coverage debt** - `--force-worktrees` flag and the `.gstack-worktrees/` refusal: reference and how-to exist in docs/uninstall.md, but docs/troubleshooting.md has no entry for that refusal's message (common gap). - Diagram drift: none; the diff touches no diagrammed entities.
Tests - [x] `bun test --timeout=30000 test/uninstall.test.ts`: 73 pass (local run, tree d1b9eb11c722) - [x] free-tests.yml run 44965912410 on head c7288d5e9: green, 37523 tests
Before/after as text ~~~diff $ gstack-uninstall --force # in a project whose .gstack/ is its own git repo, 1 local commit +kept proj-nested/.gstack/: it holds its own git repository, whose commits may exist nowhere else; check it, then remove it by hand +Removed: ~/.gstack -Removed: proj-nested/.gstack/ gstack uninstalled. exit 0 +left in .gstack/: .git, notes.md (1 local commit kept) -left in .gstack/: nothing (the folder and its local commit are gone) ~~~ Running `gstack-uninstall` in a project used to `rm -rf` the repo's whole `.gstack/` and `.gstack-worktrees/`, so a committed ship policy vanished and a worktree with uncommitted edits went with it. Now a plain uninstall keeps every file git tracks under `.gstack/` and removes only the ones git ignores. A `.gstack/` that holds its own git repository is kept with a message. A checkout under `.gstack-worktrees/` with uncommitted changes, commits no branch or tag holds, or no registration as this repo's worktree stops the uninstall with exit 2 before anything is removed, unless you pass `--force-worktrees`. A locked worktree stops it either way. The check runs again after the confirmation prompt. Install folders that are git checkouts with unpushed or uncommitted work are refused the same way, and `--keep-state` now also keeps the repo's `.gstack/` and `.gstack-worktrees/`.

title: /ship's review plan finishes on repositories with large trial files (HARN-98)
body:
/ship's review plan no longer runs out of time on results repositories whose trial files name many data files. On harness-evals #551 the scan now takes about 40 s instead of running past its limit. Why: harness-evals #551 is blocked on it. git's `grep -o` with about 80 file names took 220 s on one 16 MB trials file, and the plan timed out at 1,703 s. Nothing to do.
What changed Results repositories hit a review plan that never finished. The scan that decides whether a changed data file is read by code ran `git grep -o` with every data file name, and git's `-o` retries every name after each match, so one 16 MB trials file took 220 s. The scan now lists the files that can hold a name once per scan, finds the ones that do with `git grep -l` over a scratch index, and picks their matches itself the way `-o` does (earliest start, longest name there, then on from its end), so its output is byte-identical to the old grep. - Matching files are read a bounded amount at a time, with blobs in `git cat-file --batch` calls of at most 64 MB, working-tree files one at a time, and a file larger than the output cap goes back to git's own `-o` grep. Lines are added one at a time against the byte cap, so a file with a million matches gives git's lines or fails closed instead of crashing. - The scratch index lives under the repository's git directory, so an unwritable TMPDIR no longer fails the scan; a directory it cannot create is a named scan failure. - Untracked, unmerged and non-regular files go back to git by pathspec. Non-UTF-8 names and patterns that hold a newline keep the old whole-tree `-o` path. - `scanConsumers` credits each match through a per-depth lookup instead of testing every probe against every line (about 50 s on #551). - Docs: docs/review-policy.md (consumer scan).
